Location Summary

The plan is tied to Hauts-de-France. Cambrai / E-Valley is the leading candidate for a primary node because of its large redevelopment land. Dunkirk and Valenciennes / Denain / Escaudain are candidate split-campus nodes. Saint-Omer is a possible satellite. Each site is hypothetical until grid, land, water, permit and tenant evidence exists. The single 12.7 km square is to be stress-tested against a split model, and downsizing or cancellation remain legitimate outcomes.

Currency Strategy

This plan involves money.

Currencies

  • EUR: Primary currency for all infrastructure, land acquisition, labor, grid services, power procurement, cooling systems, fiber and connectivity, permitting, and community obligations in Hauts-de-France. Phase 0–4 capex and opex budgeted entirely in EUR (€35M–€174.6B total project cost).
  • USD: Secondary currency for GPU/TPU accelerators, international networking hardware, and select software procurement from US and global vendors. Phase 1 hardware capex €1.5B–€2.3B denominated in USD. FX exposure hedged via forward contracts matched to tenant take-or-pay lease revenue. Separate hardware vehicle recommended to isolate USD risk from infrastructure debt.

Primary currency: EUR

Currency strategy: EUR is the base for all infrastructure financing, budgeting, and reporting. USD exposure is tracked separately for hardware procurement and isolated in a separate vehicle to shield infrastructure company debt from FX volatility and vendor allocation risk. Forward-contract FX hedging is assumed for hardware costs matched to signed tenant take-or-pay leases, at estimated 0.5–2% annual cost of hedged notional. Power contracts in EUR; tenant leases in EUR with optional inflation escalation. No other currencies are material to the project. Phase 0 assume 2027–2030 EUR/USD rates in 1.08–1.12 range (placeholder; actual rates to be hedged as commitments are made).

Identify Risks

Risk 1 - Regulatory & Permitting

RTE grid hosting capacity above ~1 GW is stated as the primary kill condition. Hauts-de-France grid infrastructure may not support multi-GW connection capacity without major reinforcement; queue position, transmission reinforcement timelines and RTE's willingness to offer multi-tranche contractual commitments remain uncontrolled until RTE signs a formal connection offer. Early at-risk studies and substation pre-engineering consume capital but provide no guarantee of available capacity. Competing industrial decarbonization projects (steel, refinery, hydrogen) may saturate capacity.

Impact: If RTE offers less than ~500 MW–1 GW in the first tranche, or if reinforcement timelines stretch beyond 3–4 years, the project fails the core feasibility gate. Delay of 12–24 months to secure connection offers, plus potential cost overruns of €500M–€1.5B for transmission reinforcement if the developer must co-fund upgrades. Loss of grid queue position to competing industrial users could render the site unfeasible for hyperscale compute at the intended scale.

Likelihood: High

Severity: High

Action: Initiate formal pre-engineering dialogue with RTE and DREAL (prefectural authority) in Month 0 (2026-10-17) (no later than Month 1 = 2026-11-17). Commission an independent RTE hosting-capacity assessment identifying specific 400 kV substation locations, reinforcement scope, timeline to energization and cost allocation. Request RTE's formal technical opinion on the feasibility of phased tranches (500 MW, 1 GW, 2 GW) and associated turnaround times. Define 'adequate hosting capacity' as a firm RTE estimate of at least 1 GW available connection within 36 months; if RTE cannot commit to this, trigger the kill gate immediately. Map competing industrial load requests in the region to identify saturation risk. Structure the Phase 0 gate to require a signed RTE connection-offer letter or equivalent binding commitment for at least 500 MW before Phase 1 FID.

Risk 2 - Land Assembly & Rights

Assembling 161 km² contiguously or as a coherent semi-contiguous cluster across Cambrai / E-Valley, Valenciennes, Dunkirk and Saint-Omer faces fragmentation, farmland ownership resistance, holdouts and administrative complexity. The plan explicitly notes that 161 km² contiguous assembly is doubtful (not verified). Voluntary parcel-by-parcel purchase gives holdouts leverage and can render the single-square footprint infeasible, forcing costly pivots to a split-campus model or smaller buildout. Compulsory acquisition via public-interest designation is faster but uncontrolled until a formal State decision exists and invites legal challenge.

Impact: Inability to assemble an adequate parcel: project may fail to proceed beyond Phase 0 scoping; or forced downsizing to <500 MW footprint; or pivot to fragmented split-campus model with higher complexity, latency and per-MW cost. Land acquisition delays: 6–18 months for voluntary parcel assembly; holdout legal action could extend timelines by 12–36 months. Estimated cost overrun of €100M–€400M if forced to pay above-market premiums to holdout farmers or if compulsory-acquisition routes incur legal defense costs.

Likelihood: High

Severity: High

Action: Conduct parcel-level option surveys during Phase 0 (Months 0–3 = 2026-10-17 to 2027-01-17) across all four candidate zones, focusing on agricultural-land fragmentation, public vs. private ownership, and known holdout or environmental-activist groups. Engage municipal and prefectural land registries early to map ownership chains and identify large contiguous blocks. Develop a parallel split-campus topology option that is technically and economically viable at 2–3 separate nodes of 250–500 MW each, so that if contiguous assembly fails, a documented alternative exists. Structure Phase 0 land-assembly spend as a capped, milestone-based tranche with a decision point at Month 3 (2027-01-17): proceed with contiguous options only if ≥70% of a target parcel can be optioned non-coercively at within 15% of benchmark land values; otherwise pivot to split campus. Engage farmers' unions and regional chambers of agriculture in Month 1 (2026-11-17) to signal long-term land-use and revenue-sharing options, not acquisition threats.

Risk 3 - Power & Energy

Power procurement strategy assumes nuclear-backed baseload contracts, PPAs and BESS availability at multi-GW scale. Negotiations with EDF and RTE for dedicated nuclear-supply tranches remain uncontrolled until signed. Multi-GW baseline contracts are unprecedented and may not be available at the assumed cost (proposed EUR 50–70/MWh in the budget, not verified). Competing hyperscaler and hydrogen-production load in the region, plus France's own decarbonization targets, may constrain long-term contract availability. Geopolitical and energy-security pressures could alter EDF's willingness to sign long-dated leases to a private developer backed by foreign sovereign-fund co-investors.

Impact: Inability to secure power supply contracts at assumed cost could raise energy opex by 20–40% (€10B–€25B NPV impact over 10 years at full 9 GW). Delay of 12–24 months in securing supply agreements, extending Phase 1 timeline. If EDF or RTE condition supply on specific tenant or governance concessions, this could constrain tenant choice or require renegotiation of take-or-pay leases. Spot-price exposure without long-dated contracts could reduce tenant willingness to sign fixed-price leases, shrinking demand certainty.

Likelihood: Medium

Severity: High

Action: Commission an independent power-procurement study in Month 0 (2026-10-17), engaging EDF and RTE directly to understand multi-GW contract availability, pricing and tenor at the proposed 500 MW first tranche scale. Establish a firm Phase 0 gate criterion: secure a binding preliminary letter of intent (LOI) from EDF for at least 500 MW baseload supply at a capped EUR/MWh price (to be negotiated, but with a maximum threshold set in Phase 0) for a minimum 10-year tenor by Month 6 (2027-04-17). If EDF declines or offers unacceptable terms, reduce the first-tranche target to 250 MW and pursue a hybrid portfolio of smaller PPAs and spot-exposed BESS arbitrage. Model power-cost sensitivity scenarios at 20%, 40% and 60% above assumed baseline in the financial model, and define a cost threshold above which Phase 2 expansion is mothballed.

Risk 4 - Capital & Financing

Phase 0 budget is estimated at €250M–€750M with no committed capital until the Phase 0 gate. Phase 1 is estimated at €5B–€10B for 500 MW–1 GW. These estimates have not been validated against detailed design, procurement or geotechnical surveys. Sunk cost in Phase 0 (land options, grid studies, environmental surveys, permitting) will pressure the investment committee to proceed even if gate criteria are not met. Infrastructure-fund consortium co-investors may have capital-drawdown or return-on-investment expectations that conflict with the staged, kill-criteria discipline. FX exposure on USD GPU/TPU procurement (proposed €1.5B–€2.3B in Phase 1) is unhedged until tenant take-or-pay agreements exist, creating stranded-hardware and balance-sheet risk if demand fails.

Impact: Phase 0 sunk cost of €250M–€750M may be stranded if the RTE grid or land-assembly gates fail. Pressure to override kill criteria could commit Phase 1 capital (€5B–€10B) despite unfavorable feasibility evidence, locking in a loss. FX volatility on USD hardware: a 10% EUR/USD swing could add €150M–€230M to Phase 1 capex, eroding the margin between Phase 1 budget and actual cost. Financing refusal: lenders may demand equity cushions of 25–35% if grid, land or demand evidence is weak, raising cost of capital by 200–400 basis points and reducing project equity returns by 2–4 percentage points annually.

Likelihood: Medium

Severity: High

Action: Establish an independent investment committee in Month 1 (2026-11-17), separate from the development sponsor team, with independent directors from the infrastructure-fund consortium and an external red team. Fix numeric kill criteria in writing by Month 2 (2026-12-17): (i) RTE firm connection offer for ≥500 MW within 36 months; (ii) ≥70% of target parcel under non-coercive option; (iii) signed anchor-tenant take-or-pay covering ≥30% of Phase 1 capacity by end of Phase 0. If any criterion fails, the investment committee is empowered to pause or cancel Phase 1. Cap Phase 0 drawdown at €750M with documented abandonment conditions: if a gate criterion fails, further drawdown is forbidden without a formal committee waiver. Implement FX hedging policy: forward contracts for USD hardware procurement are allowed only against signed tenant revenue in EUR, with hedge ratio of 0.5–1.0 of notional hardware cost. Publish the investment committee's decisions and dissents quarterly to lenders and co-investors, so sunk-cost pressure is visible and accountable.

Risk 5 - Tenant Demand & Contracts

The Phase 1 and Phase 2 expansion gates require signed anchor-tenant take-or-pay capacity commitments covering ≥30–50% of the planned expansion tranche. Letters of intent, expressions of interest and non-binding allocation requests do not count. Global hyperscalers (OpenAI, Meta, Google, Microsoft, xAI) are saturating Europe with competing data-center bids, and their tenant commitments depend on sustained AI training demand growth that is not guaranteed. Sovereign-AI users (French State, European institutions) have slower procurement cycles and may demand specific security, data-residency or pricing concessions that conflict with commercial terms. Neither hyperscaler nor sovereign anchors may be ready to commit capex-equivalent take-or-pay leases at the proposed Phase 1 timescale (Month 12–36 = 2027-10-17 to 2029-10-17).

Impact: If signed anchor tenants cover <30% of Phase 1 planned capacity (500–1,000 MW) by Month 9 (2027-07-17) (critical path point to maintain Phase 1 FID on schedule), the project loses debt financing certainty and Phase 1 FID is blocked. This could trigger a 12–24 month delay while alternative demand is cultivated, or force a downsizing to 250 MW Phase 1. Loss of a major anchor tenant after Phase 1 energization (e.g., due to shifting AI training spend or tenant acquisition) could strand 100–300 MW of capacity, reducing revenue by €200M–€600M over the tenant lease term.

Likelihood: High

Severity: High

Action: Initiate anchor-tenant conversations by Month 1 (2026-11-17), targeting 2–3 global hyperscalers and 2–3 sovereign or European-consortium anchors in parallel. Develop standardized take-or-pay lease term sheets by Month 2 (2026-12-17) specifying: capacity reserved (proposed 50–500 MW per tenant), lease term (proposed 5–10 years), inflation escalation, exclusivity or non-compete terms, and PUE/latency/uptime SLAs. Require non-binding letters of intent by Month 4 (2027-02-17), binding term sheets by Month 9 (2027-07-17). Define Phase 1 FID gate: require signed take-or-pay agreements totalling ≥300 MW (30% of 1 GW planned) with minimum A-/BB+ credit rating. Offer capacity-reservation fees (proposed €10M–€50M per 100 MW) paid upfront and credited against future lease revenue, to test anchor commitment without requiring full lease signature before Phase 1 construction starts. If signed anchors do not reach 30% by Month 9 (2027-07-17), implement a contingency: reduce Phase 1 to 250–500 MW of built-out capacity, matching only the committed demand, and delay Phase 2 expansion until demand reaches ≥50% of the 500 MW Phase 2 target.

Risk 6 - Permitting & Social License

Standard ICPE and local permitting timelines are estimated at 12–18 months; environmental authorization adds 6–12 months; national-major-project fast-track status (proposed acceleration to 18–24 months) is not confirmed in final legislative form (not verified). Community opposition to industrial land use, farmland displacement, perceived security militarization, noise, and ecological impact can sustain legal appeals that extend permitting by 24–48 months. Local municipalities and prefectural authorities may demand conditions (community-benefit agreements, ecological commitments, labor-training programs) that add cost or operational constraints. Foreign co-investor involvement, data-sovereignty concerns and national-security review (uncontrolled until ANSSI or DGSI reviews the project) could add 6–12 months of delay and impose restrictions on tenant access or data flows.

Impact: Permitting delay of 12–24 months from expected timelines erodes grid queue position (RTE may release reserved capacity to competitors if connection is not energized on schedule) and extends Phase 1 timeline by 1–2 years, raising carrying costs by €200M–€500M in interest and idle land holding. Community-led legal appeals could force design changes (reduced footprint, relocated halls, additional ecological offsets) that increase capex by 5–15% (€250M–€1.5B). If national-security review blocks foreign co-investor involvement or imposes tenant-access restrictions, this could shrink the addressable market or force equity restructuring. Regulatory conditions (e.g., mandatory community benefit agreement totalling €100M–€300M) lock in costs that were not forecast.

Likelihood: Medium

Severity: High

Action: Launch formal pre-permitting engagement with DREAL, prefectural and municipal authorities in Month 0 (2026-10-17), mapping the required authorizations (ICPE, environmental authorization, urban planning, national security). Commission Phase 0 environmental baseline and social-impact assessments (Months 1–4 = 2026-11-17 to 2027-02-17) to identify the top community concerns and ecological sensitivities. Conduct early voluntary public consultation (Month 3 = 2027-01-17) with transparently posted siting rationale, design renderings, power and environmental specifications, and a publicly committal ecology and farmer-displacement mitigation plan. Establish a municipal and community liaison committee (Month 2 = 2026-12-17) with representatives from Cambrai, Valenciennes, Dunkirk, Saint-Omer and local farmer unions, committing to quarterly dialogue and published minutes. By Month 6 (2027-04-17), seek an informal prefectural opinion on the regulatory path (standard vs. fast-track potential) and on any blocking concerns (national security, ecological sensitivity, local opposition). Frame permitting as a 24-month process (Month 12–36 = 2027-10-17 to 2029-10-17 for Phase 1 start) with a permitting gate at Month 18 (2028-04-17): if critical authorizations (ICPE, EIA approval, national-security clearance) are not in formal application phase, pause Phase 1 drawdown pending resolution. Offer a binding community-benefit agreement (€50M–€150M over Phase 1–2) contingent on permit approval, to align local incentives with project success.

Risk 7 - Environmental & Water

The plan specifies zero- or ultra-low-water cooling (direct-to-chip liquid cooling with dry coolers, no evaporative water). This design basis must be validated in Phase 0 against regional hydrological constraints, summer peak dry-cooler performance, and competing water users (agriculture, industry, drinking water). Hauts-de-France has modest water stress but is not water-rich; long droughts or competing industrial water demand (refinery, chemical production) could trigger regulatory restrictions on data-center cooling. Summer peak dry-cooler performance under high ambient temperature (30–35°C) could degrade to a PUE of 1.35–1.5 (vs. target 1.15–1.25), raising electrical load by 5–15% and straining grid during peak-demand periods. Brownfield sites may have contaminated groundwater that restricts water-cooling options further.

Impact: If dry-cooler performance in summer exceeds the PUE target by >10%, the project must either accept higher power consumption (raising opex and grid curtailment risk), or retrofit to hybrid cooling with limited evaporative water (requiring groundwater permits and potential environmental opposition). Regulatory restriction on water use (e.g., drought orders limiting industrial abstractions to 50% of normal) could reduce data-center capacity utilization by 10–20% during dry periods, eroding tenant uptime commitments. Heat-reuse opportunity (proposed as unpriced upside) may not materialize if nearby district-heating or industrial heat-user offtake agreements are not signed; sunk cost for heat-distribution infrastructure (€50M–€200M) could be stranded.

Likelihood: Medium

Severity: Medium

Action: Commission a detailed hydrological and thermal-design study in Phase 0 (Months 1–4 = 2026-11-17 to 2027-02-17) covering: (i) regional water-stress profiles, including drought frequency and magnitude; (ii) vendor dry-cooler performance curves at ambient temperatures up to 35°C, and measured PUE impact; (iii) groundwater hydrology and contamination status on candidate parcels; (iv) binding opinion from regional water authorities (Agence de l'Eau Artois-Picardie and Meuse) on data-center cooling feasibility at 1 GW scale. Define the permitting gate for water/cooling: by Month 6 (2027-04-17), water authorities must confirm in writing that closed-loop direct-to-chip cooling with dry rejection is feasible at the planned scale with no material impact on drinking-water supply or competing users. Test dry-cooler performance via site-specific thermal modelling under a 35°C design day; if modelled PUE exceeds 1.30, trigger a design review and potential cost escalation for hybrid or immersion cooling. Treat heat-reuse revenue as zero unless a binding offtake agreement is signed by Month 9 (2027-07-17) of Phase 0; any heat-export infrastructure is then built as tenant-specific capex, not developer capex.

Risk 8 - Brownfield Contamination & Remediation

Candidate sites span Cambrai (former airbase surroundings), Dunkirk (heavy industrial, petrochemical), Valenciennes / Denain / Escaudain (former steel works) and Saint-Omer (former industrial zones). Legacy soil, groundwater, asbestos, slag, munitions residue and other contamination are likely but not quantified. Phase 0 intrusive surveys can bound liability per parcel, but comprehensive site remediation is expensive (€50M–€500M+ per major site) and can delay hall construction by 6–18 months if front-loaded. Back-loading remediation into Phase 1 construction risks discovering new liabilities that lenders will refuse to fund, halting construction.

Impact: Unexpected contamination discovery during Phase 1 construction (soil lead, PCBs, munitions residue) could trigger health and safety work stoppages, regulatory enforcement action, and remediation costs of €100M–€400M. Liability allocation disputes with land sellers or public bodies could tie up capital in escrow or court proceedings for 2–4 years. If remediation cost exceeds budget contingency, the project may face Phase 1 FID slippage or cancellation. Heat-reuse or water-extraction infrastructure installed during Phase 1 could encounter contamination that requires rework or abandonment.

Likelihood: Medium

Severity: High

Action: Commission Phase I (desk-top) environmental site assessments (ESAs) on all candidate parcels by Month 1 (2026-11-17). Identify sites with known industrial history (steel, refinery, munitions, chemical). By Month 3 (2027-01-17), conduct Phase II intrusive surveys (soil boring, groundwater sampling, asbestos survey) on the top 2–3 candidate sites in each zone to quantify remediation scope and cost. Establish a pre-Phase-0-gate deadline (Month 6 = 2027-04-17): shortlist only parcels whose Phase II ESA identifies remediation costs that can be bounded to within €0–€100M per site and that can be completed without blocking hall construction. Negotiate seller indemnities or remediation escrows that assign legacy-contamination liability to the seller (or to a public remediation authority) up to a capped amount, with developer liability only above that cap for discovery of new contamination during Phase 1. For public-landowner parcels (former airbases, industrial zones), seek a written agreement that the public body retains remediation liability for pre-existing contamination and certifies sites as safe for construction before hall foundation work begins. Reserve up to €100M–€300M in Phase 1 contingency for unexpected remediation; if remediation cost escalates beyond this, trigger the Phase 1 FID gate to pause construction and reassess site viability.

Risk 9 - Technical – Cooling & PUE

The cooling strategy assumes a PUE target of 1.15–1.25 via direct-to-chip liquid cooling and dry-cooler rejection, plus an optional 50–100 MW immersion-cooling pilot. These targets are at the leading edge of industry practice and depend on: (i) vendor liquid-cooling technology maturity and supply; (ii) standardized rack interfaces and form factors that integrate cooling with tenant hardware procurement; (iii) control systems that optimize cooler operation across all data halls simultaneously. Early hall construction (Phase 1) may use pioneering liquid-cooling designs that are not yet proven at 500 MW–1 GW scale; PUE degradation from 1.20 to 1.30 or higher would increase opex by 8–10% and grid load by equivalent amount. Immersion cooling is even less proven at multi-MW scale and carries risk of dielectric fluid supply constraints, hardware compatibility issues and high waste-heat concentration in localized areas.

Impact: If Phase 1 halls achieve PUE of 1.30–1.40 (vs. target 1.15–1.25) due to cooling design or execution gaps, opex increases by €50M–€150M annually at full 9 GW. This would erode tenant economics and create pressure to downsize or delay Phase 2. Immersion-cooling pilot failure (e.g., vendor dielectric-fluid supply constraint, hardware compatibility issues, local heat-concentration concerns) would strand €50M–€100M sunk cost and delay any further immersion rollout. Cooling-system outage affecting multiple halls would create emergency loss of tenant capacity, triggering SLA penalties of €10M–€50M+ and risk of tenant exit.

Likelihood: Medium

Severity: Medium

Action: In Phase 0, engage leading liquid-cooling vendors (Iceotope, Asetek, Liqid, LiquidCool Solutions, Fujitsu) to specify rack-interface standards, power density per rack, and cooling-loop configurations. Commission vendor performance guarantees (proposed PUE ≤1.25 at 30°C ambient, with penalty clauses if actual PUE exceeds 1.30). Test the chosen cooling design in a pilot 2–5 MW data hall during Phase 1 (Months 12–24 = 2027-10-17 to 2028-10-17), measuring actual PUE under production load before rolling out to remaining halls. For immersion cooling, limit the Phase 1 pilot to 10–50 MW with a dedicated tenant that accepts the technology risk; make Phase 2 immersion expansion conditional on Phase 1 pilot PUE validation (target ≤1.18). Establish a cooling-performance gate at Month 30 (2029-04-17) of Phase 1: if average PUE across commissioned halls exceeds 1.28, pause additional hall construction and conduct a root-cause review. Procure spare cooling system components (pumps, coolers, control units) during Phase 1 to ensure rapid emergency response to system outages. Require tenant SLAs to include force-majeure clauses for cooling-system outages >4 hours, limiting tenant compensation to lost margin rather than full revenue.

Risk 10 - Connectivity & Fiber

Connectivity strategy requires diverse fiber routes from the campus to Paris, London, Brussels, Amsterdam, Frankfurt, Marseille and subsea landings, with audited duct-level diversity to eliminate shared failure points. Fiber routes in France are often owned and managed by multiple carriers (Arcane, IFW, Intrinsic, Colt, Lumen, Orange, DWDM consortia), and claimed diversity often collapses at shared ducts, bridges or landing stations. Subsea cable landings near Dunkirk or Channel access are concentrated in a few facilities (UK landing stations, French coastal hubs), creating hidden single points of failure. Building dedicated fiber routes requires rights-of-way across private land, rail, canal and road corridors; permitting and land negotiation can add 12–24 months and €100M–€500M in cost.

Impact: Failure of primary fiber route (cut by construction equipment, cable-ship anchor, sabotage or natural disaster) affecting multiple carriers would isolate the campus from external networks for 2–7 days, causing total tenant revenue loss of €50M–€200M. Shared landing-point concentration (e.g., multiple carriers landing in the same UK facility or French coastal hub) means a localized disaster affects all routes simultaneously. Late-stage discovery that claimed fiber diversity is false (shared conduits disclosed during due diligence) could force rerouting, adding 6–12 months and €200M–€500M cost, delaying Phase 1 energization. Tenant demand for ultra-low latency to specific hubs (e.g., London <5 ms) cannot be met if fiber routes are routed sub-optimally or share bottlenecks.

Likelihood: Medium

Severity: Medium

Action: In Phase 0 (Months 1–6 = 2026-11-17 to 2027-04-17), commission a fiber-route audit conducted by an independent telecom engineer, requesting detailed physical-route maps from all candidate carriers serving the region. Demand specific confirmation of duct separation, bridge crossings, and landing-point facilities; do not accept marketing diversity claims without physical audits. Identify ≥2 physically separate long-haul routes (proposed minimum) to each of Paris, London, Brussels and Frankfurt, with verified duct-level separation. For subsea, map landings to ≥2 separate UK facilities (e.g., both south-coast and north-coast landings) to avoid concentrated coastal risk. By Month 9 (2027-07-17) of Phase 0, secure capacity commitments or letters of intent from carriers for Phase 1 fiber lit by Month 12 (2027-10-17) (to support Phase 1 tenant energization). If independent fiber routes are not available within cost and timeline limits, budget for a developer-owned or co-invested route along 1–2 corridors (rail, canal, highway) serving 100–200 km; negotiate rights-of-way during Phase 0 and duct installation during Phase 1 (Months 12–36 = 2027-10-17 to 2029-10-17). Define the connectivity gate for Phase 1 FID: by Month 9 (2027-07-17) of Phase 0, confirm in writing that ≥2 diverse fiber routes with ≥100 Tbps redundant capacity are available for Phase 1 energization at a cost within the project budget.

Risk 11 - Security & National-Security Review

The campus will host AI training, sovereign AI, and possibly defense-adjacent compute for French and European users. National-security review by ANSSI (Agence Nationale de la Sécurité des Systèmes d'Information), DGSI (Direction Générale de la Sécurité Intérieure) and potentially DGSE (Direction Générale de la Sécurité Extérieure) is likely but uncontrolled until the project is formally submitted. Review scope and timeline (estimated 6–12 months, not verified) depend on tenant mix, foreign co-investor involvement, and security posture. Foreign co-investors backed by sovereign funds (particularly those with geopolitical ambitions) face heightened scrutiny; data-residency and tenant-access restrictions could be imposed. Security design (hardened perimeter, anti-drone systems, cyber-OT separation, personnel vetting) adds cost (proposed €50M–€200M for Phase 1) and can create community perceptions of militarization that feed opposition to permits.

Impact: National-security review extending beyond 12 months delays Phase 1 FID and energization by equivalent duration, eroding grid queue position and raising carrying costs by €200M–€500M. Restrictions imposed by security review (e.g., limiting non-EU tenants, mandating data-residency zones, requiring state observer roles) could shrink the addressable tenant pool or force renegotiation of existing anchor-tenant leases. If ANSSI or DGSI classifies the campus as 'critical infrastructure' or 'vital-system operator,' this triggers ongoing oversight and compliance obligations that increase opex by 5–10% (€50M–€500M annually at full scale). If foreign co-investor structure is deemed a national-security risk, the project may face capital-structure constraints (e.g., forced reduction of foreign equity below 25–50%, change of control provisions) that delay financing or reduce investor returns.

Likelihood: Medium

Severity: High

Action: Initiate a confidential pre-submission dialogue with ANSSI, DGSI and the relevant DREAL/prefectural security office in Month 0 (2026-10-17) to understand the anticipated security review scope, timeline and key concerns. Prepare a security and governance white paper (Month 2–3 = 2026-12-17 to 2027-01-17) documenting: (i) tenant selection and vetting process; (ii) data-residency and national-security data handling policies; (iii) perimeter hardening, anti-drone, cyber-OT separation and personnel-clearance specifications; (iv) co-investor governance and control provisions, demonstrating how French or European public interest is protected. By Month 6 (2027-04-17), seek an informal ANSSI opinion on review timeline and any blocking concerns. Engage early with a high-level interministerial working group (SGDSN or equivalent) to build consensus on the project's national-security alignment with French AI and data-sovereignty strategies. Budget Phase 0 cost for security design review and red-teaming (€5M–€15M); identify and resolve any critical gaps before formal application. Define a security gate for Phase 1 FID: by Month 12 (2027-10-17) of Phase 0, obtain written confirmation from ANSSI that a formal security review can commence in Month 13 (2027-11-17), with a target timeline of 12–18 months to clearance. If ANSSI indicates a longer timeline or fundamental blocking concerns, trigger a Phase 1 pause or a tenant-mix redesign that resolves the concern.

Risk 12 - Political & Community Opposition

Large-scale industrial projects in France face organized opposition from environmental groups, local residents and farm-sector unions. Concerns typically include: farmland displacement and loss of agricultural production; ecological impact on wetlands, wildlife corridors and species; noise, light and visual impact; water and cooling impacts on local hydrology; security and militarization perception; foreign investment and data sovereignty; labor and wage impacts. In Hauts-de-France, agricultural land is productive (sugar beet, grains, potatoes) and politically protected; farm-sector unions (FNSEA, Confédération Paysanne) can mobilize local opposition and legal challenge. Regional environmental groups and local mayors can block permits through legal appeal or political pressure on prefectural and regional authorities.

Impact: Sustained political opposition can add 12–36 months to permitting timeline and force material design concessions (reduced footprint, relocated halls, additional ecological offsets, community-benefit commitments) that increase capex by 5–15% (€250M–€1.5B). Legal appeals by environmental or farm-sector groups can extend authorization timelines beyond the project's Phase 1 schedule, forcing delay or downsizing. A campaign by a major local politician or environmental organization can shift public and media narrative, making permit approval politically costly for the prefect or regional authorities. If a municipality formally refuses or conditions permits (e.g., by local referendum or formal municipal council vote), the project may be forced to abandon that site and pivot to alternative locations.

Likelihood: Medium

Severity: High

Action: Launch a stakeholder-engagement program in Month 1 (2026-11-17) targeting farmers' unions (FNSEA, Confédération Paysanne), environmental groups (Franceature, LPO, local conservation associations), municipality mayors, regional councillors and local media. Establish a transparent, ongoing dialogue with published consultation minutes, project updates and clear avenues for stakeholder input. Develop a binding community-benefit agreement (€50M–€150M over Phase 1–2) offering: (i) agricultural land compensation and relocation packages for displaced farmers; (ii) revenue-sharing or long-term lease options for continuation zones; (iii) ecological restoration and habitat creation on former brownfield; (iv) local employment and training commitments; (v) municipal infrastructure upgrades (roads, water, electricity). By Month 6 (2027-04-17), conduct a formal public consultation with 4-week comment period, published responses and visible incorporation of feedback into design. Seek a municipal or prefectural endorsement (non-binding) by Month 9 (2027-07-17) of Phase 0. Define a social-license gate for Phase 1 FID: by Month 12 (2027-10-17) of Phase 0, obtain written support (formal resolution or letter) from at least 2 of the 3 municipalities most affected by the project, and confirm that no major legal challenges are pending against Phase 0 activities. If majority opposition emerges or a key municipality formally refuses, trigger a Phase 1 pause and feasibility reassessment.

Risk 13 - Land Fragmentation & Split-Campus Complexity

If contiguous assembly of 161 km² fails (high likelihood per plan documents), the project must pivot to a split-campus model with 2–3 nodes across Cambrai, Dunkirk and Valenciennes. Split topology increases complexity: (i) separate grid connections and connection timelines per node; (ii) inter-node fiber links with latency and bandwidth constraints; (iii) separate permitting and security review for each node; (iv) operational overhead managing multiple sites; (v) tenant workload segmentation constraints (some workloads cannot span multiple nodes due to latency sensitivity). Early commitment to single-square topology may lock in design choices (e.g., centralized fiber landing, monolithic security perimeter) that become uneconomical or infeasible if later forced to split.

Impact: Pivot to split-campus in Phase 1 (late discovery) forces redesign and delays energization by 6–12 months (€300M–€600M carrying cost). Per-MW capex increases by 5–15% due to duplication of substations, backup power, fiber routes and security infrastructure across nodes. Coordinated tenant workload management becomes operationally complex; some tenants may refuse to span multiple nodes, shrinking addressable customer pool. If split campus is chosen from the start (Month 0 = 2026-10-17), it demands detailed topology design and separate Phase 0 validation per node, extending Phase 0 timeline and spend by 3–6 months and €100M–€250M.

Likelihood: Medium

Severity: Medium

Action: In Phase 0 Month 2–3 (2026-12-17 to 2027-01-17), commission a rigorous topology study comparing: (i) single-square 161 km² at Cambrai or nearby; (ii) two-node split campus (Cambrai primary ~500 MW, Dunkirk secondary ~250–500 MW) with fiber ring and shared tenant management; (iii) three-node split (Cambrai, Dunkirk, Valenciennes) with mesh fiber and local-grid connections. Define decision criteria by Month 4 (2027-02-17): single-square is chosen only if ≥70% of target parcel can be optioned at reasonable cost and land-use contingency; otherwise split-campus is the baseline. For split-campus, validate: (i) inter-node latency and bandwidth tolerance via tenant cluster-workload modeling; (ii) per-node grid hosting capacity and connection timelines; (iii) fiber-route diversity per node and inter-node dark-fiber cost. Develop detailed split-campus designs for the 2–3 most viable node combinations by Month 6 (2027-04-17), so Phase 1 design does not commit to single-square constraints that later become infeasible. Define modular capex estimates per node, so Phase 1 FID can proceed on the topologically feasible subset (e.g., Phase 1 = Cambrai 500 MW + Dunkirk 250 MW, deferring Valenciennes to Phase 2).

Risk 14 - Silicon Supply & USD FX Exposure

GPU/TPU and networking hardware costs are estimated at €1.5B–€2.3B in Phase 1, denominated in USD. This is the largest USD-denominated exposure in the project. FX risk depends on EUR/USD exchange rate (assumed 1.08–1.12 in Phase 0 planning, not verified), vendor allocation availability, and US export-control policy changes. If the developer procures hardware ahead of signed tenant take-or-pay agreements, the hardware sits on the developer's balance sheet as stranded asset if tenant demand fails. Vendor allocation (particularly for advanced NVIDIA GPUs or TPUs) is constrained and subject to geographic quotas, US export-control restrictions on certain countries, and competition from other hyperscalers. USD hardware procurement also ties the project to US vendor supply chains and export-control risk that is uncontrolled.

Impact: 10% EUR/USD FX move (1.08 to 1.19) increases hardware cost by €150M–€230M on a €1.5B–€2.3B procurement. Hardware procured ahead of tenant demand becomes stranded if tenant commitments fail, locking €500M–€1B in sunk cost that cannot be recovered. US export-control changes (e.g., new restrictions on advanced GPU exports to certain countries or end-users) could affect both the developer's procurement and tenant's ability to use hardware, creating renegotiation pressure or lease termination risk. Vendor allocation constraints may force the developer to accept longer lead times (12–24 months vs. 6–9 months) or higher prices, pushing Phase 1 energization into Year 3 instead of Year 2.

Likelihood: Medium

Severity: Medium

Action: Adopt a capital-structure policy in Month 1 (2026-11-17): create a separate hardware vehicle owned by tenants or a tenant-backed lessor, not by the infrastructure company. Tenants procure hardware under their own FX exposure, and the infrastructure company finances only EUR-denominated power, cooling, real estate and connectivity. Alternatively, the developer can procure hardware only against signed tenant take-or-pay leases, with forward-contract FX hedging matched to the lease term and tenant payment schedule (hedge ratio 0.5–1.0 of notional cost). By Month 6 (2027-04-17) of Phase 0, establish vendor relationships with NVIDIA and TPU suppliers to understand allocation availability, lead times and pricing for Phase 1 quantities (estimated 50,000–100,000 GPUs or equivalent TPUs). Lock vendor allocation 9–12 months ahead of Phase 1 energization (Month 3–6 = 2027-01-17 to 2027-04-17 of Phase 1) through non-binding letters of intent, at risk of loss if tenant commitments fail. Implement forward-contract FX hedging policy: 50–100% of hardware cost is hedged via EUR/USD forwards matched to signed tenant lease revenue, at a proposed hedge cost of 0.5–2% annually. If export-control policy changes during Phase 0, trigger a feasibility reassessment; define US export-control stability as a Phase 0 gate criterion.

Risk 15 - Grid Curtailment & Demand Flexibility

The proposed grid hosting strategy assumes that the campus accepts contractual curtailment and demand-flexibility commitments to RTE in exchange for connection capacity and favorable rates. A 10–20% annual curtailment allowance (proposed, to be negotiated) means the campus operates at full power only 80–90% of the time; curtailed hours typically occur during peak winter evening or summer stress periods. This reduces tenant uptime, creates revenue loss (€50M–€200M annually per GW curtailed), and may conflict with tenant SLAs that demand high availability (99.5–99.95%). Tenants may refuse to sign leases with built-in curtailment risk, or demand price concessions (5–15% lease discounts) to offset curtailment cost.

Impact: If 1 GW is curtailed at 15% annually, revenue loss is €150M–€300M over 10 years at assumed EUR 50–70/MWh rates (not verified). Tenant refusal to accept curtailment forces the developer to negotiate firm connection without flexibility, which may not be available from RTE or may require higher transmission reinforcement cost (€200M–€500M additional). Tenant lease discounts to offset curtailment reduce revenue by €50M–€150M annually, eroding project returns and lender debt-service coverage. Unplanned or excessive curtailment (due to grid stress or emergency) creates tenant disputes over SLA compliance and potential lease termination.

Likelihood: Medium

Severity: Medium

Action: During Phase 0 grid negotiations (Month 1–6 = 2026-11-17 to 2027-04-17), establish the maximum acceptable annual curtailment tolerance with RTE, proposed as ≤10% (to be negotiated with RTE). Confirm that curtailment is scheduled in advance (30–90 days notice) rather than emergency, so tenants can plan workload scheduling. Develop a campus-level BESS and demand-flexibility strategy that reduces grid stress during peak periods: propose 50–200 MWh BESS, interruptible non-critical workloads, and load shifting to off-peak hours, allowing the campus to avoid peak curtailment and serve RTE grid-balancing needs. Design tenant SLAs to carve out force-majeure exceptions for RTE-mandated curtailment, limiting tenant compensation to lost margin rather than full revenue. If RTE requires curtailment >15% annually, model the revenue impact on tenant lease pricing and investor returns; if investor returns fall below hurdle rates, reduce the Phase 1 target from 1 GW to the capacity that RTE can support without material curtailment (proposed 500–750 MW). Define the curtailment gate for Phase 1 FID: by Month 9 (2027-07-17) of Phase 0, obtain RTE's firm statement that the first tranche of 500 MW–1 GW can be connected with annual curtailment not exceeding 10–15% (to be negotiated), and that flexibility and BESS investments can further reduce curtailment.

Risk 16 - Operational – Workforce & Skills

Construction of 8–20 data halls in Phase 1, plus electrical, mechanical, cooling, and security infrastructure, requires skilled trades (electricians, mechanical engineers, cooling specialists, civil workers) that are in global shortage. Hauts-de-France has industrial heritage and a regional workforce, but wage inflation and competition for scarce trades (electrical, HVAC, cooling) during a multi-year Phase 1 build could increase labor costs by 20–40%. Operations staff for a 500 MW–1 GW campus are relatively small (proposed 50–150 FTE, not verified) but require highly trained engineers and technicians with advanced cooling, networking, security and AI-system expertise. Lack of trained operations staff risks poor PUE, security gaps and tenant SLA failures.

Impact: Wage inflation on skilled trades adds 10–20% to Phase 1 capex (€500M–€2B on a €5B–€10B budget). Labor shortages during Phase 1 cause schedule slippage of 3–9 months, raising carrying cost by €150M–€500M. If operations staff are not ready by Phase 1 energization, initial PUE and security performance falls short of targets, damaging tenant relationships and revenue. High operational labor cost (€20M–€50M annually for Phase 1, scaling to €100M–€200M at 9 GW) erodes project margins and investor returns.

Likelihood: Medium

Severity: Low

Action: Establish a regional workforce and training strategy in Phase 0 (Month 1–3 = 2026-11-17 to 2027-01-17): engage technical colleges (Université Polytechnique Hauts-de-France, IUT Dunkerque), trade unions (CFDT, CGT, FO) and employer associations to develop a training pipeline for data-center electrical, mechanical, cooling and security trades. Commit to funding a regional training academy (€10M–€30M cost) during Phase 1, producing 200–500 certified technicians over 3–5 years. Structure Phase 1 construction contracts with wage and productivity incentives to minimize labor inflation; use modular, prefabricated data-hall designs that reduce on-site labor content. Procure advanced building management and cooling systems with telemetry and remote-diagnostics capabilities to reduce on-site operations headcount. By Month 9 (2027-07-17) of Phase 0, recruit a Phase 1 operations leadership team (CTO, VP Operations, VP Security) to validate readiness and identify training gaps. Pilot operations on the first 2–3 halls during Phase 1 (Months 12–24 = 2027-10-17 to 2028-10-17) with a small team, documenting procedures and learning before full-campus operations ramp.

Risk 17 - Financial – Debt Financing & Lender Risk

Phase 1 financing (€5B–€10B capex) and Phase 2+ require debt of €3B–€8B (estimated 60–70% debt/capex ratio, to be validated). Lenders (infrastructure banks, development banks, institutional investors) will require: (i) committed grid connection from RTE; (ii) signed anchor-tenant take-or-pay leases covering ≥30–50% of capacity; (iii) bounded remediation and environmental liability; (iv) demonstrated operational performance from pilot halls; (v) stable power procurement contracts at locked-in prices. Absence of any of these elements will trigger higher cost of capital (200–400 bps spread above benchmark rates), lower debt/capex leverage (50–60% vs. 60–70%), or debt refusal. Currency mismatches between EUR-denominated infrastructure debt and USD hardware costs create balance-sheet risk if hardware is developer-financed.

Impact: If Phase 1 debt is not available on acceptable terms, Phase 1 FID is blocked and must be delayed 12–24 months pending further proof of concept. Cost-of-capital increase of 200 bps on €7B debt (midpoint of €5B–€10B) adds €140M–€280M in interest cost annually, eroding returns by 2–3 percentage points. If tenant take-or-pay leases fail to cover ≥30% of Phase 1 capacity, lenders may require additional equity or sponsor guarantees, reducing investor leverage and returns. Currency mismatches between EUR debt and USD hardware purchases create accounting losses if EUR strengthens (e.g., EUR/USD moves from 1.10 to 1.05), eroding equity value.

Likelihood: Medium

Severity: High

Action: Engage debt capital providers (EIB, KfW, French banks, infrastructure funds) in Month 3 (2027-01-17) of Phase 0 to establish lending criteria and pre-commitment signals. Commission a Phase 0 debt-financing study (Month 4–6 = 2027-02-17 to 2027-04-17) modeling debt structure, tenor, leverage, pricing and conditions for Phase 1 at various certainty levels (high certainty with signed anchors and RTE offer vs. low certainty with LOIs only). Target debt-financing commitment (non-binding LOI) by Month 9 (2027-07-17) of Phase 0, contingent on Phase 0 gate outcomes (grid, land, tenants). Define debt-financing as a Phase 1 FID gate criterion: by Month 12 (2027-10-17) of Phase 0, secure a firm debt-financing commitment for at least €3B–€5B at a cost of capital within acceptable spreads (proposed benchmark + 200 bps, to be negotiated) for a minimum 12-year tenor. If lenders decline or require unacceptable terms (higher spreads, lower leverage, additional sponsor guarantees), trigger a Phase 1 FID pause and equity-restructuring review. Implement a currency hedging policy for hardware FX exposure via forward contracts or tenant lease denominations in EUR where feasible, reducing USD balance-sheet risk.

Risk 18 - Technical – Scalability & Technology Lock-In

Phase 1 data halls and infrastructure will be designed and built to a specific technical standard (liquid-cooling interface, rack power density, networking architecture, security design). Scaling from Phase 1 (500 MW–1 GW) to Phase 2–4 (up to 9 GW) over 10–15 years creates technology-refresh risk: cooling technology, GPU/TPU architecture, networking speeds and security standards will evolve significantly. Design choices locked in Phase 1 may become suboptimal or obsolete by Phase 3–4, requiring retrofit or abandonment of early infrastructure. Long-term depreciation schedules (capex capitalized over 20–30 years) conflict with 5–7 year technology cycles in AI accelerators.

Impact: Technology refresh constraints force Phase 1 cooling to be compatible with Phase 2+ hardware, limiting optimization for early workloads. If Phase 1 cooling or rack standards become incompatible with next-generation hardware (e.g., next-gen GPUs with different power/thermal profiles), retrofit cost is €500M–€1.5B. Vendor lock-in (e.g., proprietary liquid-cooling interface that only NVIDIA or Asetek supports) limits tenant choice and increases costs. Accelerator technology obsolesce reduces asset value in later phases; if Phase 1 GPUs are fully depreciated by Year 5 but still in service, they create a legacy-asset management problem.

Likelihood: Low

Severity: Medium

Action: Design Phase 1 infrastructure using standardized, vendor-agnostic interfaces for cooling (proposed OCP or equivalent standard), power and networking. Commission a 5-year technology roadmap (Month 3–4 = 2027-01-17 to 2027-02-17 of Phase 0) from vendors and research institutes (Bell Labs, INRIA, Fraunhofer) covering: (i) cooling technology evolution; (ii) GPU/TPU power and thermal profiles; (iii) networking speeds and latencies. Plan Phase 1 cooling for modularity: halls and loops should be capable of being retrofitted or expanded with next-generation cooling without major structural rework. Separate capex depreciation schedules for infrastructure (20–30 year life) vs. accelerators (5–7 year life) to reflect economic useful life. Include technology-refresh risk in Phase 2–4 financial models: budget 10–15% of capex for retrofit and upgrades. Design Phase 1 halls with flexibility for future equipment power/thermal upgrades; limit early optimization to Phase 1 workloads rather than over-designing for hypothetical future requirements that may not materialize.

Risk 19 - Strategic – Single-Site vs. Split-Campus Topology

The plan mandates that the single 12.7 km × 12.7 km square be stress-tested honestly against a split-campus model, and explicitly allows downsizing or splitting as a legitimate outcome if feasibility fails. Commitment to single-square topology early in Phase 0 (before land assembly, grid and tenant validation) risks locking the project into an infeasible design. Conversely, postponing the topology decision until late Phase 0 (Month 10+) leaves insufficient time to develop detailed split-campus designs and grid plans, forcing a rushed, low-confidence FID decision.

Impact: Single-square commitment that later fails to assemble land or grid capacity forces expensive Phase 1 redesign or cancellation. Delaying topology decision until Month 10 (2027-08-17) of Phase 0 compresses the time available for split-campus design, fiber route planning and multi-node grid negotiations, increasing the risk of Phase 1 start slippage by 6–12 months. Split-campus choice made too early may over-complicate Phase 0 by requiring simultaneous validation of 2–3 sites, extending Phase 0 timeline by 3–6 months and spend by €150M–€300M.

Likelihood: High

Severity: Medium

Action: Establish a topology decision gate at Month 4 (2027-02-17) of Phase 0 (by Month 4 = 2027-02-17 on the project calendar = around 2027-02-17). At this gate, compare single-square vs. 2–3 node split-campus options on criteria: (i) land assemblability (% of target parcel optionable); (ii) per-node grid hosting capacity; (iii) fiber-route feasibility and cost; (iv) per-MW capex and opex; (v) operational complexity and tenant workload span-ability. Choose single-square only if ≥70% of target parcel is optionable and grid capacity is confirmed ≥1 GW in first tranche; otherwise default to split-campus. For split-campus, identify 2–3 viable node combinations and develop detailed Phase 1 capex/timeline for each, so FID can proceed on the feasible subset. Publish the topology decision in writing, with evidence and rationale, so stakeholders and lenders understand why single or split was chosen.

Risk 20 - Environmental – Ecological Impact & Compensation

The 161 km² envelope likely spans productive agricultural land, wetlands, and possibly ecological corridors or protected habitats (Natura 2000, RAMSAR wetlands, listed species). Environmental authorization and EIA (Environmental Impact Assessment) under French law require avoidance of impact where possible, reduction of unavoidable impacts, and compensation for residual impacts at a 1:1 or greater ratio (net-positive biodiversity goal). Compensating ecological impact on 100+ km² of active development may require purchasing or restoring 100–300 km² of offsite land, at a cost of €100M–€500M and with uncertain effectiveness and enforcement. Agricultural displacement of productive farmland (estimated 10,000–15,000 hectares or more) triggers compensation and relocation costs that are politically contentious.

Impact: Environmental permitting delays of 12–24 months due to EIA complexity or eco-group legal challenges. Ecological compensation cost of €200M–€500M in Phase 1–2, reducing project returns. Designation of new protected zones or expansion of Natura 2000 areas during Phase 0–1 could retroactively restrict land use, forcing design changes and cost escalation. Agricultural displacement of 10,000+ hectares triggers political opposition from farm-sector unions and can block permits or force a public referendum. Net-biodiversity targets (e.g., 'no net loss' or '+30% by 2050') may be unachievable at the proposed scale, leading to permit conditions that constrain buildout or require perpetual ecological restoration funding.

Likelihood: Medium

Severity: High

Action: Commission a Phase 0 environmental baseline and ecological survey (Months 1–4 = 2026-11-17 to 2027-02-17) covering: (i) botanical, avian, invertebrate and bat surveys across candidate sites; (ii) Natura 2000 and protected-species mapping; (iii) hydrological and soil-quality assessment; (iv) carbon storage and peat-soil inventory. Identify the 'no-build' or 'minimal-impact' core area (e.g., 50–80 km² of the 161 km² envelope) that avoids key ecological zones, and focus Phase 1 development on that core. Establish a campus-wide ecological master plan by Month 6 (2027-04-17) that pre-commits biodiversity-compensation measures: offsite habitat restoration, wetland creation, hedgerow and wildlife-corridor establishment on continuation zones. Work with environmental NGOs (Ligue pour la Protection des Oiseaux, Conservatoire Botanique) and regional conservation authorities to co-design and monitor ecological compensation. Budget €200M–€300M for ecological offset and restoration in Phase 1–2 capex. Define the environmental gate for permitting: by Month 9 (2027-07-17) of Phase 0, obtain a preliminary EIA screening opinion from DREAL confirming that ecological compensation is achievable within the proposed scale and cost; if EIA screening indicates unmanageable ecological constraint, trigger a Phase 1 redesign or site pivot.

Risk 21 - Regulatory – National Legislation & Policy Change

The project's feasibility and timeline depend on several regulatory assumptions that are not confirmed: (i) fast-track permitting status for major industrial projects (being legislated but not finalized); (ii) RTE and EDF willingness to sign multi-GW supply and connection contracts; (iii) French AI and data-sovereignty strategy remaining aligned with private-sector hyperscale data centers (policy could shift toward public or EU ownership); (iv) US export-control policy on advanced GPUs remaining stable enough to allow European deployment. Major legislative or policy changes during Phase 0–1 could render the project uneconomic or infeasible.

Impact: Legislative change delaying or eliminating fast-track permitting status extends permitting timeline by 12–24 months. Policy shift toward public-sector or EU-only data-center ownership could exclude private developers or mandate state co-investment at unfavorable terms. Export-control restrictions on advanced GPUs could eliminate hardware availability for commercial AI training, forcing the campus to focus only on sovereign AI workloads (which may not fill the capacity or pay competitive rates). Change in EDF energy strategy (e.g., pivot away from nuclear toward renewables) could make long-dated baseload contracts unavailable or uneconomical. Climate-adaptation regulations (e.g., tighter water-use limits during droughts) could force technology retrofits or capacity reductions.

Likelihood: Low

Severity: High

Action: Establish a regulatory-horizon scanning program in Phase 0 (Month 1 = 2026-11-17 onwards), monitoring: (i) French parliamentary debates on AI, data sovereignty, and fast-track permitting; (ii) EU regulations on data-center energy efficiency and environmental impact; (iii) US export-control and sanctions policy affecting GPU/TPU trade; (iv) EDF and RTE strategic statements on long-term supply and grid availability. Engage in industry associations (France Datacenter, CIGREF, MEDEF) and policy forums to understand emerging policy trends. By Month 9 (2027-07-17) of Phase 0, commission a regulatory-risk analysis updating the project's sensitivity to identified policy changes. Define a policy-change gate for Phase 1 FID: if major legislation affecting permitting, energy supply, or export controls passes during Phase 0, reassess feasibility and update project economics accordingly. Include a force-majeure clause in Phase 1 FID that allows the project to pause or exit if a fundamental regulatory change occurs (e.g., export ban on advanced GPUs, water-use ban, permitting legislation repeal).

Risk 22 - Financial – Financing Structure & Sovereign Co-Investment Terms

The project is backed by an infrastructure-fund consortium with sovereign-adjacent co-investment discussions. Sovereign co-investor terms (French State, EU, or allied governments) often include below-market returns, public-interest concessions (labor, data sovereignty, environmental commitments), governance restrictions, and slow decision-making. Reconciling sovereign-investor expectations with private-developer cost-of-capital and return targets (proposed 8–12% IRR, not specified) creates tension. Negotiating sovereign co-investment terms can take 12–24 months, delaying Phase 1 FID or forcing cost concessions that erode equity returns.

Impact: Sovereign co-investment terms requiring public-benefit spending (€100M–€500M in Phase 1–2) reduce investor equity returns by 1–3 percentage points. Governance restrictions (state board seat, veto on tenant selection, data-residency mandates) increase operational complexity and slow decision-making by 3–6 months per cycle. Negotiation delay for sovereign co-investment structure extends Phase 0 and Phase 1 timeline by 6–12 months. If sovereign terms become unacceptable, the project may lose the political support and permitting tailwind that sovereign backing provides, increasing permitting risk and cost.

Likelihood: Medium

Severity: Medium

Action: Establish a financing-structure working group in Month 1 (2026-11-17), bringing together sponsor equity, infrastructure-fund consortium representatives, and sovereign-fund representatives (if formally participating, or proposed participants). By Month 3 (2027-01-17), develop a draft co-investment term sheet outlining: (i) equity stake and return expectations; (ii) governance structure (board composition, veto rights); (iii) public-interest commitments (labor, environment, data sovereignty); (iv) decision-making timeline. Negotiate sovereign terms in parallel with Phase 0 feasibility work (Months 2–8 = 2026-12-17 to 2027-06-17), so co-investment structure is resolved before Phase 1 FID gate (Month 12 = 2027-10-17). If sovereign terms prove unacceptable (return expectations <5%, governance vetoes paralyze decisions), consider a bifurcated structure: sovereign investor takes a non-controlling stake (20–30%) with preferred-return target and board observation rights, while private sponsor retains operational control. Establish a financing gate for Phase 1 FID: by Month 12 (2027-10-17) of Phase 0, secure binding commitment from all equity sources (sponsor, infrastructure fund, sovereign co-investors if applicable) for Phase 1 capex (€5B–€10B), with agreed-upon terms, governance structure and decision-making timeline.

Risk 23 - Operational – Subsea Cable & Landing-Point Single Points of Failure

Connectivity to subsea networks and international markets depends on landings at UK, Belgium, Netherlands and France coastal facilities. These landing points are often concentrated in a few geographic locations (e.g., UK south coast, northern France coast), creating hidden single points of failure. A disaster at a primary landing station (cable-ship accident, fiber-optic cut, facility damage) could isolate the campus from international markets for days to weeks. Resilience against landing-point concentration requires geographically diverse subsea routes, which are expensive to build or lease.

Impact: Subsea cable cut or landing-point disaster isolating the campus for 3–7 days causes total tenant revenue loss of €50M–€200M. Repair of subsea cable requires 2–4 weeks; repair of landing-point damage could require 4–12 weeks. Tenants running international AI training or inference workloads cannot tolerate this level of outage; loss of anchor tenants due to unreliable connectivity could cascade into lease terminations and revenue loss.

Likelihood: Low

Severity: High

Action: During Phase 0 fiber-route audit (Months 1–6 = 2026-11-17 to 2027-04-17), audit subsea cable landing points and confirm that the campus has access to ≥2 independent landing facilities on the UK coast and ≥2 independent facilities on the French/Belgian coast, with no shared infrastructure (landing conduit, power, cooling) between them. If independent landings are not available, budget for co-investment in a new subsea cable or landing facility (€300M–€800M over Phase 1–2). Establish service-level agreements (SLAs) with subsea-cable operators requiring rapid-response repair commitments (<72 hours) and carrier guarantees of compensation for outages >4 hours. Design the campus fiber architecture with on-shore diversity, so outage of any single landing point affects <25% of total cross-border capacity; the remaining capacity continues to serve tenants. By Month 9 (2027-07-17) of Phase 0, confirm in writing that subsea connectivity redundancy is achievable within cost and timeline budgets.

Risk summary

This is a 9 GW, 161 km² hyperscale AI campus project in Hauts-de-France, France, budgeted at €100B–€140B+ over 10–15 years, with a 500 MW–1 GW Phase 1 gate. The project is intentionally framed as a stress-test of extreme ambition, with legitimate outcomes including downsizing, splitting across multiple sites, or cancellation if feasibility fails. The plan adopts a pragmatic foundation: tranche-based grid requests, milestone-capped Phase 0 capital (€250M–€750M), reservation-fee demand validation, standard permitting with early consultation, and independent investment-committee gate control. Critical success factors are RTE grid hosting capacity above ~1 GW (the primary kill condition), land assembly without major holdouts, credible anchor-tenant demand backed by signed take-or-pay agreements covering ≥30–50% of expansion tranches, social license and permitting non-blockage, and stable financing. The most critical risks are: (1) RTE grid hosting capacity constraints limiting available connection power below ~1 GW, which is the stated failure condition; (2) inability to assemble an adequate, contiguous or semi-contiguous parcel due to fragmented farmland ownership, holdouts, or limited industrial brownfield availability; and (3) absence of creditworthy anchor tenants willing to sign binding take-or-pay leases, forcing the project into speculative positioning that violates its gate discipline. Secondary risks include brownfield contamination surprises, community and political opposition sufficient to block or delay permits, water and cooling feasibility at the required PUE, financing credibility given the scale, and national-security review duration. This risk register identifies 21 material risks across regulatory, technical, financial, environmental, social and operational domains, with emphasis on the uncontrolled external dependencies and the failure modes that trigger exit or downsizing.

Make Assumptions

Question 1 - What maximum sunk cost is acceptable before the Phase 0 gate, who funds it, and how is USD hardware exposure kept separate from EUR infrastructure capital?

Assumptions: Assumption: Phase 0 is capped at €750M (user-constraint upper bound), drawn in milestone tranches from the consortium with abandonment conditions. USD hardware sits in a separate tenant-backed vehicle. Forwards are used only against signed take-or-pay, at a hedge cost of 0.5–2% a year (estimate). Rationale: staged drawdown is common in infrastructure finance and limits stranded capital.

Assessments: Title: Financial Feasibility Assessment Description: Tests whether staged capital limits sunk cost and isolates FX. Details: Phase 0 of €250M–€750M is an estimate to challenge. Phase 1 hardware of €1.5B–€2.3B in USD moves about €150M–€230M per 10% FX swing (estimate). Risk: sunk-cost pressure overrides the gate. Mitigation: an independent investment committee, drawdowns tied to grid, land and tenant evidence, and hedges only against signed leases. Opportunity: a ring-fenced hardware vehicle widens the lender pool. Full-buildout cost of €100B–€140B+ is unvalidated and credible only per tranche.

Question 2 - What is the realistic sequence and duration of Phase 0 gates, and which milestones depend on external authorities (RTE, prefecture, ANSSI) and so are uncontrolled?

Assumptions: Assumption: Phase 0 runs Months 0–12 (2026-10-17 to 2027-10-17) with a topology decision at Month 4 (2027-02-17), land and water checks by Month 6 (2027-04-17), and tenant term sheets by Month 9 (2027-07-17). The gate review is at Month 12 (2027-10-17). RTE, prefectural and ANSSI milestones are labelled uncontrolled until a signed offer or formal decision exists. Rationale: external processes in France typically take 12–24 months (estimate).

Assessments: Title: Schedule Feasibility Assessment Description: Tests whether the Phase 0 schedule is achievable given external dependencies. Details: A firm RTE connection offer within 12 months is unlikely (estimate). Permitting is 24+ months and the ~1 GW grid test may resolve only after Month 12 (2027-10-17). Risk: gate dates are set before authorities answer. Mitigation: a gate can pass with 'conditional' status, and Phase 1 FID shifts with RTE timing rather than forcing a decision. Opportunity: early topology and land checks (Months 3–4 = 2027-01-17 to 2027-02-17) can kill the single-square option cheaply, saving up to €100M–€250M (estimate).

Question 3 - What team and external advisers are needed in Phase 0, and which scarce skills (grid engineering, remediation, security, trades) are the bottleneck?

Assumptions: Assumption: Phase 0 needs a core team of about 40–60 people (estimate) plus specialist advisers for grid, hydrology, ecology, legal, land and security. An independent investment committee and red team sit apart from development. Regional offices are opened at Cambrai and Dunkirk. Rationale: comparable large-site development programmes use multidisciplinary teams of this size.

Assessments: Title: Resource Capacity Assessment Description: Evaluates availability of skills for Phase 0 and the Phase 1 build. Details: Electrical and cooling trades are scarce; wage inflation of 20–40% on trades is a risk (estimate from the risk register). Operations headcount is small (50–150 FTE for Phase 1, not verified), so employment claims must be modest. Mitigation: early framework contracts with large EPC firms, a regional training academy (€10M–€30M, estimate), and prefabricated halls. Opportunity: remediation and civil firms from the region can be certified early. Key-person dependence on the grid and permitting leads should be covered by deputies.

Question 4 - Which authorisations and reviews apply (ICPE, environmental authorisation, urban planning, national-security review, foreign-investment screening), and is fast-track status assumed?

Assumptions: Assumption: The standard route applies: ICPE and environmental authorisation take about 18–30 months, with appeal risk adding 24–48 months (estimates). Fast-track status is not assumed because it is not confirmed. National-security and foreign-investment reviews run in parallel and are uncontrolled until formal decisions exist. Rationale: a standard route avoids dependence on legislation still in progress.

Assessments: Title: Regulatory Pathway Assessment Description: Evaluates permit sequence, review burden and legal-challenge exposure. Details: Permit delay erodes RTE queue position and adds carrying cost of €200M–€500M (estimate). Foreign co-investor scrutiny could cap foreign equity or restrict tenants. Mitigation: pre-submission dialogue with DREAL, the prefecture and security authorities in Months 0–1, early voluntary consultation, and one permit file per node so a challenge does not stall all sites. A split campus multiplies files but isolates legal risk. Policy change is a gate trigger.

Question 5 - What are the principal safety and risk exposures (sabotage, grid or fiber disruption, contamination, fire, cooling failure) and what kill thresholds apply?

Assumptions: Assumption: Numeric kill thresholds are proposed in Phase 0: firm RTE offer of at least 500 MW within 36 months, at least 70% of the target parcel optioned non-coercively, and signed take-or-pay for at least 30% of Phase 1. Security is baseline campus-wide with hardened enclaves funded by sovereign tenants. Rationale: thresholds are drawn from the risk register and are proposals to be fixed by the committee.

Assessments: Title: Safety and Risk Assessment Description: Evaluates operational, security and liability risks and the strength of kill criteria. Details: Highest risks: grid below ~1 GW, land fragmentation, no creditworthy anchors (all High likelihood). Contamination can cost €100M–€400M if found late (estimate); intrusive surveys before commitment bound this. Fiber diversity often collapses at shared ducts; audit before relying on it. Single-site concentration raises sabotage and grid-loss impact; a split campus reduces it. Thresholds only bind if the committee is independent of the development team.

Question 6 - What environmental limits (water, ecology, farmland, carbon, noise, heat) cap the buildable share of the 161 km² and the tolerable cooling approach?

Assumptions: Assumption: Cooling is closed-loop direct-to-chip with dry coolers and no evaporative water. Built area is a minority of the envelope (about 30–50%, estimate), with the rest as buffers, ecology and continuing farmland. Heat reuse is valued at zero until offtake is signed. Rationale: a zero-water rule simplifies permitting; the share is a placeholder for the land-use model.

Assessments: Title: Environmental Impact Assessment Description: Evaluates water, ecology, land and thermal constraints on scale. Details: Dry cooling in 30–35°C weather may push PUE to 1.35–1.5 against the 1.15–1.25 target, raising peak grid load by 5–15% (estimate). Farmland loss of 10,000+ ha is politically contentious. Ecological compensation may cost €200M–€500M (estimate) and compete for farmland. Mitigation: ecological master plan by Month 6 (2027-04-17), written water-authority opinion, and reserving contaminated zones for energy or restoration. Opportunity: brownfield reuse and heat export strengthen the narrative if contracted.

Question 7 - Which stakeholders can enable or block the project (municipalities, farm unions, NGOs, RTE/EDF, prefecture, lenders, tenants), and what level of local support is required to proceed?

Assumptions: Assumption: Support from at least 2 of the 3 most affected municipalities is the Phase 1 gate (proposed threshold). A liaison committee and public consultation start in Months 1–3 (2026-11-17 to 2027-01-17). A community-benefit package of €50M–€150M over Phases 1–2 (estimate) is contingent on permits. A binding local veto is not adopted, but refusal by a key municipality triggers reassessment.

Assessments: Title: Stakeholder Engagement Assessment Description: Evaluates opposition risk and the legitimacy strategy. Details: Farm unions (FNSEA, Confédération Paysanne), NGOs and mayors can delay permits by 12–36 months (estimate). Benefits built on jobs lack credibility given small operations headcount. Mitigation: published minutes, lease-and-continue farming arrangements, transparent siting rationale, and funded monitoring roles for municipalities. Competing industrial users (steel, hydrogen) may contest grid capacity. Opportunity: a reindustrialisation narrative with shared infrastructure can win support.

Question 8 - What operating model will run the campus (tenant contracts, power procurement, grid flexibility, fiber, security operations, node management) and how is it tested before expansion?

Assumptions: Assumption: Capacity is sold under take-or-pay leases of 5–10 years (proposed) with reservation fees of €10M–€50M per 100 MW (proposed). Power is a blend of nuclear-linked contracts, PPAs and BESS, with curtailment at or below 10% (proposed, to be negotiated). A 2–5 MW pilot hall validates PUE before scaling. Rationale: pilot-then-scale limits systemic design errors.

Assessments: Title: Operational Systems Assessment Description: Evaluates demand contracts, power, cooling and connectivity operations. Details: Multi-GW nuclear-backed supply at the assumed €50–70/MWh is not verified; a 20–40% cost overrun would hit the economics hard. Curtailment of 15% on 1 GW could cost €150M–€300M over 10 years (estimate) and conflicts with 99.5%+ tenant SLAs. Mitigation: pass-through indexation, BESS and interruptible workloads. Expansion gate: PUE at or below 1.28 across commissioned halls, power reliability met, and signed take-or-pay for 30–50% of the next tranche. Letters of intent do not count.

Review Assumptions

Domain of the expert reviewer

Large-scale infrastructure project management and feasibility assessment, with specialization in critical grid-scale compute facilities, multi-stakeholder governance, and gated capital deployment under extreme technical and political uncertainty. Focus on identifying unexamined dependencies, uncontrolled external gates, and assumption cascades that could render the project non-viable or force costly Phase 1 restructuring.

Domain-specific considerations

  • RTE grid hosting capacity as the primary kill condition remains uncontrolled and untested until formal connection offer; no known European precedent for 1+ GW single-site allocation to private compute
  • Land assembly at 161 km² scale across fragmented French farmland with organized union opposition; compulsory acquisition uncontrolled and politically dangerous
  • Anchor-tenant demand validation limited to letters of intent (non-binding); risk of LOI manipulation or tenant reconsideration post-Phase-0 gate
  • USD hardware exposure (€1.5B–€2.3B) depends on tenant financing discipline; developer balance-sheet risk if tenants default or defer
  • National-security review duration and tenant-access restrictions uncontrolled; foreign co-investor involvement may trigger sovereignty scrutiny that delays or blocks Phase 1
  • Permitting timeline compression (18–30 months assumed) depends on fast-track legislation not yet finalized; standard route is 24–48+ months, eroding grid queue

Issue 1 - RTE Grid Hosting Capacity Remains the Uncontrolled Primary Gate: 1 GW Assumption Is Untested

The plan identifies RTE grid hosting capacity above ~1 GW as the 'primary kill condition.' However, no formal connection offer exists, RTE's multi-tranche capacity allocation policy is not confirmed, and competing industrial decarbonization projects (steel, hydrogen, refinery) may saturate regional transmission. Early at-risk pre-engineering spend (€50M–€150M estimate) provides no guarantee. A firm RTE offer is unlikely within Phase 0 (Month 12 = 2027-10-17), meaning the primary feasibility gate cannot close on schedule. If RTE offers <500 MW in the first tranche, or conditions it on unfavorable flexibility/curtailment terms (>15% annual), Phase 1 cannot proceed at the planned 500 MW–1 GW scale.

Recommendation: 1) Initiate formal RTE pre-engineering dialogue in Month 0 (2026-10-17) requesting binding technical opinion on multi-tranche feasibility (500 MW, 1 GW, 2 GW) and timelines. 2) Define the grid gate not as 'RTE offer received' but as 'RTE preliminary feasibility letter confirming ≥500 MW available within 36 months' by Month 6 (2027-04-17); if not in hand, trigger a topology review toward a split-campus model. 3) Map competing industrial load requests in real-time; if saturation is evident by Month 8 (2027-06-17), conduct a credibility reassessment and be prepared to reduce Phase 1 target from 1 GW to the available capacity. 4) Commission an independent third-party RTE hosting-capacity audit (not a developer-commissioned report); publish the findings to lenders and co-investors so the grid constraint is visible.

Sensitivity: Baseline: 1 GW available within 36 months from Month 0 (2026-10-17), so Phase 1 starts Month 36–48 (2029-10-17 to 2030-10-17). If RTE delays to Month 48 (2030-10-17), Phase 1 slips 12 months, raising carrying costs by €200M–€400M and eroding tenant demand certainty (some tenants may defect to competing sites). If RTE offers only 500 MW (50% scenario), Phase 1 capex falls from €5B–€10B to €2.5B–€5B, but margin compresses if fixed costs are unscaled. If RTE imposes curtailment of 20%+ (vs. proposed 10%), annual revenue loss is €300M–€600M at full capacity, reducing IRR by 2–4 percentage points.

Issue 2 - Anchor-Tenant Demand Validation Relies on Letters of Intent, Not Binding Commitments; 30% Take-or-Pay Gate Is Unproven

The plan correctly states that 'only signed take-or-pay or equivalent terms should count' and that 'letters of intent do not count.' However, the Phase 0 action plan still lists 'non-binding LOIs by Month 4 (2027-02-17)' and 'binding term sheets by Month 9 (2027-07-17)' without explaining how LOI-to-binding conversion is enforced or what happens if tenants back away.
