Global hyperscalers (OpenAI, Meta, Google, Microsoft) are actively comparing 10+ European competing sites; their LOIs are often non-exclusive and contingent on other site options. Sovereign AI tenants (French State, EU institutions) have procurement cycles of 18–36 months and may use LOI as a position-holding tactic rather than a commitment. If Phase 0 closes without signed take-or-pay for ≥30% of Phase 1 (300 MW on a 1 GW plan), the project lacks debt-financing credibility and Phase 1 FID is blocked.

Recommendation: 1) By Month 3 (2027-01-17), develop two tenant-term-sheet templates: a 'high-commitment' take-or-pay lease (5–10 year tenor, capacity guarantee, inflation indexing) and a 'capacity-reservation fee' (€10M–€50M per 100 MW, credited against future lease revenue, no refund if project is cancelled). 2) Distinguish between non-binding LOI (advisory only) and binding term sheet (executed, capacity reserved, payment schedule fixed). 3) Require signature on term sheets (not LOIs) by Month 9 (2027-07-17) for the Phase 0 gate; LOIs are for informational purposes only. 4) Define Phase 1 FID gate as 'signed take-or-pay agreements totalling ≥300 MW (30% of 1 GW) with minimum A-/BB+ credit rating,' not 'letters of intent.' 5) If <30% is signed by Month 9 (2027-07-17), trigger a contingency: reduce Phase 1 to 250–500 MW, matching only committed demand, and reset Phase 2 FID gate to require ≥50% of Phase 2 to be committed before expansion.

Sensitivity: Baseline: 30% (300 MW) of Phase 1 signed by Month 9 (2027-07-17); lenders approve €3B–€6B debt. Downside (20% scenario): only 200 MW signed; debt availability falls to €2B–€3B, forcing equity to cover shortfall or Phase 1 capex to be cut by €1.5B–€2B (reducing built capacity or deferring halls). Upside (50% scenario): 500 MW signed; Phase 2 FID credibility rises and larger Phase 1 expansion is viable. If no binding commitments materialize by Month 9 (2027-07-17) (0% scenario), Phase 1 does not proceed and the project pivots to Phase 0 completion only (e.g., land options held, grid pre-engineering finished, but no halls built).

Issue 3 - Land Assembly 161 km² Contiguous Assumption Is Acknowledged as Doubtful But No Credible Split-Campus Baseline Exists; Topology Decision Is Delayed Until Month 4 (2027-02-17), Compressing Split-Campus Planning

The plan explicitly states '161 km² contiguous assembly is doubtful (not verified).' However, the topology decision is deferred to Month 4 (2027-02-17)—only 4 months into Phase 0—leaving only 8 months for detailed split-campus grid, fiber, permitting and operational-complexity analysis before the Phase 0 gate (Month 12 = 2027-10-17). If contiguous assembly fails (high likelihood), Phase 1 design must pivot to 2–3 nodes (Cambrai, Dunkirk, Valenciennes), each with separate grid connections, permitting files, security perimeters and fiber routes. Late topology pivots force design rework that typically costs €200M–€500M and delays energization by 6–12 months. Additionally, tenant workload span-ability across multiple nodes (latency tolerance for tightly coupled training) has not been validated with actual tenants, risking that a chosen topology does not match workload needs.

Recommendation: 1) Advance the topology decision to Month 2 (2026-12-17) or Month 3 (2027-01-17), not Month 4 (2027-02-17), to allow 9–10 months of detailed planning before Phase 0 gate. 2) Commission detailed designs for three topology scenarios by Month 4 (2027-02-17): single-square contiguous, two-node federation (Cambrai + Dunkirk), and three-node mesh (Cambrai, Dunkirk, Valenciennes). Include capex per node, grid-connection timelines, per-MW costs, and operational overhead. 3) Solicit from anchor-tenant candidates (by Month 3 = 2027-01-17) their tolerance for inter-node latency and workload segmentation, then size topology to that constraint, not the other way around. 4) Set a contiguous-assembly go/no-go decision at Month 3 (2027-01-17): proceed with single-square only if ≥70% of target parcel can be optioned at <15% above benchmark land value; otherwise default to split-campus and begin detailed node-level design immediately. 5) Develop separate permitting and grid-connection filings per node so that one node's delay or legal challenge does not stall others.

Sensitivity: Baseline: single-square at Cambrai, 161 km² envelope, Phase 1 500 MW–1 GW, energization Month 36–48 (2029-10-17 to 2030-10-17). Downside (split-campus discovery Month 9–10 = 2027-07-17 to 2027-08-17): pivot to two-node model (Cambrai 500 MW + Dunkirk 250 MW), Phase 1 redesign adds 6–12 months, per-MW capex increases by 5–10% (€250M–€500M), energization shifts to Month 42–54 (2030-04-17 to 2031-04-17). Carrying-cost impact: €300M–€600M. Upside (early topology clarity): split-campus chosen proactively by Month 3 (2027-01-17), Node 1 (Cambrai) is energized on schedule, Node 2 (Dunkirk) follows 6–12 months later, reducing overall program risk and allowing phased tenant onboarding.

Issue 4 - National-Security Review Duration and Tenant-Access Restrictions Are Uncontrolled; Foreign Co-Investor Involvement May Trigger Sovereignty Scrutiny That Delays or Blocks Phase 1 FID

The plan proposes initiating 'confidential pre-submission dialogue with ANSSI' in Month 0 (2026-10-17) but acknowledges that review timeline (6–12 months, not verified) and findings (data-residency zones, tenant-access restrictions, state observer roles) are uncontrolled. Foreign co-investor backing (described as 'infrastructure-fund consortium with sovereign-adjacent co-investment') may elevate scrutiny if the co-investor is perceived as having geopolitical interests. If ANSSI classifies the campus as 'critical infrastructure' or requires 'vital-system operator' status, this triggers ongoing state oversight and compliance obligations (estimated 5–10% opex increase, €50M–€500M annually at scale). If Phase 1 proceeds without formal ANSSI clearance, tenants may refuse to commit capacity due to regulatory uncertainty. Conversely, if ANSSI demands structural concessions (foreign-equity cap, French board majority, state-observer seat), this could force co-investor capital restructuring and delay Phase 1 FID by 6–12 months while terms are renegotiated.

Recommendation: 1) Commission a confidential white paper on security governance by Month 1 (2026-11-17), documenting: tenant vetting process, data-residency policies, perimeter hardening, cyber-OT separation and co-investor governance. 2) Request a formal pre-submission meeting with ANSSI and DGSI by Month 2 (2026-12-17), seeking a written preliminary opinion (not binding, but indicative) on anticipated review scope, estimated timeline and any blocking concerns. Publish this opinion internally but protect confidentiality per authorities' request. 3) Prepare for three ANSSI outcomes: (a) 'low concern' – review timelines <12 months, minimal tenant-access restrictions; (b) 'medium concern' – review 12–18 months, some tenant vetting or data-residency zones; (c) 'high concern' – review 18–24 months, significant restrictions on foreign tenants or co-investor equity. By Month 6 (2027-04-17), scenario-plan for each. 4) Define a security-gate criterion for Phase 1 FID: ANSSI must issue a formal 'no objection' or conditional clearance letter (with specified conditions) by Month 18 (2028-04-17). If ANSSI has not cleared by Month 18 (2028-04-17), Phase 1 FID is conditional on authorities' indication that clearance will be completed within 6 months; otherwise Phase 1 is deferred. 5) Negotiate co-investor governance to anticipate ANSSI findings: propose French board majority and quarterly security reporting, so state expectations are pre-built into the structure.

Sensitivity: Baseline: ANSSI clearance completed by Month 12 (2027-10-17), Phase 1 FID proceeds Month 12–13 (2027-10-17 to 2027-11-17), energization Month 36–48 (2029-10-17 to 2030-10-17). Downside (high-concern ANSSI review): review extends to Month 18–24 (2028-04-17 to 2028-10-17), Phase 1 FID is delayed 6–12 months, co-investor capital structure is renegotiated (potential 2–4 month additional delay). Energization shifts to Month 42–60 (2030-04-17 to 2031-10-17). Carrying costs: €300M–€700M. Operationally, if ANSSI restricts foreign tenants, addressable market shrinks, reducing anchor-tenant pool and increasing difficulty of signing 30%+ take-or-pay. Upside: early ANSSI engagement removes surprises and lenders gain confidence in timeline and tenant eligibility.

Issue 5 - Phase 0 Sunk Cost (€250M–€750M) and Momentum Pressure Will Override Kill Gates Unless Investment Committee Independence Is Hardened in Writing in Month 1 (2026-11-17)

The plan proposes an 'independent investment committee separate from the development team' to hold kill thresholds. However, the independence and authority of this committee are not formally established in Month 0–1 (2026-10-17 to 2026-11-17), and the plan does not specify: (i) committee composition (who appoints, who votes, quorum); (ii) the specific numeric thresholds that trigger automatic review; (iii) authority to pause or cancel Phase 1 (veto power, or recommendation only); (iv) how sunk cost is accounted for in the decision (stranded-asset analysis vs. additional-investment justification); (v) public disclosure of dissent (so lenders and co-investors see the committee's reasoning, not just the outcome). Without these formalities, the investment committee will default to a 'board-level review' where sunk-cost momentum (€750M is already spent, killing the project now yields nothing) overwhelms the stated thresholds. This is a common failure mode in large infrastructure projects: the gate is set but no structure exists to enforce it.

Recommendation: 1) By Month 1 (2026-11-17), establish a formal Investment Committee Charter in writing, signed by all sponsors and co-investors. Specify: committee composition (e.g., one independent director appointed by co-investors, one representative from each sponsor, an external red-team member), voting rules (unanimous, supermajority, or independent director veto), and quorum. 2) Fix numeric kill thresholds in the Charter in Month 2 (2026-12-17): (a) RTE firm connection offer for ≥500 MW within 36 months; (b) ≥70% of target parcel under non-coercive option; (c) signed anchor-tenant take-or-pay covering ≥30% of Phase 1. If any threshold fails, the committee is empowered to pause or cancel Phase 1 with no requirement for additional sponsor approval. 3) Implement a 'stranded-asset analysis' at the Phase 0 gate: calculate the cost of stopping Phase 0 now (€250M–€750M sunk, with salvage value from land options and engineering reports) vs. proceeding to Phase 1 despite gate failures (risking €5B–€10B Phase 1 capex with lower success probability). If the analysis shows stopping is cheaper, the committee is bound to recommend stopping. 4) Publish the committee's gate decision and dissenting views (if any) quarterly to lenders and co-investors, so accountability is visible and sunk-cost pressure cannot be hidden. 5) Appoint an external red team (€2M–€5M cost) in Month 1 (2026-11-17) that reports directly to the committee, not to the development team, and publishes independent pass/fail opinions on each gate criterion.

Sensitivity: Baseline: independent committee with hardened charter; Phase 0 gate is enforced, kill criteria bind. If thresholds are breached (e.g., no RTE offer by Month 12 = 2027-10-17), Phase 1 is cancelled or downsized, and the €750M sunk cost is written off. Downside (weak committee): no formal charter, independence undermined by sponsor pressure, sunk cost overrides gates. Phase 1 proceeds despite failures (e.g., RTE offers only 250 MW, no anchor tenants signed), Phase 1 capex of €5B–€10B is committed, and by Month 24 (2028-10-17) it becomes clear the project cannot reach IRR targets. Sunk cost is now €5.75B–€10.75B. Upside (strong committee): early gate failures are recognized by Month 9–12 (2027-07-17 to 2027-10-17), project is downsized or split-campus, preventing the €5B–€10B Phase 1 write-down.

Issue 6 - Power Procurement Assumptions (€50–70/MWh, Multi-GW Nuclear-Backed Supply) Are Not Verified and May Underestimate Cost by 20–40%, Eroding Feasibility and Tenant Economics

The plan proposes 'nuclear-linked supply contracts at assumed EUR 50–70/MWh (not verified)' and assumes EDF will negotiate multi-GW long-dated baseload contracts. However: (i) France's EDF is under state pressure to supply existing industries and meet national decarbonization targets; a 1–2 GW multi-year contract to a private AI data-center developer is unprecedented; (ii) power pricing is volatile and assumes 10-year forecast prices (2027–2037) that may be 20–40% above or below the estimate; (iii) if power cost escalates from €70/MWh to €100/MWh, opex increases by €300M–€600M annually at full 9 GW scale, eroding IRR by 2–4 percentage points. The plan does not model power-cost sensitivity or establish a cost threshold above which Phase 2 expansion is mothballed. Tenants will expect to see a binding power-supply agreement in Phase 1 FID; if power cost is still uncontracted at that stage, debt-financing credibility collapses.

Recommendation: 1) Commission an independent power-market study in Month 1 (2026-11-17) analyzing current and forecast baseload pricing (2025–2035) and EDF's willingness to sign long-dated supply to large private consumers. Model three scenarios: base-case (€70/MWh), upside (€50/MWh), and downside (€100/MWh). 2) By Month 3 (2027-01-17), initiate formal negotiations with EDF (not exploratory discussions) for a preliminary letter of intent (LOI) committing to discuss a binding 500 MW baseload contract at a capped EUR/MWh price (to be negotiated, but with a maximum threshold set in Phase 0, e.g., €85/MWh). The LOI does not obligate EDF but clarifies intent and timeline. 3) Define the power-procurement gate for Phase 1 FID: by Month 9 (2027-07-17), secure either (a) a binding preliminary supply agreement (non-final but term-sheet level) with EDF for ≥500 MW at a capped price, or (b) a documented commitment to finalize supply by Month 18 (2028-04-17) of Phase 1 (before halls are energized). 4) In the financial model, calculate 'power-cost breakeven threshold': the price above which Phase 2 expansion is deferred. Publish this threshold; if market prices trend above it, trigger a Phase 2 pause decision. 5) For Phase 1 FID, model power revenue pass-through to tenants: if EDF contracts at €80/MWh vs. budgeted €70/MWh, tenants are invoiced at €80/MWh (indexed) so tenant economics do not surprise them at signature.

Sensitivity: Baseline: €70/MWh, multi-GW contract signed by Month 9 (2027-07-17), Phase 1 opex €350M–€700M annually (depending on MW built). Downside (€100/MWh scenario): opex increases to €500M–€1B annually, reducing IRR by 2–4 percentage points. If power cost is not contracted by Phase 1 FID, lenders may demand higher spreads (200–300 bps vs. 100–200 bps) or lower leverage (50% vs. 60%), adding €140M–€300M annual interest cost. Upside (€50/MWh): opex is €250M–€500M annually, IRR improves and tenant economics are more attractive, increasing demand.

Review conclusion

The plan's most critical exposure is that three primary feasibility gates—RTE grid hosting capacity (>1 GW), land assembly (≥70% of target parcel), and anchor-tenant take-or-pay (≥30% of Phase 1)—are all uncontrolled until Month 6–12 (2027-04-17 to 2027-10-17) and depend entirely on external decisions (RTE connection offer, permitting approval, tenant commitments). The plan correctly identifies these as failure conditions but does not establish how fast pivots or downsizing occur if gates fail. A late pivot to split-campus or reduced Phase 1 (Month 9–12 = 2027-07-17 to 2027-10-17) triggers 6–12 month schedule slippage and €300M–€600M carrying costs. Phase 0 sunk cost (€250M–€750M) will pressure continuation regardless of gate outcomes unless the investment committee is formally hardened in Month 1 (2026-11-17) with independence, charter, numeric thresholds and public accountability. USD hardware exposure (€1.5B–€2.3B) must be tenantfinanced or strictly hedged to avoid stranded assets. National-security review timelines are uncontrolled and foreign co-investor involvement may trigger restrictions that shrink the tenant pool or delay FID by 6–12 months. Power-procurement assumptions (€50–70/MWh, multi-GW nuclear-backed supply) are unverified and a 20–40% cost overrun would reduce IRR by 2–4 percentage points. The plan's tone is appropriately skeptical and gate-driven, but execution requires rigor in Month 0–2 (2026-10-17 to 2026-12-17) to establish independent governance, lock down early RTE and EDF dialogue, and set topology and land decisions by Month 4 (2027-02-17), not defer them. Downsizing to 250–500 MW Phase 1 or split-campus should be viewed as credible outcomes that improve risk-adjusted returns, not failures to be avoided.

Governance Audit

Audit - Corruption Risks

  • Selective vendor allocation and GPU/TPU procurement favoritism: preferential allocation to related parties, undisclosed markup on hardware purchase, or side agreements with accelerator suppliers bypassing competitive processes and inflating Phase 1 capex beyond the EUR 5B–10B budget.
  • Collusion between grid-connection advisers and RTE pre-engineering consultants to overstate required reinforcement scope or timeline, inflating estimated co-funding obligations and deterring competing bids for the project while benefiting consulting firms through extended engagement.
  • Land optioning scheme with insider knowledge: project representatives using confidential topology and zoning information to acquire adjacent parcels ahead of public announcement, or paying family members or related entities above-market fees for option agreements and easements.
  • Tenant selection bias in favor of foreign hyperscalers with sovereign-fund backing: steering toward tenants that benefit co-investors or parent companies, accepting below-market lease rates or forgiving SLA penalties in exchange for future capital commitments or board seats.
  • Permitting authority capture: offering planning authority or DREAL officials expedited reviews, consulting contracts, or post-employment opportunities in exchange for fast-tracked approvals or overlooking permit conditions that would extend timelines or increase compliance cost.
  • Security clearance withholding or conditioning: leveraging unclassified ANSSI feedback informally to exclude competitors or tenants, or conditioning national-security approval on non-binding co-investment terms that give the developer indirect control over downstream capacity allocation.

Audit - Misallocation Risks

  • Phase 0 sunk cost burden-shifting: encumbering EUR 150M–250M of Phase 0 feasibility spend (surveys, permits, land options) to a shell entity or joint venture, then abandoning the entity if the project fails, stranding sunk cost outside the developer's consolidated accounts and obscuring true Phase 0 spend to lenders and co-investors.
  • Double spending on grid and power studies: contracting independent RTE hosting-capacity audits and EDF power-market studies to different advisers without coordination, resulting in overlapping scope, duplicate site visits, and inflated advisory fees (EUR 5M–15M exposure) that could have been consolidated.
  • Land-option premium inflation without due diligence: paying EUR 15M–50M in option fees to secure parcels during Phase 0 without rigorous Phase I/II environmental or contamination surveys, leading to stranded option premiums if parcels are subsequently ruled out by DREAL or water authorities.
  • Unbudgeted community-benefit commitments: making verbal or preliminary written promises of EUR 50M–150M in social-benefit spending (training academy, municipal infrastructure, ecological restoration) without formal approval from the investment committee or capture in Phase 0 contingency reserves, exposing Phase 1 capex to unfunded add-ons.
  • Misclassified capex versus opex in pilot-hall validation: charging pilot 2–5 MW cooling system validation (EUR 10M–30M hardware and testing cost) to Phase 0 feasibility rather than Phase 1 capex, artificially constraining Phase 0 spend and deferring cost recognition to a later tranche.
  • Contingency reserve misallocation: allocating Phase 0 EUR 750M budget contingency to external party bonuses, consulting markup, or project-overhead allocations rather than reserving it for gate-critical activities (surveys, RTE pre-engineering, legal challenge defense, remediation indemnities), exposing gate achievements to under-resourcing.

Audit - Procedures

  • Monthly Phase 0 spend reconciliation and gate-milestone tracking: reconcile all Phase 0 expenditure (EUR 750M cap) against the four approved milestone tranches (EUR 150M, 250M, 200M, 150M), verify that drawdowns match gate-stage completion (Months 0–2 = 2026-10-17 to 2026-12-17, 3–6, 7–9, 10–12), and publish a variance report to the investment committee and external red team by Month 13 (2027-11-17). Require that no tranche is drawn without signed evidence of progress on grid, land, tenant and permitting gates.
  • Quarterly independent RTE and power-procurement verification: engage an external grid engineer and power-market analyst (separate from the development team) to audit all correspondence with RTE and EDF, confirm that hosted capacity, connection timelines and supply contract terms are accurately reported, and validate that any assumed hosting capacity above ~1 GW is backed by written preliminary feasibility letters or firm connection offers (not just verbal or internal notes).
  • Anchor-tenant commitment classification and signature audit: conduct a quarterly review of all tenant correspondence (LOIs, term sheets, reservation agreements, take-or-pay leases) by independent counsel to distinguish binding from non-binding commitments, confirm that only signed take-or-pay agreements are counted toward the 30–50% phase-gate threshold, and verify that counterparty credit ratings and parent guarantees are current (updated no less than semi-annually).
  • Phase I and Phase II environmental survey completion and remediation-liability mapping: track completion of Phase I desktop assessments (Target Month 1 = 2026-11-17) and Phase II intrusive surveys (Target Month 3 = 2027-01-17) across all candidate sites, and maintain a remediation-liability register mapping each parcel to bounded cost estimates (proposed EUR 0–100M) backed by ESA findings and seller/public indemnity agreements; audit the register quarterly for consistency with permit-application assumptions.
  • Topology decision gate audit at Month 4 (2027-02-17): conduct an independent verification that the topology decision (single square versus split campus) is based on documented evidence (land optioning status ≥70%, RTE written letter for ≥1 GW received, or neither), that the decision is recorded in writing with supporting rationale, and that any divergence from the proposed decision framework (e.g., proceeding with single square without RTE letter) is flagged to the investment committee with risk acknowledgment.
  • Post-gate financial and scheduling impact review at Phase 0 closure (Month 12 = 2027-10-17) and Phase 1 FID (Month 12–13 = 2027-10-17 to 2027-11-17): audit all Phase 0 gate outcomes (RTE connection offer, land assembly, tenant commitments, debt terms, permitting file status, ANSSI clearance pathway) against pre-agreed thresholds, quantify any shortfall (e.g., anchors 20% instead of 30%) and its impact on Phase 1 viability (debt capacity, lease revenue, energization timeline), and formally recommend to the investment committee whether Phase 1 should proceed, be downsized, be deferred, or be cancelled.

Audit - Transparency Measures

  • Monthly investment committee pass/fail and dissent disclosure: publish a monthly summary (public or to lenders/co-investors) documenting progress on the five Phase 0 gates (grid, land, tenants, financing, social license), marking each gate as 'on track', 'at risk' or 'failed'. Require the committee to publish dissenting opinions and minority votes, so lenders and co-investors can see when there is disagreement on gate status or Phase 1 FID recommendation.
  • Quarterly published red-team audit reports: commission an independent red team (Months 1–12 = 2026-11-17 to 2027-10-17) to issue standalone pass/fail opinions on each gate at Months 3, 6, 9 and 12 (2027-01-17, 2027-04-17, 2027-07-17, 2027-10-17), with no edit or veto by the development sponsor. Publish the reports (in redacted form as needed for confidential negotiations) to lenders and co-investors within 10 working days of issue.
  • RTE hosting-capacity letter and grid audit publication: publish a summary of RTE's preliminary feasibility assessment and final connection offer (if received by Phase 0 gate) to lenders and major stakeholders, indicating the committed MW, connection timeline, curtailment terms and estimated reinforcement cost. Publish a third-party grid engineer's audit report verifying the RTE assessment by Month 9 (2027-07-17).
  • Anchor-tenant commitment register with credit-rating and execution dates: maintain a public or lender-only register of all tenant engagements, showing (i) counterparty name, (ii) LOI or term-sheet signature date, (iii) binding status (Y/N), (iv) capacity reserved (MW), (v) credit rating or parent-guarantee status, (vi) lease term and price, and (vii) reservation-fee payment date and amount. Update quarterly and disclose the register to debt providers.
  • Permitting file and environmental baseline public posting: publish the permit application file(s) (ICPE, environmental authorization, EIA dossier) on the project website or a designated public portal as soon as filed (proposed Months 8–9 = 2027-06-17 to 2027-07-17), including the Phase I/II environmental site assessments, hydrological studies, biodiversity surveys, and remediation plans. Maintain an updated register of regulatory authority decisions and comments with resolution timelines.
  • Community engagement and public consultation minutes: publish all meeting minutes and feedback from the municipal liaison committee, public consultation, and any formal local hearings within 15 working days. Disclose the draft and final community-benefit agreement and any material changes in response to public input, along with cost estimates and funding commitments per Phase 1 and Phase 2.

Internal Governance Bodies

1. Project Steering Committee

Rationale for Inclusion: The 9 GW, 161 km², €750M Phase 0 budget is a strategic infrastructure venture with multi-billion euro Phase 1 exposure and extreme feasibility uncertainty. The sponsor, consortium co-investors, and debt/equity sources require a body that sets strategic direction, approves milestone decisions (topology, anchor-tenant strategy, permitting approach), and owns the Phase 0/Phase 1 FID recommendation. This committee harmonizes sponsor intent with co-investor expectations and coordinates responses to RTE, EDF, ANSSI and local authorities.

Responsibilities:

  • Approve Phase 0 strategy, milestone roadmap and tranche-drawdown schedules within the EUR 750M cap
  • Oversee topology decision at Month 4 (2027-02-17): single square vs. split campus
  • Review and approve anchor-tenant sourcing strategy and lease-term frameworks
  • Approve power-procurement strategy and EDF/RTE engagement approach
  • Monitor co-investor alignment and resolve conflicts between sponsor and consortium expectations
  • Recommend Phase 1 FID approval or deferral/downsizing at Month 12 (2027-10-17) gate

Initial Setup Actions:

  • Establish committee charter at Month 1 (2026-11-17) defining roles, decision rules, and escalation protocol
  • Assign sponsor CEO/CFO, infrastructure-fund lead, and at least one independent external director
  • Set three-way decision rule: sponsor, consortium co-investor and independent director must all approve Phase 1 FID
  • Publish committee composition and voting rules to lenders and equity sources by Month 1 (2026-11-17)
  • Establish quarterly meeting cadence with standing agenda items: gate status, risk register, sunk-cost assessment
  • Commission external red team to provide independent pass/fail opinions before each milestone vote

Membership:

  • Sponsor hyperscale-developer CEO and CFO
  • Infrastructure-fund consortium representative (capital and governance authority)
  • Independent external director (infrastructure or energy sector, no financial ties to sponsor or consortium)
  • Lender representative (observer, non-voting, to track debt covenants and Phase 1 financing triggers)
  • Project Director (voting, operational accountability)

Decision Rights: The committee approves all strategic decisions above EUR 50M spend (Phase 0 tranches and gate recommendations), topology choice, tenant acquisition targets, power and grid strategies, and Phase 1 FID. Below EUR 50M operational decisions delegate to the PMO. The committee's Phase 1 FID recommendation is binding if supported by 2 of 3 core votes (sponsor, consortium, independent director); if split 1–2, the decision escalates to a supermajority vote of all members.

Decision Mechanism: Decisions by majority vote (3 of 5 members minimum), with sponsor, consortium and independent director each holding one bloc vote. Phase 1 FID requires explicit two-of-three alignment among sponsor, consortium and independent director. Tie-breaker: independent director casts the deciding vote; dissent recorded and published to lenders. Monthly red-team pass/fail opinions inform but do not override committee votes.

Meeting Cadence: Monthly (Months 0–12 = 2026-10-17 to 2027-10-17) for Phase 0, with standing agenda: gate-criterion status, tranche drawdown authorization, risk escalations, red-team findings, external-authority responses (RTE, DREAL, ANSSI, EDF). Ad-hoc meetings if a gate criterion is breached or sunk-cost pressure emerges.

Typical Agenda Items:

  • RTE, EDF, ANSSI and DREAL engagement status (written evidence, preliminary opinions, timeline slippage)
  • Land assembly and topology validation (% parcel optioned, Phase II survey findings, holdout issues)
  • Anchor-tenant pipeline status (LOI vs. binding term-sheet progress, credit validation, reservation-fee timing)
  • Phase 0 spend reconciliation and tranche-drawdown authorization (actual vs. budget, next-tranche triggers)
  • Risk register update (grid, land, tenants, permitting, financing, social license) and mitigation actions
  • Red-team independent pass/fail opinions and committee response or dissent

Escalation Path: Phase 1 FID recommendation (approve, defer, downsize or cancel) escalates to the sponsor board and consortium investment committee if the Steering Committee is split or if a gate threshold is unmet. Kill criteria for Phase 1 cancellation or downsizing are formally triggered by the Gate Review and Kill Authority Committee (see below); the Steering Committee must respect those triggers unless overridden by supermajority sponsor/consortium vote with documented dissent to lenders.

2. Project Management Office (PMO)

Rationale for Inclusion: Phase 0 spans 12 months across grid, land, permitting, environmental, security, tenant and financing workstreams, with tight interdependencies and external milestones (RTE, DREAL, ANSSI). A dedicated PMO is essential to track parallel workstreams, manage deliverable timelines, reconcile Phase 0 spend against the EUR 750M cap, and escalate gate-critical risks. The PMO is operationally accountable for Phase 0 execution and reportable to the Steering Committee monthly.

Responsibilities:

  • Manage Phase 0 workstreams: grid (RTE engagement), land (options, surveys), permitting (file prep), tenants (sourcing, term sheets), financing (lender criteria), security (ANSSI dialogue), community (liaison, consultation)
  • Reconcile Phase 0 spend monthly against four milestone tranches (EUR 150M, 250M, 200M, 150M) and seek tranche authorization from the Steering Committee
  • Track external-authority milestones (RTE letter, DREAL opinion, ANSSI confirmation, EDF LOI) and escalate slippages
  • Execute Phase I/II environmental and contamination surveys, fiber audits, thermal modelling and RTE hosting-capacity audit
  • Maintain risk register (23 identified risks plus emergent risks) and escalate high-likelihood, high-severity risks to the Steering Committee
  • Coordinate Phase 0 deliverables: topology decision document (Month 4 = 2027-02-17), permitting file (Months 8–9 = 2027-06-17 to 2027-07-17), anchor-tenant term sheets (Month 9 = 2027-07-17), Phase 0 gate summary (Month 12 = 2027-10-17)

Initial Setup Actions:

  • Establish PMO with at least 40–60 FTE core team (estimate) across grid, land, permitting, environmental, tenant and finance workstreams by Month 0 (2026-10-17)
  • Commission specialist advisers: RTE hosting-capacity auditor, hydrologist, ecologist, ICPE counsel, land assembly, security liaison
  • Establish regional offices in Cambrai and Dunkirk for land, permitting and community engagement
  • Develop detailed Phase 0 workplan with weekly milestone tracking and monthly reporting to the Steering Committee
  • Establish a risk-register review cadence (monthly) and escalation protocol to the Steering Committee for risks scoring above a threshold (e.g., High likelihood + High severity)
  • Create a financial tracking system reconciling Phase 0 spend by workstream and tranche, with monthly variance reporting

Membership:

  • Project Director (overall accountability)
  • Grid and Power Lead (RTE engagement, hosting-capacity strategy, EDF coordination)
  • Land Assembly Lead (parcel acquisition, option agreements, brownfield surveys)
  • Permitting and Environmental Lead (ICPE, EIA, DREAL dialogue, ecological master plan)
  • Tenant and Revenue Lead (anchor-tenant sourcing, term-sheet negotiation, lease economics)
  • Finance and Lender Relations Lead (debt-financing criteria, Phase 0 drawdown management, cost reconciliation)
  • Security and National-Security Lead (ANSSI/DGSI dialogue, security governance framework)
  • Community and Stakeholder Lead (municipal liaison, public consultation, community-benefit agreement)
  • PMO Controller (spend reconciliation, milestone tracking, variance analysis)

Decision Rights: PMO approves operational decisions within Phase 0 tranche budgets (EUR 50M monthly run-rate, estimate). Workstream leads make day-to-day procurement and engagement decisions. Decisions exceeding EUR 50M spend, involving strategic trade-offs (e.g., split-campus pivot, tenant-acquisition priority shift), or affecting gate milestones escalate to the Steering Committee. All external-authority responses (RTE, DREAL, ANSSI, EDF) are classified as gate-critical and immediately escalated if they change feasibility assumptions.

Decision Mechanism: PMO Lead (Project Director) approves sub-EUR 50M decisions by workstream-lead consensus. Decisions involving workstream conflicts (e.g., land-assembly cost vs. timeline, permitting file scope vs. environmental scope) are escalated to the Steering Committee. Monthly PMO leadership review (all leads) validates milestone status and flags risks. Red-team opinions are reviewed monthly and factored into decision rationale.

Meeting Cadence: Weekly internal PMO standup (all leads, 1 hour) to track workstream progress and remove blockers. Monthly PMO review with external advisers (grid auditor, environmental counsel, security liaison) to validate milestone deliverables. Monthly steering-committee report (formal presentation to the Steering Committee).

Typical Agenda Items:

  • RTE, EDF, DREAL and ANSSI engagement milestones and timeline slippages (e.g., RTE letter due Month 6 = 2027-04-17, any delays flagged)
  • Land assembly: % parcel optioned, Phase II survey progress, holdouts or legal challenges, remediation-liability findings
  • Tenant pipeline: LOI vs. binding term-sheet conversions, credit validation, reservation-fee payment schedules
  • Phase 0 spend reconciliation: actual vs. planned by tranche, next-tranche authorization request to Steering Committee
  • Permitting file status: draft completion, content issues, filing date (targeted Months 8–9 = 2027-06-17 to 2027-07-17)
  • Risk register: new risks, escalations, mitigation actions, red-team findings

Escalation Path: Gate-critical risks (e.g., RTE denial of 500 MW hosting capacity, inability to option 70% of parcel, no anchor tenants by Month 9 = 2027-07-17) escalate immediately to the Steering Committee and the Gate Review and Kill Authority Committee. PMO operational decisions involving workstream conflicts or cost trade-offs escalate to the Project Director, then to the Steering Committee if unresolved. External-authority responses that change feasibility assumptions trigger a formal gate-status review within 1 week.

3. Gate Review and Kill Authority Committee

Rationale for Inclusion: The plan explicitly states that kill criteria and downsizing are legitimate outcomes, and that sunk-cost pressure typically overrides stated gate thresholds unless kill authority is vested in a body independent of the development team. This committee is chartered to enforce numeric kill thresholds—grid hosting capacity ≥1 GW (cumulative), land assembly ≥70%, anchor-tenant take-or-pay ≥30% by Month 9 (2027-07-17), debt financing ≥EUR 3B, and social license (2 of 3 municipalities). If any threshold fails by the deadline, this committee triggers a formal gate review and recommends cancellation, downsizing, deferral or split-campus pivot, with decisions published to lenders and co-investors.

Responsibilities:

  • Enforce numeric Phase 0 gate thresholds (grid ≥1 GW, land ≥70%, tenants ≥30% by Month 9 = 2027-07-17, debt ≥EUR 3B, social license ≥2 municipalities) at the Month 12 (2027-10-17) Phase 0 gate
  • Review RTE preliminary feasibility letter (or lack thereof) at Month 6 (2027-04-17) and determine whether the grid gate is on track; if not in hand, assess split-campus viability
  • Review Phase II environmental and Phase I ESA findings at Month 3 (2027-01-17) to validate land-assembly feasibility; if remediation costs exceed EUR 100M per site or contamination blocks parcels, recommend site substitution or split campus
  • Review anchor-tenant pipeline at Month 9 (2027-07-17): quantify signed take-or-pay vs. LOI, credit validation, confirm ≥30% binding commitments; if <30%, trigger Phase 1 downsizing to 250–500 MW
  • Publish monthly red-team audit opinions (independent consultants), documenting pass/fail on each gate criterion; dissent from development team opinions recorded and disclosed
  • Recommend Phase 1 FID approval, conditional approval with specific conditions, deferral pending gate resolution, downsizing, or cancellation; recommendation is binding unless overridden by supermajority Steering Committee vote with dissent published

Initial Setup Actions:

  • Charter the committee at Month 1 (2026-11-17) with composition: at least 2 independent external directors (no financial ties to sponsor or consortium), 1 lender representative, 1 infrastructure-sector expert
  • Commission an independent red team (EUR 2M–5M) to deliver monthly pass/fail opinions on each of five gate criteria (grid, land, tenants, financing, social license) from Month 1 (2026-11-17) through Month 12 (2027-10-17)
  • Fix numeric kill thresholds in writing by Month 2 (2026-12-17): grid ≥1 GW cumulative (or ≥500 MW single node + credible path to 1 GW), land ≥70% optioned at <15% above benchmark, tenants ≥30% (≥300 MW on 1 GW base, ≥150 MW on 500 MW base) signed by Month 9 (2027-07-17), debt ≥EUR 3B committed, social license ≥2 of 3 municipalities, all published to lenders
  • Establish meeting and decision protocol: monthly red-team report review + quarterly gate-status assessment (Months 3, 6, 9, 12 = 2027-01-17, 2027-04-17, 2027-07-17, 2027-10-17)
  • Define escalation protocol: if any gate threshold is breached, committee has 10 working days to issue a formal gate-status report and recommendation; recommendation is binding on the Steering Committee unless overridden by supermajority vote (2 of 3: sponsor, consortium, independent director) with full dissent disclosure
  • Appoint a dedicated chair (independent external director) with authority to call unscheduled gate reviews if red-team findings indicate threshold breach

Membership:

  • Independent External Chair (infrastructure, energy or finance sector, no affiliation with sponsor, consortium or lenders; appointed by mutual consent of sponsor and consortium at Month 1 = 2026-11-17)
  • Independent External Director 2 (technical or environmental expertise; project feasibility validation)
  • Lender Representative (debt-financing criteria and Phase 1 FID conditions, non-voting but advisory input)
  • Infrastructure-Sector Expert (independent adviser on grid, power and major-project feasibility; non-voting but provides technical opinion on RTE and EDF outcomes)
  • External Red Team Lead (independent consultant, monthly pass/fail reports, no voting role but directly inputs to committee deliberation)

Decision Rights: The committee's scope is confined to gate-threshold validation and kill/downsize/defer recommendations. It does not approve strategy (delegated to Steering Committee) or direct operations (delegated to PMO). The committee's recommendations are binding on the Steering Committee unless the Steering Committee explicitly overrides by supermajority vote (2 of 3: sponsor, consortium, independent director) with recorded dissent and public disclosure to lenders within 5 working days. If the committee recommends cancellation and the Steering Committee overrides, the override decision and dissent are disclosed to all debt and equity sources.

Decision Mechanism: Consensus where possible. If disagreement arises on gate-threshold achievement (e.g., whether a preliminary RTE letter satisfies the grid gate or whether provisional anchors qualify as 'signed'), the committee documents both positions and escalates to the Steering Committee with a recommendation of which position is more credible. Tie-breaker: the independent chair casts the deciding opinion. Red-team pass/fail opinions are advisory input, not votes.

Meeting Cadence: Monthly gate-status review (1st working day of each month, Months 1–12 = 2026-11-17 to 2027-10-17) of red-team reports and PMO milestone updates. Formal gate-assessment meetings at Months 3, 6, 9 and 12 (2027-01-17, 2027-04-17, 2027-07-17, 2027-10-17) to validate threshold achievement and issue gate-status reports to the Steering Committee and lenders.

Typical Agenda Items:

  • Red-team monthly pass/fail opinion on each of five gate criteria: grid (RTE letter received? timing on track?), land (% optioned, remediation findings), tenants (LOI vs. binding breakdown, credit validation), financing (debt commitment status, pricing acceptable?), social license (municipal letters of support in hand?)
  • External-authority milestone tracking: RTE letter (due Month 6 = 2027-04-17), DREAL opinion (due Month 9 = 2027-07-17), ANSSI confirmation (due Month 12 = 2027-10-17), EDF LOI (due Month 6 = 2027-04-17, term sheet Month 9 = 2027-07-17)
  • Phase II environmental and contamination survey findings: any sites ruled out, remediation costs exceeding EUR 100M per site, holdout issues affecting ≥30% of target parcel
  • Anchor-tenant term-sheet status: number of signed agreements, total MW, credit ratings, reservation-fee payment receipts; conversion of LOIs to binding documents
  • Debt-financing status: lender interest, term-sheet negotiations, required gate achievements for debt final commitment
  • Community-engagement and municipal-support status: liaison-committee minutes, consultation feedback, municipal letters of support in hand or on schedule

Escalation Path: If the committee determines that a gate threshold is breached (e.g., RTE letter not received by Month 6 = 2027-04-17, land optioning <70% by Month 4 = 2027-02-17, tenants <30% signed by Month 9 = 2027-07-17, debt commitment not in hand by Month 12 = 2027-10-17), the committee issues a formal gate-status report within 5 working days and recommends one of: (i) Phase 1 proceeds (all thresholds met), (ii) Phase 1 conditional approval pending specific condition (e.g., RTE letter expected by Month 18 = 2028-04-17), (iii) Phase 1 downsized (e.g., 250 MW instead of 500 MW if tenants <30%), (iv) Phase 1 deferred (6–12 months pending gate resolution), or (v) Phase 0 completion with no Phase 1 FID (project paused or cancelled). The Steering Committee may override the committee's recommendation by supermajority vote with full dissent recording and disclosure to lenders. If lenders or co-investors invoke debt covenants or capital-call conditions triggered by a failed gate, the Kill Authority Committee's recommendation is published to those parties within 2 working days of issue.

4. Compliance, Environmental & Social License Committee

Rationale for Inclusion: The project faces complex, interconnected constraints: ICPE and environmental authorization (18–30 months + 24–48 months appeal risk), ANSSI/DGSI national-security review (6–12 months, uncontrolled), GDPR and data-residency compliance (foreign co-investor, sovereign tenants, AI workloads), ecological compensation (net-biodiversity, farmland displacement of 10,000+ ha, estimated EUR 200M–500M cost), water-resource constraints (closed-loop cooling required, water-authority approval), brownfield remediation (legacy contamination EUR 0–100M+ per site, liability allocation disputes), and community social license (municipal support, farm-sector engagement, public consultation). No single person can credibly oversee all five domains (permitting, security, ecology, water, community). A dedicated committee ensures compliance risks do not fall between workstreams and that gate-critical environmental and social-license conditions are not overlooked in pursuit of schedule or cost targets.

Responsibilities:

  • Oversee ICPE and environmental authorization process, including EIA scope, file content, DREAL engagement, permit conditions and post-permit compliance monitoring
  • Manage national-security review (ANSSI, DGSI) including confidential security governance framework, tenant-vetting criteria, data-residency policies, and alignment with foreign-co-investor requirements
  • Ensure GDPR compliance for data processing at multi-tenant data center; define data-residency and sovereignty requirements with legal counsel and authorities
  • Implement ecological master plan (submitted Month 6 = 2027-04-17), manage biodiversity offsetting and compensation, coordinate with environmental NGOs and conservation authorities on net-biodiversity targets
  • Manage water-resource compliance: secure written water-authority opinion on closed-loop cooling feasibility (due Month 6 = 2027-04-17), track permitting conditions tied to water use, monitor groundwater contamination from brownfield sites
  • Oversee brownfield remediation and contamination liability: track Phase I/II ESA findings, bound liability per parcel, negotiate seller indemnities and public-remediation arrangements, escalate unexpected contamination discoveries
  • Lead community engagement and social-license strategy: establish municipal liaison committee, run early voluntary consultation (Months 1–3 = 2026-11-17 to 2027-01-17), draft and negotiate community-benefit agreement (EUR 50M–150M, due Month 6 = 2027-04-17), track farm-sector and NGO opposition, escalate legal-challenge risk
  • Coordinate integration of compliance requirements into Phase 1 permitting conditions and Phase 1 capex budget (e.g., ecological compensation cost, security hardening cost, community-benefit spend)

Initial Setup Actions:

  • Charter the committee at Month 1 (2026-11-17) with roles: ICPE/Environmental Lead, National-Security and GDPR Counsel, Ecology and Biodiversity Manager, Water Resources Manager, Community and Stakeholder Lead
  • Engage specialized counsel: ICPE expert, environmental and EIA counsel, ANSSI/security law specialist, GDPR and data-protection counsel, environmental NGO liaison, water-law specialist, land and remediation counsel
  • Commission Phase I (desktop) environmental site assessments on all candidate parcels by Month 1 (2026-11-17)
  • Commission Phase II intrusive surveys (soil, groundwater, asbestos) on top 2–3 sites per zone by Month 3 (2027-01-17), EST 1.5M–3M per zone
  • Establish ICPE and environmental file content roadmap (Month 1 = 2026-11-17): identify required studies, expert reports, baseline data, modeling and conditions
  • Initiate DREAL and prefecture pre-submission dialogue (Month 0–1 = 2026-10-17 to 2026-11-17): outline project scope, receive preliminary guidance on permit pathway, ICPE classification and fast-track status (if any)
  • Establish confidential ANSSI pre-submission engagement (Month 0–1 = 2026-10-17 to 2026-11-17): present security governance framework, understand anticipated review scope, timeline and authorities' concerns
  • Commission hydrological study and water-authority consultation (Months 1–4 = 2026-11-17 to 2027-02-17): validate closed-loop cooling feasibility, obtain water-authority preliminary opinion by Month 6 (2027-04-17)
  • Establish municipal liaison committee (Month 2 = 2026-12-17): invite mayors and representatives from at least 3 most-affected municipalities; establish monthly dialogue protocol and published meeting minutes
  • Develop draft community-benefit agreement (Months 2–4 = 2026-12-17 to 2027-02-17) covering labor, training, ecological restoration, farm relocation, and local infrastructure; bind terms by Month 6 (2027-04-17)

Membership:

  • Compliance and Regulatory Lead (overall committee accountability, ICPE and permitting authority interface)
  • National-Security and GDPR Counsel (ANSSI/DGSI liaison, security governance, data-residency requirements, foreign-co-investor compliance)
  • Ecology and Biodiversity Manager (environmental baseline, EIA content, biodiversity offsetting, NGO coordination)
  • Water Resources Manager (hydrological assessment, water-authority liaison, cooling-feasibility validation, groundwater contamination tracking)
  • Community and Stakeholder Engagement Lead (municipal liaison, public consultation, community-benefit agreement, farm-sector engagement, opposition escalation)
  • Brownfield and Remediation Counsel (Phase I/II ESA management, liability allocation, seller/public indemnities, contamination-discovery protocol)

Decision Rights: The committee advises the Steering Committee and PMO on compliance and social-license requirements, and makes day-to-day decisions on engagement with authorities, environmental consultants, municipalities and communities within the framework established by the Steering Committee. The committee has veto authority over permit-file content if it believes a proposed approach creates unacceptable legal or reputational risk; such vetoes escalate to the Steering Committee. Community-benefit agreement terms up to EUR 50M in Phase 0 pre-commitment are approved by the committee in consultation with the Steering Committee; terms above EUR 50M or with material operational implications escalate to the Steering Committee for approval.

Decision Mechanism: Decisions within the committee by consensus among the six leads. If disagreement arises (e.g., whether to pursue fast-track permitting vs. standard ICPE, whether to offer a municipal veto on certain design elements), the committee documents both positions and escalates to the Steering Committee or PMO for decision. Authority over community-benefit terms up to EUR 20M per tranche is delegated to the Stakeholder Lead in consultation with the Regulatory Lead; above EUR 20M, committee consensus is required.

Meeting Cadence: Bi-weekly workstream coordination (each lead with their specialists and external advisers) to track permitting, environmental, security and community milestones. Monthly full-committee meetings (all six leads) to integrate findings across domains and escalate material risks or changes to the Steering Committee. Ad-hoc meetings if authorities issue new guidance, legal challenges are filed, or community opposition escalates.

Typical Agenda Items:

  • ICPE and environmental authorization: file-content draft status, expert reports completion timeline, DREAL feedback, permit-application date (targeted Months 8–9 = 2027-06-17 to 2027-07-17)
  • National-security review: ANSSI pre-submission feedback (Month 6 = 2027-04-17 target), security governance framework refinement, tenant-vetting and data-residency policy drafting, anticipated formal-review start date
  • Ecological master plan: EIA scope (habitat types, species surveys), biodiversity-impact model, compensation measures (on-site and off-site), NGO consultation feedback, DREAL opinion timeline (due Month 9 = 2027-07-17)
  • Water and cooling: hydrological baseline findings, dry-cooler modelling at 35°C design day, water-authority preliminary opinion status (due Month 6 = 2027-04-17), any grounds for regulatory water-use restrictions
  • Brownfield and contamination: Phase I ESA findings, Phase II survey progress, remediation-liability estimates per parcel, site-shortlist refinement, indemnity negotiations with sellers or public authorities
  • Community engagement and social license: municipal liaison-committee meeting minutes (published), public consultation feedback, draft community-benefit agreement, farm-sector union engagement, opposition tracking and escalation
  • Permit-check at Month 18 (2028-04-17): assessment of whether initial ICPE and EIA decisions are on schedule for approval by target window (Months 26–39 = 2028-12-17 to 2030-01-17); if slippage is material (>6 months), recommend Phase 1 FID contingency

Escalation Path: Material compliance risks (e.g., ANSSI blocks the project pending data-residency restructuring, DREAL requires additional ecological compensation exceeding EUR 300M, communities block permits, water authority denies cooling feasibility) escalate to the Steering Committee within 5 working days of identification. Contamination discoveries exceeding the bounded remediation threshold (EUR 100M per site) trigger immediate PMO and Steering Committee escalation. Legal challenges to permits that could extend timelines beyond Month 26 (2028-12-17) are escalated to gate-review assessment. ANSSI findings that restrict foreign tenants or co-investor involvement are escalated immediately to the Steering Committee, as they may affect tenant strategy and financing. Community opposition that reaches organized legal challenge or formal municipal objection escalates to the Steering Committee as a social-license gate threat.

Governance Implementation Plan

1. Project Sponsor formally authorizes Phase 0 governance structure and delegates authority for committee establishment to the Project Director. Sponsor issues a written mandate defining the scope of Phase 0 (Months 0–12 = 2026-10-17 to 2027-10-17), the EUR 750M cap, the four governance bodies, and the decision-making framework. This authorization establishes the legal and organizational foundation for all subsequent governance activities.

Responsible Body/Role: Project Sponsor (or Senior Steering Body Pre-Governance)

Suggested Timeframe: Month 0 (2026-10-17), within 1 week of project kickoff

Key Outputs/Deliverables:

  • Signed Project Authorization Mandate
  • Phase 0 Scope and Budget (EUR 750M cap, four tranches, no committed capital before gate)
  • Governance Structure Charter (four bodies, roles, responsibilities)
  • Delegation of Authority to Project Director for Committee Setup

Dependencies:

  • Project sponsor board approval
  • Infrastructure-fund consortium alignment on governance framework
  • Co-investor agreement to the governance model

2. Project Director establishes the Project Steering Committee Charter and identifies initial membership. The charter documents: composition (Sponsor CEO/CFO, Consortium Lead, at least one Independent External Director, Lender Observer, Project Director); voting rules (3-of-5 majority for most decisions, 2-of-3 alignment requirement for Phase 1 FID); decision thresholds (EUR 50M and above escalate); meeting cadence (monthly); and escalation protocol. The Project Director solicits and formalizes commitments from all five designated members.

Responsible Body/Role: Project Director (in consultation with Sponsor and Consortium)

Suggested Timeframe: Month 1 (2026-11-17), within 2 weeks of project authorization

Key Outputs/Deliverables:

  • Project Steering Committee Charter (signed by all five members)
  • Committee composition and member role descriptions
  • Voting and decision-making rules (3-of-5 majority, 2-of-3 FID alignment, EUR 50M threshold)
  • Quarterly and monthly meeting schedules
  • Escalation protocol and dissent recording procedures

Dependencies:

  • Project Authorization Mandate (step 1)
  • Identification and agreement of Independent External Director (no financial ties)
  • Lender and consortium appointments confirmed

3. Project Steering Committee holds its first kick-off meeting. The committee reviews the Phase 0 roadmap, confirms the four governance bodies and their responsibilities, validates the EUR 750M four-tranche budget structure (EUR 150M / 250M / 200M / 150M), and assigns the Project Director responsibility for Phase 0 execution. The committee establishes its monthly meeting agenda template and approves the engagement approach for external authorities (RTE, EDF, DREAL, ANSSI).

Responsible Body/Role: Project Steering Committee

Suggested Timeframe: Month 1 (2026-11-17), within 1 week of charter signature

Key Outputs/Deliverables:

  • Steering Committee Kick-Off Meeting Minutes
  • Approved Phase 0 Roadmap and Milestone Schedule
  • Confirmed governance-body roles and responsibilities
  • Monthly agenda template and decision-preparation procedures
  • First Tranche Authorization (EUR 150M Months 0–2 = 2026-10-17 to 2026-12-17)

Dependencies:

  • Project Steering Committee Charter signed (step 2)

4. Project Director establishes the Gate Review and Kill Authority Committee. The Project Director recruits and formally appoints: at least 2 Independent External Directors (infrastructure or energy expertise, no financial ties to sponsor or consortium), 1 Lender Representative (non-voting, advisory), and 1 Infrastructure-Sector Expert (non-voting). The Project Director commissions an external red team (proposed EUR 2M–5M budget) to deliver independent monthly pass/fail opinions on the five gate criteria (grid, land, tenants, financing, social license). The committee chair is appointed by mutual consent of sponsor and consortium.

Responsible Body/Role: Project Director (in consultation with Sponsor, Consortium and Steering Committee)

Suggested Timeframe: Month 1 (2026-11-17), within 2–3 weeks of kickoff

Key Outputs/Deliverables:

  • Gate Review and Kill Authority Committee Charter (signed)
  • Committee composition and member roles
  • External red team engagement letter and scope (monthly pass/fail reports)
  • Committee chair appointment letter
  • Draft numeric kill thresholds (to be finalized at step 6)

Dependencies:

  • Project Authorization Mandate (step 1)
  • Steering Committee First Meeting completed (step 3)
  • Budget allocation for red team (EUR 2M–5M from Phase 0 tranche 1)

5. Project Director establishes the Compliance, Environmental & Social License Committee. The Project Director recruits and appoints six functional leads: ICPE/Environmental Lead, National-Security and GDPR Counsel, Ecology and Biodiversity Manager, Water Resources Manager, Community and Stakeholder Lead, and Brownfield and Remediation Counsel. Each lead is tasked with commissioning Phase I environmental site assessments (desktop) on all candidate parcels, initiating formal pre-submission dialogues with DREAL and ANSSI, and establishing the municipal liaison committee. The PMO Controller reports monthly to this committee on compliance-workstream spend and deliverable status.

Responsible Body/Role: Project Director (in consultation with Steering Committee PMO Lead)

Suggested Timeframe: Month 1 (2026-11-17), within 2–3 weeks of kickoff

Key Outputs/Deliverables:

  • Compliance, Environmental & Social License Committee Charter (signed)
  • Six functional-lead role descriptions and contact persons
  • Engagement letters with ICPE counsel, environmental counsel, ANSSI/security counsel, GDPR counsel, land counsel
  • Phase I ESA commission instructions (all candidate parcels) by end of Month 1 (2026-11-17)
  • Pre-submission dialogue openings with DREAL, ANSSI, prefecture by Month 0–1 (2026-10-17 to 2026-11-17)

Dependencies:

  • Project Authorization Mandate (step 1)
  • Steering Committee First Meeting (step 3)
  • Budget allocation for compliance-workstream specialists and Phase I surveys

6. Gate Review and Kill Authority Committee formally fixes numeric kill thresholds in writing and publishes them to lenders, co-investors and the Steering Committee. Thresholds are: (i) RTE grid hosting capacity at least 500 MW within 36 months (first written evidence due Month 6 = 2027-04-17); (ii) at least 70% of chosen topology's target parcel optioned non-coercively at no more than 15% above benchmark land value; (iii) signed anchor-tenant take-or-pay agreements for at least 30% of Phase 1 size by Month 9 (2027-07-17); (iv) firm debt commitment of at least EUR 3B with acceptable terms by Month 12 (2027-10-17); (v) written support from at least 2 of 3 most-affected municipalities by Month 12 (2027-10-17). The committee also publishes the decision protocol: if any threshold is breached by its deadline, the committee issues a formal gate-status report within 5 working days and recommends phase advance, conditional approval, downsizing, deferral or cancellation.

Responsible Body/Role: Gate Review and Kill Authority Committee (chaired by Independent External Director)

Suggested Timeframe: Month 2 (2026-12-17), by end of Month 2 (2026-12-17)

Key Outputs/Deliverables:

  • Published Numeric Kill Thresholds Document (signed by committee chair and all members)
  • Gate Criterion Definitions: grid (RTE letter by Month 6 = 2027-04-17), land (70% by Month 4 = 2027-02-17), tenants (30% signed by Month 9 = 2027-07-17), debt (EUR 3B by Month 12 = 2027-10-17), social license (2 municipalities by Month 12 = 2027-10-17)
  • Decision protocol and gate-status-report template
  • Distribution list for dissemination to lenders, co-investors, Steering Committee
  • Red team engagement and first pass/fail report instructions

Dependencies:

  • Gate Review and Kill Authority Committee Charter signed (step 4)
  • Committee chair appointed
  • Steering Committee aware of and endorses thresholds

7. Project Management Office (PMO) is established and staffed with a core team of 40–60 people across eight functional workstreams: Grid and Power, Land Assembly, Permitting and Environmental, Tenancy and Revenue, Finance and Lender Relations, Security and National-Security, Community and Stakeholder, and PMO Administration (Controller). Each workstream lead is assigned and given a Phase 0 detailed plan (deliverables, timelines, success criteria, escalation triggers). The PMO establishes weekly standup meetings (all leads), monthly full-team reviews, and a risk-register maintenance process. Regional offices are established in Cambrai and Dunkirk.

Responsible Body/Role: Project Director (appoints PMO Lead/Project Manager)

Suggested Timeframe: Month 1 (2026-11-17), within 3 weeks of authorization

Key Outputs/Deliverables:

  • PMO Charter and organization structure (8 workstreams, 40–60 FTE core team)
  • Workstream lead job descriptions and accountability
  • Detailed Phase 0 workplan by workstream (timelines, deliverables, success criteria)
  • Risk register template and maintenance protocol (monthly updates, escalations for High+High risks)
  • Weekly standup and monthly review meeting schedules
  • Regional office setup plan (Cambrai and Dunkirk address, staff, office equipment)

Dependencies:

  • Project Authorization Mandate (step 1)
  • Steering Committee charter signed (step 2)
  • Project Director appointed
  • Budget authority for 40–60 FTE salaries and regional offices

8. PMO commissions specialized advisers and survey firms across critical Phase 0 workstreams: (i) RTE hosting-capacity auditor (independent third-party), (ii) hydrologist and water-resource consultant, (iii) environmental and EIA counsel, (iv) ICPE specialist, (v) land-assembly and real-estate counsel, (vi) Phase I/II ESA and contamination surveyors (one team per geographic zone: Cambrai, Dunkirk, Valenciennes, Saint-Omer), (vii) security and ANSSI liaison counsel, (viii) fiber-route auditor (telecom specialist). Each adviser is tasked with delivering specific Phase 0 gate-critical outputs by agreed deadlines (e.g., RTE audit by Month 9 = 2027-07-17, Phase II surveys by Month 3 = 2027-01-17).

Responsible Body/Role: PMO Lead (Project Director) and Workstream Leads

Suggested Timeframe: Month 1 (2026-11-17), engagement letters issued by end of Month 1 (2026-11-17)

Key Outputs/Deliverables:

  • Signed engagement letters with each adviser/surveyor
  • Scope of work and deliverable specifications for each adviser
  • Budget allocation and fee schedules
  • Timeline alignment with Phase 0 gate milestones (Month 4, 6, 9, 12 = 2027-02-17, 2027-04-17, 2027-07-17, 2027-10-17)
  • Contact and escalation protocols (who reports to whom, monthly status meetings)

Dependencies:

  • PMO established and workstream leads appointed (step 7)
  • Budget approved for specialist advisers (Phase 0 tranche 1, EUR 150M)

9. PMO initiates formal pre-submission dialogue with external authorities: RTE (grid hosting-capacity assessment, connection-offer timeline, tranche availability), DREAL and prefecture (permit pathway, ICPE classification, environmental-authorization scope, fast-track status if any), ANSSI and DGSI (national-security review scope, timeline, data-residency and foreign-investment scrutiny, security-governance expectations). All dialogue is documented in writing; responses are classified as gate-critical. A formal written request is sent to each authority by Month 0–1 (2026-10-17 to 2026-11-17), with follow-up meetings scheduled by Month 2 (2026-12-17).

Responsible Body/Role: PMO Leads: Grid and Power (RTE), Permitting and Environmental (DREAL/Prefecture), Security and National-Security (ANSSI/DGSI); with support from Project Director and specialist counsel

Suggested Timeframe: Month 0–1 (2026-10-17 to 2026-11-17), dialogue initiated

Key Outputs/Deliverables:

  • Written pre-submission request letters to RTE, DREAL, ANSSI, prefecture (with project overview, siting rationale, key technical parameters, timeline expectations)
  • Meeting schedules and participant lists (internal team + authority representatives)
  • Documentation log of all authority responses (emails, letters, meeting minutes)
  • Summary of preliminary authority feedback (if any) by Month 2 (2026-12-17)
  • Gate-critical response tracking (target RTE letter Month 6 = 2027-04-17, water opinion Month 6 = 2027-04-17, ANSSI opinion Month 6 = 2027-04-17, DREAL opinion Month 9 = 2027-07-17)

Dependencies:

  • PMO established (step 7)
  • Specialist advisers identified (step 8)

10. Compliance, Environmental & Social License Committee establishes the municipal liaison committee and launches early voluntary public consultation. The committee contacts representatives from at least the three most-affected municipalities (Cambrai, Dunkirk, Valenciennes or equivalent in chosen topology), invites them to join a monthly liaison dialogue, and publishes the consultation launch with a transparent project overview, siting rationale, technical specifications (power, cooling, fiber, security), environmental and social-impact scope, and a 4-week comment period. Consultation feedback is recorded and a response summary is published by Month 5 (2027-03-17).

Responsible Body/Role: Compliance, Environmental & Social License Committee (Community and Stakeholder Lead)

Suggested Timeframe: Months 1–3 (2026-11-17 to 2027-01-17), liaison committee established by Month 2 (2026-12-17), consultation launched by Month 3 (2027-01-17)

Key Outputs/Deliverables:

  • Municipal liaison committee charter (members, meeting schedule, published minutes protocol)
  • First municipal liaison committee meeting (Month 2 = 2026-12-17)
  • Public consultation launch package (project overview, siting rationale, technical specs, environmental and social scope, 4-week comment period)
  • Published meeting minutes from at least two liaison-committee meetings
  • Public consultation feedback summary and project response (published by Month 5 = 2027-03-17)

Dependencies:

  • Compliance, Environmental & Social License Committee established (step 5)
  • Project location and topology (or alternative topologies) defined

11. PMO Land Assembly Lead and specialist real-estate counsel conduct a parcel-by-parcel option survey across all candidate sites (Cambrai, Dunkirk, Valenciennes, Saint-Omer) to assess: ownership chains (public vs. private), known holdout or activist groups, fragmentation, above-market-value expectations, and option-agreement feasibility. A preliminary go/no-go assessment is produced by Month 3 (2027-01-17) answering whether at least 70% of the single-square target parcel (or the split-campus node targets) can be optioned non-coercively at less than 15% above benchmark land value. If the single-square falls short of 70%, the assessment recommends a split-campus topology; if both fail, a further downsize or site substitution is flagged.

Responsible Body/Role: PMO Land Assembly Lead (with real-estate counsel and municipal/registry liaison)

Suggested Timeframe: Months 1–3 (2026-11-17 to 2027-01-17), assessment by end of Month 3 (2027-01-17)

Key Outputs/Deliverables:

  • Parcel-by-parcel survey report (ownership, fragmentation, holdout risk, land-value benchmarks)
  • Land-assembly feasibility assessment: single-square vs. split-campus viability
  • Topology recommendation (single square if ≥70% optionable, split campus if single square fails)
  • Phase II environmental site assessment commission instructions (identify highest-priority sites)
  • Option-agreement strategy and initial-approach outreach list

Dependencies:

  • PMO established (step 7)
  • Municipal liaison dialogue initiated (step 10) for municipal-registry and ownership-chain access
  • Candidate site map and land-use boundaries defined

12. Compliance, Environmental & Social License Committee commissions Phase II intrusive environmental site assessments (soil boring, groundwater sampling, asbestos survey) on the top 2–3 candidate sites in each geographic zone. Assessments are targeted to close by Month 3 (2027-01-17) so that contamination findings can feed the land-assembly topology decision (Month 4 = 2027-02-17). Remediation-liability estimates are produced per site; sites with bounded remediation costs below EUR 100M are shortlisted; sites exceeding this threshold are either excluded or flagged for further negotiation with the landowner or public remediation authority.

Responsible Body/Role: Compliance, Environmental & Social License Committee (Brownfield and Remediation Counsel) and PMO Environmental/Permitting Lead

Suggested Timeframe: Months 1–3 (2026-11-17 to 2027-01-17), surveys commissioned Month 1 (2026-11-17), reports closed by Month 3 (2027-01-17)

Key Outputs/Deliverables:

  • Phase II ESA engagement letters and scope (soil, groundwater, asbestos, baseline survey per site)
  • Phase II ESA reports (one per high-priority site, estimated cost EUR 1.5M–3M per zone)
  • Remediation-liability estimate per site (bounded to EUR 0–100M range preferred)
  • Site-shortlist decision (include, exclude, or conditional on seller indemnity)
  • Indemnity negotiation strategy with landowners or public remediation authorities

Dependencies:

  • Land-assembly parcel survey completed (step 11)
  • Compliance committee established (step 5)
  • Budget allocated for Phase II surveys (Phase 0 tranche 1–2)

13. PMO Grid and Power Lead commissions an independent RTE hosting-capacity assessment (third-party auditor) to estimate available 400 kV substation connection capacity at Hauts-de-France, assess transmission-reinforcement timelines and cost-sharing requirements, and model phased tranches (500 MW, 1 GW, 2+ GW). The auditor liaises with RTE to understand queue position, multi-tranche allocation policy, firm vs. conditional connection-offer timelines, and curtailment/flexibility requirements. A detailed hosting-capacity audit report is delivered by Month 9 (2027-07-17) and published to the Gate Review Committee, lenders and co-investors.

Responsible Body/Role: PMO Grid and Power Lead (with independent RTE hosting-capacity auditor)

Suggested Timeframe: Months 1–9 (2026-11-17 to 2027-07-17), audit engagement Month 1 (2026-11-17), report Month 9 (2027-07-17)

Key Outputs/Deliverables:

  • RTE hosting-capacity auditor engagement letter and scope
  • Hosting-capacity audit report (Month 9 = 2027-07-17): capacity estimates per node, transmission reinforcement scope and cost-share, queue position, connection-offer timeline by tranche
  • Grid reinforcement cost estimate (EUR 500M–1.5B range, propose risk allocation)
  • Phased connection-offer model (500 MW first tranche, pathway to 1 GW, assumptions on flexibility and curtailment)
  • Published audit summary distributed to Gate Review Committee, Steering Committee, lenders

Dependencies:

  • PMO Grid Lead appointed (step 7)
  • RTE pre-submission dialogue initiated (step 9)
  • Topology decision (Month 4 = 2027-02-17) so the auditor can focus on the chosen node(s)

14. PMO Permitting and Environmental Lead, in coordination with environmental counsel, develops detailed ICPE and environmental-authorization permit-file roadmap. The roadmap specifies: required expert reports (ecological baseline, hydrological assessment, air-quality and noise modeling, contamination survey, thermal plume modeling if water-cooling), EIA scope (avoidance-reduction-compensation hierarchy for ecological impact, biodiversity net-positive targets, farmland displacement mitigation), baseline data collection timelines, DREAL feedback integration, and targeted permit-file submission date (Months 8–9 = 2027-06-17 to 2027-07-17). This roadmap feeds into the Compliance committee's permitting-file production schedule.

Responsible Body/Role: PMO Permitting and Environmental Lead (with ICPE specialist counsel, environmental counsel, EIA specialist)

Suggested Timeframe: Months 1–2 (2026-11-17 to 2026-12-17), roadmap completed by Month 2 (2026-12-17)

Key Outputs/Deliverables:

  • ICPE and environmental-authorization permit-file roadmap (required components, baseline data, expert reports, timelines)
  • EIA scope and avoidance-reduction-compensation strategy
  • Permit-file production schedule (targeting filing Months 8–9 = 2027-06-17 to 2027-07-17)
  • Expert-report commission plan and budget allocation
  • DREAL pre-submission feedback integration plan

Dependencies:

  • Compliance committee established (step 5)
  • Pre-submission dialogue with DREAL initiated (step 9)
  • Topology decision (Month 4 = 2027-02-17) so the scope is clear

15. PMO Security and National-Security Lead, in coordination with security and GDPR counsel, prepares a confidential security governance white paper for ANSSI pre-submission. The white paper covers: tenant selection and vetting process, data-residency and national-security data-handling policies, perimeter hardening and anti-drone specifications, cyber-OT separation architecture, personnel-clearance requirements, supply-chain assurance, co-investor governance and control provisions, and alignment with French AI and sovereignty strategy. The white paper is submitted to ANSSI in advance of the formal pre-submission meeting (target Month 1–2 = 2026-11-17 to 2026-12-17) to solicit informal guidance on the anticipated review scope and any early concerns.

Responsible Body/Role: PMO Security and National-Security Lead (with security counsel and GDPR counsel)

Suggested Timeframe: Months 0–2 (2026-10-17 to 2026-12-17), white paper drafted and submitted by Month 1–2 (2026-11-17 to 2026-12-17)

Key Outputs/Deliverables:

  • Confidential security governance white paper (tenant vetting, data residency, perimeter security, cyber-OT separation, supply-chain assurance, co-investor control provisions)
  • Pre-submission meeting request to ANSSI (Months 0–1 = 2026-10-17 to 2026-11-17)
  • ANSSI confidential preliminary feedback (due Month 6 = 2027-04-17, proposed)
  • GDPR data-processing and data-residency compliance framework

Dependencies:

  • PMO Security Lead appointed (step 7)
  • Security and GDPR counsel engaged (step 8)
  • Project technical specifications defined (power, cooling, fiber, topology)

16. PMO Grid and Power Lead, in coordination with independent power-market advisers, commences multi-party power-procurement negotiations with EDF and coordinates with RTE on flexibility and BESS requirements. Negotiations target a non-binding letter of intent from EDF by Month 6 (2027-04-17) confirming willingness to discuss a multi-year baseload contract for at least 500 MW at a capped EUR/MWh price (proposed range EUR 50–70/MWh, not verified). A formal term sheet (non-binding but detailed) is targeted for Month 9 (2027-07-17). Energy pricing and curtailment assumptions are modeled in parallel; grid curtailment at or below 10% is the base assumption, with a walk-away threshold of 15%.

Responsible Body/Role: PMO Grid and Power Lead (with independent power-market adviser and EDF liaison)

Suggested Timeframe: Months 1–9 (2026-11-17 to 2027-07-17), EDF dialogue ongoing, LOI by Month 6 (2027-04-17), term sheet by Month 9 (2027-07-17)

Key Outputs/Deliverables:

  • Power-market study and pricing assessment (EUR/MWh forecast, multi-GW contract feasibility, hedging options)
  • EDF non-binding letter of intent (Month 6 = 2027-04-17): 500 MW baseload, minimum 10-year tenor, price range to be confirmed in term sheet
  • EDF formal term sheet (Month 9 = 2027-07-17): capacity, price, tenor, indexation, curtailment/flexibility terms
  • BESS and demand-flexibility modeling (50–200 MWh, grid-stress mitigation, cost estimate)
  • Power-cost sensitivity model (base case vs. +EUR 30/MWh shock scenario, impact on tenant lease pricing and project returns)

Dependencies:

  • PMO Grid and Power Lead appointed (step 7)
  • RTE pre-submission dialogue initiated (step 9)
  • Topology decision (Month 4 = 2027-02-17) so capacity targets are clear

17. Steering Committee holds a formal topology-decision meeting at Month 4 (2027-02-17). The committee reviews evidence from three sources: (i) land-assembly feasibility (% parcel optioned, contamination findings, holdout risk), (ii) RTE grid-capacity signals (preliminary letter received or timeline credible by Month 6 = 2027-04-17?), and (iii) permitting and social-license risk (single-square vs. split-campus complexity). The committee votes on single-square vs. split-campus, documents the rationale, and publishes the topology decision to lenders and co-investors. If RTE has not yet delivered a letter (due Month 6 = 2027-04-17), the split-campus default is applied; the single square can only be chosen if RTE written evidence of at least 1 GW capacity is already in hand.
