Responsible Body/Role: Project Steering Committee

Suggested Timeframe: Month 4 (2027-02-17), topology-decision meeting

Key Outputs/Deliverables:

  • Topology Decision Document (single square vs. split campus, rationale, evidence cited)
  • Land-assembly feasibility summary (% parcel optioned, contamination bounded, holdout risk)
  • RTE grid-capacity evidence (if in hand) or pathway statement (letter due Month 6 = 2027-04-17)
  • Detailed capex and timeline per topology option (single square EUR 5B–10B, split campus EUR 5.5B–9.2B, schedule difference)
  • Published topology decision distributed to PMO, Gate Review Committee, lenders, co-investors

Dependencies:

  • Land-assembly feasibility assessment (step 11)
  • Phase II ESA reports (step 12)
  • RTE pre-submission dialogue completed (step 9); letter not yet due, but dialogue status assessed

18. PMO Tenancy and Revenue Lead develops standardized high-commitment take-or-pay lease term sheets (5–10 year proposed tenor) and capacity-reservation fee structures (EUR 10M–50M per 100 MW proposed, credited against future lease revenue). Templates are finalized by Month 3 (2027-01-17) and distributed to the project's anchor-tenant acquisition team. Target anchor tenants include 2–3 global hyperscalers or AI labs (hyperscaler pool) and 2–3 sovereign-AI or European-consortium anchors (sovereign pool). Initial outreach and non-binding letter of intent collection begins in Month 3 (2027-01-17); conversion of LOIs to binding term sheets is targeted by Month 9 (2027-07-17) for at least 30% of Phase 1 capacity.

Responsible Body/Role: PMO Tenancy and Revenue Lead (with real-estate counsel and commercial advisers)

Suggested Timeframe: Months 1–3 (2026-11-17 to 2027-01-17), templates by Month 3 (2027-01-17)

Key Outputs/Deliverables:

  • Standardized take-or-pay lease term sheet (5–10 year tenor, capacity reserved, force-majeure exceptions, SLA carve-outs for grid curtailment, annual escalation)
  • Capacity-reservation fee schedule (EUR 10M–50M per 100 MW, payment timeline before construction start)
  • Tenant acquisition targeting roadmap (2–3 hyperscalers, 2–3 sovereign anchors, outreach timeline, LOI targets)
  • Tenant due-diligence criteria (credit rating BBB− minimum or parent guarantee, compute-cluster workload requirements, latency tolerance for split campus, security/data-residency requirements)
  • LOI template and non-binding engagement plan

Dependencies:

  • PMO Tenancy Lead appointed (step 7)
  • Real-estate and commercial counsel engaged (step 8)
  • Topology decision (Month 4 = 2027-02-17) so capacity targets and node specifications are clear
  • Power-procurement and grid-hosting timeline understood (so lease terms can reference power reliability and curtailment)

19. Gate Review and Kill Authority Committee implements monthly monitoring of gate-criterion achievement. Starting Month 1 (2026-11-17), the external red team delivers a monthly pass/fail opinion on each of the five gate criteria: (i) grid hosting-capacity status (RTE letter received or timeline credible?), (ii) land assembly (% parcel optioned, remediation findings), (iii) anchor-tenant pipeline (LOI vs. binding breakdown, credit validation), (iv) debt-financing status (lender interest, term-sheet progress), (v) social license (municipal support, opposition escalation). The red-team reports are reviewed by the committee in monthly gate-status sessions; any criterion showing a High-likelihood breach is flagged to the Steering Committee within 5 working days.

Responsible Body/Role: Gate Review and Kill Authority Committee (with External Red Team)

Suggested Timeframe: Monthly, starting Month 1 (2026-11-17), through Month 12 (2027-10-17)

Key Outputs/Deliverables:

  • External red-team monthly pass/fail reports (5 criteria assessed against numeric thresholds, evidence presented, risks flagged)
  • Monthly gate-status summary for the Steering Committee (which criteria on track, which at risk, recommended actions)
  • Quarterly formal gate-assessment meetings (Months 3, 6, 9, 12 = 2027-01-17, 2027-04-17, 2027-07-17, 2027-10-17) with detailed written gate-status reports
  • Escalation alerts (high-risk breaches within 5 working days to Steering Committee and PMO)
  • Published dissent log (committee disagreements on threshold achievement recorded and disclosed to lenders)

Dependencies:

  • Gate Review and Kill Authority Committee chartered (step 4)
  • External red team engaged (step 4)
  • Numeric kill thresholds published (step 6)

20. Compliance, Environmental & Social License Committee oversees the completion of hydrological study and water-authority engagement. A hydrologist assesses regional water stress, validates dry-cooler feasibility at a 35°C design-day ambient temperature, and projects the annual freshwater withdrawal (proposed target: zero evaporative water, closed-loop direct-to-chip cooling only). By Month 6 (2027-04-17), a written opinion is secured from the regional water authority (Agence de l'Eau Artois-Picardie) confirming that closed-loop cooling is permissible and that no additional water-use permits are required beyond standard stormwater management. If the water authority raises concerns, design review and cooling-technology alternatives are triggered.

Responsible Body/Role: Compliance, Environmental & Social License Committee (Water Resources Manager)

Suggested Timeframe: Months 1–6 (2026-11-17 to 2027-04-17), study by Month 4 (2027-02-17), authority opinion by Month 6 (2027-04-17)

Key Outputs/Deliverables:

  • Hydrological and water-stress assessment study (regional drought risk, competitor water demand, seasonal variation, dry-cooler performance at 35°C ambient, PUE impact modeling)
  • Water-authority consultation and engagement (letters, meetings with Agence de l'Eau Artois-Picardie by Month 3 = 2027-01-17)
  • Water-authority written preliminary opinion (due Month 6 = 2027-04-17): feasibility of closed-loop cooling, permit requirements, conditions
  • Thermal-design-day modeling (PUE at 35°C ambient, peak grid load during hot weather, grid curtailment interaction)
  • Risk triggers: if PUE exceeds 1.30 or water authority raises concerns, design review and contingency cooling options (hybrid with limited evaporative water) are activated

Dependencies:

  • Compliance committee established (step 5)
  • Water-resources counsel engaged (step 8)
  • Topology decision (Month 4 = 2027-02-17) so water-demand per node is clear

21. Compliance, Environmental & Social License Committee commissions and coordinates ecological-baseline fieldwork and develops a campus-wide ecological master plan. Botanical, avian, bat and invertebrate surveys are conducted across candidate sites; Natura 2000 designations and protected-species presence are mapped. The master plan identifies: (i) avoidance zones (no-build areas protecting key habitats or protected species), (ii) reduction measures (hall siting and design to minimize impacts), and (iii) compensation strategy (offsite habitat restoration, on-site continuation zones kept in semi-natural state or agricultural production, net-biodiversity target at least 1:1 ratio, stretch target net-positive). The master plan is completed and published by Month 6 (2027-04-17) and serves as the baseline for EIA content and DREAL permitting.

Responsible Body/Role: Compliance, Environmental & Social License Committee (Ecology and Biodiversity Manager)

Suggested Timeframe: Months 1–6 (2026-11-17 to 2027-04-17), fieldwork Months 2–5 (2026-12-17 to 2027-03-17), plan finalized by Month 6 (2027-04-17)

Key Outputs/Deliverables:

  • Ecological baseline surveys (botanical, avian, bat, invertebrate; desktop plus field assessment across all candidate sites)
  • Natura 2000 and protected-species mapping
  • Campus-wide ecological master plan (avoidance zones, reduced-impact hall siting, biodiversity-compensation strategy, net-positive target)
  • Biodiversity offsetting options (on-site continuation zones, off-site habitat creation/restoration, cost estimate EUR 200M–500M for 9 GW, Phase 1 share EUR 50M–150M estimate)
  • DREAL consultation and feedback integration

Dependencies:

  • Compliance committee established (step 5)
  • Ecology and biodiversity counsel engaged (step 8)
  • Topology decision (Month 4 = 2027-02-17) so the envelope and impact scope are defined

22. PMO Finance and Lender Relations Lead engages debt capital providers (European Investment Bank, KfW, French banks, infrastructure funds) to establish lending criteria, debt capacity, and preliminary non-binding term-sheet conditions for Phase 1. Lenders are invited to review the Phase 0 gating framework and to signal which gate achievements unlock debt commitments (typically: RTE firm connection offer, signed anchor-tenant take-or-pay for ≥30% of capacity, bounded environmental and remediation liability, firm power-supply contract or LOI, debt-service-coverage ratio above 1.30x). Lender feedback is incorporated into the PMO financial model and gate-review process. A formal debt non-binding LOI or term sheet is targeted by Month 9 (2027-07-17), conditional on gate achievements.

Responsible Body/Role: PMO Finance and Lender Relations Lead (with infrastructure finance counsel and arranger)

Suggested Timeframe: Months 2–9 (2026-12-17 to 2027-07-17), lender outreach Month 2–3 (2026-12-17 to 2027-01-17), preliminary feedback Month 6 (2027-04-17), term sheet Month 9 (2027-07-17)

Key Outputs/Deliverables:

  • Debt-financing strategy and lender-pool assessment (EIB, KfW, French banks, infrastructure funds)
  • Lender-engagement plan and term-sheet discussion schedule
  • Debt-financing criteria document (gate achievements required: RTE, tenants, liability, power, DSCR, tenor, spreads, covenants)
  • Preliminary financial model (EUR 5B Phase 1 capex base, debt capacity scenarios 50%/60%/70% leverage, DSCR under base and stress cases)
  • Non-binding debt term sheet or LOI (Month 9 = 2027-07-17): proposed debt size (EUR 3B–3.5B for 500 MW), tenor, pricing (benchmark + 200 bps estimate), gate conditions for final commitment

Dependencies:

  • PMO Finance Lead appointed (step 7)
  • Finance and infrastructure counsel engaged (step 8)
  • Phase 0 gating framework and gate criteria defined (step 6)
  • Topology and capacity targets defined (Month 4 = 2027-02-17)

23. PMO Permitting and Environmental Lead submits the formal ICPE and environmental-authorization permit application(s) to DREAL and the prefecture. One unified permit file is submitted for a single-square topology; if split-campus is chosen, one permit file per node is submitted to isolate legal-challenge risk. The filing date targets Months 8–9 (2027-06-17 to 2027-07-17) to align with the DREAL opinion gate due Month 9 (2027-07-17). The filing includes: expert reports (ecological baseline, hydrological assessment, contamination survey if remediation needed), EIA (avoidance-reduction-compensation analysis, biodiversity net-positive targets, farmland-displacement mitigation, community-benefit commitments), thermal and noise modeling, and security/resilience specifications. An electronic copy is provided to the Compliance committee and PMO for ongoing tracking.

Responsible Body/Role: PMO Permitting and Environmental Lead (with ICPE and environmental counsel)

Suggested Timeframe: Months 7–9 (2027-05-17 to 2027-07-17), target filing Months 8–9 (2027-06-17 to 2027-07-17)

Key Outputs/Deliverables:

  • Completed ICPE permit-application file (technical specification, process description, environmental protection measures, monitoring plan)
  • Completed environmental-authorization file (EIA summary, avoidance-reduction-compensation strategy, biodiversity assessment, farmland mitigation, community-benefit terms)
  • Supporting expert reports and modeling (ecology, hydrology, contamination, thermal, noise, security)
  • Letter to DREAL with filing date and timeline expectations (decision targeted 18–30 months from filing, appeal risk to be managed)
  • PMO permit-tracking protocol (application reference number, case officer contact, decision timeline milestones)

Dependencies:

  • PMO Permitting and Environmental Lead appointed (step 7)
  • Environmental and ICPE counsel engaged (step 8)
  • Ecological master plan completed (step 20)
  • Water-authority opinion received (step 19)
  • Topology decision finalized (step 17)
  • Community consultation closed and feedback integrated (step 10)

24. Compliance, Environmental & Social License Committee completes negotiations on a draft community-benefit agreement with municipalities and farm-sector representatives. The agreement specifies: (i) labor and training commitments (regional training academy, local hiring targets, apprenticeship programs); (ii) ecological restoration (EUR 50M–150M Phase 1 estimate, habitat creation, hedgerow establishment, wetland restoration); (iii) farm-sector support (compensation for displaced land, relocation assistance, revenue-sharing on continuation zones, long-term lease options); (iv) municipal infrastructure upgrades (water, roads, utilities); (v) monitoring and oversight roles (municipal and community observers on an environmental or operations monitoring committee). The draft is circulated by Month 4 (2027-02-17) and negotiations close by Month 6 (2027-04-17) so the agreement can be published and appended to the permit file as evidence of community support.

Responsible Body/Role: Compliance, Environmental & Social License Committee (Community and Stakeholder Lead)

Suggested Timeframe: Months 2–6 (2026-12-17 to 2027-04-17), draft by Month 4 (2027-02-17), signed by Month 6 (2027-04-17)

Key Outputs/Deliverables:

  • Community-benefit agreement (scope: labor, training, ecology, farm-sector support, municipal infrastructure, monitoring roles)
  • Signatory list (municipalities, farm unions, regional council, environmental NGOs as appropriate)
  • Benefit value summary (EUR 50M–150M Phase 1–2 estimate, labor commitment FTE or hours, ecological hectares, training cohorts)
  • Signed community-benefit agreement (or detailed term sheet if final signatures pending)
  • Published agreement and fact sheet (distributed to municipalities, press, lenders, co-investors as evidence of social license)

Dependencies:

  • Municipal liaison committee established (step 10)
  • Public consultation completed (step 10)
  • Ecological master plan completed (step 20)
  • Topology decision finalized (step 17) so parcel and impact scope are defined

25. PMO Tenancy and Revenue Lead closes anchor-tenant acquisition and binding term-sheet signature targets. By Month 9 (2027-07-17), signed take-or-pay lease agreements covering at least 30% of Phase 1 capacity are in hand. Acceptable anchors include: (i) global hyperscalers (NVIDIA, Meta, Google, Microsoft, Amazon, or similar, requiring A−/A+ credit rating), (ii) sovereign AI users (French State, EU consortiums, requiring sovereign guarantee or ministerial commitment), or (iii) European enterprise-AI anchors (requiring A−/BBB+ minimum). Capacity-reservation fees (EUR 10M–50M per 100 MW) are collected upfront by Month 6–9 (2027-04-17 to 2027-07-17) and credited to future lease revenue. If less than 30% signed by Month 9 (2027-07-17), the Gate Review Committee flags a threshold breach and recommends Phase 1 downsizing.

Responsible Body/Role: PMO Tenancy and Revenue Lead (with commercial advisers and legal counsel)

Suggested Timeframe: Months 3–9 (2027-01-17 to 2027-07-17), LOI collection Month 3–6 (2027-01-17 to 2027-04-17), binding term sheets by Month 9 (2027-07-17)

Key Outputs/Deliverables:

  • Anchor-tenant engagement log (target list, meeting dates, LOI dates, term-sheet negotiation timeline)
  • Signed take-or-pay lease agreements (at least 30% of Phase 1 capacity, ≥300 MW on 1 GW base; ≥150 MW on 500 MW base)
  • Tenant credit-rating validation and security assessment (BBB− minimum or parent guarantee)
  • Capacity-reservation fee receipts (EUR 10M–50M per 100 MW, received by Month 9 = 2027-07-17, credited to future lease revenue)
  • Tenant workload and compute-cluster specifications (used to validate latency tolerance for split campus and power/cooling requirements)

Dependencies:

  • Take-or-pay lease templates finalized (step 16)
  • Topology decision (Month 4 = 2027-02-17) so capacity targets and node specifications are clear
  • Power-procurement and grid-hosting timeline understood (so lease terms can reference reliability)

26. PMO Security and National-Security Lead receives ANSSI confidential preliminary feedback on the security governance white paper (due Month 6 = 2027-04-17, proposed). If ANSSI raises no blocking concerns and indicates a formal security review can commence at Month 13 (2027-11-17) after Phase 0 gate, the security pathway is on track for Phase 1. If ANSSI signals concerns (e.g., foreign co-investor involvement, data-residency restrictions, tenant-access limitations), design review and governance restructuring are triggered. The PMO documents ANSSI findings in a confidential memo for the Steering Committee and Gate Review Committee; the security gate for Phase 1 FID is confirmed (formal review starts Month 13 = 2027-11-17, clearance targeted Month 25–31 = 2028-11-17 to 2029-05-17).

Key Outputs/Deliverables:

  • ANSSI confidential preliminary opinion (due Month 6 = 2027-04-17): anticipated formal-review scope, timeline, no-go concerns (if any), tenant-access or data-residency constraints, security-design feedback
  • PMO Security Governance Roadmap (updated based on ANSSI feedback, formal-review start date Month 13 = 2027-11-17, clearance target Month 25–31 = 2028-11-17 to 2029-05-17)
  • Confidential summary memo for Steering Committee and Gate Review Committee (ANSSI findings, any design implications, security gate status)

27. PMO Grid and Power Lead distributes the published RTE hosting-capacity audit report to the Gate Review Committee, Steering Committee, lenders and co-investors by Month 9 (2027-07-17). The report summarizes RTE's assessed capacity at Hauts-de-France, the proposed connection timelines by tranche (500 MW, 1 GW, 2+ GW), transmission-reinforcement requirements and cost-sharing, queue position, and assumptions on grid flexibility and curtailment. The audit provides the Gate Review Committee with the evidence needed to assess the grid-hosting gate threshold (RTE preliminary feasibility letter for ≥500 MW within 36 months). If RTE's assessment is negative or capacity is below 500 MW, the grid gate fails and Phase 1 cannot proceed at planned scale.

Responsible Body/Role: PMO Grid and Power Lead (with RTE hosting-capacity auditor)

Suggested Timeframe: Month 9 (2027-07-17), report completion and distribution

Key Outputs/Deliverables:

  • Executive summary for lenders and co-investors (key findings on hosting capacity, transmission risk, cost-share exposure)

DREAL confirms whether an EIA is required, specifies the scope of impact assessment (ecology, hydrology, air quality, noise, contamination remediation, heat-reuse potential), and provides preliminary guidance on ICPE classification and fast-track status availability (if any, but fast-track is not assumed). Any DREAL feedback is integrated into the Phase 1 permitting plan, and permit-filing timelines are updated if needed. 29. Compliance, Environmental & Social License Committee completes fiber-route auditing and confirms that at least 2 physically separate, audited routes (no shared duct, bridge or landing facility) are available to each of Paris, London, Brussels, Amsterdam and Frankfurt, with at least 100 Tbps redundant capacity and ≤25% of cross-border capacity per landing point. Fiber carriers are engaged to provide detailed physical-route maps; an independent fiber auditor verifies true diversity. If independent routes are not available from carriers within cost and timeline, the PMO budgets for a developer-owned or co-funded route and negotiates rights-of-way and duct access. A written confirmation from carriers or a commitment to build/co-invest is secured by Month 9 (2027-07-17).

Responsible Body/Role: PMO Grid and Power Lead and/or Tenancy and Revenue Lead (with independent fiber-route auditor and carrier liaisons)

Suggested Timeframe: Months 1–9 (2026-11-17 to 2027-07-17), audits and confirmations by Month 9 (2027-07-17)

Key Outputs/Deliverables:

  • Carrier capacity commitments or letters of intent (at least 2 routes per destination, capacity reserved, lit timeline before Phase 1 energization)
  • Developer-built/co-invested fiber option (if carrier routes unavailable, budget EUR 100M–500M per 100–200 km route, rights-of-way plan, construction timeline)
  • Landing-point diversity confirmation (at least 2 independent UK landings, 2 FR/BE landings, no single landing carries >25% cross-border capacity)

30. Gate Review and Kill Authority Committee convenes for the formal Phase 0 gate review at Month 12 (2027-10-17). The committee assesses all five numeric gate thresholds: (i) RTE grid hosting capacity (firm offer or credible pathway for ≥500 MW within 36 months?), (ii) land assembly (≥70% of chosen topology's parcel optioned?), (iii) anchor-tenant take-or-pay (≥30% of Phase 1 signed?), (iv) debt financing (EUR 3B+ commitment confirmed?), (v) social license (2 of 3 municipalities' written support?). For each criterion, the committee reviews the latest red-team pass/fail opinion, supporting evidence, and any expert audits (RTE, fiber, environmental, security). The committee issues a formal Phase 0 Gate Summary report within 10 working days, recommending: (i) Phase 1 FID approval (all gates closed), (ii) conditional approval (gate(s) deferred with specific conditions, Phase 1 start pushed), (iii) Phase 1 downsizing (e.g., 250 MW instead of 500 MW if tenants <30%), (iv) Phase 0 completion with no Phase 1 (project paused or cancelled). The recommendation is published to the Steering Committee, lenders and co-investors.

Responsible Body/Role: Gate Review and Kill Authority Committee (Independent Chair, Committee Members, with External Red Team)

Suggested Timeframe: Month 12 (2027-10-17), gate review and decision by Month 12–13 (2027-10-17 to 2027-11-17)

Key Outputs/Deliverables:

  • Phase 0 Gate Summary Report (formal assessment of all five thresholds, evidence presented, pass/fail determination, risks and mitigants)
  • Red-team final pass/fail opinion (all five criteria evaluated against published thresholds, updated evidence, risks highlighted)
  • Phase 1 FID Recommendation (approve, conditional, downsize, or cancel) with rationale
  • Dissent Log (any committee member disagreements on threshold achievement recorded and disclosed to lenders)
  • Distribution to Steering Committee, lenders, co-investors within 2 working days of issuance

Dependencies:

  • Gate Review and Kill Authority Committee chartered and numeric thresholds published (step 6)
  • All Phase 0 workstreams closed or approaching closure (grid audit, land surveys, tenant term sheets, debt discussions, permit file submission, ANSSI/DREAL feedback)

31. Project Steering Committee convenes within 5 working days of the Gate Review and Kill Authority Committee's recommendation to decide on Phase 1 FID. If the committee recommends approval and all gates are closed, the Steering Committee votes to proceed with Phase 1 FID (two-of-three alignment required: sponsor, consortium, independent director). If the committee recommends conditional approval or downsizing, the Steering Committee reviews the conditions and vote accordingly. If the committee recommends cancellation and the Steering Committee votes to override, the override decision and full dissent are published to lenders and co-investors within 2 working days. A Phase 1 FID approval letter is issued by the Sponsor within 3 working days, authorizing Phase 1 budget drawdown and construction start. Phase 0 closure activities (team transition, archives, post-gate reporting) begin.

Responsible Body/Role: Project Steering Committee

Suggested Timeframe: Month 12–13 (2027-10-17 to 2027-11-17), decision and approval letter

Key Outputs/Deliverables:

  • Phase 1 FID Approval Letter (from Sponsor, authorizing Phase 1 budget and construction start, conditions if any)
  • Phase 1 Financial Close Package (debt-financing documentation, equity commitments, tenant lease executions, power-supply agreements, RTE connection agreement)
  • Phase 0 Closure Report (lessons learned, deliverable summary, cost reconciliation, gate achievements and gaps)
  • Published Phase 1 FID announcement to media, authorities, stakeholders

Dependencies:

  • Gate Review and Kill Authority Committee Phase 0 Gate Summary Report (step 30)

32. If Phase 1 FID is approved, the Project Steering Committee authorizes the transition to Phase 1 governance. The Steering Committee remains in place but expands its composition to include Phase 1 operational leads (VP Engineering, VP Operations, VP Community). The Gate Review and Kill Authority Committee's charter is updated to focus on Phase 1 expansion gates: Phase 2 FID (Months 48–54 = 2030-10-17 to 2031-04-17) will require signed take-or-pay for ≥50% of Phase 2 capacity, plus demonstration of Phase 1 operational performance (PUE ≤1.28, power reliability, security compliance). The PMO transitions to Phase 1 construction and operations mode, with Phase 1-specific workstreams (engineering, procurement, construction, commissioning, tenant onboarding). A Phase 1 Governance Roadmap is published, defining decision authorities, escalation thresholds and committee cadences for the 36-month Phase 1 build (Months 12–48 = 2027-10-17 to 2030-10-17).

Responsible Body/Role: Project Steering Committee

Suggested Timeframe: Month 13 (2027-11-17), within 2 weeks of Phase 1 FID approval

Key Outputs/Deliverables:

  • Phase 1 Governance Charter (updated Steering Committee composition, Phase 1 operational leads, committee focus shift to operational milestones)
  • Phase 2 Gate Criteria Definition (≥50% demand signed, Phase 1 operational data, PUE ≤1.28, security/community targets met)
  • Phase 1 Governance Roadmap (decision authorities, escalation thresholds, committee cadences for 36-month Phase 1)
  • Phase 1 PMO Charter and organization structure (engineering, procurement, construction, commissioning, operations, community, safety)
  • Stakeholder communication (published Phase 1 Governance Roadmap distributed to lenders, co-investors, authorities, tenants)

Dependencies:

  • Phase 1 FID approved (step 31)
  • Phase 0 gates closed or conditionally passed

33. If Phase 1 is conditionally approved or deferred, the Gate Review and Kill Authority Committee defines a Time-Bound Contingency Plan specifying when and how the deferred gate condition(s) will be resolved. For example, if RTE delays issuing a firm connection offer beyond Month 12 (2027-10-17), the plan specifies a target resolution date (e.g., Month 18 = 2028-04-17) and a Phase 1 start date contingent on RTE's response. The committee sets a decision deadline (e.g., Month 18 = 2028-04-17): if the gate condition is not resolved by then, Phase 1 FID is automatically cancelled and the project exits. Alternatively, if gate conditions are resolved before the deadline, the Steering Committee reconvenes and votes on Phase 1 FID. The contingency plan is published to lenders, co-investors and the Sponsor.

Responsible Body/Role: Gate Review and Kill Authority Committee (if conditional approval), or Project Steering Committee (if deferral)

Suggested Timeframe: Month 12–13 (2027-10-17 to 2027-11-17), if Phase 1 is conditional or deferred

Key Outputs/Deliverables:

  • Time-Bound Contingency Plan (deferred gate condition, resolution pathway, target resolution date, automatic-exit trigger date)
  • Monitoring protocol (who tracks resolution, reporting frequency, escalation if deadline is missed)
  • Phase 1 start-date contingency scenarios (if condition resolved by Date X, Phase 1 starts Month Y; if not, project exits)
  • Published Contingency Plan distributed to Steering Committee, lenders, co-investors

Dependencies:

  • Phase 1 is conditionally approved or deferred (Month 12 = 2027-10-17 gate review)

34. If Phase 0 gates fail and Phase 1 is cancelled, the PMO executes Phase 0 closure and asset preservation. Land options are extended (2–3 year renewal strategy negotiated with landowners). Grid pre-engineering reports are archived for future reference. Permit-file and community-engagement documentation are preserved. Tenant-term-sheet templates and demand-signal archives are retained. Security governance framework and ANSSI feedback are documented. The Sponsor and consortium evaluate strategic alternatives: (i) downsize and restart Phase 0 with a smaller 250 MW base, (ii) pivot to split-campus model and validate 2–3 node topology separately, (iii) defer indefinitely pending external-condition improvement (grid capacity, tenant demand, permitting regime), or (iv) cancel the project entirely. A Phase 0 Completion and Strategic-Alternatives Report is published documenting the gate failures, sunk costs, preserved assets and recommended path forward.

Responsible Body/Role: Project Sponsor, Steering Committee and PMO

Suggested Timeframe: Month 12–18 (2027-10-17 to 2028-04-17), if Phase 1 is cancelled

Key Outputs/Deliverables:

  • Phase 0 Completion and Closure Report (gate failures documented, sunk costs reconciled, preserved assets inventoried)
  • Land-option extension agreements (2–3 years, renewal strategy)
  • Strategic-alternatives analysis (downsize to 250 MW, split-campus pivot, deferral, cancellation) with pros/cons and cost implications
  • Sponsor decision and strategic-direction memo (if any path is chosen)
  • Stakeholder communication (published closure report and strategic direction to lenders, co-investors, authorities, communities)

Dependencies:

  • Phase 0 gates assessed at Month 12 (2027-10-17)
  • Phase 1 FID is not approved

Decision Escalation Matrix

RTE Grid Hosting Capacity Threshold Breach Escalation Level: Gate Review and Kill Authority Committee Approval Process: Monthly red-team assessment against numeric threshold (at least 500 MW within 36 months). If preliminary RTE letter not received by Month 6 (2027-04-17) or hosting capacity drops below 500 MW, committee issues formal gate-status report within 5 working days and recommends split-campus topology pivot or Phase 1 downsize. Recommendation binds the Steering Committee unless overridden by supermajority (sponsor, consortium, independent director) with published dissent to lenders. Rationale: Grid hosting above ~1 GW is the primary kill condition and a critical uncontrolled external dependency. RTE's connection offer directly gates Phase 1 scale and topology choice. Breach of the 500 MW first-tranche threshold makes the project infeasible at planned MW or requires architectural redesign. Early escalation to an independent committee ensures sunk-cost pressure does not override this core feasibility test. Negative Consequences: If grid hosting fails and Phase 1 proceeds anyway, the campus cannot energize on schedule (12+ month delay likely), carrying costs of EUR 200M–400M accumulate, and lenders may withdraw financing commitments. Loss of RTE queue position to competing industrial users may render the site permanently infeasible. Forced pivot to split-campus topology late in Phase 0 costs EUR 250M–500M in design rework and extends Phase 1 FID decision by 6–12 months.

Anchor-Tenant Take-or-Pay Commitment Shortfall Below 30 Percent Escalation Level: Gate Review and Kill Authority Committee Approval Process: Monthly red-team pipeline assessment compares binding lease term sheets (not letters of intent) against the 30% capacity threshold. At Month 9 (2027-07-17), if signed take-or-pay covers less than 300 MW (on 1 GW base) or 150 MW (on 500 MW base), committee issues formal gate-status report recommending Phase 1 downsizing to match actual committed demand or Phase 1 FID deferral pending tenant consolidation. Steering Committee decides within 5 working days; override requires supermajority with dissent disclosed to lenders. Rationale: Credible anchor-tenant demand is the foundation for debt financing and Phase 1 FID approval. Binding commitments (not non-binding LOIs) prove tenant credit quality and workload certainty. A 30% minimum ensures sufficient revenue visibility for lenders to underwrite the project and protects equity from stranded capacity risk. Absence of committed anchors at the Month 9 (2027-07-17) deadline signals demand has not materialized and Phase 1 must be resized or deferred. Negative Consequences: If Phase 1 proceeds without 30% signed take-or-pay, lenders refuse debt or demand higher spreads (+200–300 bps), raising annual debt service by EUR 140M–280M and eroding returns by 2–4 percentage points. Tenant pipeline failure often cascades: once lenders signal reluctance, other tenants become hesitant to commit, accelerating the shortfall. Phase 1 energization with <30% pre-leased capacity risks uncontrolled vacancy (100+ MW idle), revenue loss of EUR 50M–100M annually, and potential covenant breaches or tenant lease terminations.

Land Assembly and Parcel Option Failure (Less Than 70 Percent Optioned) Escalation Level: Gate Review and Kill Authority Committee Approval Process: Land-assembly feasibility assessments (Month 3 = 2027-01-17 and Month 4 = 2027-02-17 to 2027-02-17) measure the percentage of target parcel under non-coercive option at benchmark-aligned pricing. If at least 70% is not secured by Month 4 (2027-02-17) (proposed threshold), the committee recommends split-campus topology as the default, triggering detailed feasibility studies for 2–3 nodes. If split-campus node targets also fall short of 70–80%, committee escalates to the Steering Committee with a recommendation to downsize Phase 1 or cancel the project. Rationale: Contiguous assembly of a large envelope tests feasibility; inability to secure land non-coercively signals market resistance or high displacement costs that undermine the social-license strategy. A 70% threshold is a credibility floor: below this level, holdout risk, legal challenge exposure, and relocation premium costs spike. The topology decision (single vs. split) depends on land-assembly success; escalation ensures the decision is not deferred. Negative Consequences: Failure to assemble a contiguous parcel forces a costly late-phase pivot to split-campus topology (EUR 250M–500M capex rework, 6–12 month delay). Holdout negotiations and litigation can extend land acquisition by 12–24 months, eroding RTE queue position and permitting timelines. Elevated land-acquisition costs (paying holdouts 20–40% above market) reduce project margin by EUR 100M–300M. Forced reliance on compulsory acquisition (public-interest designation) invites political backlash and legal appeals extending land control by 24–36 months and cancelling Phase 1 risk.

Permitting Delay or Legal Challenge Blocking Schedule Escalation Level: Compliance, Environmental & Social License Committee (escalates to Steering Committee if delay exceeds 6 months from target) Approval Process: Compliance committee tracks permit-file submission (targeted Month 8–9 = 2027-06-17 to 2027-07-17) and authority decision timelines. Formal DREAL opinion due Month 9 (2027-07-17); permission filing timeline tracks decision target (18–30 months from filing = Months 26–39 = 2028-12-17 to 2030-01-17). If DREAL decision slips >6 months beyond target or a major legal challenge is filed, committee escalates to Steering Committee with revised Phase 1 timeline and cost implications. Steering Committee decides whether to defer Phase 1 FID pending permit clarity or proceed with contingent Phase 1 start date. Rationale: Permitting delay erodes the RTE queue position and extends carrying costs on Phase 0 assets (EUR 200M–500M estimated). Standard ICPE timelines are 18–30 months; appeals add 24–48 months. Early escalation allows the Steering Committee to trigger contingency options (split-campus pivot, Phase 1 deferral, reduced scope) before sunk cost becomes irreversible. A 6-month slip is the threshold because it shifts first-block energization from target Months 42–48 (2030-04-17 to 2030-10-17) into Months 48–60 (2030-10-17 to 2031-10-17), materially affecting funding costs. Negative Consequences: Unmanaged permit delay of 12–24 months directly delays Phase 1 start 12–24 months, extending carrying costs by EUR 200M–500M and pushing energization to Month 54–66 (2031-04-17 to 2032-04-17). Tenant commitments signed in Month 9 (2027-07-17) may lapse if Phase 1 cannot start by Month 36 (2029-10-17) as planned, forcing tenant re-negotiation or replacement. RTE queue position erodes if other users fill available transmission capacity during a permitting stall. Legal challenges to permits can force design rework, adding EUR 250M–1.5B capex and invalidating prior environmental assessments.

ANSSI National-Security Review Blocks or Materially Restricts Foreign Co-Investor or Tenant Access Escalation Level: Steering Committee (with Gate Review and Kill Authority Committee advisory) Approval Process: PMO Security and National-Security Lead conducts confidential pre-submission dialogue with ANSSI (Months 0–1 = 2026-10-17 to 2026-11-17). Informal opinion due Month 6 (2027-04-17); Month 12 (2027-10-17) written confirmation that formal review can start with no blocking concerns. If ANSSI signals a blocking concern (e.g., foreign co-investor capital must be capped or excluded, foreign tenants prohibited, mandatory state observer roles, extended review timeline >18 months), the Steering Committee convenes within 5 working days to reassess the financing and tenant strategy. Committee votes on restructuring (e.g., reduce foreign equity, pivot to sovereign-only anchors, accept state oversight) or defer Phase 1 pending ANSSI clarity. Rationale: National-security review outcome is uncontrolled until ANSSI formally clears the project. Foreign co-investors and hyperscaler tenants trigger heightened scrutiny; restrictions on either can materially alter the financing structure and tenant pool. Early escalation to Steering Committee ensures governance and financing decisions are not locked in before security constraints are known. ANSSI findings that constrain tenants or co-investors affect Phase 1 FID viability and must trigger strategic recalibration. Negative Consequences: If ANSSI blocks foreign co-investor equity, the project loses EUR 1B–3B of consortium backing, forcing a 6–12 month equity restructuring and raising cost of capital by 200–300 bps (EUR 140M–280M extra annual interest). If foreign hyperscaler tenants are prohibited, the addressable customer pool shrinks to EU and sovereign users only, reducing anchor-tenant demand and forcing Phase 1 downsize to 250–500 MW. ANSSI review delays of 12+ months beyond Month 12 (2027-10-17) deadline push Phase 1 FID to Month 24–30 (2028-10-17 to 2029-04-17), extending Phase 0 and eroding tenant and lender commitments.

Debt Financing Unavailable or Below EUR 3 Billion Commitment at Acceptable Terms Escalation Level: Gate Review and Kill Authority Committee (escalates to Steering Committee for Phase 1 FID decision) Approval Process: PMO Finance Lead engages lenders (Month 2–3 = 2026-12-17 to 2027-01-17) to establish debt-capacity and gate criteria. Non-binding term sheet targeted Month 9 (2027-07-17); final commitment due Month 12 (2027-10-17). If lenders offer less than EUR 3B or impose unacceptable terms (spreads >300 bps, covenant DSCR >1.40x, equity cushion >40%), Kill Authority Committee issues formal report recommending Phase 1 downsizing to 250 MW (EUR 2.5B capex, 50% debt = EUR 1.25B) or Phase 1 deferral pending equity restructuring. Steering Committee votes on downsizing, deferral or override. Rationale: Debt financing is a gate precondition for Phase 1 FID. Lenders require specific evidence: firm RTE connection offer, signed tenant take-or-pay, bounded environmental liability, firm power contract. Absence of debt at acceptable cost means equity must fund EUR 4B–5B out of EUR 5B–10B capex, far above the proposed 40% equity cap. Early escalation to Kill Authority Committee ensures financing reality is assessed before the Steering Committee votes on Phase 1 FID. Unacceptable debt terms signal market skepticism and require Phase 1 resizing. Negative Consequences: Debt financing failure forces Phase 1 downsize from 1 GW to 500 MW (losing EUR 2.5B–5B revenue growth), or Phase 1 deferral 6–12 months pending equity restructuring. If equity raises EUR 4B–5B instead of EUR 2B–4B, returns compress by 3–5 percentage points (IRR falls from 10–12% target to 5–7%), eroding co-investor appetite and extending equity close by 6–12 months. Inability to close debt in Month 12–13 (2027-10-17 to 2027-11-17) window pushes Phase 1 FID to Month 18–24 (2028-04-17 to 2028-10-17), causing tenant and lender commitments to expire and requiring costly re-engagement.

Sunk-Cost Pressure on Investment Committee to Override Kill Criteria Escalation Level: Project Steering Committee (with Gate Review and Kill Authority Committee oversight and published dissent) Approval Process: Investment Committee Charter (Month 1 = 2026-11-17) establishes veto authority and numeric kill thresholds. At Month 12 (2027-10-17) Phase 0 gate, if one or more thresholds are unmet but the Steering Committee pressures a Phase 1 FID approval, the Gate Review and Kill Authority Committee documents formal dissent and publishes it to lenders and co-investors within 2 working days. Lenders have 10 working days to invoke debt covenants or capital-call conditions; co-investors may demand governance restructuring or capital-return options. Escalation ensures sunk cost (EUR 250M–750M Phase 0) does not override stated kill criteria. Rationale: Stated kill criteria (grid >1 GW, land 70%, tenants 30%, debt EUR 3B, social license 2 municipalities) only constrain behavior if someone with no stake in continuing can enforce them. Without independent authority and transparency, sunk-cost momentum routinely overrides gates. An independent committee with veto power and published dissent makes override decisions visible to debt and equity sources, creating accountability. Published dissent also protects individual committee members from blame if Phase 1 later fails due to unmet gate criteria. Negative Consequences: If kill criteria are overridden and Phase 1 proceeds despite unmet thresholds, the project enters Phase 1 with known feasibility gaps (e.g., no firm RTE offer, <30% tenant demand, no debt financing). Phase 1 construction delays, cost overruns and potential cancellation are likely, stranding EUR 5B–10B capex and destroying equity value. Lenders who discover override decisions after the fact may invoke cross-default clauses or accelerate debt, forcing emergency equity rescue or insolvency. Co-investors may sue the developer for breach of governance, demanding return of capital or loss compensation.

Unexpected Brownfield Contamination or Remediation Cost Exceeding Bounded Estimate (>EUR 100 Million Per Site) Escalation Level: Compliance, Environmental & Social License Committee (escalates to Steering Committee and Kill Authority Committee if exceeding Phase 0 budget or Phase 1 contingency) Approval Process: Phase I desktop assessments completed Month 1 (2026-11-17); Phase II intrusive surveys Month 3 (2027-01-17) identify contamination and bound remediation to EUR 0–100M per site (proposed threshold). If Phase II findings show remediation exceeding EUR 100M for a primary site, committee escalates immediately with a site-exclusion recommendation or a renegotiation strategy with the landowner/public remediation body. If cumulative remediation across shortlisted sites exceeds the Phase 0 reserve (EUR 100M–300M estimate), the committee recommends parcel substitution or Phase 1 contingency drawdown authorization from the Steering Committee. Rationale: Brownfield contamination is the least quantifiable Phase 0 cost and carries lender and equity risk if discovered late in Phase 1. Bounding liability in Phase 0 via intrusive surveys and seller indemnities protects the project from cost escalation and schedule slippage during Phase 1. A EUR 100M per-site ceiling is realistic for legacy industrial contamination; above this, remediation becomes a project-level feasibility constraint and justifies site substitution or downsize. Negative Consequences: Contamination discovery during Phase 1 construction triggers health-and-safety work stoppages, regulatory enforcement, and unbudgeted remediation of EUR 100M–400M+. Cost overrun forces Phase 1 capex to exceed the EUR 10B ceiling, triggering debt-covenant breaches or equity restructuring. Schedule delay from remediation (6–18 months) erodes RTE queue timing and extends carrying costs by EUR 200M–500M. Liability disputes between the developer and landowner/public authority can tie up capital in escrow or litigation for 2–4 years, starving Phase 1 construction of cash flow.

Municipal or Community Opposition Blocks Permits or Forces Unacceptable Design Compromises Escalation Level: Compliance, Environmental & Social License Committee (escalates to Steering Committee if support from 2 of 3 municipalities not obtained by Month 12 = 2027-10-17) Approval Process: Community and Stakeholder Lead establishes municipal liaison committee (Month 2 = 2026-12-17) and conducts early public consultation (Month 3 = 2027-01-17, 4-week feedback). Draft community-benefit agreement (EUR 50M–150M Phase 1–2 estimate) negotiated by Month 6 (2027-04-17). Written support from at least 2 of 3 most-affected municipalities targeted by Month 12 (2027-10-17). If opposition escalates to formal municipal refusal or organized legal challenge by Month 6 (2027-04-17), committee immediately escalates to Steering Committee with revised feasibility and cost-impact assessment. Committee recommends split-campus pivot (site substitution), Phase 1 scope reduction or project deferral. Rationale: Social license from municipalities and communities is a gate condition for permitting viability. Organized opposition can sustain legal appeals extending permitting by 24–48 months, eroding feasibility. Early, transparent engagement with municipalities and structured community-benefit agreements reduce opposition risk and build political support. Escalation of opposition at Month 6 (2027-04-17) halfway through Phase 0 allows the Steering Committee to trigger topology or scope changes before permitting investment is committed. Negative Consequences: Sustained municipal opposition or formal refusal can block permits indefinitely, rendering a chosen site infeasible. Forced pivot to alternative site mid-Phase 0 triggers EUR 100M–250M additional Phase 0 spend on surveys and permitting preparation. Legal appeals to permits can extend authorization timelines by 24–48 months, pushing Phase 1 energization from target Months 42–48 (2030-04-17 to 2030-10-17) to Months 66–84 (2032-04-17 to 2033-10-17), outside the project's feasibility window. Unacceptable design compromises (reduced hall density, ecological setbacks, farmland compensation) force capex escalation of EUR 500M–1.5B or capacity reduction of 20–30%.

Monitoring Progress

1. Gate Criterion Status Tracking and Numeric Threshold Validation

Monitoring Tools/Platforms:

  • Gate Review and Kill Authority Committee monthly pass/fail reports
  • External red-team assessment dashboard (grid, land, tenants, financing, social license)
  • Phase 0 milestone tracking spreadsheet (gate deadlines, evidence receipt dates)
  • RTE hosting-capacity audit and preliminary letter repository

Frequency: Monthly (Months 0–12 = 2026-10-17 to 2027-10-17), formal gate assessment Months 3, 6, 9, 12 (2027-01-17, 2027-04-17, 2027-07-17, 2027-10-17)

Responsible Role: Gate Review and Kill Authority Committee (Independent Chair, independent external directors, with External Red Team providing pass/fail opinions); escalates to Project Steering Committee if threshold breach occurs

Adaptation Process: Monthly red-team reports assess each of five gate criteria (grid hosting ≥1 GW cumulative, land ≥70% optioned, tenants ≥30% signed, debt ≥EUR 3B, social license ≥2 municipalities) against published numeric thresholds. If any criterion shows High-likelihood breach, the committee issues a formal gate-status report within 5 working days to the Steering Committee and recommends one of: (i) Phase 1 FID approval (all thresholds met), (ii) conditional approval pending resolution, (iii) Phase 1 downsizing (e.g., 250 MW if tenants <30%), (iv) Phase 1 deferral, or (v) project exit. The Steering Committee votes within 5 working days; approval requires two-of-three alignment (sponsor, consortium, independent director). Override of the Kill Authority Committee's recommendation triggers mandatory dissent disclosure to lenders and co-investors within 2 working days.

Adaptation Trigger: Specific numeric breaches at defined deadlines: (i) RTE preliminary feasibility letter not received or hosting capacity <500 MW by Month 6 (2027-04-17); (ii) <70% of chosen parcel optioned non-coercively at <15% above benchmark by Month 4 (2027-02-17); (iii) <30% signed anchor-tenant take-or-pay by Month 9 (2027-07-17); (iv) debt commitment <EUR 3B or unacceptable terms by Month 12 (2027-10-17); (v) <2 of 3 municipalities' written support by Month 12 (2027-10-17). Any single breach triggers formal escalation; multiple breaches may recommend Phase 1 cancellation or major restructuring.

2. Grid Hosting Capacity and RTE Connection Engagement Tracking

Monitoring Tools/Platforms:

  • RTE pre-submission dialogue log (letters, meeting minutes, submitted requests)
  • Independent RTE hosting-capacity audit report (Month 9 = 2027-07-17 deliverable)
  • Grid reinforcement cost-estimate tracker (phase reinforcement, substation siting, timeline impact)
  • Connection-offer timeline and queue-position monitoring spreadsheet

Frequency: Bi-weekly PMO Grid and Power Lead + RTE liaison; monthly summary to Steering Committee; formal RTE letter or written evidence due Month 6 (2027-04-17); audit published Month 9 (2027-07-17)

Responsible Role: PMO Grid and Power Lead, with Independent RTE Hosting-Capacity Auditor, RTE liaison counsel; reports to Gate Review Committee monthly and Steering Committee quarterly

Adaptation Process: Grid hosting capacity findings feed directly into topology decision (Month 4 = 2027-02-17): single square only if RTE written evidence confirms ≥1 GW to that node; otherwise split-campus default. If RTE's preliminary letter (due Month 6 = 2027-04-17) shows hosting below 500 MW, the Kill Authority Committee recommends split-campus topology pivot or Phase 1 capacity downsize to 250 MW. If RTE offers favorable tranche-based terms (500 MW + 1 GW pathway), power-procurement strategy (EDF negotiations) and tenant-acquisition targets are confirmed as achievable; if terms are restrictive (>15% curtailment, extended connection timelines), lease pricing and BESS strategy are adjusted. If transmission-reinforcement cost-share exceeds budget (EUR 1.5B threshold), the Steering Committee decides whether to accept the cost as Phase 1 capex or request RTE cost-share under a co-development agreement.

Adaptation Trigger: RTE preliminary feasibility letter not received or capacity <500 MW by Month 6 (2027-04-17) → kill criterion breached, recommend split-campus or downsize. RTE timeline slips >6 months beyond Month 6 (2027-04-17) → Steering Committee reassesses Phase 0 and Phase 1 schedule, triggers deferral or topology re-evaluation. Transmission reinforcement cost >EUR 1.5B or timeline >48 months (2030-10-17) → cost-share negotiation or Phase 1 capacity reduction. Curtailment requirement >15% annual → walk-away trigger per power-strategy framework, Phase 1 reduced to 500–750 MW or less.

3. Land Assembly and Parcel Acquisition Feasibility Validation

Monitoring Tools/Platforms:

  • Parcel-by-parcel land survey and ownership-chain map (Phase 0 Month 3 = 2027-01-17 deliverable)
  • Option agreement tracking spreadsheet (% parcels optioned, expiry dates, holdout locations)
  • Phase I and Phase II environmental site assessment reports (contamination findings, remediation-cost bounds)
  • Land-assembly feasibility assessment report (Month 3 = 2027-01-17 and Month 4 = 2027-02-17 and 2027-02-17 decisions)

Frequency: Monthly land-assembly lead updates to PMO; formal feasibility assessments Month 3 (2027-01-17) and Month 4 (2027-02-17); Phase II ESA findings by Month 3 (2027-01-17); topology decision locked Month 4 (2027-02-17)

Responsible Role: PMO Land Assembly Lead (with real-estate counsel), supported by Phase II ESA survey teams and municipal land-registry liaisons; escalates to PMO and Steering Committee if >30% of target parcel cannot be optioned or remediation exceeds EUR 100M per site

Adaptation Process: Phase 0 Month 1–3 (2026-11-17 to 2027-01-17) land survey ranks candidate sites by assemblability, holdout risk and land cost. By Month 3 (2027-01-17), if ≥70% of the single-square parcel is optioned non-coercively at <15% above benchmark, the single square remains viable and Phase I ESA focuses on that core. If single-square assemblability falls short of 70%, split-campus topology is developed as the default: Cambrai ~500 MW node validated at ≥80% optioned, Dunkirk ~250 MW, Valenciennes ~250 MW each assessed separately. Phase II contamination findings (Month 3 = 2027-01-17) rule out sites with remediation >EUR 100M (propose bounding); shortlisted parcels have seller indemnity or public-remediation-body liability assumption negotiated. If holdout clusters (e.g., families refusing to relocate) block >20% of a primary site, the parcel is substituted or the node capacity is reduced. If Phase II finds unexpected contamination during Phase 1 construction, remediation costs exceeding the Phase 1 contingency (EUR 100M–300M) trigger debt-covenant escalation.

Adaptation Trigger: <70% of single-square parcel optioned or remediation >EUR 100M per site by Month 4 (2027-02-17) → split-campus topology forced, Phase 0 extended 3–6 months, Phase 0 spend escalates to EUR 750M. >20% of target parcel blocked by holdouts → parcel substitution or node-capacity downsize. Phase II contamination discovery after Phase 0 gate (Phase 1 construction) exceeding contingency → litigation risk, remediation delay 6–18 months, carrying cost EUR 200M–500M, Phase 1 FID contingent on revised liability allocation.

4. Anchor-Tenant Demand and Take-or-Pay Acquisition Tracking

Monitoring Tools/Platforms:

  • Tenant pipeline dashboard (LOI vs. binding term sheet status, credit validation, reservation-fee receipts)
  • Take-or-pay lease term sheets and capacity reservations log (signed agreements, MW reserved, tenor, price)
  • Tenant workload and cluster-size specifications (used to validate latency tolerance for split-campus architecture)
  • Reservation-fee payment tracking (EUR 10M–50M per 100 MW, crediting against future rent)

Frequency: Bi-weekly tenant sourcing updates; monthly pipeline status to PMO and Steering Committee; formal binding term-sheet deadline Month 9 (2027-07-17); reservation-fee payment confirmation by Month 12 (2027-10-17)

Responsible Role: PMO Tenancy and Revenue Lead (with commercial advisers and legal counsel); escalates to Gate Review Committee if signed take-or-pay falls below 30% of Phase 1 target by Month 9 (2027-07-17)

Adaptation Process: Tenant sourcing targets 2–3 global hyperscalers (A−/A+ credit) and 2–3 sovereign/European anchors (sovereign guarantee or A−/BBB+ parent) in parallel. Non-binding LOIs collected Month 3–6 (2027-01-17 to 2027-04-17) are tracked for engagement momentum but not counted toward the 30% gate criterion. Binding term sheets (5–10 year lease, capacity reserved, reservation fee EUR 10M–50M per 100 MW paid upfront) are required by Month 9 (2027-07-17); only signed agreements count. If signed take-or-pay reaches only 20% of Phase 1 (200 MW on 1 GW base) by Month 9 (2027-07-17), the Kill Authority Committee recommends Phase 1 downsize to 250–500 MW matching actual committed demand, extending Phase 1 FID to Month 18–24 (2028-04-17 to 2028-10-17) pending demand maturation. Lease price (EUR 1.1M per MW-year, non-energy) and SLA terms (99.5% uptime, curtailment carve-out to 10% annual) are confirmed in term sheets; pass-through energy indexation anchors tenants to realized EUR/MWh cost. If a committed anchor tenant requests a 10% price discount (e.g., to offset perceived curtailment risk), debt service coverage falls from 1.34x to 1.15x, requiring equity cure or debt reduction (proposed structural adaptation: negotiate curtailment exclusion rather than price discount).

Adaptation Trigger: <30% signed take-or-pay (i.e., <150 MW on 500 MW base, <300 MW on 1 GW base) by Month 9 (2027-07-17) → Phase 1 downsize to 250–500 MW or Phase 1 FID deferral 6–12 months. >20% anchor-tenant lease-price-discount requests → DSCR <1.30x, triggers debt restructuring or Phase 1 downsize. Any anchor-tenant non-renewal or early-termination signal during Phase 1 construction → revenue risk flagged, replacement-tenant sourcing accelerated, potential phase-advance slippage if replacement not secured within 6 months.

5. Power Procurement and EDF Supply Contract Negotiation Tracking

Monitoring Tools/Platforms:

  • EDF engagement log and LOI/term-sheet tracker (non-binding LOI by Month 6 = 2027-04-17, term sheet by Month 9 = 2027-07-17)
  • Power-market study and EUR/MWh pricing forecast (assumed EUR 50–70/MWh range, stress test at +EUR 30/MWh)
  • BESS and demand-flexibility feasibility assessment (50–200 MWh, cost estimate, grid-interaction modeling)
  • Energy cost pass-through agreement templates and pricing-indexation schedule (annual CPI+X% formula)

Frequency: Monthly Grid and Power Lead updates to PMO; EDF LOI due Month 6 (2027-04-17); term sheet and pricing locked Month 9 (2027-07-17); binding contract not before Phase 1 FID (Month 12 = 2027-10-17 conditional)

Responsible Role: PMO Grid and Power Lead (with independent power-market adviser, EDF liaison); escalates to Steering Committee if EDF terms are unavailable or pricing exceeds EUR 100/MWh (proposed stress threshold)

Adaptation Process: Weeks 1–8 of Phase 0 (Months 0–1 = 2026-10-17 to 2026-11-17), PMO initiates EDF negotiations for a non-binding letter of intent confirming willingness to discuss 500 MW+ baseload at a capped price range. By Month 6 (2027-04-17), EDF LOI targets ≥500 MW, ≥10-year tenor, price EUR 50–70/MWh (assumed, not verified). Phase 0 power-market study models energy cost impact: if delivered cost rises above EUR 70/MWh (e.g., EUR 80–100 due to policy shifts or grid constraints), NOI per MW falls from EUR 800k to EUR 600k (500 MW case), DSCR drops below 1.30x lender minimum, triggering either (i) lease price escalation (EUR 1.1M → EUR 1.2M+/MW-year), (ii) debt reduction from EUR 3B to EUR 2.5B (60% → 50% leverage), or (iii) Phase 2 expansion deferral. By Month 9 (2027-07-17), a detailed term sheet from EDF confirms capacity, price, tenor, curtailment/flexibility obligations and indexation formula (proposed: CPI + 50 bps indexed annually). Energy risk is passed through to tenants via indexed lease pass-through, so developer carries no volume risk beyond grid curtailment. BESS (50–200 MWh, cost EUR 20M–80M estimate) is evaluated for arbitrage value and grid-stress mitigation; if BESS ROI is positive (>5% IRR), it is funded from Phase 1 capex; otherwise optional and tenant-funded.

Adaptation Trigger: EDF LOI not received or pricing >EUR 100/MWh by Month 6 (2027-04-17) → power-gate criterion at risk, Steering Committee considers Phase 1 downsize or delay pending EDF clarity. EDF term-sheet pricing ≥EUR 80/MWh and non-indexable (fixed contract) → debt capacity drops EUR 500M–1B, equity raises required, Phase 1 FID contingent on restructured lease pricing or equity injection. Competing industrial-load requests to EDF saturate capacity <500 MW available → topology must pivot to split-campus with smaller per-node power contracts, or Phase 1 downsize to 250 MW.

6. Permitting and Environmental Authorization Timeline and Compliance Tracking

Monitoring Tools/Platforms:

  • ICPE and environmental-authorization permit-file roadmap and completion tracker (expert reports due, DREAL feedback incorporation)
  • Permit-file submission checklist and filing-date confirmation (targeted Month 8–9 = 2027-06-17 to 2027-07-17)
  • DREAL screening opinion request and timeline tracker (opinion due Month 9 = 2027-07-17)
  • Legal-challenge and appeal escalation log (none expected in Phase 0; Phase 1 monitoring plan established)

Frequency: Monthly Permitting and Environmental Lead updates; permit-file roadmap completed by Month 2 (2026-12-17); DREAL opinion due Month 9 (2027-07-17); permit-check gate at Month 18 (2028-04-17) assessing compliance with decision timeline

Responsible Role: Compliance, Environmental & Social License Committee (Permitting and Environmental Lead), with environmental and ICPE counsel; escalates to Steering Committee if DREAL timeline slips >6 months or new scope requirements emerge

Adaptation Process: Phase 0 Month 1–2 (2026-11-17 to 2026-12-17): permit-file roadmap is finalized specifying required components (ecological baseline, hydrological assessment, contamination survey, thermal modeling, security specs, community-benefit commitments). Phase I desktop ESAs and hydrological study are completed Month 1–3 (2026-11-17 to 2027-01-17); Phase II intrusive surveys (if triggered) are closed Month 3 (2027-01-17) with remediation-liability findings incorporated into permit file. Ecological master plan (completed Month 6 = 2027-04-17) provides EIA avoidance-reduction-compensation strategy. Community-benefit agreement (signed Month 6 = 2027-04-17) is appended to show local support. Permit file (single file for single-square topology, one file per node for split-campus) is submitted Month 8–9 (2027-06-17 to 2027-07-17); filing date is confirmed and tracked. DREAL screening opinion (due Month 9 = 2027-07-17) confirms EIA requirements and ICPE classification. If DREAL requires additional studies or wider EIA scope, permit-file completion date shifts from Month 9 (2027-07-17) to Month 12 (2027-10-17) and decision timeline extends from target Months 26–39 (2028-12-17 to 2030-01-17) to Months 39–52 (2030-01-17 to 2031-04-17), pushing Phase 1 energization to Month 54+ (2031-04-17+) and eroding Phase 1 schedule. Permit-check gate at Month 18 (2028-04-17): if no decision is in sight (authority response pending, legal challenge filed), Phase 1 FID becomes contingent on permit pathway clarity.

Adaptation Trigger: DREAL opinion not received or requires expanded EIA scope by Month 9 (2027-07-17) → permit timeline extends beyond target, Phase 1 decision deferred. Legal challenge to permit filed by Month 18 (2028-04-17) → appeal timeline adds 12–36 months, Phase 1 energization shifts Months 54–66 (2031-04-17 to 2032-04-17)+ (2031-04-17 to 2032-04-17+). Permit-file roadmap additions cost >EUR 20M or extend timeline >3 months → Steering Committee informed, Phase 0 tranche 4 (EUR 150M final allocation) decision may defer permitting accelerants or design refinements. ICPE classification changes to more restrictive category → Phase 1 capex +EUR 100M–300M for additional mitigation, or Phase 1 downsize if mitigation cost is unacceptable.

7. National Security Review and ANSSI Clearance Pathway Tracking

Monitoring Tools/Platforms:

  • ANSSI pre-submission confidential security governance white paper (submitted Month 1 = 2026-11-17)
  • ANSSI preliminary opinion request and timeline tracker (due Month 6 = 2027-04-17, uncontrolled)
  • Security-design framework and compliance checklist (cyber-OT separation, anti-drone systems, personnel vetting, supply-chain assurance)
  • ANSSI formal-review start confirmation (targeted Month 13 = 2027-11-17, clearance Month 25–31 = 2028-11-17 to 2029-05-17)

Frequency: Monthly Security and National-Security Lead updates to PMO; pre-submission dialogue ongoing Months 0–1 (2026-10-17 to 2026-11-17); informal ANSSI opinion due Month 6 (2027-04-17); formal review start confirmation by Month 12 (2027-10-17)

Responsible Role: PMO Security and National-Security Lead (with security and GDPR counsel, ANSSI liaison); escalates to Steering Committee immediately if ANSSI signals blocking concerns (foreign co-investor cap, tenant-access restrictions, data-residency mandates)

Adaptation Process: Phase 0 Month 0–1 (2026-10-17 to 2026-11-17): confidential pre-submission engagement with ANSSI and DGSI outlines project scope, tenant strategy (hyperscalers, sovereign AI users), foreign co-investor governance, data-residency policy, and security posture (perimeter hardening, cyber-OT separation, personnel vetting). ANSSI informal opinion due Month 6 (2027-04-17) indicates anticipated review scope, timeline and any early blocking concerns (e.g., 'foreign equity above X% is not permissible', 'non-EU tenants restricted to non-sovereign workloads'). If no blocking concerns are signaled, security gate is on track: formal ANSSI review starts Month 13 (2027-11-17, post-FID), clearance targeted Month 25–31 (2028-11-17 to 2029-05-17). If ANSSI signals blocking concerns (e.g., foreign co-investor must be limited to ≤20% equity, non-EU hyperscalers cannot access sovereign partitions), the Steering Committee convenes within 5 working days to reassess financing (consortium co-investor may need replacement) and tenant strategy (hyperscaler pool may contract). A revised security governance framework is negotiated with ANSSI; clearance pathway and timeline may extend. If ANSSI indicates formal review will take >18 months (beyond Month 31 = 2029-05-17), Phase 1 FID is contingent on ANSSI confirmation that clearance will be complete by Month 42 (2030-04-17, energization start date) or Phase 1 energization is delayed.

Adaptation Trigger: ANSSI preliminary opinion signals blocking concern (foreign co-investor cap, tenant-access restriction, data-residency mandate) by Month 6 (2027-04-17) → Steering Committee reassesses within 5 working days, may trigger financing or tenant-strategy pivot. ANSSI indicates formal-review timeline >18 months (projected clearance beyond Month 31 = 2029-05-17) by Month 12 (2027-10-17) → Phase 1 FID contingent on security-review completion by Month 42 (2030-04-17) or Phase 1 energization delayed 6–12 months. ANSSI issues final clearance restrictions on tenants or co-investor control → governance restructuring required post-FID, Phase 1 capex for security hardening may increase EUR 50M–200M if additional restrictions require design changes.

8. Community Engagement, Social License and Municipal Support Validation

Monitoring Tools/Platforms:

  • Municipal liaison committee meeting minutes (published, ongoing monthly Months 2–12 = 2026-12-17 to 2027-10-17)
  • Public consultation feedback summary and project response log (4-week comment period, feedback integrated by Month 5 = 2027-03-17)
  • Community-benefit agreement draft and final signatures (signed by Month 6 = 2027-04-17, covers labor, training, ecology, farm-sector support, municipal infrastructure)
  • Opposition escalation tracker (NGO legal challenge risk, farm-union organized action, municipal formal objection log)

Frequency: Monthly municipal liaison committee meetings (published minutes); public consultation launched Month 3 (2027-01-17), feedback closed Month 4 (2027-02-17), response published Month 5 (2027-03-17); written municipal support tracked through Month 12 (2027-10-17); legal-challenge monitoring ongoing

Responsible Role: Compliance, Environmental & Social License Committee (Community and Stakeholder Lead), with municipal and farm-sector liaisons; escalates to Steering Committee if organized opposition or formal municipal refusal emerges by Month 6 (2027-04-17)

Adaptation Process: Phase 0 Month 1–2 (2026-11-17 to 2026-12-17): municipal liaison committee is established with representatives from ≥3 most-affected municipalities; monthly dialogue is scheduled, meeting agendas and minutes are published. Month 3 (2027-01-17): public consultation is launched with transparent project overview, siting rationale, technical specs (power, cooling, footprint), environmental/social-impact scope, and 4-week comment period. Month 4–5 (2027-02-17 to 2027-03-17): feedback is compiled, project responses are drafted and published. Months 2–6 (2026-12-17 to 2027-04-17): community-benefit agreement is negotiated with municipalities, farm unions (FNSEA, Confédération Paysanne) and environmental NGOs, addressing labor/training targets (regional academy, local hiring), ecological restoration (EUR 50M–150M Phase 1–2 estimate), farm-sector support (displacement compensation, land-swap schemes, revenue-sharing on continuation zones), and municipal infrastructure upgrades. By Month 6 (2027-04-17), draft agreement is signed or a binding term sheet is in place; EUR 50M–150M Phase 1–2 commitment is contingent on permits (not Phase 0 spend). Month 9 (2027-07-17): written support letters are requested from at least 2 of 3 most-affected municipalities, indicating municipal endorsement of the project (non-binding but political signal). Month 12 (2027-10-17): formal written support (municipal council resolution or mayor letter) from ≥2 municipalities is confirmed as the social-license gate criterion. If organized opposition emerges (farm-sector legal action, environmental NGO challenge, mayor public refusal) by Month 6 (2027-04-17), the Steering Committee is informed within 5 working days and assesses whether to pivot topology (substitute site), reduce phase scope or defer permitting and land assembly.

Adaptation Trigger: Organized opposition or major legal challenge filed by a farm union or NGO by Month 6 (2027-04-17) → Steering Committee reassesses Phase 0, may trigger topology pivot or Phase 1 defer. Formal municipal refusal (mayor or council resolution against the project) in ≥2 of 3 target municipalities by Month 9 (2027-07-17) → social-license gate fails, Phase 1 FID cannot proceed, project deferral or site substitution required. Written municipal support from <2 municipalities by Month 12 (2027-10-17) → social-license gate criterion unmet, Phase 1 FID recommendation is 'conditional on achieving 2 municipal letters within 6 months' or 'project deferred'. Any municipal request for unacceptable design compromises (e.g., reduce capacity 30%, relocate all halls outside municipality) → cost escalation EUR 250M–1.5B, triggers Steering Committee scope-trade decision.

9. Phase 1 Debt Financing Credibility and Lender Engagement Tracking

Monitoring Tools/Platforms:

  • Lender outreach and engagement log (EIB, KfW, French banks, infrastructure funds, Month 2–9 = 2026-12-17 to 2027-07-17)
  • Debt-financing term sheet and non-binding LOI tracker (due Month 9 = 2027-07-17, with gate-success conditions specified)
  • Financial model and debt-service coverage sensitivity spreadsheet (DSCR base case 1.34x, stress case 1.15x)
  • Lender covenant and gate-trigger documentation (debt covenants tied to RTE, tenant, permitting gate achievements)

Frequency: Monthly PMO Finance Lead updates; lender outreach Month 2–3 (2026-12-17 to 2027-01-17), preliminary feedback Month 6 (2027-04-17), non-binding term sheet Month 9 (2027-07-17), lender final-commitment decision contingent on all Phase 0 gates Month 12–13 (2027-10-17 to 2027-11-17)

Responsible Role: PMO Finance and Lender Relations Lead (with infrastructure finance counsel and arranger); escalates to Kill Authority Committee if debt commitment <EUR 3B or terms (spread >300 bps, DSCR covenant >1.40x) are unacceptable

Adaptation Process: Phase 0 Month 2–3 (2026-12-17 to 2027-01-17): PMO Finance Lead engages prospective lenders (EIB, KfW, French banks, infrastructure funds) to present the Phase 0 gating framework and to understand debt-capacity and term-sheet conditions. Lender feedback (Month 6 = 2027-04-17) typically requires: (i) RTE firm connection offer, (ii) signed tenant take-or-pay for ≥30% of capacity, (iii) bounded environmental liability, (iv) firm power-supply contract or LOI, (v) DSCR >1.30x on stabilized assumptions. A preliminary financial model is developed (Month 4 = 2027-02-17) modeling 500 MW (EUR 5B capex, 60% debt = EUR 3B, annual debt service EUR 299M) and stress cases (tenure reduction, lease-price discount, cost overrun). Non-binding lender term sheet due Month 9 (2027-07-17) confirms debt capacity (EUR 3B–3.5B for 500 MW), tenor (12–15 years), pricing (benchmark + 200 bps estimate), and gate conditions for final commitment. If lenders signal debt <EUR 3B (capacity constraint) or spreads >300 bps (cost of capital increase), the Kill Authority Committee flags a financing-gate breach and recommends Phase 1 downsize to 250 MW (EUR 2.5B capex, EUR 1.5B debt) or Phase 1 FID deferral pending equity restructuring. Phase 1 FID approval (Month 12 = 2027-10-17) triggers final debt-commitment close (Month 13–18 = 2027-11-17 to 2028-04-17), with lenders requiring confirmations of all Phase 0 gates and post-FID financial close conditions (tenant lease executions, RTE connection agreement, power-supply contract, environmental permits on track).

Adaptation Trigger: Lender feedback (Month 6 = 2027-04-17) indicates debt capacity <EUR 3B for 500 MW → Phase 1 downsize to 250 MW or Phase 1 defer 6–12 months. Lender spreads >300 bps (raised cost of capital 2–3 pcts annually) → project economics erode, IRR falls 1–2 percentage points, Phase 1 FID contingent on equity injection or lease price escalation. Lender term sheet (Month 9 = 2027-07-17) gates final commitment on Phase 0 gate achievements not met by Month 12 (2027-10-17) (e.g., RTE letter missing, tenants <30%, ANSSI blocking) → lender commitment is void, debt unavailable, Phase 1 FID fails, project exits or defers pending gate resolution.

10. Water Resource Feasibility and Cooling Design Validation

Monitoring Tools/Platforms:

  • Hydrological and water-stress assessment study (completed Month 4 = 2027-02-17, estimate)
  • Regional water-authority consultation and preliminary opinion (due Month 6 = 2027-04-17)
  • Dry-cooler thermal-design-day modelling at 35°C ambient (PUE sensitivity, peak grid load impact)
  • Water-permitting pathway documentation (closed-loop cooling confirmed feasible, zero evaporative-water rule validated)

Frequency: Monthly water-resources management by Compliance committee; hydrology study due Month 4 (2027-02-17); water-authority opinion due Month 6 (2027-04-17); thermal modelling integrated into design reviews by Month 6 (2027-04-17); ongoing monitoring through Phase 1 permitting

Responsible Role: Compliance, Environmental & Social License Committee (Water Resources Manager), with hydrologist and water-law counsel; escalates to Steering Committee if water authority denies closed-loop feasibility or imposes restrictive abstraction limits

Adaptation Process: Phase 0 Month 1–4 (2026-11-17 to 2027-02-17): hydrological study assesses regional water stress (drought frequency and severity), competing water users (agricultural, municipal, industrial), and dry-cooler performance at extreme ambient temperatures (35°C design day). Modeling projects PUE under hot-weather scenarios (base case 1.15–1.25, hot-weather stress 1.35–1.5) and electrical load impact (peak load increase 5–15% during summer stress events). Month 3–4 (2027-01-17 to 2027-02-17): regional water authority (Agence de l'Eau Artois-Picardie) is formally consulted on closed-loop direct-to-chip cooling feasibility, water-abstraction impacts (none expected, zero freshwater withdrawal), and any permits required (stormwater management, groundwater protection). By Month 6 (2027-04-17), water authority provides written preliminary opinion confirming closed-loop cooling is permissible and no water-abstraction permits are required beyond standard stormwater authorization. If water authority raises concerns (drought vulnerability, groundwater interaction, competing demand), design review is triggered: options include hybrid cooling with limited evaporative water (risky in permitting), BESS expansion to reduce summer peak load, or capacity reduction. Thermal-design-day modeling validates PUE <1.30 at 35°C; if modelling shows PUE >1.30, design cost escalates (EUR 200M–500M for enhanced cooling or campus downsizing 20–30%) or grid peak-load impact triggers RTE curtailment negotiations.

Adaptation Trigger: Water authority opinion (Month 6 = 2027-04-17) denies closed-loop cooling feasibility or imposes water-abstraction restrictions → design review triggered, hybrid cooling option evaluated (if permissible), Phase 1 capacity downsize or site substitution. Thermal modelling shows PUE >1.30 at 35°C design day (Month 6 = 2027-04-17) → cooling-cost escalation EUR 200M–500M or Phase 1 downsize to 250 MW. Grid peak-load impact (5–15%) during summer stress exceeds RTE capacity buffer → curtailment obligation rises above 10% target, power-gate criterion at risk, Phase 1 capacity constrained by grid thermal limits rather than developer choice.

Monitoring Tools/Platforms:

  • Fiber-route audit by independent telecom auditor (physical path maps, duct-separation verification, landing-point analysis)
  • Carrier capacity commitment and letters of intent (at least 2 independent routes per destination, lit by Phase 1 energization Month 42–48 = 2030-04-17 to 2030-10-17)
  • Developer-built fiber cost and rights-of-way estimate (EUR 100M–500M per 100–200 km route, if carrier routes unavailable)
  • Landing-point concentration risk assessment (subsea cable pinch points, redundancy targets ≥2 UK, ≥2 FR/BE landings, no single landing >25% capacity)

Responsible Role: PMO Grid and Power Lead or Tenancy and Revenue Lead (with independent fiber-route auditor, carrier liaisons); escalates to Steering Committee if <2 independent routes are available or landing-point concentration risk is unmitigated

Adaptation Process: Phase 0 Month 1–3 (2026-11-17 to 2027-01-17): independent fiber auditor is commissioned to map physical-route claims from all candidate carriers (e.g., 'route A and route B are independent') and to audit actual duct paths, bridge crossings, subterranean shared facilities and landing stations. Auditor delivers detailed physical-path verification by Month 9 (2027-07-17). Month 3–9 (2027-01-17 to 2027-07-17): carriers are approached for capacity commitments (≥100 Tbps redundant capacity per route, available at Phase 1 energization). If independent carrier routes are not available (e.g., all carriers share a single landing station, rendering claimed diversity false), developer commits to build or co-invest in a separate route (EUR 100M–500M per 100–200 km), with rights-of-way negotiated along rail, canal or pipeline corridors. Subsea landings near Dunkirk or Channel access are assessed for concentration risk; if all routes funnel through one landing facility, geographic redundancy is compromised and subsea co-investment is evaluated. By Month 9 (2027-07-17), carrier LOIs or written capacity commitments confirm at least 2 independent routes to each of Paris, London, Brussels, Amsterdam, Frankfurt with ≥100 Tbps capacity and <25% per-landing concentration. If routes are not confirmed, Phase 1 design includes developer-built fiber as capex (cost EUR 100M–500M) or Phase 1 connectivity is contingent on carrier delivery by Phase 1 energization (risk of delay if carrier construction slips).
