Adaptation Trigger: Fiber audit reveals claimed-independent routes share landing station or conduit (Month 9 = 2027-07-17) → latency or resilience risk exposed, developer commits to build separate route or Phase 1 FID contingent on new fiber investment (EUR 100M–500M capex, 6–12 month construction). Carrier capacity commitments not in hand by Month 9 (2027-07-17) → Phase 1 connectivity delayed 6–12 months unless developer-built route is pre-contracted. Subsea landing-point concentration (all routes through 1 facility) not mitigated → sabotage or natural-disaster risk to all cross-border traffic, Phase 1 FID contingent on additional landing or subsea-cable co-investment.

12. Topology Decision and Feasibility Trade-Off Validation

Monitoring Tools/Platforms:

  • Topology-decision package (single-square vs. split-campus comparison, prepared Month 3–4 = 2027-01-17 to 2027-02-17)
  • Land-assemblability assessment per topology (% parcel optioned, holdout clusters, cost impact)
  • Grid-capacity per-node estimates (RTE preliminary advice per site, phased connection timelines)
  • Split-campus fiber and latency analysis (inter-node dark-fiber cost, round-trip latency vs. workload tolerance)
  • Detailed capex and per-MW cost by topology (single-square EUR 5B–10B vs. split EUR 5.5B–9.2B, schedule impact)

Frequency: Topology decision locked at Month 4 (2027-02-17); supporting analysis and evidence compiled Months 1–4 (2026-11-17 to 2027-02-17); formal vote and publication by Steering Committee at Month 4 (2027-02-17)

Responsible Role: PMO Land Assembly, Grid, and Tenancy leads (collaborative analysis); Steering Committee votes; Kill Authority Committee monitors for compliance with documented decision criteria

Adaptation Process: Phase 0 Month 1–3 (2026-11-17 to 2027-01-17): preliminary land-assemblability assessment (Month 3 = 2027-01-17) measures single-square's viability (% parcel optioned) and split-campus nodes' individual viability (Cambrai 80%+, Dunkirk 80%+, Valenciennes 80%+). RTE pre-submission dialogue (Month 1–3 = 2026-11-17 to 2027-01-17) gathers preliminary grid-capacity signals per site; written RTE preliminary letter is not due until Month 6 (2027-04-17), but early informal guidance informs topology choice. Phase 0 Month 4 (2027-02-17): topology-decision meeting is held. Single-square is selected ONLY if (i) at least 70% of target parcel is optioned, AND (ii) RTE written evidence of at least 1 GW capacity is already in hand (not due until Month 6 = 2027-04-17, so this criterion is rarely met by Month 4 = 2027-02-17). If single-square does not meet both criteria, split-campus is the default. Split-campus nodes are ranked by grid capacity per node and land-assemblability per node; typically Cambrai ~500 MW (most assemblable, largest grid offer), Dunkirk ~250 MW (heavy industrial, Gravelines nuclear nearby), Valenciennes ~250 MW (second brownfield, Brussels proximity). Latency tolerance for split-campus is assessed via tenant workload inputs (cluster sizes, inter-node communication frequency); if latent-critical training workloads are >50% of demand, split-campus becomes operationally risky and single-square is preferred if land permits. Phase 1 capex and schedule differ: single-square USD 1.0 GW centralized, ~12 months construction, energization Month 48 (2030-10-17); split-campus 2–3 nodes sequenced (Cambrai first Month 42–48 = 2030-04-17 to 2030-10-17, then Dunkirk Month 54+ = 2031-04-17+), total build 24+ months, per-MW capex higher 5–10% due to duplication. Decision is documented in a topology-decision paper, published to PMO, Steering Committee, lenders, co-investors and Kill Authority Committee.

Adaptation Trigger: Land-assemblability fails for single-square (<70% optioned by Month 4 = 2027-02-17) → split-campus forced, Phase 0 extended 3–6 months for node-level feasibility studies (EUR 100M–250M additional spend). RTE preliminary advice suggests grid capacity <1 GW total (Month 3–4 = 2027-01-17 to 2027-02-17 informal signals) → split-campus becomes default to de-risk capacity via multiple smaller nodes. Tenant workload analysis shows >50% latency-critical training workloads by Month 3 (2027-01-17) → single-square preferred on operational grounds, land-assemblability and grid must be forced to support it or Phase 1 capacity downsize. Late topology change (Month 9 = 2027-07-17 or later) → capex rework EUR 250M–500M, Phase 0 gate deferred, Phase 1 FID pushed to Month 18+ (2028-04-17+).

Governance Extra

Governance Validation Checks

  1. Completeness: All four Phase 0 governance bodies are chartered (Steering Committee, PMO, Kill Authority, Compliance Committee) with defined roles, responsibilities, and decision authorities. Phase 1 transition and Phase 2+ expansion gates are outlined. However, missing are: (1) explicit legal-entity and liability-allocation framework (who is ultimately accountable if a gate is overridden and Phase 1 fails?), (2) third-party adviser escalation protocols (how do RTE, DREAL, ANSSI findings flow back into committee decisions?), (3) conflict-of-interest and revolving-door policies for committee members and advisers, and (4) post-gate closure handoff procedures (what happens to Phase 0 governance bodies once Phase 1 begins?).
  2. Consistency: Major internal inconsistency between the Kill Authority Committee's stated veto power and the Steering Committee's stated supermajority override authority. The framework says 'recommendation is binding unless overridden by supermajority' but does not clarify: what happens if the Kill Authority recommends 'cancel' and the Sponsor/Consortium/Independent Director vote 2-1 to override? Does the Kill Authority's published dissent to lenders automatically trigger debt-covenant review? Who decides whether the override is within governance authority or a breach? This ambiguity will materialize at Month 12 (2027-10-17) if any gate fails.
  3. Gaps in decision rights and escalation: The framework allocates decisions to committees at the €50M threshold, but does not specify how the PMO resolves workstream-level conflicts below €50M (e.g., if Land Assembly and Permitting both claim limited Phase 0 tranche 2 funds [€250M], who arbitrates?). Further, PMO operational decisions triggering gate-critical outcomes (e.g., deciding not to commission a Phase II survey on a key site, deferring fiber-route audit, reducing EDA survey scope to save cost) should escalate to the Kill Authority for gate-impact review, but the framework does not mandate this. Similarly, the Compliance Committee's authority to 'veto' permit-file content for 'legal or reputational risk' is undefined—does this override the PMO Director or escalate to Steering Committee?
  4. Gaps in external-party engagement and escalation: The framework treats RTE, DREAL, ANSSI, EDF and lenders as information sources (written letters, opinions, term sheets), but does not define how preliminary or negative feedback escalates. For example, if RTE issues a preliminary feasibility letter at Month 6 (2027-04-17) saying 'capacity above 500 MW is uncertain pending further study,' does this pass or fail the grid gate? If ANSSI indicates in Month 6 (2027-04-17) that formal review will take 24 months (vs. target 12–18), is this a kill trigger or a 'conditional pass' with Phase 1 contingency? The framework lacks decision rules for ambiguous external outcomes, forcing ad-hoc Steering Committee judgment at the gate.
  5. Gaps in contingency and conditional-pass pathways: The framework allows 'conditional approval' if a gate is deferred (e.g., RTE letter due Month 6 = 2027-04-17 but Phase 0 gate at Month 12 = 2027-10-17, so a conditional pass assumes RTE will deliver by Month 18 = 2028-04-17). However, it does not define: (1) what happens if the condition is not met by the target (automatic Phase 1 cancellation?), (2) how Phase 0 team and capital are held or run down during a deferral, (3) whether land options, grid pre-engineering, and tenant term sheets remain valid or must be renewed/re-negotiated, and (4) how lender and co-investor capital commitments are structured for a conditional close (draw down tranches as conditions resolve, or wait for all conditions before any draw?). This gap is material because external authorities (RTE, DREAL, ANSSI) will almost certainly slip beyond their Month 6–9 (2027-04-17 to 2027-07-17) informal-opinion deadlines.
  6. Gaps in kill-criteria enforcement when sunk cost pressures override: The framework vests kill authority in an independent committee and mandates dissent disclosure, but does not specify the remedy if override occurs anyway. For example, if the Sponsor/Consortium vote to proceed with Phase 1 FID despite a failed grid gate (RTE offering only 250 MW vs. 500 MW minimum), and the Kill Authority publishes dissent to lenders within 2 working days, what happens next? Do lenders have a contractual right to withdraw financing, or is withdrawal optional? If lenders withdraw, does the Sponsor have 10 working days to replace them, or is Phase 1 automatically stalled? This gap leaves the framework dependent on lender discipline rather than governance structure to enforce kill criteria.

Tough Questions

  1. What specific performance metrics and evidence will the Gate Review and Kill Authority Committee require to confirm that the RTE grid-hosting threshold (at least 500 MW within 36 months) is met at Month 6 (2027-04-17)? A 'preliminary feasibility letter' is vague; does this require a signed non-binding offer, a detailed transmission-reinforcement cost-share agreement, or just written acknowledgment that the site is under study?
  2. If the Land Assembly Lead determines by Month 3 (2027-01-17) that less than 70% of the single-square parcel can be optioned non-coercively at below 15% above benchmark, who decides the topology pivot to split campus, and does Phase 0 automatically extend by 3–6 months and the budget to €750M, or can the Sponsor force a single-square continuation at higher cost/risk? What is the decision-maker's accountability if the forced single-square later fails to assemble?
  3. By Month 9 (2027-07-17), the PMO Tenancy Lead must show binding take-or-pay leases for at least 30% of Phase 1 capacity. What evidence of 'binding' satisfies the gate? Signed leases with all terms locked? Executed term sheets with only pricing indexed to be finalized at Phase 1 FID? Reservation-fee payments received? If a tenant signs but then exercises an early-termination or renegotiation clause during Phase 0, does the signed commitment count toward the 30%, or must the Kill Authority re-assess at the gate?
  4. The framework assumes EDF will provide a non-binding LOI by Month 6 (2027-04-17) and a term sheet by Month 9 (2027-07-17), but does not state what happens if EDF declines (citing policy uncertainty, competing load, or pricing volatility). What is the PMO's fallback: pursue a portfolio of smaller PPAs and spot exposure, and accept higher energy cost variance? If energy cost escalates from €50–70/MWh to €80–100/MWh and cannot be hedged, how much does Phase 1 downsize or delay, and who decides?
  5. At Month 12 (2027-10-17), if the Gate Review Committee finds that ANSSI has not issued a preliminary opinion (target Month 6 = 2027-04-17), does Phase 1 FID proceed as 'conditional on ANSSI clearance by Month 18 (2028-04-17),' or is the security gate failed and Phase 1 deferred? If conditional, what is the cost and schedule contingency for Phase 1 construction-start delay if ANSSI clears late or imposes design-change requirements?
  6. The Compliance Committee and PMO Permitting Lead must submit permit files by Months 8–9 (2027-06-17 to 2027-07-17) and receive a DREAL screening opinion by Month 9 (2027-07-17). If DREAL responds with a request for additional environmental studies or a wider EIA scope (pushing the permit-file completion to Month 12 = 2027-10-17 or beyond), does this automatically fail the permitting gate, defer Phase 1, or trigger a contingent pass? Who decides the schedule impact on Phase 1 energization (slippage from Month 48 = 2030-10-17 to Month 60 = 2031-10-17)?
  7. How will the Steering Committee or Kill Authority resolve a conflict if the PMO's red-team adviser (independent consultant) disagrees with the PMO Director on whether a gate threshold is met? For example, if the red-team says 'RTE's preliminary letter meets the 500 MW grid criterion' but the PMO Director argues 'the language is too conditional,' who has final authority, and is the dissent disclosed to lenders before the Phase 0 gate vote?
  8. If Phase 1 is conditionally approved at Month 12 (2027-10-17) pending resolution of one or more deferred gates (e.g., RTE full connection offer, DREAL permitting file decision), what is the governance cadence during Phase 1 design and early procurement (Months 12–24 = 2027-10-17 to 2028-10-17) to monitor gate-condition progress? Does the Kill Authority Committee still meet monthly, or only when a condition is resolved? If a condition fails during Phase 1 design (e.g., DREAL denies the permit), what is the authorization to stop design or procurement, and who has the authority to demand a €500M–1.5B capex write-off?
  9. The framework caps Phase 0 sunk cost at €750M in four tranches, but does not explicitly address reallocation between tranches if a workstream over-runs. For example, if the Permitting workstream needs an additional €50M for environmental studies (straining Tranche 3), can the PMO Controller reallocate from the Tenancy or Grid workstreams, or must the Steering Committee approve tranche reallocation? What is the process to avoid Phase 0 spend delays or scope cuts that trigger gate failures?
  10. What happens to the Phase 0 team, governance bodies and advisers if Phase 0 gates fail and Phase 1 is not approved at Month 12 (2027-10-17)? Does the Kill Authority Committee dissolve, or remain active to monitor deferral conditions? Are advisers (RTE auditor, ANSSI counsel, land surveyor) retained on contract or released, and what is the cost of re-engagement if Phase 1 is deferred to Month 18–24 (2028-04-17 to 2028-10-17) or cancelled?

Summary

This Phase 0 governance framework establishes a skeptical, gate-driven feasibility program (Months 0–12 = 2026-10-17 to 2027-10-17, €750M cap) with five core bodies: Steering Committee (strategy and FID approval), PMO (execution), Kill Authority Committee (numeric gate enforcement), Compliance Committee (permitting, security, environment, social license), and four tranches capping sunk cost before each gate. The framework's strength lies in separating authority (Kill Authority independent of Sponsor), publishing dissent, and binding gates to specific external milestones (RTE grid letter by Month 6 = 2027-04-17, tenants 30% signed by Month 9 = 2027-07-17, debt €3B+ committed, 2 of 3 municipalities supporting). Critical weaknesses include: vagueness on the Kill Authority's override-veto process and enforcement when the Sponsor pressures FID despite failed thresholds; incomplete specification of how advisers and external parties (RTE, DREAL, ANSSI, lenders) escalate findings back into the decision process; absent decision-rights clarity for sub-€50M workstream conflicts and operational trade-offs; and underdeveloped remediation protocols when uncontrolled external dependencies (grid, permitting, tenant credit) slip beyond gate deadlines. The framework correctly identifies the primary kill test (grid hosting ~1 GW) and anchors expansion gates to operational evidence (PUE ≤1.28, signed 30–50% demand, security and community targets), but lacks granular delegation protocols for day-to-day PMO decisions and contingency pathways for conditional Phase 1 passes when external authorities have not answered by the gate date.

Suggestion 1 - Dunkirk industrial-port grid connection programme (Grand Port Maritime de Dunkerque / RTE, incl. data-centre and decarbonisation load requests)

The Dunkirk port zone is France's largest concentration of new high-voltage industrial load requests (steel decarbonisation, electrification, batteries, data-centre sites). RTE and the port have coordinated reinforcement of the 400 kV network and site allocation through ongoing planning. Scale is in the GW range; exact queue volumes are not verified. Ongoing since the early 2020s.

Success Metrics

MW of connection requests processed by RTE (approximate, verify with RTE) Land plots allocated by the port for industrial use Time from request to energisation for first industrial users Reinforcement scope agreed and cost-sharing terms

Risks and Challenges Faced

Competing industrial loads saturating capacity: handled by RTE prioritisation and staged connection offers. Land scarcity and Seveso zoning: handled by port-led plot planning. Coastal ecology constraints: handled via EIA and compensation.

Where to Find More Information

https://www.dunkerque-port.fr https://www.rte-france.com (grid development plan, S3REnR and connection queue publications) https://www.dunkerque-promotion.com

Actionable Steps

Contact the Grand Port Maritime de Dunkerque business development / land department via the port website. Approach RTE regional customer-connection office (Nord) through the RTE site contact form requesting a pre-engineering meeting. Contact Dunkerque Promotion (economic development agency) for investor liaison.

Rationale for Suggestion

Same region and same grid operator, and it tests the primary kill condition (hosting capacity above ~1 GW) directly. Shows how RTE sequences competing industrial loads. Primary suggestion.

Suggestion 2 - Campus IA / Fluidstack France AI data-centre programme (national AI campus announcements, 2025 onward)

France's 2025 AI summit produced announcements of multi-GW AI campus plans on former industrial and brownfield sites, including a Fluidstack-led project targeting about 1 GW in the Paris region and sites identified by the State in a national list of data-centre-ready locations (including Hauts-de-France sites). Delivery status and figures are not verified; outcomes depend on RTE and permits.

Success Metrics

MW connection offers obtained from RTE (verify) Number of sites with permits filed or granted Signed anchor tenants versus announced intent Financing closed versus announced (not verified)

Risks and Challenges Faced

Grid timing: sites chosen for existing RTE capacity and State-designated priority procedures. Local opposition and land use: handled via public-interest designation and consultation, outcomes uncertain. Tenant commitment versus announcement gap: a key lesson for LOI versus take-or-pay.

Where to Find More Information

https://www.info.gouv.fr (State announcements on AI data-centre sites) https://www.fluidstack.io Business des Echos / Reuters coverage of French AI campus announcements

Actionable Steps

Contact the Fluidstack France business development or press office via its website. Contact Business France / the interministerial data-centre site programme (Ministry of Economy) for site-list access. Ask the Direction Générale des Entreprises for the process on designated data-centre sites.

Rationale for Suggestion

Closest French precedent for a GW-scale AI campus on industrial land with State involvement, the permitting route and the announcement-versus-contract gap. Primary suggestion; maturity is limited, so verify status first.

Suggestion 3 - Ireland EirGrid / CRU data-centre connection policy (Dublin grid constraint)

Ireland's data centres consume a large share of national electricity (about a fifth, approximate). EirGrid imposed a de facto moratorium on new Dublin connections to 2028, then CRU issued a 2025 policy requiring on-site dispatchable generation or storage and flexibility from new data centres. Illustrates a grid operator conditioning capacity on flexibility.

Success Metrics

Share of national demand taken by data centres (approximate) Connection decisions granted under the new CRU policy Flexibility/on-site generation obligations adopted Local grid stability events avoided

Risks and Challenges Faced

Grid saturation: handled by moratorium then conditional connections. Political backlash on energy use: handled via policy requiring on-site supply. Developer uncertainty: partly mitigated by clearer rules in 2025.

Where to Find More Information

https://www.cru.ie (Large Energy Users connection policy decision) https://www.eirgrid.ie https://www.iea.org (Energy and AI report)

Actionable Steps

Contact CRU's Large Energy Users policy team via the CRU website. Approach EirGrid's customer connections team for lessons on flexible connection terms. Speak to Irish Data Centre Association members through its website.

Rationale for Suggestion

Geographically distant, but the best documented case of a grid operator capping and conditioning data-centre capacity. Informs curtailment (10% target, 15% walk-away) and BESS commitments. Primary suggestion.

Suggestion 4 - Secondary: Nordic hyperscale and brownfield campuses (e.g., Google Hamina, Finland, former paper mill)

Google converted a former paper mill in Hamina, Finland into a data centre using seawater cooling, with later expansions. Shows brownfield industrial reuse, low-water-risk cooling and community integration. Fewer details; secondary suggestion. Scale is far below 9 GW.

Success Metrics

Operational since 2011 with expansions (verify) Heat-reuse or district-heating links announced in Finland (verify) Local employment figures disclosed (small relative to capex)

Risks and Challenges Faced

Reusing old industrial buildings and infrastructure. Cooling water permitting handled with seawater and environmental review.

Where to Find More Information

https://datacenters.google/locations/hamina-finland Finnish Ministry of Economic Affairs publications

Actionable Steps

Contact Google data centre community relations for Hamina via its locations page. Contact Haminan Kotka Business Development agency for local lessons.

Rationale for Suggestion

Secondary suggestion: northern climate and brownfield reuse parallel Hauts-de-France, but scale and grid context differ greatly.

Summary

Reference projects for a gate-driven Phase 0 feasibility of a notional 9 GW, 161 km² AI campus in Hauts-de-France. Closest real analogues: the Dunkirk-area industrial-decarbonisation and data-centre grid-queue experience in the same RTE zone, the Fluidstack/Campus IA France programme and Cambrai-area announcements (status and figures not verified), and Nordic and Irish precedents on grid-constrained hyperscale growth. No known single-site 9 GW campus exists, and French geographic analogues are limited, so distant examples (Ireland, Norway) are justified for grid-flexibility and brownfield lessons. All grid, permit and tenant outcomes remain uncontrolled until signed. Figures below are approximate or unverified; confirm with the named organisations.

1. RTE Grid Hosting Capacity and Connection Offer

RTE grid hosting capacity above ~1 GW is the primary kill-test gate. No hosting capacity exists until RTE signs a connection offer; this exposure is uncontrolled until signed and is the first feasibility filter. Grid reinforcement cost (EUR 500M–1.5B developer co-funding, estimate) is the largest contingent cost-line exposure in the Phase 1 budget.

Data to Collect

  • RTE preliminary feasibility opinion for 500 MW, 1 GW, 2 GW tranches at each candidate substation (Cambrai, Dunkirk, Valenciennes, Saint-Omer)
  • RTE estimated timeline from connection request to energization per tranche and topology
  • Transmission reinforcement scope, cost allocation (developer co-funding EUR 500M–1.5B estimate) and timeline
  • Annual curtailment allowance (target ≤10%, walk-away ≥15%) and BESS/flexibility requirements
  • Firm written connection offer for at least 500 MW by Month 12 (2027-10-17)

Simulation Steps

  • Commission independent third-party RTE hosting-capacity audit (EUR 1M–2M) using grid-modeling software (PSSE, DIgSILENT PowerFactory or equivalent RTE-compatible tools) to verify RTE's claims through network modeling; deliver findings by Month 9 (2027-07-17)
  • Run thermal and load-profile modeling (HOMER or EnergyPlan) for 500 MW (85% utilization = 425 MW average) with peak scenarios (40 MW variance in summer peak); test against candidate substation thermal constraints
  • Model three topology scenarios (single-square Cambrai 1 GW, split 2-node Cambrai 500 MW + Dunkirk 250 MW, split 3-node 250 MW each) through RTE's published network data or via RTE consultation; estimate per-node reinforcement cost using published transmission-upgrade benchmarks (EUR 50M–100M per 100 kV line upgrade, approximate)

Expert Validation Steps

  • RTE formal pre-engineering request filed in writing by Month 0 (2026-10-17); RTE's preliminary hosting-capacity opinion (month 4–6 = 2027-02-17 to 2027-04-17 estimate, uncontrolled) confirmed in writing
  • Independent grid-audit firm (third-party consultant with no developer financial interest) validates RTE's network-modeling assumptions and publishes anonymized findings to the investment committee and lenders by Month 9 (2027-07-17)
  • DREAL prefectural office confirms in writing by Month 6 (2027-04-17) that grid-reinforcement scope and environmental permits for substation upgrades are achievable within estimated timelines and cost bands

Responsible Parties

  • Grid Connection and Power Infrastructure Strategist (lead)
  • Independent RTE hosting-capacity auditor (third-party consultant)
  • Infrastructure Finance Lead (cost reconciliation against Phase 1 cap)
  • Investment Committee (gate decision at Month 12 = 2027-10-17)

Assumptions

  • High: RTE will provide a preliminary feasibility opinion within 8–12 weeks of the pre-engineering request (by Month 4–6 = 2027-02-17 to 2027-04-17). RTE's internal governance and competing requests are uncontrolled and may delay response beyond Month 6 (2027-04-17).
  • High: RTE's preliminary opinion will confirm at least 500 MW (one node) within 36 months of a formal connection request. The actual available capacity may be lower (e.g., 250 MW per node), triggering topology downsize or split-campus redesign.
  • High: Developer co-funding for grid reinforcement will be bounded to EUR 500M–1.5B (estimate) and will not exceed EUR 2.0B. Transmission reinforcement scope is uncontrolled until RTE specifies it.
  • Medium: Annual curtailment will not exceed 15% (walk-away threshold). If RTE mandates >15% curtailment, Phase 1 capex or scope is reduced to fit the grid offer, and revenue per MW declines due to lower uptime (10–15% lease discount assumed at 15% curtailment, estimate).
  • High: A firm RTE connection offer will be signed by Month 12 (2027-10-17) or Phase 1 is delayed. RTE often takes 18–36 months from request to final offer; a 12-month timeline for preliminary + final offer is aggressive but necessary for the Phase 0 gate.

SMART Validation Objective

By Month 12 (2027-10-17), obtain RTE written preliminary feasibility letter confirming at least 500 MW available within 36 months, estimated grid reinforcement cost (bounded to EUR 0–2.0B, accept ≥USD 500M as a pass if within budgeted headroom), annual curtailment not exceeding 15%, and BESS/flexibility requirements specified. If RTE cannot confirm ≥500 MW by Month 12 (2027-10-17), Phase 1 is reduced to the MW RTE offers or paused until capacity improves.

Notes

  • RTE's hosting-capacity assessment is the longest-lead external decision and the primary kill test. Month 4 (2027-02-17) topology lock depends on RTE evidence due at Month 6 (2027-04-17), inverting the sequence—mitigation: seek Month 3 (2027-01-17) interim RTE opinion or delay topology to Month 6.5 (2027-05-02).
  • Grid reinforcement co-funding exposure (EUR 500M–1.5B, estimate) overlaps with other stacked contingent add-ons (ecology, split premium, carrying, remediation, fiber) totaling EUR 1.55B–4.2B against a EUR 10B ceiling; if grid reinforcement exceeds EUR 1.0B, Phase 1 must downsize or scope is cut.
  • Curtailment risk: if RTE mandates ≥15% annual curtailment, tenant uptime SLAs (99.5–99.95% proposed) cannot be met without additional BESS or demand-flexibility investment, eroding tenant appeal and lease pricing by 5–15% (estimate).
  • Independent audit by a third-party grid specialist (not RTE internal, not developer-funded consultant) is essential to validate RTE's claims and reduce lender risk premium; cost EUR 1M–2M is justified by potential EUR 500M–1.5B co-funding exposure.

2. Land Assembly and Parcel Optionability (Topology Decision Input)

Land assembly is a primary kill test. The notional 161 km² single-square footprint is doubtful (not verified) for contiguous non-coercive assembly; fragmentation or holdouts force topology pivot to split-campus or downsize. Brownfield remediation liability (EUR 100M–400M if discovered late) is the least-quantifiable cost and can breach the Phase 1 cap if not bounded in Phase 0. Land acquisition cost (EUR 0.24B–0.40B for 16,100 ha at EUR 15,000–25,000/ha, estimate) is a major capex driver.

Data to Collect

  • Ownership maps and parcel counts for Cambrai, Dunkirk, Valenciennes, Saint-Omer candidate zones
  • Benchmark land values and acquisition-cost estimates per zone (EUR/ha)
  • Percentage of target parcel that can be optioned non-coercively at ≤15% above benchmark (target ≥70% for single-square, ≥80% per split-node)
  • Holdout count, owner types (private, agricultural, municipal), and negotiation barriers per parcel
  • Phase II brownfield surveys on shortlisted parcels: soil, groundwater, asbestos, munitions residue, remediation cost bounds per parcel (target EUR 0–100M)

Simulation Steps

  • Conduct geographic-information-system (GIS) mapping using ArcGIS or QGIS with municipal land-registry data, parcel ownership chains, and agricultural property records (Chambre d'Agriculture regional database) to produce fragmentation analysis; identify >1,000 parcels across four zones and classify by owner type, size, estimated value
  • Run land-value benchmarking using comparable-sales databases (Chambre des Notaires, SAFER regional land-transfer records) to establish baseline EUR/ha per zone and parcel category (agricultural, industrial, mixed); flag any parcel showing >2.0× benchmark as holdout-premium risk
  • Model Phase II intrusive surveys (soil boring to 2–5 m depth, groundwater sampling) at 2–3 candidate sites per zone using Phase-I-Pro or equivalent ESA software to predict remediation scope and cost; use published remediation-unit costs (EUR 1,000–5,000 per m³ contaminated soil, estimate) to bound total remediation per site
  • Conduct parcel-level assembly simulations (timeline, cost, holdout risk) for single-square Cambrai (161 km² continuous) and split-campus nodes (Cambrai 8–10 km², Dunkirk 8–10 km², Valenciennes 8–10 km²) to test the 70–80% optionability threshold

Expert Validation Steps

  • Parcel-level land-assembly feasibility study commissioned from a French real-estate advisory firm with rural and industrial land experience (EUR 200K–400K); deliver fragmentation map and holdout-risk assessment by Month 3 (2027-01-17)
  • Phase I environmental-site assessments (desktop) on all four zones by Month 1 (2026-11-17); Phase II intrusive surveys (EUR 1.5M–3M per zone) on top 2–3 sites per zone by Month 3 (2027-01-17); shortlist only parcels with Phase II findings supporting remediation ≤EUR 100M per site by Month 6 (2027-04-17)
  • Formal written opinion from DDT/DDTM (Directions Départementales des Territoires) on public-land availability, state-backed compulsory-acquisition timelines (décret de déclaration d'utilité publique, typical 6–12 months), and liability-allocation agreements for public brownfield sites by Month 4 (2027-02-17)
  • Farm-union (FNSEA and Confédération Paysanne regional chapters) and municipal-official engagement to understand landowner negotiation posture, required compensation levels (proposed 1.5–2.0× land value for displacement, EUR 15,000–25,000/ha for 8,900–10,200 ha per node, estimate), and lease-and-continue feasibility by Month 2 (2026-12-17)

Responsible Parties

  • Land Assembly and Real Estate Strategist (lead)
  • Third-party land-feasibility and ESA consultant
  • Environmental and Permitting Counsel (Phase II survey oversight and liability allocation)
  • Community Engagement and Social License Manager (farmer and municipal negotiations)

Assumptions

  • High: At least 70% of a single-square topology's target parcel (113 km² of 161 km²) can be optioned non-coercively at ≤15% above benchmark land value. Phase I assessments suggest fragmentation risk; if <70% is optionable by Month 3 (2027-01-17), single-square is abandoned and split-campus becomes the default.
  • High: Benchmark land values are EUR 15,000–25,000/ha in Hauts-de-France agricultural zones. Actual acquisition will require 1.5–2.0× benchmark (EUR 22,500–50,000/ha) due to holdout leverage and relocation premiums, adding EUR 50M–100M above base estimate (estimate).
  • High: Phase II brownfield surveys on Cambrai, Dunkirk, Valenciennes sites will identify remediation needs of EUR 0–100M per parcel. If >30% of candidate parcels show remediation costs >EUR 100M, those parcels are dropped from consideration and Phase 1 footprint is redesigned, adding cost and schedule delay.
  • Medium: Seller indemnities and public-remediation-body liability allocations will be signed and enforceable, capping developer remediation exposure to EUR 100M per site or less. Public landowners (Dunkirk port, Cambrai municipal sites) are willing to retain pre-existing contamination liability; if not, developer must fund full cleanup, escalating cost by EUR 200M–500M (estimate).
  • Medium: Lease-and-continue farming arrangements (allowing farmers to operate on buffer and continuation zones of the envelope) will satisfy >50% of landowner concerns, reducing the required cash compensation and relocation premium. If lease-and-continue is not accepted, all agricultural landowners demand full-buyout at 2.0× value, escalating cost by EUR 100M–200M (estimate).

SMART Validation Objective

By Month 3 (2027-01-17), deliver a land-assembly feasibility map confirming: ≥70% of single-square target parcel (or ≥80% per split-campus node) can be optioned non-coercively at ≤15% above benchmark; Phase II surveys identify remediation ≤EUR 100M per site on >70% of shortlisted parcels; seller/public indemnity agreements are drafted and pre-negotiated with at least 50% of target landowners. At Month 4 (2027-02-17), commit to single-square or split-campus topology based on this evidence.

Notes

  • Contiguous land assembly of 161 km² (12.7 km × 12.7 km) across four candidate zones requires coordination of >1,000 individual parcels; fragmentation is the most likely outcome, forcing split-campus topology by Month 4 (2027-02-17) unless exceptional progress is made in Months 1–3 (2026-11-17 to 2027-01-17).
  • Brownfield contamination (historical munitions, slag, asbestos, hydrocarbons from steel mills, refineries, coal mines in the region) is the highest Phase 1 cost uncertainty; front-loading Phase II surveys in Phase 0 bounds liability and allows seller/public-body liability allocation before Phase 1 FID.
  • Agricultural-sector opposition (FNSEA and Confédération Paysanne) can block permits or delay land assembly 12–36 months (estimate) unless displacement compensation and lease-and-continue terms are credible and negotiated early (Months 1–3 = 2026-11-17 to 2027-01-17).
  • Split-campus topology (3 separate 250–500 MW nodes) adds EUR 250M–500M capex (5–10% premium over single-square) for duplication of substations, fiber, security per node; cost is within EUR 10B ceiling but consumes contingency headroom.

3. Anchor-Tenant Demand Validation and Binding Commitments

Phase 1 FID gate requires signed anchor-tenant take-or-pay for ≥30% of Phase 1 capacity (proposed threshold) to support debt financing. Without proof of demand, lenders will not fund EUR 5B capex; a loose gate (LOIs accepted as commitment) is the most common mega-project failure: tenants use LOIs for site comparison without commitment and exit post-FID if conditions change. Only binding leases with cash deposits and liquidated damages prove demand.

Data to Collect

  • Identified anchor-tenant prospects (2–3 hyperscalers with published capex plans, 2–3 sovereign or EU-consortium users) and their specific power/latency/security requirements
  • Non-binding letters of intent (for market signal only; do not count toward gate) vs. binding take-or-pay term sheets (capacity reserved, payment obligation, SLA-subject; count for gate)
  • Signed take-or-pay leases or capacity-reservation agreements covering ≥30% of Phase 1 size (150 MW of 500 MW) with reservation fees (EUR 10M–50M per 100 MW) paid before construction
  • Tenant credit ratings (BBB− or better) or parent-company guarantees and letters of credit (for credit <BBB−)
  • Cluster-size and latency-tolerance validation per tenant to test split-campus feasibility (target <10 ms intra-cluster for training, <50 ms inter-node, force-majeure >4 hours)

Simulation Steps

  • Develop standardized take-or-pay lease templates (5–10 year term proposed, capacity range 50–500 MW, power price indexed or capped EUR/MWh, uptime SLA 99.5–99.95%, curtailment exceptions, force-majeure carve-outs) by Month 2 (2026-12-17) using contract-management software (Dealroom or DocuSign); model three scenarios: (i) 100% fixed power price, (ii) indexed to spot with ±3% annual cap, (iii) pass-through to tenants
  • Conduct tenant-competitive-alternative survey (Month 2–3 = 2026-12-17 to 2027-01-17) to identify 2–3 hyperscalers (e.g., Microsoft Azure, Google, Meta) and 2–3 sovereign-AI users (French State AI offices, EU CEPIs, or national-government procurement programs) that are actively evaluating sites in 2026–2028; document their published capex plans, timing, and site-selection criteria
  • Test cluster-size and latency requirements via technical interviews with top 1–2 anchors, modeling inter-node topology scenarios (single-square Cambrai 1 GW, split Cambrai 500 MW + Dunkirk 250 MW, split 3-node 250 MW each) with site-specific latency estimates based on fiber-route data; document whether training or inference workloads tolerate the split-campus round-trip latency (target <50 ms, <10 ms preferred)
  • Price capacity-reservation fees (EUR 10M–50M per 100 MW, estimate) and model NPV impact on Phase 1 financing; test whether 150 MW of signed leases (30% minimum gate) covers debt service (proposed EUR 299M annual at EUR 3B debt, approximately) or if additional 50% signed is required for DSCR >1.30x

Expert Validation Steps

  • Anchor-Tenant and Market Development Lead (dedicated full-time role) engages 4–6 prospect tenants by Month 1 (2026-11-17) with confidential site overview under NDA; obtains non-binding letters of interest from 2–3 by Month 7 (2027-05-17) (advisory, do not count); secures binding term sheets from at least 2 tenants (150 MW total minimum) with reservation fees paid in escrow by Month 9 (2027-07-17)
  • Credit validation of all anchor tenants by Month 9 (2027-07-17): obtain S&P, Moody's or Fitch credit reports for each tenant; for subsidiaries, obtain parent-company financial statements and guarantee letters; for sovereigns, obtain government-issued guarantee from Ministry of Finance or EU; confirm minimum BBB− or equivalent credit (or secured by parent guarantee/letter of credit for weaker counterparties)
  • Binding term-sheet execution by Month 9 (2027-07-17) with explicit liquidated-damages clause (10–15% of first-year lease revenue if tenant exits between FID and energization) and reservation-fee escrow arrangements; engagement of three law firms to confirm lease enforceability and remedy mechanisms under French law by Month 3 (2027-01-17)

Responsible Parties

  • Anchor-Tenant and Market Development Lead (lead)
  • Infrastructure Finance Lead (lease-pricing and NPV modeling)
  • National Security and Regulatory Affairs Lead (sovereign-tenant vetting and data-residency compliance)
  • Investment Committee (gate decision on binding-commitment sufficiency at Month 12 = 2027-10-17)

Assumptions

  • High: At least one global hyperscaler (e.g., Microsoft, Google, Meta) or credible sovereign-AI consortium will express genuine interest (site visit, technical questions, not just LOI flattery) and be willing to sign a binding term sheet for 50–150 MW by Month 9 (2027-07-17). Hyperscaler commitment timelines are typically 6–12 months ahead of power-on; LOI and binding-sheet execution must occur in Phase 0 (Months 1–12 = 2026-11-17 to 2027-10-17) or tenant demand will slip to competing sites.
  • High: Binding term sheets will include a reservation-fee cash deposit (EUR 10M–50M per 100 MW) paid in escrow by Month 9 (2027-07-17) and a liquidated-damages clause (10–15% of first-year lease revenue) if tenant exits post-FID. Without cash and damages, a 'binding' sheet is non-binding and a tenant can walk without penalty, leaving the campus operator exposed to uncontracted capacity.
  • Medium: All anchor-tenant counterparties will have a minimum credit rating of BBB− or be backed by a parent-company guarantee (A− or better) or government guarantee (for sovereigns). If credit is weaker, the tenant will post a letter of credit (2–3% annual cost, estimate) covering 1–2 years of lease payments.
  • Medium: Tenant cluster-size and latency requirements will tolerate a split-campus topology (round-trip latency 10–50 ms between nodes, depending on workload: <10 ms for synchronous training, <50 ms for inference and batch). If a key tenant requires <5 ms (demanding unified cluster), split campus is infeasible for that tenant and capacity is limited to single-node Cambrai, capping Phase 1 revenue and growth.
  • Medium: Reservation fees (EUR 10M–50M per 100 MW) are credible tenant incentives to lock commitment early. If tenants view fees as 'money spent for optionality' and prefer to delay commitment until Phase 1 detailed design (Month 20+), then fees will not be paid and demand evidence at Month 9 (2027-07-17) will remain weak (LOI-only).

SMART Validation Objective

By Month 9 (2027-07-17), execute binding take-or-pay term sheets for ≥150 MW (30% of 500 MW Phase 1) with investment-grade counterparties or parent-guaranteed subsidiaries; secure non-refundable reservation-fee cash deposits totaling at least EUR 15M–75M in escrow; confirm no liquidated-damages or exit provisions that would allow tenants to walk post-FID without financial penalty. By Month 12 (2027-10-17), if <150 MW is signed with cash and guarantees, trigger Phase 1 downsize to 250–300 MW (matching committed demand) or pause Phase 1 pending additional tenant recruitment.

Notes

  • Global hyperscalers (Microsoft, Google, Meta, Amazon) typically maintain LOI portfolios across 8–12 competitive European sites and do not commit capex-equivalent leases until 6–12 months before power-on; early Phase 0 LOI collection is market signal only and should not be treated as demand commitment.
  • Sovereign-AI procurement (French State, EU, national governments) moves slower than hyperscalers; 18–36 month procurement cycles are common, and public-sector budget cycles (annual or multi-year) often conflict with Phase 1 timelines; sovereign demand proof by Month 9 (2027-07-17) is unlikely unless a formal government RFP is issued in early 2027.
  • Reservation-fee economics: EUR 10M–50M per 100 MW (depending on lease term and scale) represents 0.2–0.5% of Phase 1 capex; fees should be sufficient to deter 'comparison shopping' LOI behavior (commitment signal) but not so large that they are prohibitive. On 150 MW signed, fees total EUR 15M–75M, funding about 2–10% of Phase 0 spend (EUR 750M cap).
  • Lease-revenue sensitivity: if only 100–150 MW (20–30%) is signed by Month 9 (2027-07-17), Phase 1 lenders will require either (i) higher debt spreads (+200–300 bps, adding EUR 100M–300M NPV interest cost), (ii) lower debt leverage (50% vs. 60%, requiring EUR 500M–1B additional equity), or (iii) Phase 1 downsize (250 MW to match committed demand). Without 30%+ signed and credible, debt financing is not available at acceptable cost.

4. Dry-Cooler PUE Validation and Water-Authority Feasibility

Cooling and water are the most operationally uncertain variables. PUE target 1.15–1.25 is optimistic; realistic hot-weather performance (1.35–1.5 PUE at 35°C design-day) adds 75–100 MW peak electrical load, straining RTE grid-curtailment budget and tenant uptime SLAs. A zero-evaporative-water constraint is permitting-friendly but may be infeasible on the proposed dry-cooler budget; hybrid cooling (capped non-potable water) reopens water-authority and permitting complexity. Early validation bounds cost and design risk.

Data to Collect

  • Dry-cooler performance curves from ≥3 manufacturers (Thermax, Hydac, Modine) at ambient temperatures 15–40°C with fouling and part-load efficiency factors
  • Site-specific thermal modeling results for 500 MW at 150 W/m² average power density, 30–35°C inlet water, on each candidate parcel; modeled PUE at 35°C design-day ambient
  • Regional hydrological data: groundwater availability, historical drought frequency and duration, summer low-flow periods on surface water, climate projections to 2035
  • Water-authority written opinion on closed-loop dry-cooler feasibility at 1 GW scale with zero evaporative water use and impact on drinking-water supply during drought years
  • Heat-demand study identifying district-heating networks and industrial heat users within 5 km of each node (identify MW offtake potential and annual capacity factor)

Simulation Steps

  • Obtain published dry-cooler performance data from vendors (Thermax, Hydac, Modine, SPX Cooling) covering capacity (100–500 MW thermal rejection range), fan power, approach temperature (Δ design-day = 10–15°C typical), part-load curves (25%, 50%, 75%, 100% load); use TRNSYS, EnergyPlus or equivalent thermal-simulation software to model hour-by-hour PUE for a representative summer (July–August) using 20 years of historical Hauts-de-France weather data (38°C peak on rarest days, 35°C on typical peak days, 60–75% relative humidity)
  • Run three power-density scenarios (100 W/m², 150 W/m², 200 W/m²) to test sensitivity; model a 500 MW data center at 150 W/m² = approximately 50,000–100,000 m² cooler area (estimate), footprint dependent on cooler type (bar-plate vs. tube-bundle), arrangement (horizontal vs. vertical), and ambient wind exposure on candidate parcels (Cambrai flat, Dunkirk near coast with wind, Valenciennes near rivers with potential temperature effects)
  • Conduct hydrological modeling (HEC-HMS, FEFLOW or equivalent) using 20-year historical weather to project groundwater levels, summer low-flow periods on surface-water bodies (Meuse, Sambre, Scheldt), and drought-frequency/duration statistics; cross-reference with Agence de l'Eau published drought-response decrees (2022, 2023) to understand constraint timelines and load-shedding triggers
  • Model heat-reuse scenario at each candidate node: identify district-heating networks (réseaux de chaleur, typical in urban areas like Dunkirk but absent in rural Cambrai) and proximate industrial users (food, brewing, paper, refining); estimate heat-delivery pipeline cost (EUR 500K–2M per km, estimate) and annual revenue (EUR 10M–30M at 20–25 MW offtake at EUR 30–60/MWh, estimate)

Expert Validation Steps

  • Independent thermal-design audit by a data-center cooling specialist (EUR 300K–600K) conducting Phase 0 modeling and delivering site-specific PUE forecast (with confidence interval) by Month 5 (2027-03-17); hard gate: if modeled PUE >1.28 at 35°C on baseline scenario (150 W/m²), recommend hybrid cooling (evaporative + dry, capped non-potable water) or load reduction.
  • Water-authority written opinion (DDT/DDTM and Agence de l'Eau Artois-Picardie) by Month 6 (2027-04-17) confirming: (i) closed-loop dry-cooler cooling acceptable at 500–1,000 MW with stated PUE range, (ii) indirect water impact (cooler air-release heat) acceptable under French environmental law, (iii) pre-agreed drought-response protocol (if drought decree issued, tenant load-shedding acceptable and covered by force-majeure lease carve-out), and (iv) whether non-potable or recycled industrial water is available as backup if dry cooling cannot meet summer peak demand.
  • Hydrologist or groundwater specialist (EUR 500K–1.5M study cost) delivering Phase 0 hydrological assessment by Month 4 (2027-02-17) addressing: groundwater availability and seasonal variation, drought-frequency analysis (20-year historical data + climate-projection models to 2035), and recommendations for water-use constraints or demand-reduction strategies if drought frequency increases.

Responsible Parties

  • Thermal, Cooling and Hydrology Engineer (lead)
  • Environmental and Permitting Counsel (water-authority engagement)
  • Infrastructure Finance Lead (thermal design cost impact on capex and contingency budget)
  • Grid Connection Strategist (peak-load forecast for RTE reinforcement and BESS sizing)

Assumptions

  • High: Dry-cooler PUE at 35°C ambient and 30–35°C inlet water will be ≤1.30 (2-point upside margin above 1.15–1.25 target) using vendor equipment at nominal fouling and part-load. If Phase 0 modeling shows >1.30, design pivot to hybrid cooling or capacity reduction is required by Month 6 (2027-04-17).
  • High: Water authorities will permit closed-loop dry-cooler cooling at 500–1,000 MW with zero evaporative water and no material impact on drinking-water supply. If water authorities require evaporative cooling as backup (e.g., 5–10% water use allowance for extreme-weather days) or restrict expansion beyond 500 MW, the zero-water design assumption is invalidated and hybrid cooling must be budgeted (EUR 50M–100M capex contingency, estimate).
  • Medium: Hauts-de-France drought frequency (current baseline ~1 event per 7 years, estimated) will not increase materially over the Phase 1–2 build period (Months 12–84 = 2027-10-17 to 2033-10-17). Climate models project increased drought risk; if frequency escalates to 1 per 3 years or more, tenant load-shedding (forced curtailment) during dry summers will increase, reducing uptime SLAs and tenant satisfaction.
  • Medium: Heat-reuse offtake (15–30 MW at 20–25 MW sustained) from district heating or industrial users will be contracted and paying by Year 2 of Phase 1 operations (about Month 54 = 2031-04-17). If no binding heat offtake is signed by Month 9 (2027-07-17), heat-delivery infrastructure (EUR 50M–100M estimated capex) is removed from Phase 1 scope.
  • Medium: Peak electrical load for 500 MW at 150 W/m² average density with 1.20–1.25 PUE will be approximately 625–650 MW (500 MW compute + 125–150 MW cooling and auxiliary). A 1.35–1.40 PUE pushes peak to 675–700 MW, adding 75–100 MW unplanned load to the RTE feeder; RTE's grid-reinforcement and curtailment assumptions must account for this variance.

SMART Validation Objective

By Month 5 (2027-03-17), deliver site-specific thermal modeling confirming modeled PUE ≤1.28 at 35°C design-day on baseline scenario (500 MW, 150 W/m²), or commit in writing to hybrid-cooling design or Phase 1 capacity reduction. By Month 6 (2027-04-17), obtain written water-authority opinion confirming closed-loop dry-cooler feasibility with zero evaporative water and acceptable indirect-water-impact (cooler air release). By Month 7 (2027-05-17), identify at least one credible heat-offtake prospect (10+ MW, investment-grade or municipal credit); if no offtake is signed by Month 9 (2027-07-17), remove heat infrastructure from Phase 1 capex.

Notes

  • PUE upside risk is a hidden cost driver. A 10-point escalation (1.20 to 1.30 PUE) adds 150–200 MW peak load on hot days; if RTE's grid reinforcement and BESS assumptions are based on 1.20 PUE, discovery of 1.30+ PUE in Phase 1 forces retrofits (EUR 200M–400M for hybrid cooling or battery storage) or load shedding (curtailment clauses in tenant leases).
  • Water-authority permitting is often the bottleneck for large-scale cooling. Hauts-de-France sits in a water-stressed catchment (Artois-Picardie Agence de l'Eau); pre-emptive dialogue with water authorities (Months 1–2 = 2026-11-17 to 2026-12-17) and a pre-agreed drought-response protocol (load shedding up to X% during declared drought, with tenant lease carve-out) reduce mid-Phase-1 permitting surprises.
  • Heat-reuse infrastructure (EUR 50M–100M insulated pipelines, heat exchangers, pump stations) is sunk cost if no offtake is signed; many data-center projects plan heat reuse as a community benefit but fail to close commercial contracts, leaving infrastructure dormant. Early identification of credible heat customers (Months 2–4 = 2026-12-17 to 2027-02-17) and binding offtake agreements (Months 5–9 = 2027-03-17 to 2027-07-17) are essential to justify capex.
  • Phase 1 design-day thermal validation (35°C ambient, full 500 MW load, worst-case cooler fouling) must be stress-tested against RTE's grid-reinforcement budget and BESS sizing; if peak load forecast escalates late in Phase 0 or early Phase 1, carrying cost and redesign cost are substantial.

5. ANSSI National-Security Review Pathway and Foreign Co-Investor Clearance

Foreign co-investor involvement and sovereign-AI tenants trigger national-security review by ANSSI/DGSI, which is the longest-lead external decision (12–18 months, uncontrolled until started). Blocking concerns on foreign ownership or data-residency policies can emerge late and force co-investor restructuring or tenant-mix redesign mid-Phase-1. Early ANSSI engagement (Months 0–1 = 2026-10-17 to 2026-11-17) and a clear security-design governance roadmap reduce surprise delays.

Data to Collect

  • ANSSI/DGSI preliminary opinion on data-residency policies, foreign co-investor governance restrictions, and foreign-ownership limits acceptable for this site
  • Foreign-investment screening clearance (CFIUS if any US hyperscaler is involved; EU foreign-direct-investment review if non-EU sovereign co-investors are involved)
  • Security-design governance roadmap: perimeter hardening, anti-drone systems, OT-network cyber separation, personnel security clearance requirements (SB–Défense or equivalent)
  • Timeline for formal ANSSI national-security review starting Month 13 (2027-11-17) and target completion (12–18 months estimated, all uncontrolled until ANSSI issues review schedule)
  • Data-residency and tenant-access control policies for sovereign vs. hyperscaler vs. general-commercial tenants

Simulation Steps

  • Develop a security-design governance white paper (10–15 pages) by Month 2 (2026-12-17) covering: (i) anticipated tenant mix (e.g., 30% hyperscaler, 50% sovereign-AI, 20% commercial), (ii) data-residency requirements (e.g., all data must reside on French territory, no transatlantic routing), (iii) foreign co-investor structure and voting rights, (iv) preliminary security architecture (perimeter security, OT-network isolation, supply-chain vetting), (v) governance structure (board composition, state-observer roles if required). Use this as an ANSSI engagement document.
  • Conduct a security architecture and design roadmap study (EUR 500K–1.5M) by Month 2 (2026-12-17), engaging a high-assurance security consultant with ANSSI/DGSI experience to specify: baseline perimeter design (height, anti-climb, setbacks per security standard), CCTV and access-control architecture, OT-network logical separation (air-gap vs. 2-factor authentication), personnel-clearance process (SB–Défense threshold for certain roles), supply-chain security vetting for critical components. Use this roadmap to inform ANSSI's preliminary assessment.
  • Model three tenant-governance and data-residency scenarios: (i) hyperscaler-only (standard governance, data residency France), (ii) mixed hyperscaler + sovereign (dual-zone architecture with segregated high-security halls), (iii) EU-public-consortium (multi-country data-residency and governance complexity). Estimate capex and timeline impact per scenario (sovereign partitions add EUR 50M–200M security investment, dual-zone fiber routing adds EUR 100M–300M, estimate).

Expert Validation Steps

  • Confidential pre-submission meeting with ANSSI/DGSI (proposed Month 0, 2026-10-17, or Month 1 = 2026-11-17, led by sponsor CEO and legal/security leads) to present the white paper and preliminary security-design roadmap; request ANSSI's informal guidance on foreign co-investor acceptability, data-residency requirements, and formal review timeline.
  • ANSSI written preliminary opinion (Month 6 = 2027-04-17 target, uncontrolled) confirming: (i) formal security review can commence at Month 13 (2027-11-17) (one month after Phase 1 FID), (ii) no fundamental blocking concerns on foreign equity or tenant mix, (iii) security-design roadmap is acceptable at a high level, (iv) estimated formal-review timeline (typically 12–18 months from initiation).
  • Foreign-investment screening clearance (CFIUS if a US hyperscaler is a material tenant, or EU foreign-direct-investment review if non-EU sovereign funds are co-investors) should be pre-tested in parallel (Months 1–6 = 2026-11-17 to 2027-04-17) with informal guidance from relevant authorities; binding clearance is not required for Phase 1 FID but unresolved issues should be flagged by Month 9 (2027-07-17).

Responsible Parties

  • National Security and Regulatory Affairs Lead (lead, ANSSI/DGSI liaison)
  • Security Architect (security-design roadmap development)
  • Infrastructure Finance Lead (co-investor governance structure and compliance with capital-control regulations)
  • Anchor-Tenant and Commercial Lead (tenant mix impact on security and data-residency requirements)

Assumptions

  • High: ANSSI will issue a preliminary opinion by Month 6 (2027-04-17) confirming that formal security review can start by Month 13 (2027-11-17) with no fundamental blocking concerns on foreign co-investor involvement or data-residency policies. ANSSI review timelines are uncontrolled; preliminary opinions often take 3–4 months, and blocking concerns can emerge requiring significant co-investor restructuring.
  • High: Foreign co-investors (proposed infrastructure funds with possible EU sovereign-fund involvement) will be acceptable to ANSSI provided they hold no control stake (board seat, veto rights) and are EU-domiciled. If non-EU or China-linked capital is involved, ANSSI review will be more intensive and may impose restrictions on tenant access, data flows, or technology.
  • Medium: Formal ANSSI national-security review will commence at Month 13 (2027-11-17) (one month post-Phase-1 FID) and complete within 12–18 months (by Months 25–31 = 2028-11-17 to 2029-05-17). If review is delayed or unresolved at first-block energization (Month 42 = 2030-04-17), some tenants (particularly sovereign-AI users) may defer commitments pending clearance, affecting Phase 1 revenue ramp.
  • Medium: Security-design governance roadmap (perimeter, OT separation, personnel vetting) will satisfy ANSSI's preliminary expectations. If ANSSI's formal review uncovers additional requirements (e.g., state observer role, real-time monitoring of certain data flows, export-control compliance), security capex and operational complexity escalate (EUR 100M–300M additional, estimate), potentially triggering Phase 1 budget breach.
  • Low: Sovereign-AI and defense-adjacent tenants (e.g., French State AI office, NATO-member defense agencies) will be attracted to the campus due to the hardened security posture and domestic location, paying lease premiums (5–15% higher than commercial hyperscalers, estimate) to offset the security capex and operational overhead.

SMART Validation Objective

By Month 6 (2027-04-17), obtain ANSSI written preliminary opinion confirming: (i) no fundamental blocking concerns on foreign co-investor involvement or tenant mix, (ii) formal security review can commence within one month of Phase 1 FID submission (Month 13 = 2027-11-17), (iii) security-design roadmap is acceptable at a high level. By Month 12 (2027-10-17) Phase 1 FID, document ANSSI's review timeline and any interim compliance conditions (e.g., personnel-clearance process start, interim access controls). If ANSSI signals a review timeline beyond Month 30 (2029-04-17) or identifies fundamental blocking concerns, Phase 1 is paused and co-investor/tenant mix is reassessed.

Notes

  • ANSSI review is the slowest external gating decision (12–18 months uncontrolled); early pre-submission dialogue (Months 0–1 = 2026-10-17 to 2026-11-17) and a credible security-design roadmap reduce surprise delays, but no guarantee of fast-track exists.
  • Foreign co-investor involvement (proposed infrastructure funds with potential EU sovereign co-investors) is politically sensitive; ANSSI will scrutinize ownership structures, beneficial owners, capital-control compliance, and geopolitical affiliations. A transparent co-investor governance structure (non-controlling stakes, EU domicile, published board composition) helps ANSSI clearance.
  • Sovereign-AI tenants (French State, EU CEPIs) may require segregated high-security compute halls, dedicated fiber routing, and state-observer rights; these requirements add security capex (EUR 50M–200M, estimate) and operational complexity. Early tenant engagement (Months 2–4 = 2026-12-17 to 2027-02-17) on security requirements informs Phase 1 design and ANSSI roadmap.
  • US hyperscaler involvement triggers CFIUS review (Committee on Foreign Investment in the US); if the hyperscaler is classified as 'critical-infrastructure-dependent' or handles sensitive datasets, CFIUS may require long-form review (6–12 months, estimate) before the lease is finalized. Pre-testing CFIUS appetite for this campus (Months 3–6 = 2027-01-17 to 2027-04-17) via informal inquiry reduces late-stage surprise delays.

6. Municipal and Community-Stakeholder Engagement and Social-License Gate

Social license and permitting (Decisions 4 and the permitting outcome) depend on municipal and community support. Farmland displacement of 10,000+ ha is contentious; farm-union opposition (FNSEA, Confédération Paysanne) can delay permits by 12–36 months or force design changes increasing capex 5–15% (EUR 250M–1.5B, estimate). Early engagement (Months 1–3 = 2026-11-17 to 2027-01-17) and binding community benefits (Months 5–9 = 2027-03-17 to 2027-07-17) reduce opposition escalation.

Data to Collect

  • Municipal liaison-committee outcomes: attendance, positions (support, neutral, opposition), blocking concerns identified from mayors, regional councillors, NGO representatives
  • Social-impact study findings: farmer concerns (displacement, compensation level, lease-and-continue feasibility), resident concerns (noise, light, security perception, employment benefits), NGO positions (ecological impact, water use, farmland loss)
  • Community-benefit package: signed commitment from ≥2 of 3 most-affected municipalities (Cambrai, Dunkirk, Valenciennes or Saint-Omer) endorsing Phase 1
  • Binding community-benefit agreement: EUR 50M–150M commitments (direct income to municipalities, farm-relocation packages, ecological restoration, local employment, infrastructure upgrades), contingent on Phase 1 permits
  • Permitting-timeline feedback from DREAL and prefectures: any anticipated blocking concerns, required design modifications (e.g., ecological offsets, buffer zones, alternative sites)

Simulation Steps

  • Conduct social-impact survey (USD 300K–600K) by Month 1 (2026-11-17), targeting ≥100 farmers (interviews), ≥500 residents (survey questionnaire), ≥5 environmental NGOs (meetings); document top concerns, willingness-to-accept thresholds for displacement and ecological trade-offs, and perceived benefits (jobs, infrastructure, heat reuse). Use survey software (Qualtrics, SurveySparrow) and qualitative-research methods (focus groups, key-informant interviews) to triangulate findings.
  • Model community-benefit package scenarios: (i) EUR 50M package (EUR 10M to municipalities, EUR 20M farm relocation, EUR 15M ecology, EUR 5M training), (ii) EUR 100M package (EUR 20M to municipalities, EUR 40M farm relocation, EUR 25M ecology, EUR 15M training), (iii) EUR 150M package (EUR 30M to municipalities, EUR 60M farm relocation, EUR 35M ecology, EUR 25M training). Estimate willingness-to-accept improvement as benefit scale increases; target the minimum package that overcomes majority opposition in each zone.
  • Run permitting-timeline simulations with DREAL and prefecture: estimate 18–30 months for standard ICPE and environmental authorization, plus 24–48 months for legal appeals if opposition is organized. Model the impact of ecological offsets, buffer-zone redesign, and permit conditions on Phase 1 capex and schedule (assume 5–15% cost escalation for design modifications, 3–6 month schedule slip for appeal periods, estimate).

Expert Validation Steps

  • Municipal Liaison Committee meetings (quarterly, Months 1, 4, 7, 10 = 2026-11-17, 2027-02-17, 2027-05-17, 2027-08-17) with published minutes within 2 weeks; committee includes mayors, regional councillors, farm-union representatives, environmental NGOs (minimum 5–8 members per committee), and a neutral facilitator. Committee members are invited to provide feedback on draft Phase 1 design, permitting strategy, and community-benefit proposals.
  • DREAL prefectural office consultation (Months 1–2 = 2026-11-17 to 2026-12-17) to present the Phase 0 approach, environmental baseline, and permitting strategy; obtain informal feedback on anticipated blocking concerns and permit-pathway recommendations (standard ICPE vs. environmental authorization prioritization, ecological-compensation feasibility).
  • Binding community-benefit agreement signed by ≥2 of 3 most-affected municipalities by Month 9 (2027-07-17); agreement specifies EUR amounts (direct income indexed to inflation, farm relocation at 1.5–2.0× land value, ecological restoration EUR/ha, training program enrollment targets), implementation timeline (percent of Phase 1 capex), and accountability (third-party monitoring role for municipalities/NGOs). Legal binding and financial commitment are essential; non-binding 'memoranda of understanding' do not satisfy the gate.

Responsible Parties

  • Community Engagement and Social-License Manager (lead, liaison committee chair)
  • Environmental and Permitting Counsel (ecology and permit-strategy coordination)
  • Land Assembly and Real Estate Strategist (farm-relocation packages and lease-and-continue terms)
  • Infrastructure Finance Lead (community-benefit budget integration into Phase 1 capex)

Assumptions

  • High: At least 2 of the 3 most-affected municipalities will sign a binding community-benefit agreement by Month 9 (2027-07-17), committing to Phase 1 permitting support. If fewer than 2 municipalities sign, social-license gate fails and Phase 1 is paused pending redesign or alternative-site evaluation.
  • High: A community-benefit package of EUR 50M–150M (over Phases 1–2) will overcome majority opposition from farmers and residents, conditional on credible implementation (binding agreement, third-party monitoring, real-time fund disbursement). If opposition persists despite benefits, permits may be blocked or conditions imposed that increase capex >15%.
  • Medium: Farm-displacement compensation of 1.5–2.0× benchmark land value (EUR 22,500–50,000/ha) will satisfy >70% of affected farmers. If market conditions or holdout leverage drive required compensation to >2.0× (EUR 30,000–75,000/ha), land-acquisition cost escalates by EUR 100M–300M (estimate).
  • Medium: Lease-and-continue farming arrangements (allowing farmers to operate on buffer and continuation zones for the lifecycle of the campus) will be accepted by >50% of agricultural landowners, reducing cash-compensation and relocation-package costs. If lease-and-continue is not accepted, all agricultural land must be purchased at full premium, escalating cost.
  • Medium: Ecological compensation and monitoring will be co-managed with environmental NGOs and conservation bodies, building credibility with permitting authorities and reducing appeal risk. If NGOs view compensation as inadequate and launch legal challenges, permits are delayed 12–24 months.

SMART Validation Objective

By Month 9 (2027-07-17), secure written support (formal resolution or signed letter) from at least 2 of the 3 most-affected municipalities, with a binding community-benefit agreement totaling EUR 50M–150M over Phases 1–2, specifying direct municipal income, farm-relocation packages (1.5–2.0× land value), ecological restoration (EUR/ha), local employment targets, and monitoring roles. By Month 12 (2027-10-17) Phase 0 gate, confirm no major legal challenges pending and majority stakeholder-engagement outcomes documented.

Notes

  • Farm-sector opposition in Hauts-de-France is organized and powerful (FNSEA, Confédération Paysanne have political leverage in regional councils); early engagement (Months 1–2 = 2026-11-17 to 2026-12-17) and credible relocation/lease-and-continue terms are essential to convert opposition into neutrality or support.
  • Environmental NGO support (or at least neutrality) is a permit-application prerequisite in France; ecological offsetting and co-management arrangements (e.g., NGO role in monitoring habitat restoration) reduce appeal risk from environmental groups.
  • Municipal signatures on the community-benefit agreement carry political weight with prefectural authorities (DREAL, prefecture); mayors' endorsement signals that local concerns have been addressed and strengthens permit applications.
  • Community-benefit budget (EUR 50M–150M, estimate) sits outside or overlaps with the Phase 1 capex (EUR 5B–10B); clarification of funding source (phase-1 capex, separate sponsor equity, or third-party grants) is essential by Month 12 (2027-10-17) to reconcile budget headroom.

Summary

This phase-0 feasibility plan for a notional 9 GW, 161 km² AI campus in Hauts-de-France is a gate-driven, evidence-based stress-test that validates or kills the project based on six critical data-collection areas: (1) RTE grid hosting capacity (primary kill test, ≥500 MW by Month 6 = 2027-04-17), (2) land assembly (≥70% contiguous or split-campus feasibility by Month 4 = 2027-02-17), (3) anchor-tenant binding commitments (≥30% of Phase 1 signed by Month 9 = 2027-07-17), (4) thermal design and water-authority clearance (PUE ≤1.28 modeled, dry-cooler feasibility confirmed by Month 6 = 2027-04-17), (5) ANSSI national-security review pathway (preliminary opinion by Month 6 = 2027-04-17, formal review timeline confirmed), and (6) community and municipal social license (≥2 of 3 municipalities signed and supportive by Month 9 = 2027-07-17). A Phase 0 budget cap of EUR 750M (four milestone tranches) and an independent investment committee with numeric kill thresholds, external red-team oversight, and supermajority override authority enforce gate discipline against sunk-cost momentum. Phase 1 FID (Month 12 = 2027-10-17) is contingent on all six gates passing (or conditional pass with documented mitigation); failure on any gate triggers downsize, split-campus pivot, delay, or cancellation. Simulation steps use industry-standard tools (RTE-compatible grid modeling, GIS parcel mapping, thermal modeling, ESA software, tenant-finance modeling); expert validation steps require written engagement and formal opinions from RTE, DREAL, water authorities, ANSSI, lenders, and municipalities. Key sensitivities: RTE's response timeline is uncontrolled and may invert the topology-decision sequence (mitigation: move topology gate to Month 6.5 = 2027-05-02); land assembly is doubtful for 161 km² contiguous (mitigation: split-campus design in parallel); anchor-tenant LOIs are non-binding (mitigation: require cash reservation fees and liquidated-damages clauses); thermal validation is deferred (mitigation: commission independent audit and hard PUE gate by Month 5 = 2027-03-17); social-license shortfall can delay permits 12–36 months (mitigation: early municipal engagement and binding community-benefit agreement by Month 9 = 2027-07-17). Immediate actions: (1) Charter the independent investment committee and lock numeric kill thresholds by Month 1 (2026-11-17); (2) file RTE pre-engineering request and commission independent grid audit by Month 0 (2026-10-17); (3) launch land-assembly surveys and environmental baselines by Month 1 (2026-11-17); (4) initiate ANSSI and water-authority pre-submission dialogue by Month 0 (2026-10-17); (5) identify anchor tenants and launch reservation-fee discussion by Month 1 (2026-11-17); (6) establish municipal liaison committee and commission social-impact study by Month 1 (2026-11-17). Success measure: Phase 1 FID with signed debt (≥EUR 3B), anchor tenants (≥30% of 500 MW), and Phase 2 demand (≥50% signed) unlocked by Month 36 (2029-10-17) energization. Failure or downsize is a legitimate outcome if gates fail.

Documents to Create

Create Document 1: Investment Committee Charter and Governance Protocol

ID: 1dd7e8cb-6bf6-477d-a5fc-598a99eea13e

Description: Formal charter establishing the independent investment committee's composition (≥2 external directors, lender/co-investor observers), voting rules (supermajority two-thirds override, published dissent), numeric kill thresholds locked in writing (RTE ≥500 MW, ≥70% land optioned, ≥30% anchor-tenant take-or-pay, ANSSI pathway, ≥EUR 3B debt by Month 12 = 2027-10-17), red-team reporting protocols (direct to committee, monthly pass/fail), and dissent-publication mechanics to lenders within 5 business days. Primary audience: sponsor board, lenders, co-investors, investment committee members. Enforces gate discipline and prevents sunk-cost override.

Responsible Role Type: Independent Investment Committee Chair and Governance Officer

Primary Template: Project Finance Investment Committee Charter Template (Project Management Institute or World Bank Project Finance Handbook)

Secondary Template: Megaproject Gate Governance Protocol (Infrastructure UK / Crossrail lessons-learned documents)

Steps to Create:

  • Engage external counsel to draft charter language compliant with French law and lender expectations.
  • Define numeric kill thresholds in table form with explicit pass/fail and conditional-pass criteria.
  • Establish voting mechanics: simple majority for continuation, supermajority for override, single external-director veto authority.
  • Specify red-team reporting line (direct to committee, not to sponsor), confidentiality protocols, and dissent-publication cadence (monthly to lenders, quarterly to co-investors).
  • Obtain written signatures from all sponsors, lenders and co-investors before Phase 0 Tranche 1 (EUR 150M) is drawn.

Approval Authorities: Sponsor board, Chief Lenders (EIB, KfW or equivalent), Infrastructure Fund Co-Investors, External Committee Chair

Essential Information:

  • Define the investment committee's composition: minimum 2 external independent directors, lender observer(s), co-investor observer(s), sponsor representative(s); specify independence criteria (no financial interest in project beyond lender/investor role, minimum term 3 years).
  • Establish numeric kill thresholds in tabular form locked by Month 2 (2026-12-17): (i) RTE firm letter for ≥500 MW by Month 12 (2027-10-17); (ii) ≥70% of target parcel optioned non-coercively by Month 12 (2027-10-17); (iii) Signed take-or-pay for ≥30% of Phase 1 (≥300 MW) by Month 9 (2027-07-17); (iv) ANSSI confirmation of formal review initiation with no stated blocking concerns by Month 12 (2027-10-17); (v) Binding debt commitment ≥EUR 3B for 500 MW tranche by Month 12 (2027-10-17).
  • Detail voting mechanics: simple majority for continuation, supermajority (two-thirds) for gate override, single external-director veto authority over sunk-cost decisions, published dissent to lenders within 5 business days of any vote.
  • Define red-team reporting protocols: independent red team reports directly to committee (not sponsor), monthly pass/fail opinion on each gate criterion, access to all Phase 0 audit/study findings, confidentiality with external-director sign-off, dissent recording mechanics (minority report, reasoning, confidence level).
  • Establish tranche-release mechanics: Phase 0 draws in 4 tranches (EUR 150M/250M/200M/150M, Months 0–2 = 2026-10-17 to 2026-12-17/3–6/7–9/10–12 = 2026-10-17 to 2026-12-17, 2027-01-17 to 2027-04-17, 2027-05-17 to 2027-07-17, 2027-08-17 to 2027-10-17) tied to milestone completion, committee approval required for each tranche draw, abandonment conditions (write-off of remaining tranche and Phase 1 pause/cancel).
  • Specify conditional-pass mechanics: if external authority (RTE, ANSSI, DREAL) has not delivered final written opinion by the gate date, committee may vote a 'conditional pass' (e.g., Phase 1 FID decision deferred to Month 15 = 2028-01-17 pending authority decision), with go/no-go trigger defined in writing.
  • Describe dissent-publication protocol: quarterly summary to lenders and co-investors of any committee disagreement (yes/no votes, minority reasoning, external director reservations); publication within 10 business days of vote; lender has right to request unpublished meeting minutes (under confidentiality agreement).
  • Articulate charter amendments and restatement: charter may be amended only by unanimous vote of all committee members plus sponsor board approval; full restatement required if numeric thresholds are adjusted post-Month 2 (2026-12-17).
  • Define conflict-of-interest and recusal protocols: external director may not recuse on any gate threshold; lender/co-investor observer may not vote but may request minority opinion; all advisers to the committee must sign engagement letters prohibiting other work for any party with interest in the project outcome.

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • Weak independence language allows sponsor to dominate committee; sunk-cost pressure overrides stated kill thresholds in practice, leading to Phase 1 FID despite failed gates (primary risk per plan, user concern).
  • Vague numeric thresholds (e.g., 'adequate grid capacity' instead of '≥500 MW') create interpretation disputes at gate review; lenders and co-investors cannot assess compliance, reducing financing credibility.
  • Lack of formalized red-team reporting lets sponsor suppress or delay unfavorable findings; gate review proceeds without transparent evidence of feasibility failures.
  • No tranche-release discipline allows Phase 0 spending beyond EUR 750M without committee check; sunk cost balloons uncontrollably, weakening negotiating power with RTE, landowners and permitting authorities.
  • Absent dissent-publication mechanism means lender and co-investor concerns are not recorded; if Phase 1 fails post-FID, no accountability trail or evidence of governance failure exists.
  • Conditional-pass ambiguity (no definition of what triggers a true pass vs. deferred decision) creates confusion; Phase 1 FID is delayed indefinitely pending unclear authority deliverables.
  • No abandonment conditions mean Phase 0 sunk cost is irrecoverable if gates fail; project momentum and equity pressure override rational exit decision.
  • Charter without enforceability mechanisms (no trustee, no third-party arbitration, no lender consent clause) is advisory only; sponsor board can override or reinterpret the charter unilaterally at any gate.

Worst Case Scenario: The investment committee is chartered but composed of sponsor-aligned directors with no independent authority.
