Numeric kill thresholds are written but vaguely (e.g., "adequate grid capacity" rather than "≥500 MW"). Red-team findings of grid constraints, land fragmentation or tenant shortfall are submitted to the committee but sponsor argues they are "manageable risks." The committee votes 5–2 (sponsor majority) to approve Phase 1 FID despite RTE offering only 250 MW, <50% of land optioned, and no binding tenants. Phase 0 sunk cost of EUR 750M is cited as the reason to "protect the investment" and proceed anyway. Phase 1 begins with EUR 5B–10B capital commitment. By Month 36 (2029-10-17), RTE has not issued a connection offer, permitting stalls with legal challenge, land assembly hits holdouts and major contamination is discovered. Phase 1 is halted after EUR 2B–3B is spent. No dissent record exists; lenders and co-investors have no evidence that committee governance failed or that red-team warnings were overridden. Sponsor claims unforeseen circumstances; co-investors lose EUR 1.5B–2B and the project is abandoned with stranded assets and regulatory liability. The absence of a credible independent gate mechanism turns the stated kill criteria into fiction and exposes all stakeholders to cascading losses from sunk-cost override.

Best Case Scenario: The charter is signed by all sponsors, lenders and co-investors in Month 1 (2026-11-17) with independent external directors, formalized numeric kill thresholds and red-team reporting directly to the committee. Red-team monthly reports and gate analyses are transparent to lenders and co-investors; dissent is published quarterly. By Month 9 (2027-07-17), red-team evidence shows RTE will not offer >250 MW, land assembly stalls at 55%, and tenants are offering only non-binding LOIs. Committee holds a formal vote in Month 11 (2027-09-17); the two external directors and lender observer vote no-proceed, citing threshold failures on all three gates. Sponsor argues for a conditional pass but is outvoted supermajority (4–1, sponsor alone voting yes). The committee directs Phase 1 cancellation and Phase 0 completion only (EUR 400M sunk, EUR 350M budget preserved). Phase 0 deliverables (RTE feasibility studies, land options, permitting file, tenant term-sheet templates) are preserved for a potential restart. Sponsor pivots to a scaled 250 MW node in Month 12 (2027-10-17) using preserved assets, reducing equity at-risk and allowing lenders to re-evaluate at a credible scale. The independent committee's credible veto signals market discipline and protects all co-investors from catastrophic sunk-cost overextension. The kill criteria are proven real, not negotiable.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • If independent-director recruitment is difficult or delayed: retain an external governance adviser (not a lender or co-investor) to chair the committee and hold veto authority; require all equity sources to nominate one observer plus sponsor; use the adviser's casting vote on deadlock rather than supermajority rule.
  • If numeric thresholds cannot be locked by Month 2 (2026-12-17) due to external uncertainty: issue a preliminary charter with qualitative thresholds ('RTE shows credible pathway to ≥500 MW'), a monthly red-team re-calibration process, and a Month 6 (2027-04-17) 'threshold lockdown' review; condition Phase 1 FID only on revised, locked thresholds from Month 6 (2027-04-17) onwards.
  • If formal red-team independence is costly or resisted by sponsor: hire the red team through a trustee (e.g., lender's independent technical adviser) rather than sponsor procurement; pay fee from Phase 0 budget with no sponsor discretion over publication.
  • If dissent-publication to lenders is challenged as breaching confidentiality: separate published dissent (summary opinion, not detailed rationale) from confidential minutes (full reasoning, withheld from co-investors unless specifically requested and authorized by committee).
  • If sponsor board refuses a two-thirds override rule as too restrictive: accept simple-majority voting but add a mandatory 30-day 'cooling-off' period after any vote overriding red-team no-proceed finding; during the cooling-off, the project pauses and either new evidence is submitted or the no-proceed decision stands.
  • If tranche-capped drawdown is resisted due to funding logistics: allow accelerated draws but require committee pre-approval and a formal explanation of accelerated spend to lenders within 5 business days of each draw; any draw exceeding budget by >5% triggers an emergency committee meeting.
  • If conditional-pass ambiguity cannot be resolved at charter-drafting time: define a 'decision-deferral schedule' in the charter specifying maximum deferral windows (e.g., if RTE decision is pending, Phase 1 FID can defer to Month 15 = 2028-01-17 maximum; if ANSSI decision is pending, defer to Month 18 = 2028-04-17 maximum). If authority does not deliver by the deferred date, the gate fails automatically.
  • If charter enforceability is questioned: make the charter a binding schedule to all Phase 1 financing agreements and the sponsor's equity commitment, so breaches trigger lender remedies (acceleration, security interests) or co-investor puts (forced buyout of their stake at book value).

Responsible Role Type: Grid Connection and Power Infrastructure Strategist

Primary Template: RTE Connection Offer Template and Technical Feasibility Letter

Secondary Template: Independent Grid Audit Report (e.g., by Tractebel Engineering or equivalent)

Steps to Create:

  • File formal, dated RTE pre-engineering request (Month 0 = 2026-10-17) specifying four tranches, maximum PUE, average load profile, desired energization windows.
  • Request RTE preliminary opinion by Month 4 (2027-02-17) and firm preliminary letter by Month 6 (2027-04-17).
  • Commission independent RTE hosting-capacity auditor (Month 1 = 2026-11-17) to parallel-verify RTE claims using third-party network modeling tools (PSSE, DIgSILENT).
  • Obtain written confirmation from RTE of: available MW per node, reinforcement scope and cost split, timeline to energization, curtailment terms and BESS requirements.
  • Reconcile RTE letter with topology decision: if RTE offers <500 MW per node, document implications for split-campus default.
  • Publish auditor findings (anonymized if needed) to investment committee and lenders by Month 9 (2027-07-17).

Approval Authorities: RTE (Réseau de Transport d'Électricité), Independent RTE Auditor, Investment Committee

Essential Information:

  • Identify the specific RTE grid hosting capacity available at each candidate node (Cambrai, Dunkirk, Valenciennes, Saint-Omer) for 250 MW, 500 MW, 1 GW and 2 GW tranches, with firm timelines to energization per tranche and required transmission reinforcement scope.
  • Document RTE's queue position for the campus relative to competing industrial load (steel decarbonization, hydrogen production, refinery upgrades) in the region and assess saturation risk.
  • Quantify the developer's co-funding obligation for transmission reinforcement (EUR 500M–1.5B estimate) and confirm cost allocation between RTE and developer.
  • Specify annual curtailment allowance (target ≤10%, walk-away ≤15% proposed) in contractual terms, including notice period (30–90 days minimum) and BESS/demand-flexibility requirements to offset curtailment.
  • Validate that at least 500 MW can be connected within 36 months of the formal request (Month 0 = 2026-10-17) to meet the Phase 0 gate at Month 12 (2027-10-17).
  • Provide independent third-party verification of RTE's hosting-capacity claims via parallel network modeling (audit due Month 9 = 2027-07-17).
  • Compare single-square and split-campus topologies on per-node grid hosting, reinforcement cost and timelines to inform the topology decision at Month 4 (2027-02-17).

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • RTE offer of <500 MW in the first tranche, or reinforcement timelines >36 months, fails the primary feasibility gate and triggers Phase 1 cancellation or 12–24 month delay.
  • Omission of competing industrial load analysis may underestimate grid saturation risk and overstate available capacity, stranding land and capital investments.
  • Unclear cost allocation between RTE and developer invites disputes and potential budget overruns of EUR 200M–500M mid-Phase-1.
  • Curtailment terms >15% annually or lacking advance notice erode tenant uptime certainty, causing lease-pricing disputes and potential anchor-tenant exit.
  • Independent audit findings contradicting RTE's preliminary estimate undermine lender and co-investor confidence, delaying or blocking debt financing.
  • Failure to validate split-campus node connectivity and separate grid timelines forces late-stage redesign and 6–12 month Phase 1 delay.

Worst Case Scenario: RTE declines to offer grid hosting above 250–500 MW at any node, or conditions multi-GW access on developer co-funding of EUR 2B+ transmission reinforcement with no timeline certainty. Competing industrial users saturate regional transmission before the campus can secure queue position. An independent grid audit contradicts RTE's preliminary estimate, destroying lender confidence. Phase 1 FID is blocked; Phase 0 sunk cost of EUR 400M–750M is stranded. The project pivots to a much smaller footprint (≤250 MW, single hall) or exits the site entirely, forcing land-option abandonment and renegotiation of all tenant and financing commitments.

Best Case Scenario: RTE issues a firm written connection offer for at least 500 MW within 36 months at the preferred Cambrai node by Month 6 (2027-04-17), with reinforcement costs and timelines clearly bounded and developer co-funding capped at EUR 500M–750M. Curtailment is locked at ≤10% annually with 90 days' notice. Independent audit confirms RTE's estimates. Grid assessment supports both single-square (1+ GW per node) and split-campus options, enabling topology flexibility at Month 4 (2027-02-17). RTE's written evidence allows the investment committee to approve Phase 1 FID at Month 12 (2027-10-17) with high confidence, unlocking debt financing and Phase 1 energization on the baseline Months 42–48 (2030-04-17 to 2030-10-17) schedule.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • If RTE preliminary feasibility letter is not in hand by Month 6 (2027-04-17): immediately trigger the topology decision at Month 4 (2027-02-17) as a split-campus model with 2–3 nodes of 250–500 MW each, default to Dunkirk (port/generation assets) and Valenciennes (industrial heritage) as primary candidates, defer Cambrai to Phase 2 if grid capacity there remains uncertain.
  • If RTE curtailment allowance exceeds 15%: reduce Phase 1 base case from 500 MW to 250–300 MW or shift to a powered-shell model where tenants accept firm but lower power and share curtailment upside via BESS/arbitrage, reducing developer's firm-power obligation.
  • If independent grid audit contradicts RTE's estimates by >20%: commission a second parallel audit by a different vendor; if both audits diverge, escalate to DREAL for mediation and treat the RTE preliminary letter as non-binding, conditional on Phase 1 FID with lender due diligence.
  • If competing industrial load is confirmed to saturate regional transmission: accelerate discussion of co-development with the industrial consortium (steel, hydrogen, refinery users) to share reinforcement costs and enter the grid queue as a unified reindustrialization package, negotiating a blended allocation.
  • If Phase 0 grid assessment reveals that no single node can reliably host ≥500 MW: abandon the single-square topology entirely at Month 4 (2027-02-17), adopt a minimum-viable split-campus model (Dunkirk 250 MW + Valenciennes 200 MW = 450 MW for Phase 1), and defer Cambrai and larger expansion to Phase 2 pending further reinforcement.
  • If RTE cannot commit to energization within 36 months of the formal request: structure Phase 1 with a phased energization plan (first 250 MW at Month 36 = 2029-10-17, second 250 MW at Month 48 = 2030-10-17) to compress the grid connection schedule and accept higher carrying costs.

  • Present the single-square vs. split-campus land-assemblability comparison with explicit go/no-go recommendation by Month 4 (2027-02-17) for the topology decision.

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • Incomplete parcel mapping or omitted holdout identification causes Phase 1 design delays and cost escalation when assembly falters mid-construction; at-risk exposure EUR 200M–500M (estimate).
  • Overoptimistic assemblability claims (e.g., treating pending municipal approvals as 'secured') lead to Phase 1 FID on a parcel base that collapses, forcing redesign or cancellation after EUR 250M–500M sunk cost.
  • Inaccurate land valuation or failure to establish the 15% benchmark threshold allows overpayment by EUR 50M–200M (estimate) or triggers lender concerns about inflated asset basis.
  • Missed or underestimated Phase II ESA contamination findings defer true liability to Phase 1 construction, exposing the project to EUR 100M–400M surprise costs, regulatory enforcement and schedule slips of 6–18 months.
  • Vague or non-binding option-agreement terms leave parcels unprotected; competitors or land speculators can block or delay options, and landowners can demand renegotiation closer to Phase 1.
  • Failure to document activist-group and farm-union opposition early allows organized resistance to crystallize and undermine community-benefit negotiations, extending permitting by 12–36 months (estimate).
  • Absence of a clear single-square vs. split-campus recommendation at Month 4 (2027-02-17) delays topology decision, compresses the remaining Phase 0 timeline (Months 5–12 = 2027-03-17 to 2027-10-17) for split-campus grid, fiber and permitting work, and risks missing the Month 12 (2027-10-17) gate.
  • Weak compulsory-acquisition feasibility assessment understates political and legal risk, leading to false confidence in a single-square option that later proves infeasible, forcing emergency pivot to split campus with late redesign and cost overrun.

Worst Case Scenario: By Month 9 (2027-07-17), mid-Phase 0, parcel assembly stalls: voluntary options fail on 40–60% of the single-square target due to underestimated holdouts (FNSEA opposition, municipal land-registry delays, unknown owners), and Phase II ESA reveals EUR 150M–300M remediation liability on the primary Cambrai parcel, invalidating seller indemnity assumptions. Simultaneously, a competing hydrogen-production project pre-empts RTE's available 1 GW capacity, reducing the Cambrai node offer to 500 MW. The investment committee must downsize Phase 1 to 250 MW (increasing per-MW capex), pivot to a fragmented split-campus topology (requiring 4–8 weeks of emergency grid, permitting and financing rework, breaching the Month 12 (2027-10-17) Phase 0 gate and delaying Phase 1 by 6–12 months), or recommend Phase 0 completion without Phase 1 FID, stranding EUR 500M–750M and signalling project failure to co-investors and lenders. The project loses momentum; Phase 2 FID (contingent on Phase 1 success) is indefinitely deferred or cancelled.

Best Case Scenario: By Month 4 (2027-02-17), the Land Assembly Feasibility report certifies that 75–85% of the single-square Cambrai/E-Valley target parcel (115–137 km² of 161 km²) is optionable at 8–12% above benchmark, with three anchor landowners (including the Cambrai economic-development agency and a regional remediation authority) committing to non-coercive sales or long-term leases by Month 6 (2027-04-17). Phase II ESA bounds remediation to EUR 50M–80M across the top five parcels, with seller indemnities covering EUR 40M–60M. The report recommends the single-square topology for Phase 1, supported by written RTE technical opinion (Month 6 = 2027-04-17) confirming 1+ GW available to Cambrai. Land optioning accelerates through Months 5–12 (2027-03-17 to 2027-10-17); by Month 12 (2027-10-17), ≥70% is under signed option agreement at acceptable cost. The Phase 0 gate passes; Phase 1 FID proceeds on schedule. Land-assembly certainty enables lenders to commit EUR 3B (60% of EUR 5B Phase 1 capex); Phase 1 construction starts Month 13 (2027-11-17) and stays on track for energization Month 42–48 (2030-04-17 to 2030-10-17). Agricultural displacement is packaged into a EUR 50M–100M relocation/revenue-sharing benefit (part of the EUR 50M–150M community-benefit package), reducing farm-union opposition and supporting permitting. Success of the single-square model enables later Phase 2–4 growth on the same landbase, minimizing topology complexity and operational overhead.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • If single-square assemblability remains uncertain at Month 3 (2027-01-17), immediately accelerate split-campus detailed design (Months 3–4 = 2027-01-17 to 2027-02-17) using pre-prepared node templates (Cambrai 500 MW ~8.9 km², Dunkirk 250 MW, Valenciennes 250 MW), so the topology decision at Month 4 (2027-02-17) can choose split campus with confidence; budget EUR 100M–150M (estimate) additional Phase 0 cost for multi-node environmental baselines, grid pre-engineering and permitting file preparation.
  • If parcel optionability stalls below 70% by Month 4 (2027-02-17), commission a rapid compulsory-acquisition feasibility study (2–3 weeks, Months 4–5 = 2027-02-17 to 2027-03-17) with French administrative-law counsel to quantify timeline and cost of State-backed public-interest designation; if compulsory acquisition is viable (12–18 month timeline, EUR 100M–300M cost), proceed; if not, trigger split-campus pivot.
  • If Phase II ESA remediation costs exceed EUR 100M per site, prioritize low-remediation parcels for Phase 1 hall siting (reducing Phase 1 capital at risk), and defer high-remediation areas to Phase 2 or buffer/ecological zones; request public remediation authority (ADEME, BRGM) co-funding or take-over of contamination liability for designated brownfield zones.
  • If activist opposition (farm unions, NGOs) blocks voluntary land assembly by Month 6 (2027-04-17), pivot immediately to a lease-and-continue farming model: offer long-term land leases (20+ years) with revenue-sharing to incumbent farmers, so parcels remain in agricultural use in off-built zones (continuation areas = 50–70% of node envelope); this converts opponents into stakeholders and de-risks farm-sector political blockage.
  • If RTE's written technical opinion (due Month 6 = 2027-04-17) indicates the Cambrai node can support only 500 MW (not 1 GW) due to transmission constraints, accept the 500 MW Phase 1 base case and pursue Phase 2 expansion to a second node (Dunkirk or Valenciennes) contingent on full signed demand and RTE capacity offer for that node; this preserves Phase 1 FID on a lower risk profile.
  • If municipal or prefectural land-registry delays prevent option-agreement closure by Month 9 (2027-07-17), secure a legal lock-in instrument: a formal municipal 'reservation' (réservation) holding the land off the open market for up to 24 months (renewable), with a committed purchase or lease option, while resolving registry and ownership disputes in parallel; cost EUR 5M–20M (estimate), delays gate by 3 months.
  • If Phase 0 timeline pressures make simultaneous single-square and split-campus detailed assemblability work infeasible within the EUR 750M cap, commission only the single-square parcel mapping and Phase II ESA for the Months 0–6 (2026-10-17 to 2027-04-17) period (EUR 250M–350M), and defer split-campus node-level assemblability to Month 4–6 (2027-02-17 to 2027-04-17) using shell template costs and preliminary grid/permitting assumptions; this fits the Phase 0 milestone but requires a 2-week Month 4 (2027-02-17) topology-decision acceleration to finalize the split-campus recommendation by early Month 5 (2027-03-17).

Create Document 4: Anchor-Tenant Term-Sheet Template and Demand Validation Framework

ID: 81dcdb35-531f-4ec4-a728-fecfbd5ab50d

Description: Standardized take-or-pay lease template (deliverable Month 2 = 2026-12-17) specifying capacity reservation (50–500 MW per tenant), lease term (5–10 years), reservation fee (EUR 10M–50M per 100 MW, paid before construction and credited to rent), power price (indexed or capped EUR/MWh with ±3% annual escalation cap proposed), uptime SLA (99.5–99.95%, force-majeure carve-outs for curtailment and cooling outages >4 hours), take-or-pay clause, and liquidated-damages provision (10–15% of first-year lease revenue if tenant exits post-FID). Document distinguishes binding term sheets (exclusive, payment commitment) from non-binding LOIs (site-comparison tool, do not count toward gates). Includes process for securing cash reservation-fee deposits in escrow, parent-company guarantees for sub-investment-grade tenants, and credit-rating monitoring (S&P, Moody's quarterly updates). Primary audience: commercial development team, anchor tenants, lenders.

Responsible Role Type: Anchor-Tenant and Market Development Lead

Primary Template: Master Service Agreement (MSA) Template for Data Center Capacity Leases (AWS, Microsoft or equivalent precedent)

Secondary Template: Take-or-Pay Lease Agreement with SLA and Force-Majeure Carve-Outs (project-finance standard form)

Steps to Create:

  • Engage commercial counsel to draft term-sheet language covering capacity, pricing, term, SLAs, take-or-pay mechanics, and exit penalties.
  • Define what constitutes 'binding' (reservation-fee cash, liquidated damages, parent guarantee if credit <BBB−).
  • Specify force-majeure carve-outs: RTE curtailment >15% annual, cooling outage >4 hours, ANSSI clearance delay >X months.
  • Develop power-price pass-through mechanics: indexed to EDF/RTE settlement price with tenant cap (e.g., ±3% escalation).
  • Create tenant credit-monitoring protocol: counterparty rating downgrade >1 notch triggers collateral posting (12-month lease escrow).
  • By Month 3 (2027-01-17), identify 2–3 anchor-tenant prospects by name and pre-brief on terms.
  • By Month 9 (2027-07-17), execute binding term sheets with ≥150 MW (30% of Phase 1) and confirm reservation-fee cash deposits in escrow.
  • Document tenant credit quality (A− to BB+ minimum) and any parent-company guarantees.

Approval Authorities: Anchor-Tenant Lead, General Counsel, Investment Committee (for gate approval)

Essential Information:

  • Define the contractual structure of binding take-or-pay leases specifying: capacity reserved (50–500 MW per tenant), lease term (5–10 years proposed), reservation fee mechanism (EUR 10M–50M per 100 MW, paid before construction, credited against rent), and power pricing (indexed or capped EUR/MWh with ±3% annual escalation cap proposed).
  • Establish the legal distinction between binding term sheets (exclusive capacity reservation, non-refundable fees, liquidated-damages clause for early termination) and non-binding letters of intent (site-comparison advisory, no payment commitment, do not satisfy Phase 0 or Phase 2 FID gates).
  • Specify uptime and service-level agreements: 99.5–99.95% availability (proposed threshold), force-majeure carve-outs for RTE curtailment >15% annual (walk-away threshold), cooling outages >4 hours, and ANSSI clearance delay >X months (to be defined).
  • Define counterparty credit and risk mitigation: minimum credit rating A−/BB+ (proposed threshold), parent-company guarantees or letters of credit for sub-investment-grade tenants, quarterly S&P/Moody's monitoring with collateral posting triggered by >1-notch downgrade.
  • Document the reservation-fee escrow and cash-deposit mechanism: fees held in third-party escrow, released at Phase 1 FID contingent on all gates closing, forfeiture if tenant exits post-binding, credited EUR-for-EUR against first 12–36 months of lease rent.
  • Include power-price pass-through mechanics: indexed to EDF/RTE settlement price or capped at a defined EUR/MWh range (proposed EUR 50–70/MWh base, ±3% annual escalation), tenant liable for delivered cost (network tariffs, taxes) above the capped wholesale price (mechanism to be validated with EDF).
  • Specify liquidated-damages for tenant breach or early exit post-FID: 10–15% of first-year lease revenue (propose EUR 55M–82.5M per 500 MW at EUR 550M/year stabilized revenue), payable within 30 days, in addition to lease termination and facility damages.
  • Define force-majeure and curtailment accommodation: RTE-mandated curtailment up to 10% (proposed) is not force-majeure; curtailment 10–15% (walk-away) is shared cost (tenant takes 50% revenue loss, developer absorbs grid costs); curtailment >15% is force-majeure, tenant may exit. BESS dispatch to minimize curtailment is developer responsibility.
  • Establish process timeline for securing term-sheet signatures: identify 2–3 anchor-prospect tenants by Month 3 (2027-01-17), pre-brief on commercial terms Months 3–6 (2027-01-17 to 2027-04-17), execute binding term sheets with at least 30% of Phase 1 capacity (150 MW of 500 MW; 300 MW of 1 GW) by Month 9 (2027-07-17), confirm reservation-fee escrow deposits by Month 12 (2027-10-17) gate review.
  • Detail tenant-classification framework: hyperscaler (multi-hundred-MW commitment, high credit, negotiated power discounts), sovereign AI (French/EU public-sector or defense, slower procurement, may demand segregated security zones, data-residency constraints), and mixed/secondary (smaller tenants, faster deployment). Term-sheet variants per class.
  • Document the gate criterion for Phase 1 FID and Phase 2 expansion: Phase 1 gate requires ≥30% (150 MW of 500 MW baseline) signed, at least 300 MW if 1 GW baseline. Phase 2 gate requires ≥50% (user floor 30–50%) of next-tranche expansion, plus 12 months' Phase 1 operating data proving uptime and power availability. Letters of intent do not count toward either gate.
  • Provide template language and checklists for: (i) capacity, term and pricing definition; (ii) reservation-fee mechanics and escrow; (iii) force-majeure and SLA carve-outs; (iv) credit monitoring and collateral; (v) liquidated-damages triggers; (vi) counterparty representation and authority; (vii) governing law (proposed French law) and dispute resolution (mediation, then arbitration under ICC rules).

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • Ambiguity between binding and non-binding terms allows tenants to claim non-binding LOI as equivalent to a signed term sheet, invalidating the gate criterion (30% signed capacity required). This risks Phase 0 gate failure if the investment committee cannot distinguish executed leases from advisory mail.
  • Weak or missing reservation-fee mechanism (e.g., fees not in escrow, refundable after signing) allows tenants to reserve capacity without financial commitment, reducing leverage if tenant demand later evaporates or tenants negotiate price concessions post-FID.
  • Imprecise force-majeure language (e.g., no threshold for curtailment tolerance, vague SLA carve-outs) leads to disputes during Phase 1 when RTE curtailment hits 12–15% or cooling systems fail. Tenant claims force-majeure and exits; developer loses revenue and cannot meet debt covenants (DSCR minimum 1.30x, current 1.34x; 10% lease discount drops to 1.15x gap).
  • Missing or overly broad parent-guarantee waiver for sub-investment-grade tenants (e.g., 'BB' rating without guarantee) exposes the developer if the tenant's credit deteriorates post-signature; no collateral posting mechanism to protect lease revenue during Phase 1 construction (18-month gap between FID and revenue start).
  • Unclear power-price pass-through mechanics (e.g., tenant cap vs. developer pass-through exposure) create disputes when EDF supply cost rises above assumed EUR 50–70/MWh. If EUR 30/MWh overrun is not passed through, developer absorbs EUR 112M annual cost at 500 MW (36% of estimated NOI EUR 300M pre-tax), breaching lender DSCR covenant.
  • Liquidated-damages clause missing or too low (e.g., 5% of revenue vs. proposed 10–15%) allows tenant to treat the penalty as a negotiable option cost rather than a real deterrent to exit. Early post-FID tenant withdrawal to a cheaper competing data center becomes rational if penalty is <EUR 27.5M vs. EUR 55M–82.5M first-year lease value.
  • No credit-monitoring schedule or collateral-posting trigger allows a tenant to slip from A− to BB− without the developer triggering escrow increases or parent-guarantee recalls, leaving Phase 1 revenue exposed to tenant financial stress.
  • Insufficient detail on reservation-fee escrow mechanics (e.g., what triggers release, who authorizes draws, what happens if FID is delayed or cancelled) leads to disputes with the escrow agent and tenants over access to deposits, delaying Phase 1 financing closure and drawdown authorization.
  • Generic or template SLA language (e.g., 'commercially reasonable efforts') without defined uptime percentages, curtailment limits or monetary remedies leaves no clarity on what constitutes tenant SLA breach vs. force-majeure, inviting litigation if Phase 1 halls miss commissioning targets or experience cooling/power issues.
  • Omission of tenant-workload segregation and latency-tolerance specifications (relevant to split-campus topology) prevents the developer from assessing which tenants can span multiple nodes or require co-location, undermining the Phase 0 topology decision (Month 4 = 2027-02-17) which depends on confirmed tenant-cluster-size requirements.

Worst Case Scenario: By Month 9 (2027-07-17) of Phase 0, only non-binding LOIs are in hand (e.g., 200 MW from hyperscalers phrased as "letters of intent, not commitments"). The investment committee correctly rejects these toward the 30% gate threshold (150 MW for 500 MW baseline). Phase 0 gate fails on the anchor-tenant criterion (Month 12 = 2027-10-17). Without signed take-or-pay, debt financing is withdrawn or downgraded to 50% leverage (EUR 2.5B vs. EUR 3B), requiring EUR 2.5B additional equity and raising cost of capital by 200+ basis points. Phase 1 FID is cancelled or deferred 12–24 months. The Phase 0 sunk cost (EUR 250M–750M) is stranded, and the project enters a 18–24 month holding pattern waiting for tenant demand signals to crystallize. If demand eventually firms only at a lower scale (e.g., 250 MW instead of 500 MW), Phase 1 capex falls from EUR 5B to EUR 2.5B, but per-MW fixed costs (substation, grid, security, permitting) cannot scale down proportionally. The project's return-on-equity collapses below the hurdle rate (proposed 8–12% IRR, not specified), and co-investors may force a reassessment or exit. Alternatively, weak term sheets (high cancellation-penalty waivers, low power-price pass-through caps) allow tenants to negotiate margin-eroding concessions post-signature, reducing Phase 1 operating-margin from proposed EUR 400M (550 revenue − 150 opex) to EUR 250M–300M, dropping DSCR from 1.34x to 0.84–1.0x and triggering technical default on debt covenants within 24 months of Phase 1 energization.

Best Case Scenario: By Month 9 (2027-07-17), the commercial team has executed binding term sheets from three anchor tenants (e.g., two hyperscalers at 150 MW + 100 MW, one sovereign AI consortium at 100 MW) for 350 MW total (70% of 500 MW baseline, exceeding the 30% gate minimum). Reservation fees of EUR 15M per 100 MW (EUR 52.5M total) are deposited in escrow. Power-price cap is locked at EUR 68/MWh with ±2% escalation, aligned with preliminary EDF supply LOI. Force-majeure carve-outs are tight: curtailment >15% is walk-away, <10% is accepted, 10–15% is shared cost. Credit ratings are A− (hyperscalers) and BBB (sovereign via state parent guarantee), qualifying under the A−/BB+ threshold. Parent guarantees are in place for any sub-investment-grade tenants; quarterly credit monitoring is triggered with collateral posting on downgrade. The Phase 0 gate closes in Month 12 (2027-10-17) with signed demand covering 70% of Phase 1, enabling debt financing at 60% leverage (EUR 3B on EUR 5B), cost of capital at 5.5% all-in (benchmark + 100 bps), and Phase 1 FID authorization. Phase 1 energization begins Months 12–36 (2027-10-17 to 2029-10-17) with revenue ramping starting Month 42 (2030-04-17). By Months 48–54 (2030-10-17 to 2031-04-17), the 500 MW asset is stabilized at 500 MW utilization, generating EUR 550M lease revenue, EUR 223M energy pass-through, EUR 150M opex, and EUR 400M NOI, servicing EUR 299M debt with 1.34x DSCR and EUR 101M annual equity distributions. Phase 2 FID (Month 48–54 = 2030-10-17 to 2031-04-17) proceeds with 12 months' operating data validating PUE 1.20–1.25, uptime >99.6%, security clearance, and signed demand from Phase 1 tenants and new anchors for the 2 GW Phase 2 expansion (reaching 50% threshold). The project is on track for 3 GW by Month 84 (2033-10-17) and 9 GW by Month 180 (2041-10-17), subject to subsequent gates.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • If binding term-sheet signatures are difficult to obtain by Month 9 (2027-07-17), pivot to a tiered demand structure: secure at least 30% (150 MW) in binding term sheets by Month 9 (2027-07-17), allow non-binding LOIs from an additional 20–30% (100–150 MW) with a contingent binding-upgrade deadline by Month 18 (2028-04-17). Reframe the Phase 0 gate (Month 12 = 2027-10-17) as 'conditional pass' if the 30% binding threshold is met plus a credible path to 50% (250 MW) by Phase 1 energization (Month 42 = 2030-04-17). This allows Phase 1 FID to proceed with lower initial utilization (25–30% of capacity on opening), ramping to 50% within 12 months as LOI tenants convert.
  • Develop a capacity-reservation-fee structure that reduces tenant cash commitment but increases financial penalty: lower upfront fee (EUR 5M–10M per 100 MW vs. EUR 10M–50M) but increase liquidated-damages to 20–25% of first-year revenue (vs. 10–15%) and require a parent-company guarantee letter of credit (rather than guarantee) to back early-exit penalties. This makes the financial exposure transparent without requiring large upfront escrow from tenants with volatile balance sheets.
  • If major hyperscalers refuse to commit before seeing Phase 1 operational data (common in the industry), launch a 'fast-follower' tier: accept non-binding LOIs from hyperscalers contingent on Phase 1 performance (PUE, uptime, security clearance), paired with a binding commitment from 1–2 sovereign or European consortium anchors that provide the 30% minimum demand. This splits the risk: sovereign tenants lock in capacity (de-risking financing), hyperscalers reserve spots with performance optionality, and Phase 1 revenue comes from a mix of paying anchors and eventual hyperscaler conversion.
  • If power-price pass-through cannot be agreed (e.g., tenants push back on indexed caps, demand full fixed-price leases), split the power risk: negotiate fixed-price leases for the 30% anchor-demand base (revenue locked at EUR 550M at 500 MW) and offer floating-price leases for secondary/overflow tenants at EUR/MWh settlements. This concentrates fixed-price cost exposure on the creditworthy anchors and preserves upside if power prices fall, while accepting downside on secondary capacity.
  • If the template term sheet proves too commercially aggressive (high reservation fees, strong liquidated-damages, tight force-majeure), develop a 'light' variant for secondary tenants: lower fees (EUR 5M–10M per 100 MW vs. EUR 10M–50M), longer payment terms (rent-to-own after 3–5 years rather than immediate lease), and broader force-majeure (curtailment >10% vs. >15%), paired with a higher base capacity price (EUR 1.2M–1.3M per MW-year vs. EUR 1.1M). This broadens the addressable tenant pool for the 40–70% non-anchor portion of the campus, accepting margin compression for utilization.
  • Commission a third-party tenant-demand study (Month 2 = 2026-12-17) if term-sheet negotiations are moving slowly, to validate whether the Phase 0 gate (30% demand) is achievable in the 12-month timeline. If the study indicates demand will not materialize until Month 18–24 (2028-04-17 to 2028-10-17), replan Phase 0 as a 18–24 month effort, extending the gate to Month 24 (2028-10-17) and Phase 1 FID to Month 30 (2029-04-17). Adjust the Phase 0 tranche drawdown schedule accordingly (e.g., four tranches over 24 months vs. 12 months).
  • If executed term sheets exceed the Phase 0 demand ceiling (e.g., 300 MW of binding interest vs. 150 MW 30% requirement), repurpose the excess as oversubscription options: structure 200 MW as binding for anchor tenants and 100 MW as oversubscription rights exercisable in Phase 2, tied to Phase 1 operational performance. This locks in the 30% minimum (200 MW of 500 MW baseline is 40%, above the 30% threshold) and creates Phase 2 pipeline demand.
  • Prepare a backup term-sheet template with financing-structure alternatives if standard take-or-pay leases prove unpalatable: (i) Powered-shell model (developer sells capacity, tenants procure and finance hardware separately under their own FX and obsolescence risk); (ii) Revenue-sharing model (developer and tenant split uptime and power-cost overruns rather than fixed lease rate); (iii) Throughput-based model (tenant pays per GPU-hour of utilization vs. reserved MW, reducing upfront commitment). Each variant has different gating implications (powered-shell narrows addressable market; revenue-sharing adds operational complexity; throughput-based delays revenue recognition), so document the trade-offs and decision rules for each.

Create Document 5: National Security and Foreign Investment Screening Assessment

ID: 15ad112b-b9b8-4ca8-9541-acfa10700686

Description: Confidential white paper and formal assessment (Month 6 = 2027-04-17 informal opinion, Month 12 = 2027-10-17 clearance-pathway confirmation) documenting: project scope, tenant types and data-residency requirements, foreign co-investor shareholding and governance, proposed security architecture (perimeter hardening, anti-drone, cyber-OT separation, personnel vetting), and anticipated national-security review scope and timeline with ANSSI, DGSI and DGSE. Identifies potential blocking concerns (foreign equity restrictions, data-residency zones, state observer roles) and proposes mitigation (governance restructuring, data policies). Includes confidential ANSSI/DGSI pre-submission meeting summary (Month 0–1 = 2026-10-17 to 2026-11-17) and formal preliminary opinion letter confirming that security review can start (Month 13 = 2027-11-17) with 12–18 month target clearance. Primary audience: ANSSI/DGSI, foreign co-investors, investment committee, Phase 1 security design team.

Responsible Role Type: National Security and Regulatory Affairs Lead

Primary Template: ANSSI/DGSI Pre-Submission White Paper (confidential, French government format)

Secondary Template: Foreign Investment Screening Impact Assessment (CFIUS precedent or EU equivalent)

Steps to Create:

  • Draft white paper (10–15 pages) covering tenant mix, foreign co-investor details, data-residency policies, security design baseline.
  • Schedule confidential pre-submission meetings with ANSSI, DGSI and DGSE (Month 0 = 2026-10-17).
  • Commission high-assurance security-design roadmap (EUR 500K–1.5M, Month 2 = 2026-12-17) covering perimeter, OT separation, supply-chain vetting, personnel clearance standards.
  • Share roadmap informally with ANSSI (Month 3 = 2027-01-17) for preliminary feedback.
  • Obtain written ANSSI preliminary opinion (Month 6 = 2027-04-17) confirming review timeline and blocking concerns (if any).
  • By Month 12 (2027-10-17), secure written confirmation that formal security review can start (Month 13 = 2027-11-17) with no fundamental blocking concerns.
  • Coordinate with foreign co-investor legal counsel on governance and investment-screening mitigation.

Approval Authorities: ANSSI, DGSI, DGSE (French national-security agencies), Foreign Co-Investor Legal Counsel, Investment Committee

Essential Information:

  • Identify the foreign co-investor stakeholders by name, equity stake, jurisdiction and any sovereign or state-backed affiliation; clarify governance voting rights and veto powers held by each party.
  • Document the proposed tenant mix: hyperscaler or AI lab name, workload type (general training, sovereign AI, defense-adjacent), data classification (unclassified, confidential, secret), data-residency requirements (EU-only, FR-only, on-site storage).
  • Map tenant tenancy structure: separate hall allocations, network isolation (air-gapped or logically segregated), physical security zones (high-assurance enclaves), personnel access controls (cleared vs. uncleared).
  • Specify the proposed security architecture baseline applicable to all halls: perimeter hardening (fence, CCTV, detection), anti-drone systems, cyber-OT separation (industrial control networks isolated from tenant networks), personnel security vetting (level of background check, national-security clearance), supply-chain vetting (hardware vendors, contractors).
  • Define escalated security postures for sovereign or defense-adjacent partitions: hardened enclaves, air-gapping, 24/7 armed security, state observer roles, audit frequency and escalation procedures.
  • Quantify the national-security review scope and anticipated timeline based on confidential pre-submission dialogue with ANSSI, DGSI and DGSE (Month 0–1 = 2026-10-17 to 2026-11-17): review duration (proposed 12–18 months from formal start at Month 13 = 2027-11-17), phases (preliminary assessment, formal review, interim clearance, full clearance), documentation requirements, and test/audit timelines.
  • Identify potential blocking concerns or conditions that may emerge from the review: restrictions on foreign equity stake (proposed cap or divestment timeline), tenant-access restrictions (hyperscaler exclusion, EU-only requirement), data-residency mandates (on-site storage, no transmission outside FR), state observer or monitoring roles, periodic re-certification cycles.
  • Document the foreign co-investor mitigation strategy: revised governance structure (e.g., supermajority voting for data-policy decisions, veto by French director on tenant access), data-residency and national-security data-handling policies (encryption at rest, network segmentation, audit trails, incident response), operational compliance (regular security red teams, third-party audits, ANSSI liaison officers), and timeline to achieve compliance (targeted before Phase 1 energization, Months 42–48 = 2030-04-17 to 2030-10-17).
  • Propose the gate criteria for Phase 1 FID: written confirmation from ANSSI by Month 12 (2027-10-17) that formal security review can commence (Month 13 = 2027-11-17) with no fundamental blocking concern identified; formal clearance is proposed as a Phase 1 energization condition (Months 42–48 = 2030-04-17 to 2030-10-17) but may run in parallel if interim clearance for limited initial operations is available.
  • Establish escalation and decision procedures if ANSSI or DGSI issues conditional clearance (e.g., restricted-tenant list, mandatory state observers): who decides (investment committee, sponsor board, foreign co-investor), timeline for remedy (6–12 months), fallback options (tenant substitution, security upgrade, reduced Phase 1 size), and exit provisions (force majeure, equity buyout trigger).

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • Absent or ambiguous foreign co-investor identification and governance structure leaves ANSSI unable to assess national-security risk, blocking formal review start and delaying Phase 1 FID by 6–12 months (carrying cost €300M–600M estimated).
  • Vague tenant-mix definition (hyperscaler names, workload types, data classification not specified) prevents ANSSI from determining review scope and potential blocking concerns (e.g., US-headquartered hyperscaler training unclassified models vs. French sovereign classified AI); ANSSI may demand a revised tenant strategy post-Phase-0, forcing anchor-tenant renegotiation.
  • Incomplete specification of security-architecture baseline and escalated postures allows ANSSI to demand costly retrofits post-FID (e.g., air-gap requirements, hardware encryption mandates, armed 24/7 security); Phase 1 capex exposed to €50M–200M (estimate) unbudgeted security additions.
  • Lack of pre-submission dialogue with ANSSI/DGSI by Month 1 (2026-11-17) delays informal opinion to Month 12 (2027-10-17) or beyond, compressing time available to address blocking concerns before Phase 1 FID gate at Month 12 (2027-10-17); exit or renegotiation forced at last minute.
  • Failure to quantify ANSSI review timeline and phases leaves debt-financing and Phase 1 schedule dependent on uncontrolled authority timelines; lenders may refuse debt commitment if security clearance is not a Phase 1 FID gate, citing regulatory risk.
  • Absence of written mitigation strategy for foreign-equity restrictions (e.g., proposed governance restructuring, data-policy commitments) leaves co-investor at risk of forced equity sale or governance veto post-gate; equity value and IRR eroded, co-investor legal challenge possible.
  • Unspecified escalation procedure for conditional clearance (e.g., state observer mandate, tenant-access restrictions) leaves the project without a framework to respond; repeated ANSSI requests for design change or operational constraint add cost, delay, or force Phase 1 redesign.
  • No documented force-majeure clause or exit provision in case ANSSI clearance is refused or made contingent on unacceptable terms (e.g., state majority ownership, zero-foreign-tenant rule) leaves Phase 1 FID at legal and financial risk if clearance becomes unachievable or incompatible with investor expectations.

Worst Case Scenario: If the National Security and Foreign Investment Screening Assessment is incomplete, ambiguous or absent, ANSSI formal review may be blocked or delayed until Phase 1 FID (Month 12 = 2027-10-17) or beyond. Unidentified foreign-equity concerns or tenant-mix incompatibilities may trigger ANSSI conditional clearance (e.g., mandatory state observer, foreign-equity cap, hyperscaler-tenant exclusion) requiring Phase 1 redesign, anchor-tenant renegotiation or co-investor equity restructuring. Phase 1 FID is delayed 6–12 months; debt financing withdrawn unless security clearance is no longer a gate condition (increasing lender risk premium by 200–400 bps). Carrying costs €300M–600M (estimate). Co-investor threatens legal action over governance changes or forced equity sale. Phase 1 energization slips to Months 48–60 (2030-10-17 to 2031-10-17), eroding RTE grid queue position and tenant demand certainty. Alternatively, ANSSI refusal to clear the project (if foreign-investor or hyperscaler-tenant composition is deemed incompatible with French national interest) blocks Phase 1 entirely, leaving Phase 0 sunk (€250M–750M) and triggering investor disputes over whose approval failure caused the loss.

Best Case Scenario: A comprehensive, transparent National Security and Foreign Investment Screening Assessment, developed in partnership with ANSSI, DGSI and co-investor legal counsel by Month 6 (2027-04-17), enables ANSSI to issue an informal preliminary opinion confirming that formal security review can commence on a defined timeline (12–18 months) with no fundamental blocking concerns. Governance structure, foreign-equity restrictions, data-residency commitments and security-architecture design are pre-agreed with authorities, removing surprise conditions at Phase 1 FID. Tenant mix is verified compatible with national-security requirements; hyperscaler and sovereign-AI partitions are segregated per ANSSI recommendation, reducing inter-tenant risk. Formal security clearance is achieved by Phase 1 energization (Months 42–48 = 2030-04-17 to 2030-10-17) or interim clearance allows limited initial operations. Co-investor governance and foreign-equity stake are finalized without post-gate renegotiation, protecting equity value and Phase 1 financing. Debt financing commitment is achieved (Month 12 = 2027-10-17) because security clearance is a quantified gate criterion met on schedule. Phase 1 FID proceeds on plan; energization at Months 42–48 (2030-04-17 to 2030-10-17) and grid queue position are held.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • Commission a simplified confidential white paper by Month 3 (2027-01-17) covering only the foreign co-investor shareholding, governance voting rights, data-policy framework and tenant-access restrictions; schedule informal ANSSI coffee meeting (unminuted, non-binding) by Month 4 (2027-02-17) to solicit preliminary feedback on showstoppers. Document outcomes in a single-page memo; if no blocking concerns are flagged, proceed with Phase 0 gate assuming ANSSI dialogue can be formalized post-FID.
  • Bifurcate the investment structure: separate the foreign co-investor equity from operational control by vesting campus-company voting and tenant-access decisions with an independent French board majority (≥2 of 3 directors) backed by French pension funds or institutional investors, not the foreign sovereign fund. Reduce foreign-investor role to non-voting preferred equity; this may reduce ANSSI scrutiny and eliminate the need for a lengthy pre-submission security assessment.
  • Defer sensitive tenant-commitment discussions (hyperscaler names, workloads, data classification) until after ANSSI informal opinion (Month 6 = 2027-04-17) is in hand. Phase 0 white paper references 'undisclosed multinational AI labs' and 'European sovereign users' without names. Once ANSSI has indicated review scope and timeline, tenants are locked in (binding term sheets by Month 9 = 2027-07-17) and the formal security assessment covers only the final tenant mix.
  • Engage a boutique firm specializing in French national-security reviews (e.g., Eurasia Group, Control Risks) to prepare the assessment and manage ANSSI pre-submission dialogue (Months 0–1 = 2026-10-17 to 2026-11-17). Provide the white paper in French; use ANSSI's preferred documentation format (SDIS template or equivalent) to reduce friction. Estimated cost €500K–1.5M; this accelerates Month 6 (2027-04-17) informal opinion and reduces Phase 0 timeline risk.
  • Establish a separate 'national-security governance committee' reporting to the investment committee (not the full board), with ANSSI liaison officers, a French co-director and the Chief Security Officer. Hold monthly meetings (first Month 2 = 2026-12-17 onwards) and publish minutes to ANSSI; this signals continuous compliance and may allow ANSSI to issue preliminary clearance earlier (Month 3–4 = 2027-01-17 to 2027-02-17 vs. Month 6 = 2027-04-17). Estimated cost €1M–2M annually.
  • Condition the Phase 1 FID gate not on full ANSSI security clearance (which may extend to Phase 1 energization, Months 42–48 = 2030-04-17 to 2030-10-17) but on formal ANSSI confirmation by Month 12 (2027-10-17) that review can start (Month 13 = 2027-11-17) with no anticipated blockage. Interim clearance for limited initial operations (e.g., unclassified hyperscaler workloads only, restricted personnel access) allows Phase 1 energization to proceed while formal clearance runs in parallel over 12–18 months. Risk: ANSSI may issue full clearance condition post-FID with costly retrofit requirements.

Create Document 6: Environmental Baseline Assessment and EIA Strategy

ID: 7d3dc740-7c95-43a7-a7f1-7d4c818e85a5

Description: Comprehensive environmental assessment (Phase 0 deliverable, with DREAL screening opinion by Month 9 = 2027-07-17) covering Phase I/II ESA, hydrology and water-balance, ecology and biodiversity (Natura 2000, protected species, habitat surveys), soil and groundwater contamination, and stormwater/drainage. Produces a campus-wide ecological master plan (due Month 6 = 2027-04-17) with avoidance-reduction-compensation strategy; remediation liability allocation (private sellers, public bodies, escrow); water-authority opinion on dry-cooling feasibility at zero evaporative water; and preliminary EIA scope for one or more permit filings (single application for integrated campus vs. per-node filings). Identifies any contamination or ecological constraints that would trigger topology pivot or Phase 1 downsize. Primary audience: DREAL, prefecture, water authority (Agence de l'Eau), lenders, permitting counsel.

Responsible Role Type: Environmental and Permitting Counsel

Primary Template: Phase I/II Environmental Site Assessment Report (French BRGM or USEPA format)

Secondary Template: EIA Scoping Document and Ecological Compensation Master Plan (per French Code de l'environnement Articles R.181 et seq.)

Steps to Create:

  • Commission Phase I desktop assessments (Month 1 = 2026-11-17) on all candidate parcels.
  • Commission Phase II intrusive surveys (Month 1 = 2026-11-17, delivered Month 3 = 2027-01-17, EUR 1.5M–3M per zone) covering soil boring, groundwater sampling, asbestos inventory, ordnance risk.
  • Engage environmental baseline team (ecology, hydrology, soil specialists) to conduct summer field surveys (botanical, avian, invertebrate, bat) across all candidate sites; deliver by Month 4 (2027-02-17).
  • Commission hydrological study (EUR 800K–1.5M) covering water balance, drought frequency, and cooler performance at 35°C; deliver by Month 5 (2027-03-17).
  • Draft ecological master plan (Month 5 = 2027-03-17) with avoidance zones (no-build areas protecting Natura 2000), mitigation (landscaping, habitat creation), and compensation parcels (offsite restoration); due Month 6 (2027-04-17).
  • Obtain written water-authority opinion (Month 6 = 2027-04-17) on dry-cooler feasibility at zero evaporative water.
  • Prepare preliminary EIA file for DREAL screening (Month 6 = 2027-04-17); obtain formal screening opinion by Month 9 (2027-07-17).
  • Identify any Phase II results (contamination >EUR 100M, protected-species conflict, water-authority restriction) that would trigger topology pivot or capacity downsize; escalate to investment committee.

Approval Authorities: DREAL (Directions Régionales de l'Environnement, de l'Aménagement et du Logement), Regional Water Authority (Agence de l'Eau Artois-Picardie), Environmental Counsel

Essential Information:

  • Deliver a Phase I Environmental Site Assessment (desktop survey, records review) covering all candidate parcels across Cambrai/E-Valley, Dunkirk, Valenciennes/Denain/Escaudain and Saint-Omer by Month 1 (2026-11-17); identify sites with known industrial history or environmental sensitivity.
  • Commission and complete Phase II intrusive surveys (soil boring, groundwater sampling, asbestos inventory, ordnance/munitions risk assessment) on the top 2–3 candidate sites per zone by Month 3 (2027-01-17), with cost EUR 1.5M–3M per zone (estimate); bound remediation liability to EUR 0–100M per site as a gate criterion.
  • Conduct and document environmental baseline field surveys (botanical, avian, invertebrate, bat surveys; Natura 2000 and protected-species mapping) across all candidate sites by Month 4 (2027-02-17); identify avoidance zones (no-build areas) and biodiversity hotspots.
  • Commission hydrological study (EUR 800K–1.5M estimate) covering regional water stress, summer drought frequency and severity, and dry-cooler thermal performance at 35°C ambient; deliver by Month 5 (2027-03-17).
  • Obtain written opinion from Agence de l'Eau Artois-Picardie confirming that closed-loop direct-to-chip cooling with dry coolers (zero evaporative water) is technically and legally feasible at the planned scale (500 MW–1 GW) by Month 6 (2027-04-17).
  • Draft campus-wide ecological master plan by Month 5 (2027-03-17) and finalize by Month 6 (2027-04-17), incorporating avoidance (no-build buffers around Natura 2000 and protected habitats), reduction (landscaping, habitat enhancement on working land) and compensation (offsite restoration or habitat creation, estimated EUR 200M–500M); define net-positive biodiversity strategy and habitat equivalence calculations.
  • Identify remediation-liability allocation strategy: distinguish private-landowner sites (require Phase II and seller indemnity or escrow EUR 50M–250M estimate), public-land sites (require public remediation body to retain liability and certify clean-up), and insurance-eligible sites; shortlist parcels by Month 6 (2027-04-17) with bounded remediation exposure.
  • Prepare preliminary EIA scoping document for DREAL screening (French Code de l'environnement Articles R.181–R.189 et seq.) by Month 6 (2027-04-17); obtain formal DREAL screening opinion (scoping decision) by Month 9 (2027-07-17) confirming EIA scope, single vs. multi-site permitting strategy, and any blocking environmental sensitivities.
  • Assess and escalate to the investment committee any Phase II findings that would trigger topology pivot or Phase 1 capacity downsize: contamination remediation >EUR 100M (estimate), Natura 2000 or protected-species conflict requiring major hall relocation, or water-authority restriction on cooler feasibility; document decision and rationale by Month 7 (2027-05-17).
  • Quantify and disclose all environmental cost exposures in Phase 0: Phase II survey EUR 1.5M–3M per zone (estimate); ecological compensation EUR 200M–500M (estimate); remediation reserve EUR 100M–300M Phase 1 (estimate); describe how each is funded (Phase 0, Phase 1 capex, contingency, tenant or public contribution).

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • Incomplete Phase II surveys or late discovery of major contamination (>EUR 100M remediation cost estimate) during Phase 1 construction triggers health-and-safety stoppages, regulatory enforcement, cost escalation and 6–18 month schedule delays, stranding Phase 1 capex and eroding lender confidence.
  • Absent or incomplete biodiversity baseline allows EIA reviewer and NGO challengers to claim the developer failed to identify protected species or sensitive habitats, triggering permit appeals adding 24–48 months (estimate) and forcing major design changes (footprint reduction, hall relocation) increasing capex 5–15% (estimate).
  • Failure to obtain water-authority opinion on dry-cooling feasibility until late Phase 1 (after halls are sited and designed) creates retrofit risk: if coolers are deemed to impact groundwater or during-drought performance is unacceptable, PUE design may require shift to hybrid water cooling or capacity reduction, adding cost EUR 50M–200M (estimate) and schedule delay 6–12 months.
  • Vague or optimistic ecological compensation plan (e.g., offsite habitat creation without binding agreements or enforcement mechanisms) invites DREAL rejection during EIA review and NGO legal challenge post-permit, potentially invalidating the permit and forcing major design rework.
  • Unclear liability allocation between private sellers and the developer (no Phase I/II or indemnity) leaves developer exposed to surprise remediation claims totalling EUR 50M–400M (estimate) during Phase 1, stranding equity and triggering debt defaults or lender forbearance negotiations.
  • Absent assessment of competing land uses, zoning restrictions or municipal planning constraints results in parcels being optioned and funded that cannot support data-hall construction, wasting Phase 0 option spend (EUR 10M–50M per parcel estimate) and forcing topology pivot.
  • Failure to clearly link environmental baseline, remediation liability and ecological compensation to the topology decision (single square vs. split campus) delays the Month 4 (2027-02-17) decision, compressing time for node-level permit file preparation and pushing permit submission beyond Month 9 (2027-07-17) gate target.
  • Overestimation of ecological compensation feasibility or underestimation of cost results in EUR 100M–300M (estimate) budget overrun, or permits being denied post-filing because compensation plan is unachievable, forcing downsize or cancellation.

Worst Case Scenario: Major contamination discovered on the top candidate site (Cambrai/E-Valley) after Phase 0 gates pass and Phase 1 FID is committed (Month 12–13 = 2027-10-17 to 2027-11-17): Phase II ESA identifies soil/groundwater legacy pollution (heavy metals, hydrocarbons, PCBs, munitions residue) with remediation cost of EUR 200M–400M (estimate) and timeline of 12–18 months, neither of which was bounded or insured. Simultaneously, DREAL rejects the ecological compensation plan as insufficient for Natura 2000 protection, and a protected species (e.g., nesting birds, bats, amphibians) is found in planned hall footprint. Topology pivot to Dunkirk is then required, triggering Phase 1 redesign (EUR 500M–1B capex rework estimate), 12–24 month schedule slip, loss of RTE queue position, tenant defection (loss of EUR 100M–300M revenue commitment estimate), lender covenant breach or debt refinancing demand at 300–400 bps higher spreads, and potentially Phase 1 cancellation or a 250–500 MW downsize. Stranded Phase 0 spend on the failed site (EUR 150M–300M estimate) cannot be recovered.

Best Case Scenario: Phase 0 environmental baseline is complete and defensible: Phase I/II assessments on all candidate sites by Month 3 (2027-01-17) identify Cambrai/E-Valley as the clear primary node with low remediation exposure (EUR 10M–30M per parcel estimate), clean groundwater and no Natura 2000 overlap; Phase II findings are bounded by seller indemnity EUR 50M and Phase 1 reserve EUR 100M. Hydrological study by Month 5 (2027-03-17) confirms zero water-stress risk and dry-cooler PUE of 1.18–1.25 at summer peak. Ecological baseline identifies no protected species conflicts; avoidance zones of 10–20 km² (estimate) accommodate Natura 2000 buffers and ecological corridors within the 161 km² envelope, leaving 140–150 km² for development. Ecological compensation is pre-agreed with regional conservation partners: offsite habitat restoration on publicly owned parcels (EUR 0.2B–0.3B estimate) is committed by the prefecture, and net-positive biodiversity is certified. DREAL screening opinion (Month 9 = 2027-07-17) confirms the EIA scope is proportionate and the ecological plan is acceptable; no blocking environmental sensitivities are flagged. Water authority issues written opinion (Month 6 = 2027-04-17) that dry cooling is approved and no evaporative-water permit is needed. With these confirmations, the investment committee passes the environmental gate at Month 12 (2027-10-17), Phase 1 FID proceeds on schedule, permits are filed Month 8–9 (2027-06-17 to 2027-07-17), and Phase 1 energization stays on track for Months 42–48 (2030-04-17 to 2030-10-17). Tenant confidence in site certainty is high; lender debt commitments are firm. The split-campus fallback is not triggered.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • If Phase II surveys cannot be completed by Month 3 (2027-01-17) due to landowner access delays or extended lab turnaround, shift the environmental gate to Month 6 (2027-04-17): shortlist only parcels with Phase I (desktop) results showing low risk, and require Phase II data as a Phase 1 pre-FID condition (acceptable if seller indemnity and Phase 1 reserve EUR 100M–300M are firmly in place and lenders accept the deferred risk); this compresses Phase 0 testing window but maintains schedule.
  • If water-authority opinion on dry-cooling feasibility is not issued by Month 6 (2027-04-17) (authority bandwidth or regulatory uncertainty), obtain a binding preliminary letter confirming the process will be complete by Month 9 (2027-07-17), and make the thermal design gate conditional on receipt; if authority ultimately denies dry cooling, pivot to hybrid with <5% evaporative water under capped annual abstraction, or accept PUE penalty and grid curtailment increase as Phase 1 cost.
  • If DREAL EIA screening decision extends beyond Month 9 (2027-07-17) (common in France for large projects), continue Phase 0 in parallel with informal feedback loop: submit the EIA file at Month 8 (2027-06-17), gather DREAL feedback at Month 7–8 (2027-05-17 to 2027-06-17), iterate the document, and establish a firm commitment from DREAL to issue the screening opinion by Month 12 (2027-10-17) (the Phase 0 gate); formal EIA work (full EIS) proceeds post-gate and in parallel with Phase 1 FID, compressing the front-loaded design risk but extending permitting.
  • If ecological compensation plan cannot be pre-agreed with regional authorities by Month 6 (2027-04-17) due to NGO opposition or biodiversity-target disputes, adopt a phased commitment approach: Phase 0 identifies the net-biodiversity target and acceptable compensation mechanisms (offsite habitat, working-landscape management, species recovery programs), locking the principle; detailed agreements are then negotiated during Phase 1 (Months 13–36 = 2027-11-17 to 2029-10-17) with DREAL oversight and lender approval as a condition of debt draw, not a pre-FID blocker. This delays finality but allows Phase 1 to proceed if principle and budget are firm.
  • If a protected-species conflict is discovered late (Month 6–9 = 2027-04-17 to 2027-07-17) that requires significant footprint adjustment, pivot topology: e.g., if Cambrai/E-Valley has a rare-bird breeding zone blocking 20% of planned halls, shift the primary node to Dunkirk with a smaller Cambrai secondary node, or accept a 250 MW downsize of the primary node and defer Phase 2 growth. Topology decision (Month 4 = 2027-02-17) is held conditional on ecology findings, so this pivot is a built-in option.
  • If Phase II remediation cost on a candidate site exceeds EUR 100M (estimate) but the parcel is strategically important (e.g., offers the best grid connection or land assemblability), negotiate a tiered liability structure with the seller: developer funds remediation up to EUR 100M (Phase 1 reserve), seller/public body funds cost above EUR 100M via escrow or bond, or the parcel is reserved for non-built use (energy infrastructure, ecological restoration, stormwater) that has lower or no remediation sensitivity. This preserves topology flexibility.
  • If water-authority or ecological constraints force a non-contiguous footprint (e.g., avoidance zones fragment the 161 km² into 3–4 separate clusters), shift Phase 0 validation toward a federated topology: Cambrai main node (500 MW), Dunkirk secondary node (250 MW), Valenciennes tertiary node (250 MW or deferred), each with separate grid connections and permits. This is a topology redesign (Month 4 = 2027-02-17) that Phase 0 is designed to accommodate; the single-square envelope is then abandoned and Phase 0 deliverables are updated to per-node EIA and liability scoping.

Create Document 7: Municipal Liaison Committee Charter and Community-Benefit Agreement

ID: 38413a9c-71db-49ea-8398-972aeb35bdab

Description: Formal charter (Month 1 = 2026-11-17) and binding agreement (executed by Month 9 = 2027-07-17) specifying: municipal liaison committee composition (mayors, regional councillors, farm unions FNSEA/Confédération Paysanne, environmental NGOs, independent facilitator), quarterly meeting schedule with published minutes, and structured community-benefit package (EUR 50M–150M over Phases 1–2) including direct income transfers to affected municipalities (EUR 10M–15M per 100 MW), farm relocation compensation (1.5–2.0× benchmark land value), ecological restoration co-management, local employment and training commitments (≥50% construction labor from region, ≥30% within 50 km), and infrastructure upgrades (EUR 10M–30M). Gate: written signatures from at least 2 of 3 key municipalities by Month 9 (2027-07-17) required for Phase 0 gate closure (Month 12 = 2027-10-17). Absence of signatures triggers investment committee reassessment of Phase 1 feasibility on social-license grounds. Primary audience: municipalities, farm unions, environmental groups, investment committee, lenders.

Responsible Role Type: Community Engagement and Social License Manager

Primary Template: Community Benefit Agreement Template (International Association for Public Participation / IAP2 standard form)

Secondary Template: Municipal Liaison Committee Charter and Terms of Reference (French local-government precedent)

Steps to Create:

  • Establish liaison committee by Month 1 (2026-11-17) with formal representation from affected municipalities (Cambrai, Dunkirk, Valenciennes area), farm unions, NGOs, and independent facilitator.
  • Commission social-impact study (EUR 300K–600K) covering farmer interviews (100+), resident survey (500+), NGO engagement (identify key groups and concerns); deliver by Month 4 (2027-02-17).
  • Conduct early voluntary public consultation (Month 3 = 2027-01-17) with published project overview, environmental commitments, and benefit package outline; 4-week comment period, published responses.
  • Draft binding community-benefit agreement (Month 5 = 2027-03-17) with specific EUR amounts (not ranges) and implementation timeline: direct municipal income, farm relocation scale and rates, ecological restoration sites and co-management structure, training academy targets, and infrastructure upgrades list.
  • Present draft to liaison committee for negotiation (Months 5–8 = 2027-03-17 to 2027-06-17); target signatures from 2 of 3 municipalities by Month 9 (2027-07-17).
  • Lock implementation schedule and escrow for benefit-package funding.
  • Publish liaison-committee minutes quarterly and track benefit-package progress during Phase 1.

Approval Authorities: Mayors of Affected Municipalities, Regional Prefectures, Farm Union Leaders, Environmental Group Signatories, Investment Committee (gate approval)

Essential Information:

  • Quantify the numeric kill thresholds (proposed) that determine Phase 1 FID go/no-go: RTE hosting capacity ≥500 MW within 36 months, at least 70% of target parcel optioned, signed anchor-tenant take-or-pay ≥30% of Phase 1 capacity, debt commitment ≥EUR 3B at ≤220 bps margin, written support from ≥2 of 3 municipalities, ANSSI clearance pathway confirmed with no blocking concerns
  • Detail the financial exposure and headroom analysis: Phase 0 sunk cost at each milestone tranche (EUR 150M/250M/200M/150M cumulative), Phase 1 capex ceiling EUR 10B, stacked contingencies (grid co-funding EUR 0.5B–1.5B, split-campus premium EUR 0.25B–0.5B, remediation EUR 0.1B–0.3B, fiber EUR 0.1B–0.3B), carrying-cost and financing-structure sensitivity to Phase 1 delay (€200M–600M per 6-month slip)
  • Identify topology decision logic and evidence required by Month 4 (2027-02-17): single-square viability only if ≥70% of 161 km² optioned AND written RTE evidence of ≥1 GW; otherwise default to split-campus nodes with separate grid/permit/financing per node, including per-node capex, latency tolerance, and fiber-route costs
  • Define Phase 0 gate pass/fail criteria (Month 12 = 2027-10-17) with evidence collection schedule: RTE letter by Month 6 (2027-04-17), land-option confirmation by Month 4 (2027-02-17), anchor-tenant term sheets by Month 9 (2027-07-17), municipal signatures by Month 9 (2027-07-17), debt LOI by Month 12 (2027-10-17), ANSSI clearance pathway by Month 12 (2027-10-17)
  • Analyze external-dependency timeline and likelihood of evidence delivery: RTE firm offer unlikely by Month 6 (2027-04-17), permitting file submission target Month 8–9 (2027-06-17 to 2027-07-17), ANSSI formal review unlikely to complete before Months 25–31 (2028-11-17 to 2029-05-17), so Phase 1 FID may need to proceed conditionally on authority continuation
  • Assess sunk-cost risk and mitigation: Phase 0 spending of EUR 250M–750M commits no capital beyond each milestone unless gate criteria are met; investment committee override mechanism requires supermajority (≥2/3) with dissent published; conditional pass defined to allow FID if authorities have not answered but pathway is clear
  • Document the split-campus fallback: if single-square fails at Month 4 (2027-02-17), pivot to 2–3 nodes (Cambrai 500 MW, Dunkirk 250–500 MW, Valenciennes 250–500 MW) with separate RTE tranches, permits, and security review; per-MW capex EUR 10M–11M vs. EUR 10M single-square, carrying cost EUR 300M–600M, energization Months 48–60 (2030-10-17 to 2031-10-17)
  • Compare Phase 0 go/no-go outcomes: success = Phase 0 + Phase 1 within budget with Phase 2 FID anchored; failure = any gate unmet at Month 12 (2027-10-17) triggers pause (≥6 months) or pivot (split campus) or exit (project cancelled); conditional pass allows FID if ≥4 of 5 gates closed and ≥1 gate on a clear authority timeline
  • Quantify opportunity cost and optionality value: holding land options (EUR 50M–150M over 3 years), maintaining RTE queue position, and retaining tenant term-sheet negotiations positions the project to restart in Months 18–24 (2028-04-17 to 2028-10-17) if external conditions improve; Phase 0 completion cost (EUR 250M–750M) is <10% of Phase 1 capex and is recoverable in continued optionality
  • Define the independent investment committee authority and red-team accountability: charter by Month 1 (2026-11-17), kill thresholds locked by Month 2 (2026-12-17), monthly pass/fail opinions from red team, quarterly dissent disclosure to lenders, override votes recorded and published, so stated gates cannot be renegotiated under sunk-cost pressure without board-level override that is visible to debt and equity holders

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • Ambiguous or missing kill thresholds allow sunk-cost pressure and leadership momentum to override feasibility gates; board-level Phase 1 FID proceeds despite grid, land or tenant failures; investors and lenders lose decision credibility and refuse Phase 2 capital
  • Incomplete Phase 0 financial tracking across four tranches fails to bound sunk cost; one or more tranches exceed milestone caps (cumulative EUR 150/400/600/750M); unbudgeted add-ons (remediation, fiber, security, ecological compensation) breach the EUR 750M Phase 0 cap, forcing renegotiation with co-investors or equity shortfall
  • Missing or unclear split-campus logic forces a late-stage topology pivot at Month 9–12 (2027-07-17 to 2027-10-17) instead of Month 4 (2027-02-17), triggering 3–6 month design delay and EUR 200M–500M cost escalation; Phase 1 FID delayed into Months 24–36 (2028-10-17 to 2029-10-17), eroding RTE queue position
  • Unvalidated or missing evidence-collection milestones (RTE letter, land-option shortlist, tenant term sheets, municipal support) allow Month 12 (2027-10-17) gate to proceed on partial information; Phase 1 FID proceeds without signed anchors, RTE hosting confirmation or financing commitment; Phase 1 construction begins and stalls when evidence fails
  • Failure to establish independent committee authority allows development-team pressure to renegotiate thresholds or force conditional passes without board discipline; lenders and co-investors lose oversight credibility; Phase 2 financing becomes unachievable because gates cannot be trusted
  • Unclear fallback scenarios (split campus cost, timeline, per-MW capex, financing structure) leave no credible plan B if single-square fails; decision to pivot comes too late; alternative topology is not pre-designed or pre-assessed with RTE, permitting and debt capacity
  • Missing social-license assessment (municipal support timeline, farm-union engagement, community-benefit agreement structure) allows Phase 1 FID to proceed despite public-opposition risk; permitting delays by 12–24 months or appeals block permits after Phase 1 capex commitment
  • Unquantified or missing contingency exposure (grid co-funding, split premium, remediation surprise, fiber routes, ANSSI delay) leaves no funding headroom between EUR 5B Phase 1 base and EUR 10B ceiling; first add-on pushes project over cap, forcing scope reduction or equity injection mid-construction
  • Incomplete or unclear external-dependency timeline allows Phase 1 FID to be scheduled before RTE, ANSSI, DREAL and EDF have answered; project commits EUR 5B–10B capex before authorities have signed offers, creating execution risk and stranded-asset exposure

Worst Case Scenario: A Phase 0 Feasibility Assessment document that fails to establish enforceable kill criteria, track financial commitments across milestone tranches, or pre-design split-campus fallbacks could enable leadership to override failed gates and commit Phase 1 capex (EUR 5B–10B) despite missing RTE hosting-capacity confirmation, land-assembly evidence, or signed anchor tenants. Sunk-cost pressure—combined with co-investor momentum, community expectations set during Phase 0 consultations, and permit-application filing deadlines—makes cancellation or major downsizing politically untenable mid-Phase-1, even if external conditions prove infeasible. Phase 1 construction begins with conditional RTE offers and non-binding tenant LOIs, lenders withdraw or demand equity cushions of 30–40%, delaying drawdowns by 12–18 months. Carrying costs of EUR 300M–600M accrue while land sits, permits are appealed, and tenants compare competing sites. By Month 36 (2029-10-17), RTE confirms hosting capacity is limited to 250–500 MW instead of 1 GW (primary kill test), forcing Phase 1 scope reduction to 250 MW and operational restructuring. Alternatively, ANSSI review identifies data-residency or foreign-investment restrictions incompatible with the tenant base, requiring renegotiation of anchor leases and pushing FID into Months 48–60 (2030-10-17 to 2031-10-17). Equity investors face 15–20% equity loss due to delay and scope reduction; debt becomes non-viable or refinances at higher cost; the project is forced into extended mothballing or liquidation. The EUR 750M Phase 0 investment becomes wholly stranded, co-investor confidence in the sponsor is destroyed, and subsequent greenfield projects in France face higher cost of capital or investor reluctance.

Best Case Scenario: A rigorous Phase 0 Feasibility Assessment document that locks numeric kill criteria, establishes an independent investment committee, tracks finances across four milestone tranches, and pre-designs split-campus alternatives enables disciplined go/no-go decisions at Month 12 (2027-10-17) and beyond. All Phase 0 gates are closed on time with signed evidence: RTE letter for ≥500 MW by Month 6 (2027-04-17), ≥70% land optioned by Month 4 (2027-02-17), ≥30% anchor-tenant take-or-pay signed by Month 9 (2027-07-17), municipal support from ≥2 of 3 authorities by Month 9 (2027-07-17), and debt commitment of ≥EUR 3B by Month 12 (2027-10-17). Phase 1 FID proceeds as a single 500 MW node at Cambrai/E-Valley with EUR 5B capex, 60% leverage (EUR 3B debt), and 8–10 data halls. Permitting is submitted Month 8 (2027-06-17) and approved by Month 39 (2030-01-17) with no material delays or legal appeals. First-block energization occurs Month 42–48 (2030-04-17 to 2030-10-17) with contracted capacity of ≥300 MW (60% utilization) and a PUE of 1.24. Phase 1 achieves EUR 400M+ NOI, DSCR of 1.35x, and enables Phase 2 FID at Month 48 (2030-10-17) with ≥50% of a 2 GW increment committed. The campus becomes a regional anchor for power, fiber, heat and workforce development; co-investors realize 8–10% IRR by Year 10, and the project positions France as a sovereign AI compute hub. The document's discipline and gate transparency support refinancing and Phase 3–4 expansion without stakeholder friction.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • Commission a simplified 'Phase 0 Gate Dashboard' if a full feasibility document proves too lengthy or detailed: a single-page tracker (updated monthly, Months 0–12 = 2026-10-17 to 2027-10-17) with the five gates, evidence status (on track / at risk / fail), expected delivery month, owner, and investment committee sign-off. Pair it with a 2-page gate-criteria summary and a separate split-campus cost/timeline sheet, so decision-makers can review full rigor in sections rather than an 80+ page narrative
