  • Structure the feasibility assessment as a modular set of workstream reports (grid, land, tenant, financing, permitting, security, environmental) with a separate executive gate-summary cover sheet and numeric threshold table, allowing lenders and co-investors to review specific risks without waiting for a monolithic document
  • Engage the investment committee to define kill thresholds in a facilitated 2-day workshop (Month 1 = 2026-11-17) rather than staffing a long document-drafting process; capture outputs in a short charter (5–10 pages) with numeric thresholds and redteam accountability, then anchor Phase 0 workstreams to the charter
  • If RTE, ANSSI, DREAL or EDF are slow to provide written opinions by the scheduled gates, establish a 'conditional pass' framework built into the assessment: define the interim evidence (non-binding LOI, preliminary study opinion, scheduled formal-review date) that allows Phase 0 to close at Month 12 (2027-10-17) with Phase 1 FID contingent on formal authority sign-off by an agreed future date (e.g. Month 18 = 2028-04-17 for ANSSI)
  • Separate the Phase 0 assessment into two documents: (i) a 20-page Gate Criteria and Evidence Summary (Month 9 = 2027-07-17) for lenders and committee decision-making; (ii) a detailed workstream-findings appendix (40–60 pages) published separately for transparency and stakeholder reference, reducing review burden on decision-makers
  • If split-campus analysis requires independent feasibility studies per node, commission a simplified 'multi-node financial model' (one spreadsheet with three node scenarios: single-square, two-node, three-node) rather than separate full feasibility reports; use it to compare capex, per-MW cost, financing structure and Phase 1 start date across topologies
  • Partner with an independent feasibility/due-diligence firm (EUR 5M–10M) to author or validate the assessment, ensuring red-team credibility is seen as external and defenses against sunk-cost override are backed by a third party; publish the firm's monthly findings so lenders and co-investors see independent evidence, not sponsor narrative

Create Document 8: Phase 1 Cost Baseline and Budget Reconciliation Model

ID: f61c6bf5-e1b8-4289-b590-5df88ab6a3cd

Description: Detailed financial model (deliverable Month 9 = 2027-07-17) reconciling all Phase 1 cost lines against the EUR 10B user ceiling (user constraint) for the 500 MW base case. Breaks down capex into: (i) committed cost lines with ≤5% uncertainty (shell, power, primary cooling, main fiber, perimeter) estimated EUR 4.0B–4.5B; (ii) contingent-but-likely costs (grid co-funding EUR 0.5B–1.5B, remediation EUR 0.1B–0.3B, secondary fiber EUR 0.2B–0.6B, ecological compensation EUR 0.2B–0.3B) at 60% probability of occurrence; (iii) low-probability exposures (contamination discovery, ANSSI retrofit, subsea build, long-delay carrying cost) EUR 0.2B–0.5B at 20–30% probability. Maps each cost line to funding source (debt EUR 3.0B, equity EUR 2.0B, or risk transfer via insurance/indemnity). Identifies which stacked-contingent add-ons (grid reinforcement, split-campus premium, ecological, fiber, subsea) must be cut if total exceeds EUR 10B. Tests DSCR under stress (10% lease discount, EUR 30/MWh energy shock, 15% capex overrun) and shows Phase 1 downsize trigger if DSCR falls below 1.15x. Primary audience: lenders (debt underwriting), investment committee (budget gate), Phase 1 FID decision-makers.

Responsible Role Type: Infrastructure Finance and Capital Structure Lead

Primary Template: Project Finance Cost Estimate and Contingency Analysis (PMI Project Management Body of Knowledge / PMBOK)

Secondary Template: Risk-Adjusted Capex Model with Sensitivity Analysis (infrastructure-fund precedent)

Steps to Create:

  • Compile bottom-up capex estimates from all workstream leads (grid EUR 50M–500M, cooling EUR 400M–800M, security EUR 50M–200M, etc.); reconcile into base case.
  • Stratify cost lines by uncertainty: committed (design-complete, vendor quotes locked) vs. contingent (scoped but not finalized) vs. exploratory (optional, low probability).
  • Map contingencies to probability-weighted cost ranges; consolidate overlapping exposures (e.g., grid co-funding and split-campus both trigger on RTE capacity shortfall).
  • For each contingency, identify funding source: debt (constrained by covenant), equity (subject to co-investor approval), or third-party transfer (insurance, seller indemnity, public grant).
  • Model DSCR sensitivity: base case 1.34x at 500 MW EUR 550M lease revenue, EUR 60/MWh energy; stress scenarios with 10% lease discount (1.15x), 20% energy shock (1.04x), 15% capex overrun (1.28x).
  • Define Phase 1 downsize rules: if total capex forecast reaches EUR 8.0B (300 MW budget remaining), reduce Phase 1 target to 375 MW or defer expansion.
  • Publish model to lenders and investment committee by Month 9 (2027-07-17) with assumptions and risk ratings.
  • Lock revised Phase 1 ceiling (proposed EUR 8.0B for 500 MW, leaving EUR 2.0B contingency within the EUR 10B ceiling) by Month 12 (2027-10-17).

Approval Authorities: Finance Lead, Lenders, Investment Committee, Phase 1 FID Board

Essential Information:

  • Reconcile all Phase 1 capex cost lines (shell, power, cooling, fiber, perimeter, grid co-funding, remediation, ecological compensation, contingencies) against the EUR 10B user ceiling for the 500 MW base case, showing cumulative totals and headroom.
  • Stratify costs by certainty level: committed cost lines with ≤5% uncertainty (estimate EUR 4.0B–4.5B); contingent-but-likely costs at 60% probability (grid co-funding EUR 0.5B–1.5B, remediation EUR 0.1B–0.3B, secondary fiber EUR 0.2B–0.6B, ecological EUR 0.2B–0.3B); low-probability exposures at 20–30% probability (EUR 0.2B–0.5B).
  • Model DSCR (debt-service coverage ratio) sensitivity under base case and stress scenarios: base 1.34x (500 MW, EUR 550M lease revenue, EUR 60/MWh energy), 10% lease discount scenario 1.15x, EUR 30/MWh energy shock scenario 1.04x, 15% capex overrun scenario 1.28x.
  • Identify which stacked contingent add-ons (grid reinforcement, split-campus premium, ecological, fiber, subsea, extended delay carrying) must be cut or deferred if total capex forecast exceeds EUR 8.0B (proposed trigger), leaving EUR 2.0B headroom for Phase 1 unknowns within the EUR 10B ceiling.
  • Define Phase 1 downsize rule: if 500 MW capex forecast reaches EUR 8.0B, reduce Phase 1 to 375 MW or 250 MW or defer Phase 2, with revised capex, lease revenue, debt service and DSCR.
  • Map each cost line to funding source: debt (EUR 3.0B at 60% leverage for 500 MW case, constrained by DSCR ≥1.30x covenant), equity (EUR 2.0B subject to co-investor approval), or third-party transfer (insurance, seller indemnity, public grant, RTE/EDF cost-sharing).
  • For each contingency, document trigger condition (e.g., grid contingency triggers if RTE offer is <1 GW or demands co-funding >EUR 1.0B), probability (60%, 20–30%, etc.), and mitigation (reduce scope, defer to Phase 2, or equity cure).
  • Test capex model against canonical facts: Phase 1 range EUR 5B–10B for 500 MW–1 GW, estimated EUR 10M per MW; Phase 1 financing 60% debt/40% equity on 500 MW; debt all-in 5.5%, 15-year amortization; annual debt service EUR 299M on EUR 3.0B; Phase 2 FID requires signed take-or-pay ≥50% of tranche (user floor 30–50%).
  • Reconcile overlap and unfunded exposure: identify cost lines that double-count (e.g., split-campus capex premium overlaps with remediation exposure if Dunkirk site has higher contamination), and allocate union of risks, not sum.
  • Publish assumptions, risk ratings and sensitivity ranges to lenders (debt underwriting), investment committee (budget gate authority) and Phase 1 FID decision-makers by Month 9 (2027-07-17); lock revised Phase 1 ceiling (EUR 8.0B base for 500 MW) by the Month 12 (2027-10-17) gate.

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • Stacked contingencies not identified: if grid co-funding (EUR 0.5B–1.5B) and split-campus capex premium (EUR 250M–500M) and ecological compensation (EUR 0.2B–0.3B) and fiber build (EUR 0.2B–0.6B) and remediation (EUR 0.1B–0.3B) are modelled as independent additive risks rather than overlapping exposures, total capex forecast balloons to EUR 7.05B–10.35B and appears near the EUR 10B ceiling with no room for real overruns or discoveries, leading lenders to demand 50% leverage (EUR 2.5B debt) instead of 60%, cutting debt availability by EUR 500M and forcing equity cushion or Phase 1 cancellation.
  • DSCR stress not linked to downsize trigger: if the model shows 10% lease discount (EUR 495M revenue) pushes DSCR to 1.15x but no formal rule exists to cut debt from EUR 3.0B to EUR 2.66B or reduce Phase 1 to 250–375 MW, lenders will refuse to commit because covenant coverage is substandard, blocking Phase 1 FID.
  • Contingency probability and funding not clear: if 'grid co-funding contingent at 60% probability' is not tied to a funding source or offset (RTE partial cost-share, developer equity injection, or deferred to Phase 2), Phase 1 FID assumes the best case (RTE covers 100% of reinforcement) and discovers EUR 1.0B–1.5B liability mid-Phase-1 build, forcing a funding crisis or work stoppage.
  • Split-campus capex premium not quantified: if the model assumes EUR 5.0B for single-square 500 MW at Cambrai but does not show a separate line for 'split topology upside cost EUR 250M–500M (grid duplication, separate substations, fiber inter-node links, redundant security)', Phase 0 topology decision at Month 4 (2027-02-17) cannot compare single vs. split economics, forcing topology choice in the dark.
  • Energy cost pass-through not validated: if the model assumes EUR 60/MWh energy is passed through to tenants in full but does not state the mechanism (indexed lease term, separate energy invoice, or tenant-procured power) or lender assumptions, a 20–40% overrun (EUR 30/MWh shock) could be absorbed by the campus company as opex cost, not tenant revenue, reducing NOI by EUR 112M–224M and DSCR to 0.96x, breaching debt covenant and triggering cross-default.
  • Debt tenor and amortization mismatch: if senior debt is structured as a traditional 15-year amortizing loan (annual debt service EUR 299M on EUR 3.0B) but Phase 1 lease revenue ramps from 30% to 100% over 18–24 months post-energization, cash flow in Months 13–24 (2027-11-17 to 2028-10-17) of Phase 1 construction is negative (hard capex spend, no revenue), and debt cannot be drawn. Model must show draw schedule matching capex milestone and specify if a construction-period interest reserve is needed (EUR 100M–300M estimate).
  • Lender covenant and trigger thresholds not published: if the model does not explicitly state the lender's minimum DSCR covenant (proposed 1.30x) or link capex forecast to a downsize trigger (if capex forecast exceeds EUR 8.0B, cut to 375 MW), Phase 1 FID decision-makers and investment committee cannot hold the model accountable; model approval becomes a vague 'financeable at 60% leverage' opinion instead of a rigorous pass/fail gate.
  • Contingency overlap and union not modelled: if the model sums independent probabilities (grid contingency 60%, remediation contingency 60%, ecological contingency 50%, fiber contingency 40%, subsea contingency 20%) without modelling joint occurrence (e.g., grid contingency + split-campus topology + higher remediation at Dunkirk node = simultaneous capex shocks), the expected-value cost range understates tail risk, and Phase 1 FID is blindsided by 2–3 simultaneous contingencies occurring together.
  • Phase 2 downsize and optionality not locked in: if the model does not specify cost levels at which Phase 2 is deferred (proposed trigger: if Phase 1 DSCR falls below 1.30x due to cost overrun or revenue shortfall, Phase 2 FID is delayed 12–24 months), investment committee and lenders cannot enforce the stated gate criteria, and momentum pressure keeps Phase 2 on original schedule despite weak economics.
  • Third-party cost-sharing not quantified: if the model does not show which costs are potentially shared with RTE, EDF, municipalities or public remediation bodies (e.g., grid reinforcement EUR 200M–500M, remediation EUR 50M–250M escrow, ecological EUR 100M–200M public funding), Phase 1 FID assumes the developer bears 100% cost, overstating capex exposure and understating headroom to EUR 10B ceiling.

Worst Case Scenario: Phase 1 FID meeting at Month 12 (2027-10-17) discovers that stacked contingencies (grid co-funding EUR 1.5B, split-campus topology premium EUR 500M, remediation surprise EUR 300M, ecological compliance EUR 300M, fiber build EUR 600M, subsea landing EUR 200M, carrying cost from permitting delay EUR 400M) total EUR 4.2B above the EUR 5.0B committed base, pushing total capex to EUR 9.2B. Investment committee and lenders demand updated DSCR before releasing Phase 1 capital; model shows DSCR 1.18x under base-case assumptions (below the 1.30x minimum covenant). Lenders refuse debt funding at 60% leverage and offer only 50% (EUR 2.5B instead of EUR 3.0B), requiring EUR 500M additional equity. Co-investors balk at raising incremental equity without a clear path to returns, triggering a 6–12 month Phase 1 delay while capital structure is renegotiated. Topology contingency begins to actualize (RTE offer is only 500 MW at Cambrai, not 1 GW; Dunkirk node requires separate connection application adding 12–18 months). Phase 1 must be downsized to 250 MW to fit capex within lender comfort (EUR 2.5B at 50% leverage), but anchoring tenants walk away because reserved capacity shrinks below their minimum take-or-pay thresholds. Project enters a 12–24 month funding and demand restructuring, missing the Months 12–36 (2027-10-17 to 2029-10-17) Phase 1 build window and pushing first energization to Months 48–60 (2030-10-17 to 2031-10-17) or later.

Best Case Scenario: Phase 1 cost model published at Month 9 (2027-07-17) clearly stratifies costs by certainty, shows committed base EUR 4.0B–4.5B with contingencies summing to EUR 0.5B–1.5B at expected value, and identifies stacked-overlap scenarios (grid contingency + split-campus cost premium = EUR 0.9B–2.0B joint exposure, not EUR 2.0B independent sum). Model demonstrates DSCR 1.34x under base case (500 MW, EUR 550M lease revenue, EUR 60/MWh energy) and defines downsize trigger: if total capex forecast reaches EUR 8.0B, reduce Phase 1 to 375 MW with revised debt/equity and DSCR confirmation ≥1.30x. Lenders review model, confirm debt commitment EUR 3.0B at benchmark +200 bps, and issue binding LOI by Month 12 (2027-10-17) conditioned on final capex lock ±5% by Month 18 (2028-04-17). Investment committee uses model to enforce kill criteria: if RTE offers only 500 MW (grid contingency triggers), committee approves topology pivot to split-campus Cambrai + Dunkirk without Phase 1 delay, because capex model already shows per-node financials for 250 MW at Dunkirk (EUR 2.5B) and allows independent permitting and grid application. Phase 1 FID clears at Month 12 (2027-10-17) with lender certainty and co-investor confidence; construction mobilization begins Month 13 (2027-11-17), on schedule for first-block energization Month 42–48 (2030-04-17 to 2030-10-17).

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • If full-model build is resource-constrained or time-compressed: develop a simplified 'skeleton model' by Month 6 (2027-04-17) showing committed base capex (EUR 4.0B–4.5B) plus the single largest contingency exposure (e.g., grid co-funding EUR 0.5B–1.5B as the swing line) and DSCR base case. Treat other contingencies (remediation, ecology, fiber, subsea) as qualitative risk factors documented in a separate risk register (mapping to the Risk Register document). At Month 9 (2027-07-17), layer in detailed contingency sensitivities for the top 3–4 risks (grid, split-campus, remediation, fiber) using the working group's latest estimates, and publish the partial model to lenders with a note that detailed build-out of overlap, funding sources and downsize rules will follow by Month 12 (2027-10-17). This allows lenders to commence debt-underwriting process in parallel while the finance lead completes the full model.
  • If tenant lease-revenue validation is delayed beyond Month 9 (2027-07-17): use a conservative proxy revenue assumption (e.g., EUR 500M per year = EUR 1.0M per MW over 500 MW at EUR 25M/year per 50 MW, 80% of the EUR 550M target) and stress the DSCR to 1.20x in the base case, triggering the downsize rule at a lower capex threshold (EUR 7.5B instead of EUR 8.0B). Publish the model as 'conservative base case pending final tenant term-sheet validation,' and commit to a rerun at Month 12 (2027-10-17) once anchor tenants are signed. This avoids over-optimism in the FID recommendation and forces investment committee to acknowledge downside if anchors slip.
  • If RTE's capex cost-share guidance is not available by Month 6 (2027-04-17): model grid contingency as a range (EUR 0 if RTE funds 100%, EUR 1.5B if developer funds 100%), with intermediate scenarios (RTE 50/50 = EUR 750M developer share). For the Phase 0 gate report at Month 12 (2027-10-17), publish the capex model under each scenario and recommend a specific cost-allocation structure (proposed: developer funds up to EUR 500M, RTE above that, or developer cost-shares at 50% up to EUR 1.5B cap). Allow Phase 1 FID to proceed conditional on RTE signaling its cost-share commitment within 30 days of FID approval, with Phase 1 capex draw phased to match RTE's signed agreement. This avoids freezing a gridcontingency number prematurely and keeps Phase 1 flexible.
  • If permitting delay risk is high (e.g., DREAL screening opinion at Month 9 = 2027-07-17 indicates 30+ month timeline instead of 18–24 months): model carrying cost as a separate capex line item (EUR 100M–300M over Phase 1 extension) and publish it as a discrete downsize trigger. For example: 'If permitting decision is not final non-appealable by Month 30 (2029-04-17), Phase 1 carrying cost exceeds EUR 200M, total capex reaches EUR 7.2B, and Phase 1 is capped at 375 MW.' This gives the investment committee an explicit early-warning rule and triggers Phase 2 deferral before Phase 1 cash burn accelerates.
  • If contingency overlap and union modelling is too complex: use a Monte Carlo simulation run by a third-party risk model (EUR 50K–100K, 4–6 week turnaround). Input the probability distributions for each cost line (grid contingency 60% normal, median EUR 1.0B; remediation 60% normal, median EUR 200M; etc.) and correlations (e.g., split-campus and grid contingency are 70% correlated because split-campus is triggered by low RTE capacity). Run 10,000 iterations to generate capex probability distribution, showing the 10th-percentile (EUR 5.5B), 50th-percentile (EUR 6.8B), and 90th-percentile (EUR 8.2B) outcomes. Use the 90th-percentile scenario as the Phase 1 downsize trigger (if capex reaches EUR 8.2B, cut to 375 MW). Publish the Monte Carlo results in the month 9 (2027-07-17) report and update quarterly as contingency probabilities change.
  • If lender-covenant and funding-source detail is beyond the finance lead's capacity by Month 9 (2027-07-17): commission a debt-financing consultant (EUR 200K–500K) to develop a separate 'debt underwriting memorandum' that maps each cost line to a funding source (e.g., committed debt EUR 2.5B, equity EUR 1.5B, RTE/EDF cost-share EUR 500M, insurance/indemnity EUR 300M) and spells out lender covenant mechanics (DSCR ≥1.30x, DCR at stabilization ≥1.50x, leverage ≤60%, no additional senior debt without lender consent). The consultant produces a standalone memo that the finance lead integrates into the cost model's assumptions section, avoiding duplication of effort. Lenders use the memo as their term-sheet template, accelerating debt negotiation post-FID.
  • If Phase 1 downsize rule is contentious (co-investors or project sponsors resist cutting to 375 MW): define a phased downsize path: if capex reaches EUR 7.0B, reduce Phase 1 to 400 MW; at EUR 8.0B, reduce to 300 MW; above EUR 8.5B, Phase 1 is deferred 12 months pending Phase 0 reopening. Publish the rule in advance so co-investors and lenders know the trade-off between capex overrun and timeline slip, and do not expect the investment committee to magically absorb a EUR 3.2B blowout (EUR 5.0B base + EUR 3.2B contingency = EUR 8.2B, but still under the EUR 10B ceiling) by doubling leverage or extending Phase 1. This forces a deliberate choice at each threshold rather than a crisis decision late in Phase 1 build.

Create Document 9: Debt Financing Framework and Term-Sheet Template

ID: 7da4f58a-af0c-490c-8539-a83ab5722a72

Description: Non-binding debt-financing study (Month 4 = 2027-02-17, EUR 200K–400K) and lender-engagement roadmap defining Phase 0 pre-screening (Month 3 = 2027-01-17) with 2–3 lead lenders (proposed EIB, KfW, French banks), lending criteria, leverage targets (60% for 500 MW, EUR 3B senior debt), tenor requirements (minimum 12 years, proposed 15 years), pricing benchmarks (proposed benchmark +200 bps all-in at 5.5% estimate), and covenant framework (DSCR floor 1.30x, leverage ceiling 60% LTV). Includes DSCR stress model under key-risk scenarios and identifies which cost lines and tensor reductions trigger debt-cap enforcement. Non-binding term-sheet from lead lender(s) targeted Month 9 (2027-07-17); firm commitment by Month 12 (2027-10-17) contingent on Phase 0 gates closing. Specifies drawdown tranches tied to Phase 1 milestones (grid connection signed, first hall operational, stabilized PUE). Primary audience: lenders, investment committee, Phase 1 FID sponsor.

Responsible Role Type: Infrastructure Finance and Capital Structure Lead

Primary Template: Project Finance Term Sheet Template (EIB or World Bank precedent)

Secondary Template: Debt Covenant and Financial-Ratio Monitoring Framework (project-finance standard form)

Steps to Create:

  • Engage 2–3 lead lenders (Month 1 = 2026-11-17) with preliminary project overview and financing requirements.
  • Commission independent debt-structuring study (Month 3 = 2027-01-17) modeling leverage, tenor and cost-of-capital for 500 MW and 1 GW cases at various certainty levels (100% demand, 70% demand, 50% demand).
  • Develop term-sheet template (Month 2 = 2026-12-17) specifying: loan amount (EUR 3.0B for 500 MW), tenor (15 years proposed), pricing (benchmark +200 bps, 5.5% all-in estimate), financial covenants (DSCR ≥1.30x, leverage ≤60%), drawdown conditions (grid connection, minimum anchors signed, first-hall energization), and other-debt restrictions.
  • By Month 6 (2027-04-17), brief lenders on Phase 0 findings (RTE letter, land assembly, ANSSI clearance path, water authority opinion) to signal project maturity.
  • Distribute non-binding NBCE (non-binding credit estimate) from lenders by Month 9 (2027-07-17), committing to term-sheet finalization by Month 12 (2027-10-17).
  • Lock covenants with lenders: DSCR floor 1.30x (1.15x emergency waiver clause with 12-month cure), leverage ceiling 60%, and annual debt-service reserve-account minimum equal to 1.5× upcoming annual debt service.
  • Require lender sign-off on Phase 1 capex budget reconciliation (Month 9 = 2027-07-17) before term sheet can be finalized.

Approval Authorities: Lead Lenders (EIB, KfW, French Banks), Infrastructure Fund Co-Investors, Investment Committee

Essential Information:

  • Define the scope, audience and primary use case for the Debt Financing Framework: is it a pre-screening diagnostic for lenders (Month 3 = 2027-01-17), a binding term-sheet template (Month 9 = 2027-07-17), or a detailed debt-covenant monitoring protocol for Phase 1 operations (post-FID)?
  • Establish the debt structure: senior debt amount (EUR 3.0B proposed for 500 MW), tenure (15 years proposed), all-in pricing (benchmark +200 bps, ~5.5% estimate), and the tranche-drawdown schedule tied to Phase 1 milestones (grid connection signed, first hall energized, PUE stabilized).
  • Specify financial covenants and trigger thresholds: minimum debt-service coverage ratio (DSCR floor 1.30x, proposed), maximum leverage ratio (60% LTV proposed), reserve-account requirements (1.5× upcoming annual debt service proposed), and cure periods for covenant breaches (12 months proposed for emergency DSCR waiver to 1.15x).
  • Model DSCR and leverage sensitivity under key-risk scenarios: 100% tenant demand (base case), 70% demand (downside), 50% demand (stress), and identify which cost lines (grid co-funding EUR 500M–1.5B, split-topology premium EUR 250M–500M, contamination EUR 100M–400M) trigger debt-cap enforcement and reduce available debt.
  • Quantify energy-price pass-through and curtailment-discount impacts on debt service: if tenants absorb a 10% lease discount for curtailment acceptance, revenue falls from EUR 550M to EUR 495M annually (500 MW), NOI drops from EUR 400M to EUR 345M, and DSCR falls to 1.15x; define lender tolerance and cure mechanisms (e.g., debt reduction to EUR 2.66B or equity cure).
  • Define drawdown conditions and gatekeeping: debt drawn only as Phase 1 capex incurs, with lender sign-off on each tranche release tied to Phase 1 milestones (grid offer signed, anchors at ≥30% Phase 1 capacity, first-block energization).
  • Establish the relationship between the debt facility and the investment committee's kill criteria: if Phase 0 gates fail (RTE <500 MW, land <70%, tenants <30%), does debt commitment automatically lapse, or is there a conditional restart provision if gates are re-tested by Month 18 (2028-04-17)?
  • Detail other-debt restrictions and leverage caps: are there restrictions on adding subordinated debt, mezzanine financing or tenant-backed equipment leasing (for USD hardware) that would subordinate or dilute senior-lender claims?
  • Specify reporting and monitoring: quarterly financial statements, DSCR and leverage tracking, tenant-lease covenant compliance, operational-performance dashboards (PUE, power reliability, security incidents), and annual debt-service reserve funding certification.
  • Document lender protections and remedies: security package (first-priority pledge of campus company assets, tenant leases, power contracts, concession agreements), default triggers (DSCR <1.20x, lease revenue <70% of forecast, security breach, material tenant exit), and acceleration/cross-default clauses.

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • Weak or missing DSCR/leverage modeling leads to lender rejection or 200–400 bps higher pricing; Phase 1 cost of capital increases by EUR 140M–280M annually on EUR 7B debt.
  • Vague covenant triggers and cure periods allow sunk-cost pressure to override lender discipline; debt continues being drawn despite deteriorating Phase 1 fundamentals (tenant shortfall, grid constraints, contamination discoveries).
  • Omission of energy-price pass-through or curtailment-discount impact on cash flow creates false confidence in debt servicing; when a 10% lease discount is needed to secure anchors, NOI drops to EUR 345M and DSCR falls to 1.15x, triggering breached covenants and lender intervention.
  • Unclear relationship between Phase 0 gates and debt commitment leaves lenders without clear exit options if RTE, land or tenant gates fail; sunk Phase 0 cost (EUR 250M–750M) and debt-commitment fees make cancellation politically and financially difficult, forcing continuation into Phase 1 despite inadequate feasibility.
  • Insufficient sensitivity analysis of cost-line contingencies (grid co-funding, split-topology premium, contamination remediation, fiber diversity, subsea landings) leaves lenders and the investment committee unaware that stacked add-ons total EUR 1.55B–4.2B and exceed the Phase 1 budget headroom.
  • Missing or incomplete monitoring framework allows operational performance (PUE, power reliability, tenant SLA compliance) to diverge from assumptions without triggering intervention; by the time lenders discover average PUE is 1.35 instead of 1.25, Phase 1 capex is committed and cannot be adjusted.
  • Inadequate detail on USD hardware financing and FX hedging policy leaves lenders exposed to undisclosed hardware procurement by tenants or a separate lessor; if hardware is procured ahead of signed take-or-pay, lenders' collateral claims on the campus company do not extend to hardware assets.
  • Loose definition of 'anchor-tenant commitment' allows lenders to be misled: if LOIs, non-binding reservations or parent-company comfort letters are counted as equivalent to signed take-or-pay, the base-case 30% demand assumption is unvalidated and DSCR and leverage models collapse.

Worst Case Scenario: A debt-financing framework lacking clear covenants, scenario modeling and tie-in to Phase 0 gates enables the project to proceed into Phase 1 despite failure of one or more critical feasibility gates (RTE <500 MW offer, land assembly <70%, anchors <30% signed, contamination EUR 400M+). Phase 0 sunk cost of EUR 750M is non-recoverable; Phase 1 capital commitment rises from EUR 5B to EUR 6.5B–9.2B (with overlapping add-ons), overshooting the EUR 10B ceiling and the lender's DSCR floor (DSCR falls to 1.15x under a 10% curtailment-driven lease discount). Debt repricing or refusal in Month 12–18 (2027-10-17 to 2028-04-17) forces either an unscheduled equity raise (damaging existing investor returns), a project pause or downsize (eroding grid queue position and tenant confidence), or lender-driven restructuring that shifts risk onto tenants (higher leasing costs, tighter SLAs) and community (unmet benefit commitments). The project becomes an example of sunk-cost escalation, where a poorly gated feasibility study locks EUR 6B–10B into infrastructure that cannot sustain its debt obligations under realistic operating assumptions.

Best Case Scenario: A rigorous, scenario-tested debt-financing framework with numeric covenants, clear gatekeeping and sensitivity modeling enables lenders to commit firm, competitive debt (EUR 3B at benchmark +150–200 bps, ~5.5% all-in) by Month 12 (2027-10-17), accelerating Phase 1 FID and investor confidence. The framework explicitly ties debt drawdown tranches to Phase 0 gate closures (RTE letter, land assembly, anchor-tenant term sheets, ANSSI clearance) and Phase 1 milestones (grid connection signed, first-block energization, PUE stabilization), so if any gate fails, debt commitment lapses without lender capital loss. Sensitivity models show DSCR and leverage impact of the top 8–10 cost-line contingencies (grid co-funding EUR 500M–1.5B, contamination EUR 100M–400M, split topology EUR 250M–500M, etc.), enabling the investment committee and lenders to allocate EUR 2.95B–0.8B headroom against stacked risks. Energy-price pass-through and curtailment-discount scenarios are quantified (10% lease discount drops NOI from EUR 400M to EUR 345M, DSCR to 1.15x, requiring debt cut to EUR 2.66B), clarifying tenant and lender tolerance. Quarterly covenant monitoring and operational dashboards (PUE, power reliability, lease revenue, security incidents) enable early detection of performance divergence and allow corrective action (operational improvements, tenant SLA renegotiation, Phase 2 deferral) before debt service is threatened. The framework enables Phase 1 financing to close within 8–12 weeks of FID (by Month 13–14 = 2027-11-17 to 2027-12-17), avoiding carry-cost delay and enabling Phase 1 to start Month 15 (2028-01-17).

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • If the full debt-financing framework study (EUR 200K–400K, 3–4 months) is too slow or expensive, use an expedited pre-screening by a single lead lender (EIB or KfW) in Month 2 (2026-12-17) to establish rough leverage targets and pricing guidance (EUR 2.5B–3.5B at benchmark +200–250 bps); defer detailed term-sheet work to Month 6–9 (2027-04-17 to 2027-07-17), once Phase 0 gates begin to resolve and cost certainty improves.
  • Adopt a staged debt-commitment strategy: commit non-binding credit estimate (NBCE) in Month 9 (2027-07-17) subject to Phase 0 gate closure, and finalize binding term sheet only at Phase 1 FID (Month 12–13 = 2027-10-17 to 2027-11-17); this avoids carrying debt-commitment fees if gates fail but compresses the time between FID decision and debt-facility closure to 8 weeks, creating schedule risk if lender due diligence lags.
  • Structure debt drawdown in smaller tranches (EUR 300M–500M per block) released only against executed Phase 1 capex contracts, grid milestones and first-block energization, rather than a single EUR 3B commitment; this reduces lender risk exposure if Phase 1 encounters delays or cost overruns, but adds flexibility and transparency at cost of higher administrative burden and potential mid-project repricing.
  • If senior-debt markets are unfavorable or lenders decline to commit, explore alternative financing: mezzanine debt (EUR 500M–1B at 8–12% coupon) from infrastructure funds or pension investors, tenant-backed equipment financing for USD hardware (shifting FX and obsolescence risk to tenants), or partial asset-level financing (e.g., fiber route securitization as a standalone EUR 200M–500M vehicle), so campus-company balance-sheet debt is reduced to EUR 2.0B–2.5B and leverage managed at 40–50% LTV.
  • Commission an independent debt-covenant audit by a third-party credit specialist (Ernst & Young, Deloitte, or similar) in Month 9 (2027-07-17) to validate DSCR and leverage calculations and flag hidden sensitivities (e.g., interdependencies between energy cost, curtailment tolerance and lease-discount concessions) before binding commitment; costs EUR 50K–150K but can prevent undersized covenant buffers and surprise breaches.
  • Adopt a scenario-gated drawdown mechanism: trigger automatic debt-facility suspension if DSCR falls below 1.20x or leverage exceeds 62% LTV for two consecutive quarters; restart only after lender approves a remediation plan (operational improvement, tenant SLA adjustment, Phase 2 deferral, or equity cure); this creates contractual discipline around the investment committee's kill authority and prevents sunk-cost override.

Create Document 10: Topology Decision Framework and Scenario Modeling

Includes detailed split-campus node designs for (Cambrai 500 MW + Dunkirk 250 MW), (Cambrai 500 MW + Valenciennes 250 MW), and (all three 250 MW each), with per-node capex, grid-connection timelines, permitting parallelization, and inter-node fiber-latency constraints. Model shows topology lock cannot be final until RTE evidence (due Month 6 = 2027-04-17) arrives, so Month 4 (2027-02-17) decision is conditional unless RTE preliminary-feasibility is already in hand. Responsible Role Type: Phase 0 Program Manager and Red Team Lead

Secondary Template: Topology and Scaling Analysis (data-center feasibility template)

Steps to Create:

  • By Month 4 (2027-02-17), publish topology recommendation to investment committee with pass/fail on each criterion.

Approval Authorities: Investment Committee, Grid Connection Lead, Land Assembly Lead

Essential Information:

  • Compare single-square (161 km², Cambrai/E-Valley) vs. split-campus (2–3 nodes: Cambrai 500 MW, Dunkirk 250 MW, Valenciennes 250 MW) topologies against numeric pass/fail criteria: (1) RTE grid capacity (≥1 GW = single-square viable, <1 GW = split default); (2) land assemblability (≥70% optionable ≤15% above benchmark = single-square viable, <70% = split); (3) capex (single 500 MW EUR 5.0B Months 12–36 = 2027-10-17 to 2029-10-17 vs. split EUR 6.5B–7.5B Months 12–42 = 2027-10-17 to 2030-04-17); (4) schedule impact (single 24 months build vs. split 30 months phased).
  • Develop detailed per-node designs for 2–3 viable split combinations: node capex, grid-connection timelines per RTE, permitting parallelization (one file per node), inter-node fiber-latency constraints (training tolerance 50 ms, inference 10 ms), operations complexity.
  • Document decision logic: single-square only if BOTH RTE ≥1 GW written evidence AND ≥70% of target parcel optioned by Month 4 (2027-02-17). Because RTE letter due Month 6 (2027-04-17), split campus is default at Month 4 (2027-02-17) unless RTE evidence already in hand.
  • Quantify cost and schedule impact of topology pivot mid-Phase-0: redesign EUR 100M–250M (estimate), schedule slip 6–12 months, stranded Phase 0 work on abandoned single-square studies.
  • Model per-topology sensitivity: +10% per-MW capex impact of split (multi-site duplication), +6 months financing ramp if split-campus decision is late, +EUR 200M–300M fiber-ring cost for inter-node connectivity.
  • Establish decision document evidence thresholds: what specific RTE outputs (preliminary-feasibility letter scope, hosting-capacity confirmation, tranche-sizing methodology) allow single-square to remain viable at Month 4 (2027-02-17).
  • Publish recommendation to investment committee with explicit pass/fail on each criterion and financial/schedule consequences, prepared for Month 4 (2027-02-17) decision gate.

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • Topology decision deferred or ambiguous past Month 4 (2027-02-17): Phase 1 design team cannot lock grid connection strategy, land-acquisition scope, or permitting file structure; delays Phase 0 design work 3–6 months, compressing time available for split-campus validation and risking Phase 0 gate breach.
  • Single-square commitment based on incomplete RTE evidence (LOI or non-binding feasibility sketch vs. firm preliminary-feasibility letter): Phase 1 FID proceeds on unvalidated grid assumption; RTE formal offer in Month 6 (2027-04-17) or later reveals hosting capacity <500 MW, forcing emergency Phase 1 redesign or cancellation, stranding EUR 250M–500M Phase 0 spend.
  • Split-campus topology chosen without validated inter-node latency tolerance: Phase 1 tenant workloads cannot span nodes, reducing addressable customer pool and forcing downsize or reconfiguration mid-Phase-1, eroding revenue credibility with lenders.
  • Permitting-file strategy not aligned to topology: single-square permits filed before topology confirmed, later split-campus decision requires duplicate permitting work; split-campus permitting filed for all nodes before demand is proven, stranding EUR 20M–50M per extra node file.
  • Split-campus capex estimates not credible (underestimate of duplication, fiber cost, or operations overhead): Phase 1 FID capital request increases 10–20% after Month 4 (2027-02-17) decision, exceeding EUR 10B ceiling or forcing re-gating with lenders.
  • Land-assemblability analysis incomplete or optimistic: topology decision assumes 70% optionable but Phase 0 land work (Months 3–4 = 2027-01-17 to 2027-02-17) reveals <50% in hand, forcing topology pivot after decision is published, eroding credibility with investment committee and lenders.
  • Fiber and security costs omitted from split-campus models: topology recommendation appears EUR 1.5B–2.5B cheaper than reality, Phase 1 FID discovers EUR 0.3B–0.7B additional cost, exceeding cabinet approval authority.
  • Document is narrative without numeric decision thresholds: investment committee cannot apply the recommendation mechanically; subjective judgment prevails, enabling sunk-cost override and weakening gate discipline.

Worst Case Scenario: Topology decision is deferred, ambiguous, or wrong, leading to a Phase 1 FID (Month 12 = 2027-10-17) locked into single-square design on the assumption of ≥1 GW RTE capacity. RTE formal connection offer in Month 13 (2027-11-17) reveals only 500 MW available at the Cambrai node, plus EUR 500M co-funding demand for transmission reinforcement, and curtailment ≥15% annually. Simultaneously, land-assembly negotiations (ongoing into Phase 1) reveal that the full 161 km² envelope cannot be optioned at reasonable cost: holdout farmers demand above-market premiums or public compulsory acquisition, adding 12–18 months to assembly and creating political liability. Grid capacity is thus committed to a single node that cannot be fully developed, and land assembly extends past Months 24–36 (2028-10-17 to 2029-10-17) when Phase 1 construction is supposed to be active, forcing design revision from single-square to split-campus mid-Phase-1. Phase 1 capex explodes from EUR 5B to EUR 7.5B+, exceeding the EUR 10B ceiling and requiring a new funding ask. Phase 1 energization slips from Month 48 (2030-10-17) to Month 54+ (2031-04-17+), eroding grid queue position (RTE offers are time-conditional) and losing 12–18 months of tenant revenue. Cost overrun and schedule slip combine to reduce debt service coverage to <1.2x, triggering lender covenant breach and potential loan restructuring (cost 200+ bps) or demand for additional equity (EUR 1B–2B). Tenant anchors signed in Phase 0 hold the campus to take-or-pay commitments for 2024 demand profiles that are now obsolete by 2031; renegotiation demands from both sides create friction and potential lease terminations. Investment committee is discredited for approving FID without locking topology, and board-level confidence in the sponsor's delivery capability erodes, affecting future capital raises. Project survives but in degraded form (smaller, later, more expensive) or is written down.

Best Case Scenario: Topology Decision Framework, completed by Month 4 (2027-02-17), rigorously compares single-square vs. 2–3 viable split-campus options with numeric criteria for RTE capacity, land assemblability, capex, schedule and per-node financing. The document shows that single-square requires firm evidence of ≥1 GW from RTE by Month 4 (2027-02-17) (or conditional pass if RTE letter is in hand by Month 6 = 2027-04-17). Investment committee adopts the framework and declares single-square the working assumption, conditional on RTE's Month 6 (2027-04-17) letter. Phase 1 design team locks grid-connection strategy (single substation, dedicated 400 kV lines) and permitting file (single coordinated ICPE application). Land-assembly team focuses validation on Cambrai/E-Valley core parcel (90 km² of the 161 km²) by Month 6 (2027-04-17), confirming ≥70% optionable at benchmark cost. RTE issues its preliminary-feasibility letter in Month 6 (2027-04-17), confirming 500 MW available in first tranche within 36 months and pathway to ≥1 GW if flexibility conditions are met. Framework's split-campus designs are held as read-to-activate contingencies, requiring only 2–3 weeks reactivation if conditions change. Lenders see a disciplined topology decision backed by numeric thresholds and contingency designs, increasing confidence in Phase 1 FID. Tenants understand single-square is firm (lower operational complexity) and sign leases accordingly. Phase 1 FID (Month 12 = 2027-10-17) proceeds with clear grid, land and financing strategy, reducing FID decision time by 2–4 weeks. Phase 1 capex stays within EUR 5B–6B (single node with modest contingency for grid co-funding). Phase 1 build (Months 12–36 = 2027-10-17 to 2029-10-17) executes on a stable topology with locked permitting path and validated land, reducing design rework and schedule variance. First-block energization targets Months 42–48 (2030-04-17 to 2030-10-17) and is credible to tenants and lenders, supporting demand certainty and financing syndication. Framework enables evidence-based decisions, reduces sunk-cost pressure and hardens gate discipline, positioning Phase 0 for a high-confidence pass or an early, low-impact downsize/defer.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • If RTE hosting-capacity evidence is unavailable by Month 2 (2026-12-17): treat RTE capacity as a gate blocker and default to split-campus topology (2–3 independent nodes, each ≤500 MW) as the working assumption in the framework, with single-square kept only as an Option A contingency if RTE evidence arrives early. This allows Phase 1 design to proceed on split-campus infrastructure (independent grid connections, parallel permitting, inter-node fiber) while holding the option to revert to single-square without redesign if RTE later offers ≥1 GW to one node.
  • If land-assemblability analysis reveals <50% of any single target parcel optionable by Month 3 (2027-01-17): immediately pivot to a fragmented split-campus topology using smaller, independently optionable parcels (Cambrai 300 km², Dunkirk 150 km², Valenciennes 150 km²) on independent grid connections. Simplify the framework to model only split options, with 2–3 node designs at 250–500 MW each, rather than spending Phase 0 effort on a single-square topology that cannot assemble.
  • If RTE curtailment requirements exceed 15% or indicate >18 month delay to first connection: reframe the topology decision around grid-constrained capacity rather than land-constrained geography. Design Phase 1 to target the subset of capacity RTE can support reliably (e.g., 300–500 MW instead of 1 GW) and stage expansion to later tranches only as grid reinforcement completes. This makes the topology secondary to the grid constraint and shortens Phase 0 validation.
  • If tenant latency tolerance for training workloads proves >50 ms (making inter-node span operationally infeasible): eliminate split-campus as an option and focus the framework on a single-node topology only, with capacity limited to the hosting available at that one node from RTE. Accept that the 9 GW vision is infeasible and design Phase 1 for 500 MW–1 GW at one location, treating Phase 2+ as dependent on building additional single-node campuses at other locations (separate sites, not split campuses).
  • If Phase 0 timeline compression (Month 4 = 2027-02-17 decision) proves infeasible (RTE, DREAL, land surveys not ready): defer topology decision to Month 6 (2027-04-17) or Month 9 (2027-07-17), accepting a 2–3 month compression of Phase 0 deliverables. Publish a preliminary topology recommendation (single-square with split contingency) at Month 4 (2027-02-17) and a final decision at Month 6 (2027-04-17) once RTE letter is in hand. Phase 1 design team uses the preliminary recommendation to begin grid and permitting work in parallel.
  • If Phase 0 budget constraints (EUR 750M cap) make split-campus detailed designs unaffordable: develop a single split-campus reference design (Cambrai 500 MW + Dunkirk 250 MW) as a template, rather than modeling 3–4 node combinations in detail. Apply the reference design to each plausible pair of sites, accepting higher uncertainty in per-node capex and latency, to stay within budget. Upgrade to detailed per-node designs only if topology decision pivots to split and enters Phase 1.
  • Commission an independent topology-decision consultant or red team (EUR 1M–2M, estimate) to peer-review the framework before Month 4 (2027-02-17) gate, reducing reliance on the development team's analysis and hardening investment-committee confidence in the decision. The consultant assesses the RTE evidence, land-assembly findings and capex models against industry benchmarks and flags any analysis gaps.

Create Document 11: Phase 0 Risk Register and Red-Team Monthly Status Reports

ID: eff08abf-5ab6-49d8-8c08-ae2eba2558b1

Description: Living risk register (initiated Month 1 = 2026-11-17, updated monthly through Month 12 = 2027-10-17) tracking 23 material risks across regulatory, technical, financial, environmental, social and operational domains (per canonical facts risk taxonomy). Each risk entry specifies: title, description, impact/likelihood/severity, current status (red/yellow/green), actions taken, responsible owner, and escalation trigger. Red-team monthly status reports (1-page pass/fail summary per gate criterion: RTE, land, tenants, ANSSI, water, ecology, permitting, financing) published to investment committee and lenders by the 15th of each month, with any trend toward threshold breach flagged as yellow (>20% failure risk) or red (>50% failure risk). Month 12 (2027-10-17) final red-team opinion (signed) summarizes evidence for each gate and any dissent. Primary audience: investment committee, lenders, Phase 1 FID decision-makers.

Responsible Role Type: Phase 0 Program Manager and Red Team Lead

Primary Template: Project Risk Register (PMI PMBOK or Infrastructure UK Standard)

Secondary Template: Monthly Project Health Report (traffic-light scoring per gate criterion)

Steps to Create:

  • Initialize risk register in Month 1 (2026-11-17) with 23 canonical risks from risk-assessment documents.
  • For each risk, define: trigger indicator (how to measure if risk is materializing), owner (workstream lead responsible for mitigation), action plan (specific steps and timeline), and escalation path (to investment committee if risk status turns yellow or red).
  • Commission external red team (EUR 2M–5M contract, Month 1 = 2026-11-17) to publish monthly pass/fail assessments independent of development team.
  • Red team delivers 1-page monthly summary by 15th of each month (Months 1–12 = 2026-11-17 to 2027-10-17) covering: RTE status (confidence in 500 MW letter by Month 6 = 2027-04-17?), land assembly (% optioned, holdout risk), tenant commitments (MW signed, cash deposited), ANSSI clearance (timeline credible?), permitting (filing on track for Month 9 = 2027-07-17?), water-authority opinion (received?), financing (lender appetite confirmed?). Each item rated green (on track), yellow (at risk), or red (threshold breach likely).
  • Escalate any red-status item immediately to investment committee with recommended action (proceed, pause, downsize, kill).
  • Month 12 (2027-10-17): red team delivers signed final opinion on all five Phase 0 gates, with any dissent or contested assumptions appended.

Approval Authorities: External Red Team Lead, Investment Committee, Lenders (observers)

Essential Information:

  • Document purpose: A living risk register initiated in Month 1 (2026-11-17), updated monthly through Month 12 (2027-10-17), tracking 23 material risks (regulatory, technical, financial, environmental, social, operational) with current status (red/yellow/green), mitigation actions, responsible owners, and escalation triggers.
  • Red-team monthly status reports (1-page pass/fail summaries) due by the 15th of each month, covering five Phase 0 gate criteria: RTE grid hosting (≥500 MW letter by Month 6 = 2027-04-17), land assembly (≥70% optioned by Month 4 = 2027-02-17), anchor-tenant take-or-pay (≥30% signed by Month 9 = 2027-07-17), ANSSI clearance pathway (confirmed by Month 12 = 2027-10-17), and permitting on track (file submitted Month 8–9 = 2027-06-17 to 2027-07-17).
  • Risk register structure: title, description, impact (qualitative EUR/MW/timeline), likelihood (Low/Medium/High), severity (Low/Medium/High), trigger indicator (how to measure if materializing), owner (workstream lead), action plan (specific steps and timeline), and escalation path (to investment committee if yellow >20% threshold breach or red >50% breach).
  • Red-team independence: external contract (EUR 2M–5M), separate from development team, with monthly scoring (green=on track, yellow=at risk, red=threshold breach likely) and formal signed opinion at Month 12 (2027-10-17) including any dissent or contested assumptions appended.
  • Escalation protocol: any red-status item triggers immediate investment-committee notification with recommended action (proceed with conditions, pause Phase 0 spend, downsize Phase 1, or kill). Yellow-status items monitored; trend toward red-status documented.
  • Gate evidence thresholds (from canonical facts): RTE written letter for ≥500 MW within 36 months by Month 6 (2027-04-17); land ≥70% optioned and ≥80% if split-campus nodes by Month 4 (2027-02-17); anchor-tenant term sheets for ≥30% of Phase 1 (150 MW of 500 MW base case) by Month 9 (2027-07-17), signed and non-binding LOI excluded; ANSSI written confirmation that formal review can start at Month 13 (2027-11-17) with no identified blocking concern; permitting file submitted by Month 8–9 (2027-06-17 to 2027-07-17) on track for decision within 24–30 months.

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • Sunk-cost momentum overrides kill criteria: without monthly red-team accountability and published dissent, Phase 1 proceeds despite failed gates, wasting Phase 1 capital (EUR 5B–10B) on unproven grid, land or tenant conditions.
  • Late-discovered threshold breaches: if risk status is not tracked monthly, red-flag conditions (e.g., RTE negative preliminary opinion, land holdout increase to >30%, anchor-tenant term-sheet failure) are discovered in Month 10–11 (2027-08-17 to 2027-09-17), leaving no time for Phase 1 FID pause or redesign.
  • Uncoordinated team actions: without a single authoritative risk register, workstream leads (grid, land, tenants, permits, security) manage their own risks in isolation, miss cross-dependencies (e.g., land delay eroding RTE queue position), and present inconsistent evidence to the investment committee.
  • Lender and co-investor blind spots: if risk status is not published monthly, lenders and co-investors cannot challenge the development team or propose mitigation before Phase 1 commitment, discovering issues only at FID gate.
  • Red-team capture or alignment: if the red team reports to the development sponsor, conflict of interest incentivizes soft assessments; dissent is suppressed, turning the register into a compliance exercise rather than genuine scrutiny.

Worst Case Scenario: The risk register is initialized but not maintained with rigorous monthly discipline. Red-team assessments become infrequent or soft, missing the deterioration of grid, land, tenant or permitting status through Months 3–9 (2027-01-17 to 2027-07-17). By Month 10–11 (2027-08-17 to 2027-09-17), RTE signals lower-than-expected hosting capacity, a major landowner holdout emerges, and anchor tenants defer term-sheet signature citing market uncertainty. The investment committee meets at Month 12 (2027-10-17) with no prior warning, faces a binary decision without time to restructure Phase 0 or Phase 1, and either commits Phase 1 despite failed gates or cancels, stranding EUR 500M–750M Phase 0 spend with minimal salvage value. Subsequent project restart requires 12–24 months of condition-improvement waiting, during which grid queue position, land options and tenant interest decay.

Best Case Scenario: The risk register is operational by Month 1 (2026-11-17), with red-team monthly assessments published to the investment committee, lenders and co-investors by the 15th of each month. By Month 3–4 (2027-01-17 to 2027-02-17), early yellow flags on land assembly (holdout count rising) and grid (RTE pre-engineering delays) trigger escalation and mitigation: the land team intensifies option negotiations and offers revised parcel boundaries, while the grid team negotiates interim RTE feedback and prepares split-campus designs. By Month 6 (2027-04-17), RTE preliminary letter arrives on schedule, water opinion confirms feasibility, and ANSSI signals no blocking concern. By Month 9 (2027-07-17), anchor-tenant term sheets are signed, permitting file is submitted, and the red team publishes a pass recommendation on all five gates. By Month 12 (2027-10-17), Phase 0 concludes within budget (EUR 250M–750M), Phase 1 FID proceeds with high confidence, and financing closes at favorable terms. Assets generated during Phase 0 (land options, grid pre-engineering, tenant frameworks, permitting file, security governance roadmap) are in the hands of experienced teams ready for Phase 1 execution.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • If external red team cannot be secured by Month 1 (2026-11-17): commission an internal red team reporting directly to the investment committee (not the sponsor development team) with charter signed by all co-investors; rotate membership quarterly to prevent alignment; require monthly written opinions with dissent appended; publish summaries (redacted of confidential findings) to lenders.
  • If monthly reporting cadence is infeasible (e.g., long sales cycles for anchor tenants make monthly updates unreliable): shift to milestone-driven risk reporting at fixed events (Month 2 = 2026-12-17, Month 4 = 2027-02-17, Month 6 = 2027-04-17, Month 9 = 2027-07-17, Month 12 = 2027-10-17, 2027-02-17, 2027-04-17, 2027-07-17, 2027-10-17), with hot-topic escalations between milestones if a risk status turns red before the next scheduled report.
  • If a full 23-risk register is too unwieldy: consolidate into 5–7 critical risks (grid, land, tenants, ANSSI, permitting, financing, community) and track secondary risks by workstream; allocate 50% of red-team effort to critical risks and 50% to secondary/workstream oversight.
  • If investment-committee overhead is high (monthly meetings infeasible): adopt a written-report model with in-person monthly committee review for red-status items only, allowing virtual or asynchronous review of green/yellow items.
  • If dissent disclosure feels politically risky to co-investors: structure the red-team opinion with majority findings and a separate 'alternative assessment' or 'dissenting view' section, published together but clearly separated, so lenders see both the consensus and the disagreement without implying failure.

Steps to Find:

  • Access RTE's GARE (Guichet d'Accès au Réseau pour les EnR) online portal or contact RTE's Nord regional customer-connection office directly (Rue du Faubourg de Roubaix, Lille) for current queue data and connection-request status.

Access Difficulty: Medium.
