Response timeline typically 4–8 weeks. A formal pre-engineering request from the sponsor to RTE (filed in Month 0 = 2026-10-17) is the standard path.

Essential Information:

  • Current RTE queue positions and available hosting capacity at Hauts-de-France 400 kV substations (Cambrai/E-Valley, Dunkirk, Valenciennes, Saint-Omer), with timeline from connection request to energization for each node.
  • Existing and committed industrial loads competing for RTE capacity in the Nord region (steel mills, hydrogen projects, refinery decarbonization) and their expected drawdown dates.
  • RTE's multi-tranche allocation policy: whether the operator will offer capacity in staged tranches (500 MW, then 1 GW, then 2 GW+) or require a single full filing, and the contractual flexibility (curtailment, BESS, load-shedding) RTE will accept for each tranche.
  • Transmission-reinforcement scope and cost allocation for each candidate node: 400 kV substation upgrades, line reinforcement, and whether RTE or the developer bears study and construction cost.
  • RTE's formal preliminary feasibility letter or written estimate for the first 500 MW tranche, due by Month 6 (2027-04-17), stating available capacity, connection timeline (months to energization), and required flexibility/curtailment terms.
  • Published S3REnR (Schéma Régional de Raccordement) roadmap for Hauts-de-France covering renewable and industrial load integration through 2030.

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • Absence of written RTE hosting-capacity evidence by Month 6 (2027-04-17) leaves the primary kill test unvalidated; Phase 0 gate cannot close and Phase 1 FID is blocked.
  • Underestimated competing load from decarbonization projects (hydrogen, steel) saturates regional grid capacity, reducing available MW from assumed 1+ GW to <500 MW, forcing immediate topology pivot or project cancellation.
  • Incomplete or outdated RTE queue data delays the topology decision at Month 4 (2027-02-17), compressing time for split-campus design and permitting separation by 4–8 weeks.
  • Mischaracterized transmission-reinforcement cost allocation (developer liability assumed at EUR 200M–500M, actual EUR 800M–1.5B) breaches Phase 1 budget headroom and erodes equity returns by 3–5 percentage points.
  • Unconfirmed multi-tranche policy forces a full 9 GW filing rather than staged 500 MW first request, triggering regulatory pushback and queue-position loss to other users.
  • Obsolete or incomplete queue data (>6 months old) fails to reflect recent industrial requests or grid reinforcements, giving false confidence in available capacity.

Worst Case Scenario: RTE written capacity offer is delayed beyond Month 12 (2027-10-17) or limited to <300 MW in the first tranche, or RTE conditions all capacity on >20% annual curtailment. Result: the primary kill test (grid hosting >~1 GW) fails; Phase 1 cannot proceed at intended 500 MW scale, forcing downsizing to 250 MW or less; topology and permitting assumptions collapse; Phase 0 sunk cost (EUR 250M–750M) is stranded unless an alternative site or much-reduced scope can be justified. If RTE's answer comes only in Month 18–24 (2028-04-17 to 2028-10-17), the grid queue position is lost to competing users, and the project timeline slips 12–24 months, raising carrying costs by EUR 300M–600M.

Best Case Scenario: RTE publishes a written preliminary feasibility letter by Month 6 (2027-04-17) confirming at least 1 GW available capacity across two tranches (500 MW + 500 MW) within 36 months, with annual curtailment capped at 10% and flexible load-shedding acceptable via BESS. Transmission-reinforcement cost is shared with regional industrial projects (hydrogen, steel), capping the developer's contribution to EUR 200M–300M. The single-square Cambrai/E-Valley node is confirmed viable; land assembly, permitting, and fiber routing are streamlined to a single file. Phase 0 gate closes on schedule (Month 12 = 2027-10-17) with Phase 1 FID authorized, energization targeted Months 42–48 (2030-04-17 to 2030-10-17), and Phase 2 FID pathway credible.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • If RTE capacity data is incomplete or delayed, commission an independent RTE hosting-capacity audit (EUR 500K–1.5M) from a specialist grid-engineering firm with direct RTE access; escalate to the RTE regional director for a formal response within 4 weeks (by Month 2 = 2026-12-17).
  • If competing decarbonization projects saturate capacity, pivot to a split-campus model with dedicated grid connections per node (Cambrai 500 MW, Dunkirk 250 MW) or a much-reduced Phase 1 (250 MW) on the most favorable node, by Month 4 (2027-02-17).
  • If RTE multi-tranche policy is unclear, submit a formal written request for a pre-engineering study of a phased connection (500 MW Year 1, +500 MW Year 3, +1 GW Year 5+), with contractual flexibility for load reduction or curtailment, asking for a 90-day response by Month 2 (2026-12-17).
  • If transmission-reinforcement cost is above budget headroom (>EUR 500M), negotiate a cost-sharing agreement with competing industrial users (hydrogen production, steel decarbonization) who benefit from the same reinforcement, or request that a regional development agency or the State co-fund the substation (escrow agreement by Month 9 = 2027-07-17).
  • If RTE's answer remains uncertain at Month 12 (2027-10-17), defer Phase 1 FID and hold Phase 0 optionality (land options extended 2–3 years, permitting file prepared but not submitted) pending RTE clarity within 6 months; reset gate to Month 18 (2028-04-17) with contingency carry costs of EUR 150M–300M.

Find Document 2: Hauts-de-France Regional Land Ownership and Agricultural Land-Value Benchmark Data

ID: c753ec15-8b01-435b-a4d1-702eb2d2bfeb

Description: Cadastre (official land registry) maps and land-value statistics for candidate zones (Cambrai/E-Valley, Dunkirk industrial area, Valenciennes/Denain/Escaudain, Saint-Omer). Includes parcel-level ownership (public/private/agricultural), recent sales-price comps (EUR/ha), and municipal zoning (industrial, agricultural, protected). Benchmark land value needed to evaluate the 70% optionability test (non-coercive options at ≤15% above benchmark). Intended audience for analysis: land-assembly lead and investment committee.

Recency Requirement: Most recent available (2024–2025 land-value benchmarks from SAFER France or DDT/DDTM local registries); historical 3–5 year trend helpful.

Responsible Role Type: Land Assembly and Real Estate Strategist

Steps to Find:

  • Contact the Chambre d'Agriculture Hauts-de-France (regional agricultural chamber) for land-value benchmarks per zone and known FNSEA member interests.
  • Access the French cadastre online (cadastre.gouv.fr) to search parcel ownership by commune and assess fragmentation.
  • Request municipal planning documents (Plans d'Urbanisme Local, PULs) from each affected municipality (Cambrai, Dunkirk, Valenciennes, Saint-Omer) showing current zoning and land-use plans.
  • Contact the regional SAFER (Société d'Aménagement Foncier et d'Établissement Rural) to understand agricultural-conservation policies and land-transfer procedures for the region.

Access Difficulty: Easy to Medium. Cadastre.gouv.fr is freely accessible online. Municipal zoning maps are public. Agricultural land-value benchmarks require contact with SAFER (typically responsive within 2–4 weeks) and the Chamber of Agriculture.

Essential Information:

  • Parcel-level ownership mapping (public/private/agricultural) across Cambrai/E-Valley, Dunkirk, Valenciennes/Denain/Escaudain and Saint-Omer zones via cadastre and municipal records.
  • Recent land-value benchmark data (EUR/ha) per zone and land use (industrial, agricultural, protected) from SAFER France and DDT/DDTM registries, 2024–2025 or most recent available.
  • Historical 3–5 year land-price trends per zone to establish volatility and real appreciation.
  • Fragmentation analysis: count and average parcel size by municipality to assess assemblability; identify known holdouts or activist groups blocking sales.
  • Zoning and planning status (PLU, PUL, protected areas, Natura 2000, RAMSAR wetlands) to confirm industrial and buildable land designation.
  • Agricultural land-use preservation policies and SAFER intervention rights that may constrain private purchase or require public co-investment.
  • Comparison of benchmark land value to option prices negotiated or proposed in Phase 0 (to verify the 70% optionability test at ≤15% premium).

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • Inaccurate or outdated land-value benchmarks lead to overestimation of option-price feasibility; Phase 0 land-assembly spend may be stranded if benchmark is wrong by >20%.
  • Incomplete ownership data hides holdouts or fragmentation, forcing late discovery (Month 6–9 = 2027-04-17 to 2027-07-17) that triggers topology pivot and costly redesign.
  • Missing or misinterpreted zoning and Natura 2000 designations cause permit delays or design constraints discovered at Month 6 (2027-04-17) or later, compressing Phase 0 schedule.
  • Lack of historical price trends obscures whether current benchmark is inflated or suppressed, creating false confidence in optionability or false rejection of feasible sites.
  • Absence of SAFER and farm-union engagement data leaves political resistance and acquisition constraints unquantified, undermining the Phase 0 land gate (Month 4 = 2027-02-17) decision.

Worst Case Scenario: Land-value benchmarks are 25–40% below actual market prices in Cambrai and Dunkirk due to outdated SAFER data (last refreshed 2022), and ownership fragmentation is not identified until Phase 0 Month 8–9 (2027-06-17 to 2027-07-17). The topology decision at Month 4 (2027-02-17) proceeds on false assumptions, confirming single-square at Cambrai. At Month 9 (2027-07-17), option negotiations reveal that 60% of target parcels are held by 3–5 holdouts refusing to sell below EUR 35,000/ha (vs. EUR 20,000 benchmark), and 15% overlap Natura 2000 wetlands blocking development. Phase 0 land-assembly spend (EUR 50M–100M estimate in tranches 1–2) is stranded; topology must pivot to split-campus in Month 10–11 (2027-08-17 to 2027-09-17), compressing design to 1 month before the Phase 0 gate. The gate is delayed 2–3 months and Phase 1 FID slips to Month 15–18 (2028-01-17 to 2028-04-17), eroding RTE queue position and adding EUR 300M–500M carrying cost.

Best Case Scenario: Benchmark data identifies Cambrai/E-Valley and Dunkirk as having adequate industrial and agricultural land at EUR 18,000–22,000/ha with no major Natura 2000 overlap. Ownership is concentrated (60%+ in 2–3 public/industrial landowners and 3–4 farmer co-operatives), and SAFER confirms no compulsory-acquisition barriers. Phase 0 Month 1–3 (2026-11-17 to 2027-01-17) option negotiations lock 75–80% of single-square target at EUR 20,500/ha (within 2.5% of benchmark), with public landowners committing to a lead position. The topology decision at Month 4 (2027-02-17) confirms single-square at Cambrai, and land-assembly spend (EUR 80M–120M in tranches 1–3) closes with confidence. By Month 9 (2027-07-17), at least 85% of target parcel is optioned. The Phase 0 gate at Month 12 (2027-10-17) passes on land with room for Phase 1 contingency and split-campus optionality deferred.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • If benchmark data is unavailable or stale (>2 years old), commission a rapid Phase 0 primary market survey (EUR 1.5M–3M, Months 1–3 = 2026-11-17 to 2027-01-17) via a local real-estate firm (e.g., Cushman & Wakefield Nord, JLL France), targeting 50–100 recent (2023–2025) land sales comps per zone and expert opinion on current-market premiums and holdout risk.
  • Engage the Chambre d'Agriculture Hauts-de-France and SAFER directly in Month 1 (2026-11-17) for written opinions on land-assemblability, historical price trends, and FNSEA/Confédération Paysanne positions; treat their informal input as an interim gate (Month 3 = 2027-01-17) to validate benchmark viability before heavy Phase 0 spend on options.
  • Cross-check benchmark data against recent industrial-zone parcel sales (brownfield redevelopment) in Dunkirk and Valenciennes to distinguish industrial-land pricing (higher, often EUR 30,000–50,000/ha) from agricultural (EUR 12,000–20,000/ha); site-specific benchmarks per zone reduce false assumptions.
  • If contiguous single-square assembly appears unachievable by Month 3 (2027-01-17), immediately pivot to split-campus topology and re-baseline per-node land costs; avoid sunk cost on single-square options beyond Month 3 (2027-01-17).
  • Establish a price-escalation clause in Phase 0 land-option agreements: if land benchmark inflation exceeds 10% year-on-year during Phase 0, trigger a topology and cost review at Month 6 (2027-04-17); if escalation tops 20%, activate the split-campus fallback or 250 MW downsizing.

Find Document 3: French Phase I and Phase II Environmental Site Assessment Standards and Template Guidance

ID: b80cda5f-14a9-416c-900f-9b41fec15293

Description: Official guidance on Phase I and Phase II intrusive environmental surveys (soil boring, groundwater, asbestos) per French BRGM (Bureau de Recherches Géologiques et Minières) or equivalent standards. Includes soil-contamination thresholds for heavy metals (lead, cadmium, mercury), petroleum hydrocarbons, and hazardous-waste indicators relevant to industrial brownfield sites. Needed to scope Phase II surveys and bound remediation-liability estimates. Intended audience for analysis: environmental counsel and remediation lead.

Recency Requirement: Current French environmental standards (AFNOR NF X31-600 or equivalent) and BRGM guidance on soil thresholds (Valeurs de Fond Géochimique and Valeurs de Référence).

Responsible Role Type: Brownfield Remediation and Environmental Liability Counsel

Steps to Find:

  • Consult BRGM online portal (brgm.fr) for published soil-contamination reference values and methodology for Phase I/II assessments.
  • Access AFNOR standards via French environmental or geological societies (Société Géologique de France).
  • Contact regional DREAL or DDT offices for local contamination histories and known industrial-legacy sites in candidate zones.

Access Difficulty: Medium. BRGM publishes standards freely; AFNOR standards may require a subscription. Regional DREAL/DDT guidance is typically provided on request (2–4 week response).

Essential Information:

  • Define the soil-contamination reference thresholds (Valeurs de Fond Géochimique and Valeurs de Référence) specific to northern France heavy-industrial sites (Hauts-de-France)', including trigger levels for lead, cadmium, mercury, petroleum hydrocarbons, and hazardous-waste indicators per AFNOR NF X31-600 or equivalent current standard
  • Specify the Phase I desktop-assessment methodology: what data sources (BRGM historical mining/industrial maps, regional DREAL archives, municipal records), what trigger conditions warrant Phase II intrusive surveys, and what output documentation (ESA report format, recommendations) is standard
  • Detail the Phase II intrusive-survey scope: soil boring depth and spacing for a 500 MW node (estimate ~9 km² per node, estimate 8-10 data halls), groundwater sampling (aquifer depth, flow direction, contamination pathways), asbestos and building-material surveys for demolition-candidate structures, and chain-of-custody and analytical protocols
  • Specify remediation-cost estimation methodology and liability-allocation scenarios: what cost ranges (EUR per m³, EUR per site) are typical for common contaminants (heavy metals, slag, munitions residue) in former steel, coal, industrial and airbase sites; how long-term monitoring or engineering controls factor into remediation cost
  • Provide templates or checklist forms for Phase I and Phase II reporting, including: executive summary, site history and baseline conditions, analytical results with comparison to reference thresholds, risk characterization, remediation recommendations, closure letters or regulatory approval pathways, and contingencies for unexpected findings during construction
  • Identify the regulatory approval bodies (DREAL, DDT, regional environmental agency) and approval timelines for Phase I findings and Phase II remediation plans; specify what constitutes 'bounded liability' acceptable to insurers or lenders

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • Incorrect or outdated soil-contamination thresholds lead to underestimation of actual remediation liability; Phase 1 discovery of unbudgeted contamination forces construction delay and cost overrun of EUR 100M–400M (estimated), triggering Phase 1 FID renegotiation or cancellation
  • Phase II survey scope that is too narrow (insufficient boring density, shallow depth) misses deep groundwater plumes or subsurface munitions residue; latent discoveries during Phase 1 excavation or pile-driving stop construction for 3–12 months (estimate) and compound cost
  • Ambiguous Phase I/II templates or missing regulatory approval pathways create confusion about when liability is 'bounded'; lenders require clear ESA closure or a written regulatory opinion before construction finance release; absence of this documentation can block drawdown tranches
  • Failure to distinguish between historical-baseline contamination (seller/public liability) and project-induced impacts (developer responsibility) creates indemnity disputes; properly structured Phase I/II reports with clear liability allocation preserve recovery against sellers and reduce sunk-cost risk
  • Phase II cost estimates that omit long-term remediation verification, engineering controls, or monitoring obligations understate true lifecycle remediation cost; later discovery that closure requires 10+ years of groundwater pumping or deed notices erodes project margin

Worst Case Scenario: ["Absence of clear AFNOR-compliant Phase II survey methodology and thresholds: a 500 MW node at Cambrai with estimated 9 km² footprint and multiple brownfield parcels is surveyed with outdated or non-standard protocols. During Phase 1 excavation (Months 13–24 = 2027-11-17 to 2028-10-17), deep-subsurface munitions residue, slag contamination or persistent groundwater plumes are discovered that do not appear in Phase II. Remediation of the affected building footprints (estimated 2–4 of 8–10 halls) requires stop-work orders, hazmat emergency response (EUR 5M–20M), extended investigation (6–9 months), and remedial design and implementation (EUR 50M–150M). Construction schedules slip 9–18 months. Phase 1 debt service accrues on unfinished infrastructure (estimated EUR 150M–300M carrying cost). Lenders trigger remediation-reserve drawdowns, exhausting contingency and forcing additional equity injection or Phase 1 FID renegotiation. Project energization slips from Months 42–48 (2030-04-17 to 2030-10-17) to Months 48–60 (2030-10-17 to 2031-10-17) (estimated), eroding grid queue position and tenant lease certainty. Estimated total impact: EUR 300M–500M+ cost, 12–18 month delay, credit impact on sponsors and co-investors."]

Best Case Scenario: ["Robust AFNOR NF X31-600–compliant Phase I and Phase II assessment standards and templates enable systematic contamination baseline at all four candidate zones (Cambrai, Dunkirk, Valenciennes, Saint-Omer) by Month 3 (2027-01-17). Phase II intrusive surveys identify contamination profiles per parcel and bound remediation liability to EUR 0–100M per site (per risk register). All liability for pre-existing contamination is contractually allocated to land sellers or public remediation bodies via signed indemnities or escrow by Month 6 (2027-04-17). Phase 0 environmental gate closes cleanly, with DREAL confirmation that identified remediation is achievable and permits can proceed. Phase 1 construction begins with complete baseline knowledge; any unexpected contamination discovered during excavation is minor, remediated within budgeted contingency (EUR 100M–300M reserve), and does not block schedule. Lenders release debt tranches on time. First-block energization occurs at Month 42–48 (2030-04-17 to 2030-10-17) as planned, tenant leases proceed without delay, and grid queue position is preserved."]

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • If official BRGM or AFNOR ESA guidance documents are unavailable or outdated: engage a European environmental-assessment firm (e.g. Arcadis, Ramboll, or French firms Burgeap, BEAL) to commission a bespoke Phase I/II assessment protocol aligned with current French regulations and compatible with lender/insurer expectations. Cost estimate EUR 3M–8M for a full four-zone Phase I/II program; timeline 4–6 months (overlaps with Phase 0 design). Deliverable: site-specific remediation-liability estimates and regulatory approval pathways. Risk mitigation: third-party protocol carries higher professional-liability insurance and lender credibility.
  • If intrusive Phase II surveys on all four zones are unaffordable or infeasible within Phase 0 budget (Phase 0 cap EUR 750M): prioritize Phase II on the top 2–3 candidate sites per zone (estimated EUR 1.5M–3M per zone, total EUR 6M–12M) by Month 3 (2027-01-17). Use Phase I findings to shortlist only parcels with low historical contamination risk; defer full Phase II on non-priority parcels to Phase 1, conditioned on a seller/public indemnity capping remediation liability to EUR 50M–150M per site. This staged approach reduces Phase 0 spend and compresses timeline but increases Phase 1 remediation risk.
  • If regulatory closure letters or written approval from DREAL/DDT for Phase II findings are not available before Month 12 (2027-10-17) gate: structure Phase 1 FID with a conditional contingent liability cap. Define in debt and equity documents that remediation beyond EUR 100M–300M (per Phase 1 reserve) triggers a sponsor cure obligation or debt-covenant reset. Require sellers or public bodies to post indemnity letters or escrows equal to the gap between Phase 0 ESA estimates and lenders' maximum-liability tolerance. This preserves Phase 1 FID timing but shifts risk explicitly to sponsors.
  • If Phase I/II survey discovers extensive contamination (EUR 300M–500M+ remediation) that cannot be bounded or shifted to sellers: initiate public-sector remediation dialogue with regional or national remediation bodies (ADEME, CEREMA, or regional prefectural remediation programs). Propose that the project contribute to a co-funded brownfield-restoration program in exchange for liability cap and regulatory support. This converts a project liability into a regional reindustrialization narrative, though it extends dialogue timeline (6–12 months, estimated) and may impose operational constraints (scheduling, monitoring, deed notices).

Find Document 4: French ICPE (Installations Classées pour l'Environnement) and Environmental Authorization Permitting Timeline and EIA Scope

ID: ab1b6923-81c8-4e90-9ca6-58b33abca732

Description: Official DREAL guidance on ICPE classification for data centers (power consumption thresholds triggering 'Autorisation' vs. 'Déclaration' vs. 'Enregistrement'), environmental-authorization scoping (EIA mandatory scope per Article L.122-1 to L.122-3 Code de l'environnement), and published permitting timelines (18–30 months for Authorization route, +24–48 months for appeals). Includes case studies or examples of recent industrial permits (refinery, power plant expansions) to benchmark timeline realism. Needed to validate Phase 0 permitting schedule (file submission Month 8–9 = 2027-06-17 to 2027-07-17, decision Month 26–39 = 2028-12-17 to 2030-01-17 estimated). Intended audience for analysis: environmental-permitting counsel and Phase 0 program manager.

Recency Requirement: Current ICPE and EIA rules (updated 2022 under French environmental law reforms); typical permitting timelines from 2023–2025 cases.

Responsible Role Type: Environmental and Permitting Counsel

Steps to Find:

  • Access DREAL Hauts-de-France website (dreal.hauts-de-france.gouv.fr) for published ICPE guidance, EIA scoping templates, and recent permit decisions (anonymized).
  • Request a pre-filing scoping meeting with DREAL (standard practice, Month 1–2 = 2026-11-17 to 2026-12-17) to clarify EIA scope and likely permitting timeline.
  • Review published French court decisions (Conseil d'État) on environmental permit appeals to understand typical delay patterns and legal-challenge grounds.
  • Consult recent environmental-impact assessments for comparable industrial projects in the region (available in DREAL public databases).

Access Difficulty: Medium to Easy. DREAL is responsive to pre-filing inquiries (2–4 week turnaround); published case law and scoping templates are freely available online.

Essential Information:

  • Clarify the French ICPE classification threshold for data centers: at what power consumption (MW) does a 'Déclaration' escalate to 'Autorisation' versus 'Enregistrement'?
  • Confirm mandatory EIA scope triggers under Article L.122-1 to L.122-3 Code de l'environnement for a 500 MW–1 GW campus; identify whether the 161 km² envelope automatically triggers EIA or if it is parcel-dependent.
  • Publish 2–3 recent case studies (2023–2025) of comparable industrial permits (e.g. refinery expansion, power plant retrofit, or large manufacturing facility) filed in Hauts-de-France or northern France, with documented timelines from filing to final non-appealable decision.
  • Establish the standard permitting timeline for ICPE Authorization without appeals (baseline 18–30 months); quantify typical appeal duration and grounds (environmental, procedural, data-sovereignty) with frequency data.
  • Map the specific DREAL pre-filing scoping process: turnaround time for a scoping opinion (target Month 1–2 = 2026-11-17 to 2026-12-17), required application materials, and whether scoping opinion is binding or advisory.
  • Detail any accelerated or fast-track permitting paths available under recent French legislation (e.g., national-priority projects, renewable-energy or hydrogen expedited routes); confirm current legislative status (enacted, proposed, not verified).
  • Identify the scope and timeline of concurrent environmental-authorization and planning-permission processes; clarify whether they run in parallel or sequentially, and whether one can block the other.
  • Quantify the typical cost and team size (FTE) required to prepare and shepherd a permit application of this scale (data center, 500 MW–1 GW, multi-year) through DREAL and prefectural review.

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • Misclassification of the data center under ICPE (e.g., treating it as 'Déclaration' instead of 'Autorisation') could lead to permit invalidation post-FID, forcing resubmission, appeal vulnerability, and 12–24 month delay.
  • Incomplete EIA scope at filing triggers DREAL requests for supplementary information, extending review by 6–12 months and increasing legal-appeal grounds.
  • Absence of recent case-study timelines encourages unrealistic Phase 0 permitting schedule (targeting decision Month 18–24 = 2028-04-17 to 2028-10-17 vs. realistic Months 26–39 = 2028-12-17 to 2030-01-17), causing Phase 1 FID delay and eroding grid queue position.
  • Unconfirmed fast-track availability treated as baseline risks locking Phase 0 and Phase 1 timelines into infeasibility; permit delay becomes the critical path and triggers cascade overruns.
  • Lack of clarity on concurrent vs. sequential permitting processes leads to duplicate applications, missed approval deadlines, or approval of one stream without the other (e.g., planning granted but environmental authorization blocked).
  • Unknown permitting cost and team scale in Phase 0 budgeting (EUR 750M cap) could exhaust Phase 0 budget before land assembly or grid work is funded.
  • Unfamiliar DREAL pre-filing protocol risks non-standard scoping opinion or misalignment with authorities, delaying permit-file preparation and formal submission.

Worst Case Scenario: Permit application filed at Month 8 (2027-06-17) is rejected or requires major supplementary information at Month 18 (2028-04-17) due to incorrect ICPE classification or incomplete EIA scope. DREAL requests resubmission, extending review by 18–24 months; appeals filed by environmental groups add another 24–36 months. Permitting decision does not arrive until Month 60–72 (2031-10-17 to 2032-10-17). By then, RTE grid queue position is lost to competing projects, anchor tenants have signed leases elsewhere, and Phase 1 FID is abandoned. Campus is cancelled. Phase 0 sunk cost of EUR 250M–750M is stranded.

Best Case Scenario: Scoping opinion obtained Month 2 (2026-12-17) confirms data center is ICPE Autorisation, EIA mandatory, and DREAL targets 20-month decision window. Permit file filed Month 8 (2027-06-17) is complete on submission; DREAL completes review by Month 26 (2028-12-17). One municipal appeal is filed but rejected by Conseil d'État by Month 33 (2029-07-17). Final non-appealable authorization is issued Month 33 (2029-07-17), aligning with Phase 1 energization timeline (Months 42–48 = 2030-04-17 to 2030-10-17) and preserving RTE queue position. Phase 1 FID proceeds on schedule.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • Engage DREAL for a pre-filing scoping meeting in Month 1 (2026-11-17), requesting both a written scoping opinion and a published case study from recent comparable permits. If DREAL cannot provide or timeline is unclear, commission an independent environmental-law firm to benchmark permitting timelines against 3–5 recent industrial authorizations filed in the region.
  • Request DREAL's standard ICPE classification schedule and confirm data-center power thresholds in writing by Month 2 (2026-12-17); if the threshold is unclear, model two scenarios (Déclaration vs. Autorisation) with corresponding timelines and submit both at filing to preserve optionality.
  • If fast-track status is not confirmed by Month 3 (2027-01-17), remove it from the Phase 0 schedule immediately and adopt the standard 18–30 month baseline plus 24–48 month appeal exposure, pushing permitting decision to Month 39–60 (2030-01-17 to 2031-10-17) and triggering a Phase 1 FID delay contingency.
  • Commission a permit-strategy consultant (EUR 0.5M–2M) to prepare a detailed phase map showing all concurrent authorizations (ICPE, environmental, planning, water, ecology), decision points, appeal mechanisms and typical timelines by Month 2 (2026-12-17); use this to lock Phase 0 permit-preparation milestones.
  • If DREAL pre-filing dialogue indicates EIA scope uncertainty, submit a formal 'avis à titre préalable' (preliminary opinion request) on EIA requirements by Month 1 (2026-11-17) and obtain written confirmation by Month 4 (2027-02-17) before finalizing the permit file.
  • Establish a permit-risk gate at Month 12 (2027-10-17) Phase 0 review: if the permitting timeline is still unconfirmed or DREAL indicates blocking concerns, implement a six-month Phase 0 extension (Months 12–18 = 2027-10-17 to 2028-04-17) with a secondary permit-decision gate at Month 18 (2028-04-17) before Phase 1 FID is greenlit.

  • Identify the capacity-expansion targets and timeline for at least 2–3 major global hyperscalers (Microsoft, Google, Meta) announced for 2024–2025, with specific MW, location preferences (Ireland, Netherlands, Germany, France), and planned energization months.
  • List the power-consumption requirements and PUE efficiency claims stated by each hyperscaler for new data-center projects, to benchmark against the planned campus's PUE target of 1.15–1.25.
  • Document the committed or pipeline data-center projects in France and the EU announced by hyperscalers or sovereign-AI initiatives (e.g. Campus IA), including capacity in MW, location, timeline, and whether capacity is reserved or competitive.
  • Quantify the competitive landscape: how much data-center capacity (MW) is currently or planned to be built in Ireland, Netherlands, Germany, Northern France over Months 12–36 (2027-10-17 to 2029-10-17), to establish market saturation risk.
  • Extract the lease or SLA terms mentioned in announcements (power pricing, uptime SLAs, lease tenor, reservation or flexibility terms), to validate the campus's proposed take-or-pay lease structure (5–10 year tenor, 99.5%+ uptime).
  • Identify stated or implied power-price expectations from hyperscalers (EUR/MWh or equivalent) to validate the campus's assumed EUR 50–70/MWh nuclear-backed supply strategy.
  • List any public statements by hyperscalers, EDF, or EU authorities on willingness to commit to long-dated (10+ year) power-supply contracts at data-center scale, to de-risk the Phase 1 power-procurement gate.

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • If hyperscaler capacity-expansion plans are outdated or incomplete, the anchoring demand for the campus may be overestimated, forcing Phase 1 FID downsizing or cancellation when signed take-or-pay fails to reach the 30% gate threshold (proposed 300 MW on 1 GW).
  • Without current information on hyperscaler power-price expectations, the campus's EUR 50–70/MWh assumption may be uncompetitive or infeasible, eroding tenant lease viability and lender debt-service coverage below the proposed 1.30x minimum.
  • If the document omits Irish, Dutch or German capacity announcements, the competitive positioning analysis is incomplete, and the investment committee cannot assess the risk that global hyperscalers choose alternative sites over Hauts-de-France, eliminating Phase 1 FID demand.
  • If SLA uptime terms (99.5%, 99.95%, etc.) and curtailment tolerance stated by hyperscalers are not captured, the campus may offer incompatible terms (e.g., 10% annual curtailment when hyperscalers demand <5%), forcing lease renegotiation or tenant rejection post-FID.
  • Absence of current EDF or EU sovereign-AI power-supply commitments leaves the nuclear-backed contract assumption entirely unvalidated, risking a Phase 1 power-procurement gate failure or cost escalation of +EUR 30–60/MWh (estimate), eroding project returns by 2–4 percentage points.

Worst Case Scenario: If this document is incomplete or outdated, Phase 1 anchor-tenant commitments may fall short of the 30% (300 MW) gate threshold because the investment committee lacks current competitive and demand intelligence. The campus loses anchor credibility with lenders, debt financing (proposed EUR 3B for 500 MW) is refused or repriced at +300–400 bps, and Phase 1 FID is blocked or delayed 12–24 months. Alternatively, if hyperscaler power-price expectations exceed the campus's EUR 70/MWh assumption, tenants refuse lease signature, forcing the developer to absorb the cost differential (EUR 30–60/MWh delta = EUR 112–224M annually on 500 MW), eroding equity returns to below hurdle and forcing equity withdrawal. The full 9 GW buildout (Months 0–180 = 2026-10-17 to 2041-10-17+) is abandoned, leaving Phase 0 sunk cost of EUR 250M–750M unrecovered and regional infrastructure unbuilt.

Best Case Scenario: Current, comprehensive data on hyperscaler capacity and power-price expectations confirms that 2+ major anchors (e.g., Microsoft and Google) are expanding European data-center footprints and are actively seeking 200–500 MW partnerships in France or Hauts-de-France specifically. Signed or binding LOIs naming the campus are obtained by Month 9 (2027-07-17), validating market demand and accelerating anchor-tenant term-sheet closure to >30% (300 MW) by the Phase 0 gate. Lender confidence and debt pricing improve (margin benchmark +150–200 bps vs. +250–300 bps), reducing all-in cost of capital and improving Phase 1 project returns by 0.5–1.5 percentage points. Power-price competitiveness is confirmed at EUR 50–70/MWh, validating lease pricing and tenant acquisition, and enabling Phase 2 FID and 9 GW expansion with high confidence.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • If published announcements are unavailable or outdated, commission direct market-research interviews with 3–5 hyperscaler (Microsoft, Google, Meta, Amazon) real-estate and capacity-planning executives during Month 1–3 (2026-11-17 to 2027-01-17) to obtain current expansion priorities, power-price thresholds, and France/Hauts-de-France appetite. Offer anonymized survey participation or NDA-protected discussions.
  • Engage an independent data-center industry analyst firm (Gartner, IDC, TeleGeography, or Cushman & Wakefield) in Month 1 (2026-11-17) to conduct a competitive-positioning study: capacity pipeline in Ireland/Netherlands/Germany/France, pricing trends, and anchor-tenant demand drivers over Months 12–60 (2027-10-17 to 2031-10-17).
  • Conduct a reverse-engineering demand model: estimate global AI training workload growth (from public sources: Hugging Face, OpenAI, academic papers on compute demand) and allocate capacity to European hubs to infer hyperscaler and sovereign demand for the campus's timeframe (Months 12–36 = 2027-10-17 to 2029-10-17).
  • If real-time announcements prove unavailable, fall back to the conservative anchor-demand gate: require signed binding term sheets (not LOIs) from at least 2 creditworthy counterparties by Month 9 (2027-07-17) covering ≥30% of Phase 1 size, validated by the investment committee and lender due diligence; if unavailable, reduce Phase 1 to 250 MW (matching the committed demand) and defer Phase 2.

Strengths

  • Hauts-de-France offers brownfield and industrial land (Cambrai/E-Valley, Dunkirk, Denain/Escaudain), rail, canal and port access, and a reindustrialization narrative that is stronger than a greenfield story.
  • Low-carbon French grid and nearby nuclear generation (Gravelines) support a credible clean-power story, though supply terms are uncontrolled until signed.
  • The plan is gate-driven and skeptical: Phase 0 is capped at EUR 750M (user constraint) in four tranches (150/250/200/150 EUR M), with no committed capital before Month 12 (2027-10-17).
  • Kill criteria are numeric (proposed thresholds): RTE letter for at least 500 MW, at least 70% of the parcel optioned, binding tenant term sheets for at least 30% of Phase 1.
  • An independent investment committee and red team are designed in, with override only by two-thirds supermajority and published dissent.
  • The 500 MW Cambrai base case, with an option to reach 1 GW, and a split-campus default at Month 4 (2027-02-17) keep the plan flexible and let downsizing count as a legitimate result.
  • A zero-evaporative-water design basis and a 35°C design-day test simplify the water and permitting story.
  • USD hardware (EUR 1.5B–2.3B) is ring-fenced with tenants or a lessor, so the campus company holds no unhedged USD.
  • Cooler climate and low latency to Paris, London, Brussels, Amsterdam and Frankfurt suit batch inference and sovereign workloads.

Weaknesses

  • The headline scale (9 GW, 161 km²) has no precedent, and its EUR 100B–140B+ cost is unvalidated and credible only per tranche (estimate).
  • Contiguous assembly of 161 km² is doubtful. Farmland displacement of 10,000–15,000+ ha (estimate) would be contentious, and the sponsor has no land control yet.
  • No signed anchor tenants exist, and demand evidence so far is only announcements, which are not commitments.
  • Operations headcount is small (50–150 FTE, not verified), so a jobs-based social-license story is weak.
  • Stabilized 500 MW economics are thin: DSCR 1.34x against a 1.30x lender minimum (estimate). A 10% curtailment discount cuts it to 1.15x, and without energy pass-through it falls to 0.96x.
  • Stacked contingent add-ons of EUR 1.55B–4.2B on the 500 MW base are unfunded and overlap. Other cost lines could push the total to EUR 10.35B, above the EUR 10B ceiling.
  • Gate dates assume authority answers (RTE, ANSSI, DREAL) that the sponsor cannot control. A firm RTE offer by Month 12 (2027-10-17) is unlikely.
  • The Month 4 (2027-02-17) topology decision falls before the RTE written letter (Month 6 = 2027-04-17), so split campus becomes the default by timing rather than evidence.
  • Split-from-the-start would breach the Phase 0 cap by up to EUR 250M and slip the gate.
  • It is an open decision whether the user's EUR 5B–10B includes USD hardware.

Opportunities

  • Staged 500 MW tranches with BESS and curtailment at most 10% (proposed) can earn later RTE tranches and avoid looking speculative.
  • Learning from the Dunkirk grid-queue programme and the Irish CRU flexibility policy can shape realistic connection terms.
  • Split-campus nodes (Cambrai 500 MW, Dunkirk 250 MW, Valenciennes/Denain 250 MW) allow independent permits, grid offers and legal isolation.
  • Redeployable substations and open fiber leave regional value if the campus is downsized.
  • Sovereign AI zones with segregated halls could anchor demand if ANSSI sets clear expectations.
  • Reservation fees (EUR 10M–50M per 100 MW, proposed) test demand early and fund pre-construction work.
  • Lease-and-continue farming, brownfield restoration and a regional training academy can win municipal support.
  • Heat reuse is unpriced upside (EUR 0 until a binding offtake exists).
  • Co-investing with regional industry and fiber carriers could share reinforcement cost and lift regional connectivity.
  • A 2–5 MW pilot hall can validate PUE and cooling before scaling.

Threats

  • RTE hosting capacity above ~1 GW is the primary kill test. Competing steel, hydrogen and refinery loads may saturate the Nord 400 kV network, and reinforcement co-funding could cost EUR 500M–1.5B (estimate).
  • Multi-GW nuclear-backed supply at EUR 50–70/MWh is not verified. A +EUR 30/MWh shock adds about EUR 112M per year at 500 MW and about EUR 2.0B per year at 9 GW.
  • Standard permitting takes 18–30 months plus 24–48 months for appeals (estimates). Fast-track is not assumed, and delay erodes queue position and adds EUR 200M–500M carrying cost.
  • ANSSI/DGSI and foreign-investment review may restrict tenants or foreign equity, and its timeline is uncontrolled.
  • Farm unions, NGOs and mayors can delay permits by 12–36 months (estimate).
  • Tenants may use LOIs to compare 10+ European sites without committing, and AI demand or hyperscaler capex may soften.
  • Late-found contamination (EUR 100M–400M) and shared fiber ducts or landings are hidden single points of failure.
  • Hot-weather dry-cooling PUE of 1.35–1.5 raises peak grid load by 5–15%, and drought rules could restrict water.
  • US export-control changes and EUR/USD moves (EUR 150M–230M per 10%) could disrupt tenant hardware.
  • Financing could be refused or priced higher if grid, tenant or liability evidence is weak.
  • Sunk cost (up to EUR 750M) pressures sponsors to override gates.

Recommendations

  • Month 1 (2026-11-17) (owner: sponsor board and consortium): sign the investment committee charter with at least 2 external directors, a two-thirds override rule and published dissent. Commission the red team (EUR 2M–5M). Fix numeric kill thresholds in writing by Month 2 (2026-12-17).
  • Months 0–1 (2026-10-17 to 2026-11-17) (owner: grid lead): file written pre-engineering requests with RTE and DREAL for 500 MW, 1 GW and 2 GW tranches, and commission an independent hosting-capacity audit. Target the RTE preliminary letter by Month 6 (2027-04-17) and treat it as uncontrolled until received.
  • Months 1–3 (2026-11-17 to 2027-01-17) (owner: land lead): run parcel and holdout surveys in all four zones. At Month 3 (2027-01-17), test whether at least 70% can be optioned at no more than 15% above benchmark. At Month 4 (2027-02-17), default to split campus unless RTE written evidence for 1 GW is in hand.
  • Months 1–9 (2026-11-17 to 2027-07-17) (owner: commercial lead): issue standard take-or-pay and reservation-fee term sheets by Month 2 (2026-12-17). Target binding sheets for at least 150 MW of a 500 MW tranche by Month 9 (2027-07-17). Count only binding sheets, and test the offer with a reservation-fee presale.
  • Months 1–6 (2026-11-17 to 2027-04-17) (owner: environment lead): commission Phase I and II brownfield surveys, a hydrology and 35°C thermal study, and a fiber audit. Obtain the written water opinion by Month 6 (2027-04-17) and shortlist parcels with remediation bounded to EUR 0–100M.
  • Months 0–6 (2026-10-17 to 2027-04-17) (owner: security and legal lead): hold confidential ANSSI/DGSI pre-submission dialogue and seek an informal opinion by Month 6 (2027-04-17).
  • Months 1–5 (2026-11-17 to 2027-03-17) (owner: community lead): set up a liaison committee with published minutes and draft the community-benefit agreement by Month 5 (2027-03-17), aiming for signatures from 2 of 3 municipalities by Month 9 (2027-07-17).
  • Month 1 (2026-11-17) (owner: finance lead): resolve whether USD hardware sits inside the EUR 5B–10B. Fund the stacked add-on exposure explicitly, or reduce Phase 1 scope to 250 MW if it cannot be funded.

Strategic Objectives

  • By Month 2 (2026-12-17), charter the independent investment committee and red team and lock numeric kill thresholds in writing, with Phase 0 spend held within the EUR 750M cap and its four tranches.
  • By Month 4 (2027-02-17), publish the topology decision (single square or split campus) based on at least 70% optioned parcel evidence and per-node grid timelines. Obtain the RTE written 500 MW preliminary letter by Month 6 (2027-04-17) (uncontrolled).
  • By Month 9 (2027-07-17), obtain binding tenant term sheets covering at least 30% of Phase 1 size (150 MW of 500 MW), with investment-grade or guaranteed counterparties, and executed agreements with reservation fees by Month 12 (2027-10-17).
  • By Month 12 (2027-10-17), hold the gate review with a firm debt commitment of at least EUR 3B (12-year tenor or longer), written support from 2 of 3 municipalities, and bounded brownfield liability. Pass, conditionally pass, downsize, split or cancel on evidence.
  • By Month 9 (2027-07-17), confirm in writing at least 2 audited diverse fiber routes per core hub, and by Month 6 (2027-04-17) a water-authority opinion and a modelled PUE of at most 1.30 on a 35°C design day.

Assumptions

  • The sponsor is a private developer backed by an infrastructure-fund consortium. Phase 0 spend is exploratory, with no committed capital before the Month 12 (2027-10-17) gate.
  • The 161 km² square is a notional envelope, and split campus is the default at Month 4 (2027-02-17) unless RTE written evidence exists.
  • Phase 1 base case is 500 MW at Cambrai/E-Valley; 1 GW only against signed demand and a grid offer.
  • All RTE, EDF, ANSSI/DGSI, prefecture and tenant outcomes are uncontrolled until backed by a contract, permit, formal decision or signed term sheet.
  • Financing: 60% debt and 40% equity at 5.5% over 15 years (estimates). Lease price is EUR 1.1M per MW-year, excluding energy (estimate).
  • Energy is EUR 60/MWh (range 50–70, not verified) and passed through to tenants.
  • Fast-track permitting is not assumed.
  • USD hardware is financed by tenants or a lessor, and EUR/USD planning is 1.08–1.12 (not verified).

Missing Information

  • Actual RTE hosting capacity, queue position and competing load requests at Cambrai, Dunkirk and Valenciennes substations.
  • Delivered power cost, including network tariffs and taxes, and whether EDF will contract multi-GW volumes to a private developer.
  • Which tenants exist, their cluster-size and latency needs, and what early evidence would reveal a compelling reason to choose this site (for example which prospects pay reservation fees or return for site tours, and what they ask for first).
  • Parcel ownership maps, holdout counts and benchmark land values in each zone.
  • Phase II contamination results and the creditworthiness of sellers and public bodies offering indemnities.
  • ANSSI/DGSI expectations and foreign-investment screening limits for sovereign-adjacent co-investors.
  • Local water-authority position on dry cooling and drought rules.
  • Whether the EUR 5B–10B includes USD hardware, and how the EUR 1.55B–4.2B contingent add-ons are funded.
  • Fiber duct-level route data, and lender and co-investor appetite and terms.
  • Status of French AI campus precedents (Fluidstack, State site list), not verified.

Questions

  • If RTE offers only 250–500 MW per node, would the project still be worth building, and who decides that?
  • What evidence would persuade the investment committee to cancel after EUR 400M–750M of spend, and is that threshold already agreed in writing?
  • Which tenant would pay a reservation fee today, and what specific advantage of this site (power, latency, sovereignty, price) drives that choice?
  • Can the thin 500 MW economics (DSCR 1.34x against a 1.30x minimum) survive curtailment discounts, energy price shocks and the unfunded add-ons?
  • Which municipalities, farm groups and competing industrial users can block the project, and what would each need to see before supporting it?

Roles Needed & Example People

Roles

1. Grid Connection and Power Infrastructure Strategist

Contract Type: full_time_employee

Contract Type Justification: Grid Connection and Power Infrastructure Strategist owns the primary kill-test gate (RTE hosting capacity ≥500 MW by Month 6 = 2027-04-17) and leads continuous dialogue with RTE and EDF through Phase 0 and Phase 1. This role requires sustained, strategic presence over 24+ months, deep institutional knowledge of multi-tranche grid negotiation, and real-time responsiveness to RTE's phased connection offers. Cannot be outsourced or part-time; full accountability for power-procurement strategy and grid-hosting decisions across the critical path.

Explanation: Leads dialogue with RTE and EDF on hosting capacity, transmission reinforcement, nuclear-backed supply contracts, and curtailment terms. Owns the primary kill-test gate (≥500 MW connection offer by Month 6 = 2027-04-17). Manages pre-engineering studies, multi-tranche phasing strategy, and BESS/demand-flexibility architecture. Directly unblocks or kills the project depending on RTE's written feasibility letter.

Consequences: RTE engagement defaults to administrative communication rather than strategic dialogue. Multi-GW connection offers are not secured; grid hosting capacity above 1 GW remains unconfirmed, triggering the primary kill gate. At-risk Phase 0 pre-engineering spend EUR 50M–150M is wasted without credible path to commitment. Power procurement risk (EUR 50–70/MWh vs. EUR 80–100/MWh) is not hedged, eroding 2–4 percentage points of project IRR.

People Count: 1 lead (VP or Director level) + 2–3 specialists (grid engineer with RTE experience, power-market analyst, BESS/flexibility engineer), depending on project scale and complexity of multi-tranche negotiations. Total: min 1, max 4, depending on RTE engagement intensity and number of parallel tranches being negotiated.

Typical Activities: Monthly RTE technical meetings with hosted-capacity audit teams; drafting connection request tranches (500 MW, 1 GW, 2 GW) with flexibility and curtailment terms; co-authoring grid reinforcement cost-sharing proposals; tracking grid queue position and competing industrial load requests; negotiating BESS and demand-response commitments; validating thermal modelling of substation capacity under peak summer and winter scenarios; reviewing EDF baseload-contract term sheets; escalating grid-capacity gate outcomes to the investment committee; managing relationships with RTE regional customer-connection offices across Nord and Pas-de-Calais.

Background Story: Dr. Henri Leclerc, 52, based in Brussels. Spent 15 years at RTE as a grid-development engineer, focusing on 400 kV substations and industrial load integration across northern France. Left RTE in 2019 to lead power-infrastructure strategy for a pan-European energy trader, negotiating multi-GW renewable PPAs and grid-connection agreements. Fluent in French grid law, RTE queue dynamics, and nuclear-backed baseload contracting. Recruited for this project to replicate his RTE insider knowledge and multi-tranche phasing expertise. Known for translating technical grid constraints into commercial negotiation leverage.

Equipment Needs: Grid analysis and power modelling software (PSSE, DIgSILENT PowerFactory or equivalent RTE-compatible tools); high-security VPN access to RTE and EDF networks for connection-request tracking and multi-tranche pre-engineering dialogue; thermal modelling and BESS simulation tools (HOMER, EnergyPlan); video-conferencing and secure telephony for confidential RTE and EDF negotiations; project-management and gate-tracking systems (Smartsheet, MS Project); desktop workstations with dual monitors; secure document storage and version control.

Facility Needs: Regional office at Cambrai or Dunkirk with secure meeting room for RTE and EDF technical discussions (not public-facing); high-bandwidth internet (100+ Mbps) for grid-data uploads and real-time modelling collaboration; proximity to RTE regional customer-connection office (Nord) for monthly pre-engineering meetings; access to secure meeting facilities in Brussels (RTE EU coordination) and Paris (EDF HQ) for quarterly strategic dialogues; temporary mobile office for site surveys and grid-node field assessments.

2. Land Assembly and Real Estate Strategist

Contract Type: full_time_employee

Contract Type Justification: Land Assembly and Real Estate Strategist manages the topology decision (Month 4 = 2027-02-17), land optionability surveys (≥70% threshold check Month 3 = 2027-01-17), and multi-zone parcel negotiations across Cambrai, Dunkirk, Valenciennes and Saint-Omer. Owns the land-assembly gate, which is a primary kill condition. Requires continuous presence for negotiations, phase II survey oversight, and liability-allocation agreements with sellers and municipalities. Full accountability for a feasible contiguous or split-campus footprint; cannot be delegated part-time.

Explanation: Assembles target parcels through option agreements, lease structures, and liability allocation. Conducts fragmentation analysis and parcel-level optionability surveys (70% threshold by Month 3 = 2027-01-17). Structures lease-and-continue farming arrangements, negotiates seller indemnities for brownfield contamination, and coordinates Phase I/II environmental site assessments. Owns the land-assembly gate and the topology (single-square vs. split-campus) decision at Month 4 (2027-02-17).

Consequences: Land assembly defaults to reactive option-buying or compulsory acquisition with minimal negotiation. Contiguous assembly of 161 km² remains infeasible; the project is forced to split or downsize. Holdouts and political opposition emerge unchecked, extending permitting by 12–36 months. Brownfield liability is not bounded; remediation cost escalates from EUR 0–100M (forecast) to EUR 200M–500M (actual), eroding Phase 1 capex cushion.

People Count: 1 lead (Director of Land Acquisition) + 1–2 real estate advisers + 1–2 legal counsel (French real estate and contamination specialists), depending on parcel fragmentation, holdout complexity, and number of candidate zones. Total: min 1, max 5, depending on whether assembly is 1 zone (simple) or 4 zones with many small parcels (complex).

Typical Activities: Weekly parcel-level fragmentation surveys across Cambrai, Dunkirk, Valenciennes and Saint-Omer zones (mapping owner types, known activists, land-value benchmarks); negotiating non-coercive option agreements with 20+ landowner and farmer groups; structuring lease-and-continue farming arrangements with revenue-sharing pools; preparing Phase I/II environmental site assessments and coordinating with sellers on indemnity escrow agreements; tracking option-renewal cycles and holding-cost accrual; drafting topology recommendations (single square vs. split campus) with per-node parcel cost and assemblability estimates; presenting land-assembly gate evidence to the investment committee; liaison with municipalities on public-land availability and process timelines.

Background Story: Martine Rousseau, 48, formerly Head of Land Acquisition for a French construction and real-estate developer specializing in brownfield industrial conversion in northern France. Assembled 2,400+ hectares for automotive and logistics parks over 12 years, navigating French agricultural law, compulsory-acquisition procedures, and fragmented smallholder negotiations in rural Hauts-de-France. Left development to lead a boutique real-estate advisory firm focusing on large-scale industrial-land assembly for energy and data-centre projects. Expert in French farmland valuation benchmarks, farmer-union negotiation tactics, and remediation-liability allocation with sellers and municipalities. Bilingual French-English; advises on topology trade-offs between parcel contiguity and holding-cost exposure.

Equipment Needs: Geographic information systems (GIS) software (ArcGIS or QGIS) for parcel-level land mapping, ownership chain tracking and holdout-risk analysis; land valuation and benchmark tools (comparable sales databases, municipal property records); Phase I/II environmental site assessment (ESA) software and databases (Phase I Pro, EnviroMapper); legal contract management system (Dealroom or equivalent) for tracking option agreements and liability indemnities; spreadsheet and database tools for parcel inventory tracking (1,000+ parcels across 4 zones); desktop workstations with multiple large displays for map work.

Facility Needs: Regional offices in both Cambrai and Dunkirk with local land-registry access (e.g., via DDT/DDTM connections) and secure space for confidential negotiations with landowners and farmers; high-speed internet for GIS and document uploads; meeting rooms suitable for farmer and agricultural-union discussions (neutral, non-corporate); proximity to municipal town halls and land-registry offices (Chambéry des Notaires) for deed and ownership verification; secure document storage for option agreements and Phase II survey results; temporary field office near candidate sites for parcel surveys and soil-boring coordination.

3. Environmental and Permitting Counsel

Contract Type: full_time_employee

Contract Type Justification: Environmental and Permitting Counsel manages ICPE, environmental authorization, water, biodiversity, and EIA permits across all nodes. Owns the critical path to permit filing (Months 8–9 = 2027-06-17 to 2027-07-17) and the DREAL screening opinion gate (Month 9 = 2027-07-17). Requires continuous coordination with DREAL, prefecture, and water authorities; drafting of ecological master plan by Month 6 (2027-04-17); and legal authority over permitting strategy. Part-time or contract counsel would create response delays in a permitting process where regulatory feedback shapes design. Full-time ensures embedded accountability for permit timelines and risk mitigation.

Explanation: Manages ICPE, environmental authorization, water, biodiversity and EIA permitting across 1–3 nodes. Coordinates with DREAL, prefecture and Agence de l'Eau on regulatory pathway. Develops ecological master plan and compensation strategy, delivers DREAL screening opinion by Month 9 (2027-07-17). Coordinates Phase 0 environmental baseline (hydrology, ecology, soil) and validates dry-cooling and water-abstraction feasibility. Owns permit-filing timeline (Months 8–9 = 2027-06-17 to 2027-07-17) and tracks appeal risk.

Consequences: Permitting file is submitted late or incomplete, missing Month 8–9 (2027-06-17 to 2027-07-17) target. Authorization timeline slips from 18–30 months to 36–48 months, delaying energization by 12–24 months and eroding grid queue position. Water-authority sign-off on dry cooling is not obtained; cooling strategy defaults to hybrid with evaporative risk, conflicting with the zero-water project constraint. Ecological compensation is not pre-committed, triggering legal challenge during Phase 1 based on unmitigated impact.

People Count: 1 lead (Director of Permitting) + 1–2 environmental engineers (hydrology, ecology) + 1–2 legal counsel (French environmental and ICPE specialists), depending on project complexity (single node simpler, 3-node split requires per-node filings). Total: min 1, max 5.

Typical Activities: Confidential pre-submission meetings with DREAL (Nord and Pas-de-Calais prefectures) and Agence de l'Eau Artois-Picardie on regulatory pathway and anticipated blocking concerns; commissioning Phase I desktop environmental assessments and Phase II intrusive soil/groundwater surveys; drafting the environmental baseline and ecological master plan (due Month 6 = 2027-04-17); coordinating hydrological and thermal-modelling studies on dry-cooler feasibility and water-authority sign-off; preparing ICPE and environmental-authorization permit files (one per node or single, depending on topology); engaging with conservation NGOs and local environmental groups on ecological compensation strategy; tracking appeal risk and legal-challenge timelines; liaising with municipalities on stormwater, biodiversity and land-use conditions.

Background Story: Dr. Fabienne Arnaud, 55, environmental lawyer and EIA specialist with 20 years' experience in French ICPE (Installations Classées pour l'Environnement) permitting and industrial land-use authorization. Formerly lead counsel for a multi-GW renewable-energy and grid-infrastructure developer, securing ICPE, environmental and water permits for 15+ projects across France. Expert in pre-filing engagement with DREAL, prefecture and regional water agencies; navigation of Natura 2000 and ecological-compensation requirements; and mitigation of appeals-based legal risk. Advises water authorities and conservation bodies as an expert witness. Deep knowledge of fast-track major-project designation rules (being legislated) and likelihood of qualification for this campus.

Equipment Needs: Environmental impact assessment (EIA) and ICPE permitting software (Covadis, EIA databases); hydrological and water-quality modelling tools (HEC-HMS, FEFLOW or equivalent for groundwater); ecological survey data management (BSBI, GBIF databases, Natura 2000 mapping tools); GIS for baseline mapping (habitat, water, contamination zones); thermal performance modelling tools for dry-cooler design (TRNSYS, EnergyPlus); phase I/II ESA document management; legal permitting-timeline and regulatory-tracking systems; video-conferencing for DREAL and water-authority engagement.

Facility Needs: Regional office near DREAL office (Nord prefecture, Lille) for pre-submission meetings and ongoing regulatory dialogue; proximity to Agence de l'Eau Artois-Picardie (Douai) for water-authority sign-off process; meeting rooms for confidential negotiations with environmental agencies and NGO stakeholders; secure storage for phase II survey data (soil cores, groundwater samples handled via external labs); access to regional ecological data repositories (e.g., natural-history museums, university departments); temporary site offices near candidate parcels for baseline survey work and thermal-modelling field validation (microclimatic data collection); high-bandwidth internet for large GIS files and remote collaboration with EIA specialists.

Contract Type: full_time_employee

This role demands continuous tenant relationship management, rapid iteration on commercial terms, and accountability for the debt-financing gate (which requires proof of demand). Cannot be outsourced; tenants expect direct engagement with a committed leader. The distinction between non-binding LOI and binding take-or-pay is operationally critical and requires full-time ownership.

Explanation: Develops take-or-pay lease templates, launches conversations with 4–6 anchor prospects (hyperscalers and sovereign-AI users), distinguishes non-binding LOIs from binding term sheets, and closes at least 300 MW (30% of Phase 1) in signed commitments by Month 9 (2027-07-17).
