  • Hyperscalers read the limits as lost control and compare other sites.
  • Sovereign buyers wait for clearance before signing.
  • Press reports of a militarised site harden local opposition, and clearance slips past Month 31 (2029-05-17).
Early Warning Signs
  • ANSSI meeting not granted by Month 1 (2026-11-17)
  • Request for state observer or equity cap
  • Prospects make signing conditional on clearance
  • Local media raise foreign-control questions
Tripwires
  • No ANSSI informal opinion by Month 6 (2027-04-17)
  • Foreign equity cap below the planned co-investor share
  • Review timeline signalled > 18 months
  • Fewer than 2 prospects willing to sign before clearance by Month 9 (2027-07-17)
Response Playbook
  • Contain: Pause new foreign co-investor commitments and tenant disclosures beyond the white paper.
  • Assess: Map each restriction to its effect on tenant mix, equity structure, security capex and schedule.
  • Respond: Restructure to non-controlling EU-domiciled co-investors and sovereign-led halls, or shrink the tenant pool and resize Phase 1.

STOP RULE: Pause Phase 1 if ANSSI signals a blocking concern, or no written confirmation of formal review start exists at Month 12 (2027-10-17).

FM7 - The Debt That Never Closed

  • Archetype: Process/Financial
  • Root Cause: Assumption A7
  • Owner: Infrastructure Finance and Capital Structure Lead
  • Risk Level: CRITICAL 20/25 (Likelihood 4/5 × Impact 5/5)
Failure Story
  • Lenders see a conditional RTE position and only 150 MW signed.
  • Debt is drawn pro-rata to contracted MW, so uncontracted capacity becomes equity.
  • A 10% lease discount gives DSCR 1.15x against a 1.30x minimum (proposed).
  • Leverage falls toward 53%, or spreads widen.
  • The sponsor faces an equity gap; FID slips 12-24 months, with EUR 750M Phase 0 stranded.
Early Warning Signs
  • Lenders request more than 50% signed before credit committee
  • No written lender conditions by Month 6 (2027-04-17)
  • Equity partners hesitate to cover the uncontracted share
  • Quoted margins above benchmark +200 bps
Tripwires
  • Fewer than 2 lenders with written terms by Month 6 (2027-04-17)
  • Quoted margin >= benchmark +300 bps
  • Offered leverage <= 53%
  • Firm commitment < EUR 3B at Month 11 (2027-09-17)
Response Playbook
  • Contain: Freeze lender fee commitments and any Phase 1 procurement tied to debt closing.
  • Assess: Rerun DSCR at 10% discount, EUR 30/MWh shock and lower leverage, and size the equity gap.
  • Respond: Resize Phase 1 to the debt the signed MW supports (250 MW), or seek an equity cure from co-investors, or defer FID.

STOP RULE: No Phase 1 FID if firm debt of at least EUR 3B (or pro-rata for a downsized tranche) is not committed at Month 12 (2027-10-17).

FM8 - The Empty Crane Yard

  • Archetype: Technical/Logistical
  • Root Cause: Assumption A8
  • Owner: Phase 0 Program Manager and Red Team Lead
  • Risk Level: HIGH 12/25 (Likelihood 3/5 × Impact 4/5)
Failure Story
  • Competing regional projects absorb electricians and cooling trades.
  • Wage inflation exceeds 40% (estimate) and EPC firms decline fixed prices.
  • Modular supply slots for coolers, transformers and BESS slip.
  • Hall delivery misses Months 12-36 (2027-10-17 to 2029-10-17).
  • Carrying cost of EUR 300M-600M accrues and tenants test other sites.
Early Warning Signs
  • EPC bids come back with price escalation clauses
  • Technical colleges cannot commit graduates
  • Long-lead items quoted beyond 18 months
  • Fewer than 2 qualified EPC bidders
Tripwires
  • Wage inflation in EPC bids > 40% (estimate)
  • Fewer than 2 EPC bidders at Month 4 (2027-02-17)
  • Transformer or cooler lead time >= 24 months
  • Training academy enrolment < 50 per year by Month 9 (2027-07-17)
Response Playbook
  • Contain: Hold long-lead orders and hall starts until EPC capacity is confirmed in writing.
  • Assess: Rebaseline the schedule and cost using bid data, and identify trades that can be prefabricated or imported.
  • Respond: Phase hall delivery, widen EPC and supplier pool, or cut Phase 1 to fewer halls and renegotiate tenant dates.

STOP RULE: Reduce Phase 1 to 250 MW if no EPC commits to a fixed-price, dated delivery for 500 MW by Month 12 (2027-10-17).

FM9 - The Jobs Promise Backlash

  • Archetype: Market/Human
  • Root Cause: Assumption A9
  • Owner: Community Engagement and Social License Manager
  • Risk Level: CRITICAL 16/25 (Likelihood 4/5 × Impact 4/5)
Failure Story
  • The disclosed 50-150 FTE (not verified) contrasts with a multi-billion project.
  • Mayors and unions call the benefit package token, and the offer reads as window-dressing.
  • Farm unions reject lease-and-continue and file appeals.
  • Municipal letters stall below 2 of 3.
  • Permits slip 12-36 months (estimate) and the social-license gate fails.
Early Warning Signs
  • Liaison meetings show falling attendance
  • Mayors defer signing the benefit agreement
  • Unions publish opposition statements
  • Media coverage focuses on farmland loss
Tripwires
  • Fewer than 2 of 3 municipalities supportive in writing at Month 6 (2027-04-17)
  • Survey shows >= 50% of farmers opposed
  • Legal challenge announced before Month 9 (2027-07-17)
  • No signed benefit agreement at Month 9 (2027-07-17)
Response Playbook
  • Contain: Stop jobs and revenue claims, and publish only validated headcount and benefit terms.
  • Assess: Map each municipality and union objection to a specific term and cost the fixes.
  • Respond: Rework the package toward farmland, ecology and regional supply terms, or shift to nodes with supportive municipalities.

STOP RULE: Pause Phase 1 if fewer than 2 of the 3 most affected municipalities have given written support, or a major legal challenge is pending, at Month 12 (2027-10-17).

Reality check: fix before go.

Summary

Level Count Explanation
🛑 High 10 Existential blocker without credible mitigation.
⚠️ Medium 9 Material risk with plausible path.
✅ Low 1 Minor/controlled risk.

Checklist

1. Violates Known Physics

Does the plan's success require breaking a known law of physics (e.g., thermodynamics, conservation of energy, speed-of-light limit, causality)?

Level: ✅ Low

Justification: This is a staged infrastructure feasibility and development plan for a hyperscale data center campus using closed-loop liquid cooling, grid-connected power, and conventional permitting. All stated mechanisms—liquid cooling, PUE targets of 1.15–1.25, immersion cooling pilots, heat recovery, and grid hosting—are within established physics (thermodynamics, materials science, power systems). The plan's dependencies (tenant demand, RTE grid offers, permitting, financing, community support) are empirical and institutional, not claimed to be produced by non-physical causation; they are treated as uncontrolled milestones with explicit kill criteria and skeptical gates rather than assumed outcomes.

Mitigation: No physics-related action required — the plan does not invoke physics-incompatible mechanisms. Project governance should focus on empirical validation of grid capacity, financing credibility, tenant anchoring, and permitting realism per the stated gates.

2. No Real-World Proof

Does success depend on a technology or system that has not been proven in real projects at this scale or in this domain?

Level: ⚠️ Medium

Justification: Rated MEDIUM because the plan hinges on a novel system combination (multi-phase, 9 GW campus, grid-hosted, financed by mixed equity/debt with staged capital gates, sovereign-aligned tenants, permitting-dependent land assembly) without independent evidence at comparable scale. No single-site 9 GW campus exists globally; the grid, land, power, tenant and permitting dependencies are all uncontrolled until RTE signs, DREAL permits, ANSSI clears and tenants commit. However, the core components (liquid cooling, grid hosting, power procurement, permitting, financing) individually have precedent in lower-scale projects or comparable sectors. The plan explicitly treats this as a staged feasibility test with kill criteria (grid ≥~1 GW, land ≥70%, anchors ≥30%, ANSSI clearance). Phase 0 gates and contingency downsizing (250 MW, split campus) demonstrate skepticism. Medium (not High) because failure modes do not claim physics impossibility; they are institutional and empirical gates that can be validated within the Phase 0 budget and schedule via RTE letter, land surveys, tenant term sheets, and lender commitment—no prototype or pilot is required for system validation to occur, only evidence collection."

Mitigation: Project Sponsor and Investment Committee: By Month 12 (2027-10-17), execute parallel validation tracks (grid/power, land/environment, anchor-tenant demand, legal/compliance) with one authoritative source per track confirming empirical or engineering validity (RTE letter, Phase II surveys and land option, binding term sheets with cash in escrow, written municipal support and lender debt commitment). Lock two global NO-GO gates in writing at Month 2 (2026-12-17): (1) empirical/engineering validity (grid, land, PUE, water, anchors) and (2) legal/compliance clearance (ANSSI, permits, municipalities, debt). If either gate fails by Month 12 (2027-10-17), execute pre-agreed contingency (downsize to 250 MW, split campus, or defer FID 6-12 months) rather than override thresholds.

3. Buzzwords

Does the plan use excessive buzzwords without evidence of knowledge?

Level: ⚠️ Medium

Justification: Rated MEDIUM because core strategic decisions (grid, capital, anchors, permitting, governance) are named and linked to Phase 1 viability, yet decision ownership is distributed across multiple roles without a consolidated registry, the causal link between decision failure and Phase 1 consequences is implicit rather than explicit, social-license thresholds are partly qualitative, and no unified strategic thesis knits the 15 decisions into a coherent hypothesis. The plan lacks one-pagers for Decisions 1–5 that explicitly state inputs→process→customer-value flows and measurable outcomes with decision-maker accountability.

Mitigation: Strategic-Clarity Lead: Produce a Decision Charter (Month 1–2 = 2026-11-17 to 2026-12-17) and one-pagers for Decisions 1–5 (grid, capital, anchors, permitting, governance) with explicit inputs, process, customer-value, success metrics, failure thresholds, Phase 1 impact, and owner accountability. Assign owners to secondary decisions; publish updates to investment committee monthly.

4. Underestimating Risks

Does this plan grossly underestimate risks?

Level: ⚠️ Medium

Justification: Rated MEDIUM because the risk register identifies 23 cascading second-order hazards (permit delay → RTE queue erosion → DSCR breach; energy shock → anchor-tenant collapse → FID fail; sunk-cost → threshold override → cost overrun). However, three gaps: (1) gate enforcement relies on committee independence, not contractual debt tranches; (2) dual/triple cascades during Phase 1 build (Months 18–30 = 2028-04-17 to 2029-04-17) not stress-tested; (3) reputational cascade impact on tenant recruitment is qualitative, not quantified or gated.

Mitigation: Finance and Governance Lead: Embed gate authority in a tri-party binding agreement (sponsor, lenders, co-investors) by Month 1 (2026-11-17) that ties Phase 1 debt tranches to committee sign-off, publishes monthly dissent to lenders, and pre-defines dual-/triple-event Phase 1 stress scenarios (permit delay + energy shock + 10% cost overrun) with a shared DSCR covenant floor (1.30x proposed lender minimum; base 1.34x) and automatic refinance triggers. Deliver Phase 1 stress covenant summary by Month 12 (2027-10-17).

5. Timeline Issues

Does the plan rely on unrealistic or internally inconsistent schedules?

Level: 🛑 High

Justification: Rated HIGH because the Phase 0 topology decision (Month 4 = 2027-02-17) precedes the RTE written preliminary feasibility letter (Month 6 = 2027-04-17) by two months, forcing a split-campus default by calendar before evidence arrives. Additionally, standard permitting (18–30 months from filing, plus 24–48 months for appeals) will delay Phase 1 energization beyond the base-case Months 42–48 (2030-04-17 to 2030-10-17) if challenges emerge; fast-track status is not confirmed (not verified). The plan lacks a critical-path diagram with dated predecessors and no-go slip thresholds. Long-lead items (transformers, coolers, BESS, subsea cable) are not locked to delivery dates in Phase 0. Permit check at Month 18 (2028-04-17) is too late to prevent Phase 1 design commitments.

Mitigation: Project Controls Lead: By Month 1 (2026-11-17), build a detailed critical-path network with dated predecessors (RTE preliminary Month 3 = 2027-01-17, water opinion Month 6 = 2027-04-17, ANSSI pathway Month 6 = 2027-04-17, permit submission Month 8–9 = 2027-06-17 to 2027-07-17, Phase 1 FID Month 12 = 2027-10-17). Lock permit-critical thresholds and no-go slip dates per the regulatory roadmap. Establish vendor commitment gates (cooler/BESS/cable selection by Month 6 = 2027-04-17). Publish monthly schedule variance and critical-path burn-down to lenders and the investment committee.

6. Money Issues

Are there flaws in the financial model, funding plan, or cost realism?

Level: ⚠️ Medium

Justification: Rated MEDIUM because Phase 0 funding is sponsor equity committed in principle (EUR 750M capped tranches) with no signed master drawdown agreement or lender co-commitment; Phase 1 financing is indicative only (non-binding lender indications expected Month 6 = 2027-04-17, firm commitment only if Phase 0 gates pass at Month 12 = 2027-10-17). Financing gates and covenants are stated in the plan but not embedded in debt documents or equity agreements. Stacked contingent add-ons total EUR 1.55B–4.2B against EUR 5.0B base, leaving only EUR 0.8B–3.45B headroom to EUR 10B ceiling; cost allocation is undefined.

Mitigation: Finance and Governance Lead: By Month 2 (2026-12-17), execute a tri-party binding agreement (sponsor, lead lenders, co-investor consortium) vesting Phase 0 tranche releases to investment-committee gate sign-off and locking Phase 1 financing conditions (≥EUR 3B debt term sheet, equity commitments, covenant floor DSCR ≥1.30x, no-go acceleration if gates fail). By Month 9 (2027-07-17), publish unified Phase 1 cost-stack reconciliation assigning funding sources and contingencies; by Month 12 (2027-10-17), confirm debt and equity commitments in writing or trigger Phase 1 downsize.

7. Budget Too Low

Is there a significant mismatch between the project's stated goals and the financial resources allocated, suggesting an unrealistic or inadequate budget?

Level: 🛑 High

Justification: Rated HIGH because the plan states Phase 1 capex of EUR 5B–10B without a detailed line-item breakdown, vendor quotes, or scale-normalized benchmarks (EUR/m² or EUR/MW) to substantiate the figures. Stacked contingent add-ons (grid co-funding EUR 500M–1.5B, split-campus premium EUR 250M–500M, remediation EUR 100M–300M, ecology EUR 200M–300M, fiber EUR 100M–300M) total EUR 1.55B–4.2B, leaving free headroom to the EUR 10B ceiling of only EUR 0.8B–3.45B. The plan does not specify which add-ons are funded from the EUR 5B base, which sit outside, or what triggers cost cuts if the unified stack exceeds EUR 10B. No comparable data-center projects at 500 MW or 1 GW scale are cited to validate per-MW or per-m² cost assumptions.

Mitigation: Finance Lead: Deliver a detailed Phase 1 capex model by Month 6 (2027-04-17) with ≥3 vendor quotes or benchmarks per major line item (halls, coolers, transformers, security, fiber, BESS), normalized cost per m² and per MW against global and Western European data-center comparables at 100 MW, 500 MW and 1 GW scales. Publish cost-reconciliation statement assigning funding sources and contingencies; obtain lender and investment-committee written approval.

8. Overly Optimistic Projections

Does this plan grossly overestimate the likelihood of success, while neglecting potential setbacks, buffers, or contingency plans?

Level: 🛑 High

Justification: Rated HIGH because the plan presents key projections as single-point estimates without ranges, confidence intervals, or explicit alternative scenarios. Revenue stabilized 500 MW is stated as EUR 550M annually (lease) + EUR 223M (energy) = EUR 773M, with no low/base/high case. Phase 1 capex is EUR 5.0B–10B (a range, but not conditioned on explicit scenario assumptions). DSCR is 1.34x at stabilized baseload without stress-case sensitivities documented until the risk register. Energy cost is assumed EUR 60/MWh (range 50–70, not verified) without modeled impact on affordability or lease renegotiation if it reaches EUR 100/MWh. Energization window is Months 42–48 (2030-04-17 to 2030-10-17) base case, Months 48–60 (2030-10-17 to 2031-10-17) downside, but no probability weighting or go/no-go contingency for Months 60+. Phase 0 is EUR 250M–750M (a wide range, no decision rule for when the cap is triggered). The plan lacks a unified base/mid/high case showing how grid, tenant, power, permitting and capital variables interact.

Mitigation: Finance and Planning Lead: By Month 9 (2027-07-17), deliver three scenarios (low/base/high) for Phase 1 stabilized state (Months 54–60 = 2031-04-17 to 2031-10-17), each with stated assumptions on RTE curtailment (10%/15%/20%), energy cost (EUR 50/70/100 per MWh), tenant credit (BBB+ / BB+ / BB−), power reliability (99.5% / 99.0% / 97.5%), and schedule slip (0 / 6 / 12 months). Calculate NOI, DSCR and equity IRR per scenario. Gate Phase 1 FID on commitment to deliver quarterly actual-vs.-forecast variance (±10% on revenue, opex, cost of capital) and a reforecast trigger if variance exceeds ±15%.

9. Lacks Technical Depth

Does the plan omit critical technical details or engineering steps required to overcome foreseeable challenges, especially for complex components of the project?

Level: 🛑 High

Justification: Rated HIGH because the plan identifies 9 build-critical components (grid hosting, land assembly, anchor-tenant demand, power procurement, cooling/PUE, water authority clearance, ANSSI security clearance, permitting/DREAL opinion, and financing commitment) yet lacks formal engineering artifacts for most. Grid hosting capacity is uncontrolled until RTE signs (Month 6 = 2027-04-17), with no pre-engineering specs or interface contract. Land assembly has no parcel-level engineering or surveying plan before topology locks (Month 4 = 2027-02-17). Cooling targets PUE 1.15–1.25 but thermal modeling is not due until Month 5 (2027-03-17), after topology commits. Power procurement assumes EUR 50–70/MWh but no binding supply contract or interface specification exists. Fiber diversity is audited but not contracted. Permitting file is to be submitted Month 8–9 (2027-06-17 to 2027-07-17) but preliminary DREAL opinion is not until Month 9 (2027-07-17). No integration plan ties these components to a unified Phase 1 design or a single FID checklist. Acceptance tests (DSCR thresholds, PUE floor, connection offer, permit decision, security clearance) are stated in the risk register but not formalized as engineering gates with measurable pass/fail criteria or sign-off authority.

Mitigation: Engineering Leadership (Grid, Land, Power, Cooling, Security, Permitting): By Month 3 (2027-01-17), produce a unified Phase 1 Technical Specification Document covering grid interface (RTE connection terms, substation SLD, curtailment protocol), land/topology (parcel map, layout, remediation scope), thermal design (cooler specs, PUE test plan, 35°C validation), power (EDF contract template, energy SLA), fiber (route map, diversity audit), security (enclave specifications), and permitting (ICPE file content plan). Define acceptance tests per component: RTE letter, DREAL opinion, thermal validation report, water authority letter, fiber diversity audit, security roadmap sign-off. Assign owner and sign-off authority per component. Reconvene at Month 9 (2027-07-17) to confirm all component specs are complete and non-conflicting before Phase 1 FID (Month 12 = 2027-10-17).

10. Assertions Without Evidence

Does each critical claim (excluding timeline and budget) include at least one verifiable piece of evidence?

Level: 🛑 High

Justification: Rated HIGH because the plan makes nine critical claims (RTE grid offer, EDF power contract, 150 MW signed anchors, ANSSI clearance, municipal support, water opinion, EUR 3B debt, fiber diversity, Phase II remediation) that lack verifiable artifacts today. Each is marked "uncontrolled" or "not verified." All are gates: absence of any one triggers Phase 1 downsize/cancel. No external-stakeholder binding commitment mechanism exists to guarantee evidence delivery on schedule (Month 6, 9, 12 = 2027-04-17, 2027-07-17, 2027-10-17).

Mitigation: Investment Committee Chair and Program Manager: Establish signed "Evidence Commitment" protocols with RTE, EDF, ANSSI, DREAL, lenders, municipalities confirming artifact delivery by gate date, or state inability. Publish Monthly Evidence Dashboard (Months 1–12 = 2026-11-17 to 2027-10-17) tracking status. Escalate missing artifacts 30 days before gate date to investment committee with contingency (delay, downsize, exit). Target: Protocols signed by Month 1 (2026-11-17); Dashboard by Month 2 (2026-12-17).

11. Unclear Deliverables

Are the project's final outputs or key milestones poorly defined, lacking specific criteria for completion, making success difficult to measure objectively?

Level: 🛑 High

Justification: Rated HIGH because the Phase 1 deliverable—the first major operational milestone—is mentioned as "about 8–10 data halls" and "500 MW energized by Months 42–48 (2030-04-17 to 2030-10-17)" without specific, verifiable qualities. The plan defines PUE targets (1.15–1.25) and expansion thresholds but does not specify hall-by-hall commissioning criteria, operational acceptance gates, tenant capacity allocation, connectivity validation, or security clearance status at energization. A range ("about 8–10") is not a fixed deliverable; no baseline operational SLA is defined for Phase 1 go-live.

Mitigation: Program Manager: Define SMART Phase 1 Energization Acceptance Criteria by Month 9 (2027-07-17) including (1) exact hall count and power distribution map, (2) per-hall commissioning schedule (Months 42–48 = 2030-04-17 to 2030-10-17), (3) measured PUE ≤1.28 KPI across all halls by Month 50 (2030-12-17), (4) connectivity validation (both audited fiber routes lit and tested), (5) security clearance signoff, and (6) operational SLA baseline (99.5% uptime target, <50 ms latency to Paris). Gate Phase 1 FID on written lender and anchor-tenant approval of acceptance criteria by Month 12 (2027-10-17).

12. Gold Plating

Does the plan add unnecessary features, complexity, or cost beyond the core goal?

Level: 🛑 High

Justification: Rated HIGH because the immersion-cooling pilot (50–100 MW, EUR 50M–100M capex, unproven at scale) does not directly support either of the two core Phase 1 objectives: (i) energize 500 MW with baseline direct-to-chip liquid cooling and PUE ≤1.30, and (ii) achieve Phase 1 FID with DSCR ≥1.30 and ≥30% anchors signed. The plan labels it "optional" and acknowledges "pilot failure risks EUR 50M–100M sunk cost," confirming speculative status. No tenant, lender or contractual requirement mandates immersion; the baseline design alone satisfies all stated constraints. This is classic gold plating: discretionary complexity and cost added to the core deliverable.

Mitigation: Project Finance and Engineering Lead: Produce a one-page Immersion-Cooling Benefit Case Review by Month 6 (2027-04-17) justifying pilot inclusion with a KPI (e.g., achieve PUE ≤1.18 in pilot halls by Month 54 = 2031-04-17), owner accountability, and confirmed cost (EUR 50M–100M), or move the pilot to Phase 2 or the backlog. Gate Phase 1 FID approval on this decision.

13. Staffing Fit & Rationale

Do the roles, capacity, and skills match the work, or is the plan under- or over-staffed?

Level: 🛑 High

Justification: Rated HIGH because Grid Connection and Power Infrastructure Strategist is the unicorn role: owns the ~1 GW hosting-capacity kill test (uncontrolled until RTE signs, Month 6 = 2027-04-17), shapes the topology decision (Month 4 = 2027-02-17) by two months before RTE's evidence arrives. Requires rare expertise: RTE operational history, PSSE/DIgSILENT modeling, multi-tranche phasing, French DREAL coordination, competing industrial-load intelligence. Few professionals in Northern Europe combine these credentials. Role departure or inadequacy during Month 0–6 (2026-10-17 to 2027-04-17) breaks the grid gate, forces split-campus redesign (EUR 250M–500M Phase 0 sunk cost, EUR 300M–600M carry cost), and stalls Phase 1 by 6–12 months.

Mitigation: Hiring Lead: Identify and vet the candidate Grid Connection and Power Infrastructure Strategist by Month 1 (2026-11-17) with four validation gates: (1) RTE Director-level contact with pre-engineering response commitment in writing by Month 2 (2026-12-17); (2) grid-modeling credentials (PSSE/DIgSILENT) via completed multi-GW study in Western Europe past 5 years, deliverable reviewed; (3) technical interview with independent auditor confirms coordination feasibility; (4) written RTE pre-engineering request sent by Month 2 (2026-12-17) with acknowledgment from RTE. Stop rule: if any gate fails, escalate to investment committee with fallback recruiting plan or recommend 250 MW Phase 1 downsize contingency.

14. Legal Minefield

Does the plan involve activities with high legal, regulatory, or ethical exposure, such as potential lawsuits, corruption, illegal actions, or societal harm?

Level: ⚠️ Medium

Justification: Rated MEDIUM because a legal/regulatory pathway exists (ICPE, environmental authorization, water, agriculture, foreign-investment screening, ANSSI national-security review named explicitly) with early regulator engagement planned (pre-submission dialogues Months 0–1 = 2026-10-17 to 2026-11-17, liaison committees, milestone gates Months 6, 9, 12 = 2027-04-17, 2027-07-17, 2027-10-17). However, critical gaps remain: ANSSI formal clearance timeline (12–18 months from Month 13 = 2027-11-17) extends into Phase 1 build (Months 13–36 = 2027-11-17 to 2029-10-17), creating blocking risk if delayed; no formalized NO-GO protocol exists if DREAL, ANSSI or foreign-investment authorities issue adverse findings; and foreign-investment-screening outcome is entirely uncontrolled until Month 9 (2027-07-17), potentially forcing capital restructuring during Phase 1 FID. Permitting timelines (18–30 months + 24–48 month appeal risk) extend beyond the base-case Phase 1 energization window (Months 42–48 = 2030-04-17 to 2030-10-17), creating 12–24 month downside risk. A fatal-flaw analysis and NO-GO procedure are mentioned in risk language but not yet embedded in formal governance charter or debt covenants.

Mitigation: Investment Committee Chair and General Counsel: Execute a "Regulatory NO-GO Protocol" document by Month 2 (2026-12-17) specifying blocking-finding criteria and decision rules per authority (RTE <500 MW = auto-downsize to 250 MW; DREAL denial or >24-month delay = Phase 1 pause; ANSSI blocking concern = sovereign co-investor restructure or 6-month reassessment; foreign-investment veto = capital restructure or exit). Embed the protocol in the investment committee charter and debt documents. Conduct monthly regulatory-status dashboard (Months 1–12 = 2026-11-17 to 2027-10-17) tracking RTE, DREAL, ANSSI and CFIUS milestones; escalate any slippage >30 days before gate date. Obtain written formal opinions from each authority confirming review timeline and no blocking concern by Month 12 (2027-10-17), or trigger Phase 1 FID pause and contingency assessment.

15. Lacks Operational Sustainability

Even if the project is successfully completed, can it be sustained, maintained, and operated effectively over the long term without ongoing issues?

Level: ⚠️ Medium

Justification: Rated MEDIUM because post-Phase-1 operational sustainability depends on five uncontrolled variables: (1) ongoing energy costs (EUR 60/MWh assumed, range 50–70, not verified; +EUR 30/MWh shock reduces NOI from EUR 400M to EUR 288M at 500 MW, DSCR to 0.96x, breaching the 1.30x lender floor); (2) tenant demand retention and lease renegotiation risk (phase-by-phase FID gates require 30%→50% signed, but AI training demand beyond 3–5 years is unvalidated); (3) maintenance of specialized cooling, security and network assets at 1.15–1.25 PUE target in a 15-year operation (thermal performance degradation, vendor lock-in, parts obsolescence unaddressed); (4) personnel sustainability (50–150 FTE ops headcount not verified; specialized skills in liquid cooling, high-assurance security, and fiber diversity are scarce); (5) technology obsolescence of GPU/TPU and power-delivery standards over 10–15 years of service (5–7 year vendor cycles vs. 15-year debt tenor create mismatch). The plan states revenue stabilization (EUR 550M lease + EUR 223M energy per year at 500 MW) and DSCR 1.34x as targets, but no operational sustainability plan, failure-mode recovery mechanisms, or contingency for sustained demand shortfall exists.

Mitigation: Operations and Finance Lead: Develop a comprehensive Operational Sustainability Plan by Month 9 (2027-07-17) covering: (1) energy-cost hedging strategy and tenant pass-through mechanic for sustained cost >EUR 75/MWh; (2) tenant demand-retention roadmap with lease-renewal triggers and ramp-up contingencies for Phase 2–4 if demand <50% of targets; (3) maintenance schedule and spare-parts inventory strategy for critical cooling, security and fiber assets with vendor lock-in mitigation; (4) operations staffing model and succession plan for roles with specialized skills; (5) technology refresh roadmap for power-delivery and accelerator standards. Lock the plan in Phase 1 financing covenants; commit to quarterly operational-sustainability dashboard tracking actual vs. forecast (energy cost, tenant utilization, unplanned downtime, maintenance cost, staffing turnover). If sustained demand drops >20% below forecast by Month 48 (2030-10-17) energization, trigger Phase 2 FID pause and strategic reassessment.

16. Infeasible Constraints

Does the project depend on overcoming constraints that are practically insurmountable, such as obtaining permits that are almost certain to be denied?

Level: ⚠️ Medium

Justification: Rated MEDIUM because the plan does not verify that hard regulatory constraints (zoning/land-use compatibility, occupancy/egress codes, fire load limits, structural capacity, noise bylaws, permit-path feasibility) can be satisfied at the proposed 500 MW scale in the Cambrai/E-Valley and candidate split-campus zones. The plan names the constraint categories (ICPE, environmental authorization, water, biodiversity) but does not present: (1) a zoning letter or land-use opinion from the municipalities confirming the data-center use is permitted on target parcels; (2) an occupancy/egress and fire-load assessment for the proposed 8–10 halls and their geometric layout; (3) a structural-capacity study validating that candidate parcels can bear a 500 MW load at the planned power density; (4) a noise-impact and vibration study confirming compliance with local noise bylaws (typically 55–60 dB in rural/industrial zones). The plan states 'DREAL screening opinion by Month 9 (2027-07-17)' but that is not a binding approval, only a preliminary pathway confirmation. Permits are not targeted before Months 26–39 (2028-12-17 to 2030-01-17), so hard-constraint verification occurs 12+ months after the Phase 0 gate (Month 12 = 2027-10-17) when land options and grid pre-engineering are already committed. If hard constraints are discovered to be unsatisfiable after Phase 0 sunk cost is incurred (EUR 400M–750M by Month 12 = 2027-10-17), the project faces a costly pivot to alternative sites or downsizing.

Mitigation: Environmental and Permitting Counsel: Conduct a Fatal-Flaw Constraint Screen by Month 6 (2027-04-17) covering zoning opinion (written municipal confirmation that data-center use is permitted on each target parcel), occupancy/egress code assessment (preliminary life-safety design for the proposed hall envelope and utility routing), fire-load and structural limits (professional engineering opinion on site-bearing capacity and load-capacity compliance), noise-impact model (35 dB baseline measurement plus 3D prediction of plant and hall noise), and permit-path timeline confirmation (written DREAL opinion on ICPE, environmental-authorization and water-permit feasibility within the proposed schedule). Publish the screen with a NO-GO threshold: if any hard constraint cannot be satisfied on the chosen topology, trigger immediate Phase 0 reassessment and potential pivot to alternative sites or downsizing.

17. External Dependencies

Does the project depend on critical external factors, third parties, suppliers, or vendors that may fail, delay, or be unavailable when needed?

Level: ⚠️ Medium

Justification: Rated MEDIUM because the plan identifies critical external dependencies (RTE grid hosting, land assembly, anchor-tenant demand, ANSSI clearance, DREAL permits, municipal support, debt financing) that are uncontrolled until backed by signed offer, deed, term sheet, formal decision or written commitment. Each dependency arrives at a gate (Month 6, 9, or 12 = 2027-04-17, 2027-07-17, 2027-10-17) and failure of any one triggers downsize, delay or cancellation. However, partial redundancy exists: split-campus topology provides a fallback to single-square; 250 MW downsize is a default if grid or demand fail; lease-and-continue farming and split liability allocation offer partial mitigation to holdout and contamination exposure. The plan explicitly treats all major outcomes as uncontrolled and gates them rather than assuming success.

Mitigation: Investment Committee Chair: By Month 2 (2026-12-17), execute a tri-party binding agreement (sponsor, lead lenders, co-investor consortium) embedding Phase 0 tranche releases to committee gate sign-off and locking Phase 1 financing conditions (≥EUR 3B debt term sheet, equity commitments, DSCR floor 1.30x). Commission monthly Evidence Dashboard (Months 1–12 = 2026-11-17 to 2027-10-17) tracking artifact delivery (RTE letter, water opinion, ANSSI opinion, fiber audit, DREAL pre-opinion, tenant term sheets, lender commitment, municipal support) against gate dates; escalate any slippage >30 days to committee with contingency (downsize, delay, cancel) rather than proceeding with unmet thresholds.

18. Stakeholder Misalignment

Are there conflicting interests, misaligned incentives, or lack of genuine commitment from key stakeholders that could derail the project?

Level: ⚠️ Medium

Justification: Rated MEDIUM because the plan identifies two stakeholders—Infrastructure Finance Consortium (lenders, co-investors) and Development Sponsor—with opposing incentives: consortium prioritizes capital preservation and hard kill gates; sponsor prioritizes momentum and ambition scale. However, the conflict is implicit, not explicitly articulated. The plan states governance intentions (independent committee, supermajority override, dissent publication) but does not define a shared measurable objective (OKR) that aligns both parties on trade-offs between risk mitigation and growth. The topology decision rule (Month 4 = 2027-02-17 before RTE evidence Month 6 = 2027-04-17) and Phase 0 budget breach risk (EUR 250M–500M split-campus pivot) exemplify unresolved tension.

Mitigation: Investment Committee Chair and Finance Lead: By Month 2 (2026-12-17), co-author a written Stakeholder Alignment OKR document with sponsor and consortium specifying one shared, measurable objective: Phase 0 gate pass only if RTE ≥500 MW confirmed AND land ≥70% optioned AND anchors ≥30% signed by Month 12 (2027-10-17), or a coordinated downsize/split decision. Embed the OKR in the governance charter and debt documents with explicit override costs (additional equity, lender consent, timeline slip) to make trade-offs visible and accountable.

19. No Adaptive Framework

Does the plan lack a clear process for monitoring progress and managing changes, treating the initial plan as final?

Level: 🛑 High

Justification: Rated HIGH because the plan lacks a formalized, binding feedback loop with enforceable kill criteria. The plan states intentions ("independent investment committee," "numeric kill thresholds locked by Month 2 = 2026-12-17," "external red team with monthly pass/fail opinions") but does not embed these in contractual debt covenants, tri-party binding agreements, or operational procedures. Governance remains advisory: "dissent publication to lenders and co-investors" creates transparency but not authority to halt drawdowns or cancel Phase 1 if thresholds fail. The sponsor board retains overridable discretion. Sunk-cost pressure (EUR 400M–750M Phase 0 by Month 12 = 2027-10-17) will routinely override stated gates absent a mechanism that ties tranched capital release to committee sign-off and lender consent. No monthly KPI dashboard or change-control process with rethreshold triggers exists yet.

Mitigation: Investment Committee Chair and Finance Lead: Execute a tri-party Binding Governance and Gate Enforcement Agreement (sponsor, lead lenders, co-investor consortium) by Month 1 (2026-11-17) vesting Phase 0 tranche releases in the independent committee, locking numeric kill thresholds (grid ≥500 MW, land ≥70%, anchors ≥30% signed, ANSSI clearance pathway confirmed, municipal support ≥2 of 3) in the debt documents, and establishing a monthly KPI dashboard (revenue ramp, DSCR, tenant commitments, grid/permit status, cost variance) with automatic covenant acceleration if thresholds are breached.

20. Uncategorized Red Flags

Are there any other significant risks or major issues that are not covered by other items in this checklist but still threaten the project's viability?

Level: 🛑 High

Justification: Rated HIGH because four strongly coupled risk cascades exist: (1) RTE grid <1 GW → split-campus topology pivot → EUR 250M–500M Phase 0 rework + EUR 300M–600M carrying cost + lender repricing +100 bps; (2) EDF energy cost >EUR 75/MWh → anchor-tenant demand collapse → signed commitment <30% → financing loss → Phase 1 delay 12–24 months; (3) ANSSI investment-restriction regime → co-investor capital restructuring → debt covenant renegotiation → tenant lease cascades; (4) sunk-cost momentum EUR 400M–600M by Month 9 (2027-07-17) + weak governance enforcement (charter not yet in debt documents) → override of kill criteria → locked financial stress. No unified interdependency map or combined heatmap with contingency thresholds exists to surface multi-node cascades.

Mitigation: Risk Leadership and Investment Committee Chair: Deliver a unified Risk Interdependency Map (bow-tie or FTA diagram) by Month 6 (2027-04-17) identifying four critical cascades (grid→topology→capital, energy→demand→finance, regulation→equity→operations, sunk-cost→override→breach), assign owner and NO-GO/contingency thresholds per cascade (e.g., RTE <500 MW triggers auto split-campus and lender renotification within 5 days), embed thresholds in debt covenants by Month 12 (2027-10-17).

1. Phase 1 window (Months 12-36) vs energization, permits and ANSSI clearance (🔴 High) — needs a project decision

  • Pitch (Project Overview, Metrics for Success); executive summary (Timeline); project plan (Time-bound): Pitch: "Phase 1 delivers 500 MW by Months 12-36" and "Phase 1 Baseline (Months 12-36): 500 MW energized, 8-10 halls online". Project plan and executive summary also give Phase 1 as Months 12-36.
  • Pitch (Key Milestones, Risk section); executive summary; canonical permitting_and_schedule_realism: First-block energization at Months 42-48 (downside 48-60). Permit decisions are expected at Months 26-39 and ANSSI formal clearance at about Months 25-31. Stabilized demand is reached only at Months 54-60.
  • Why it conflicts: The Phase 1 window closes before the base-case energization, and the Months 54-60 stabilization falls outside it too. Build starts at Month 12, before the permit decision and ANSSI clearance. The pitch states both 'energized within Months 12-36' and 'energization at Months 42-48'. The user's success definition (Phase 2 FID backed by anchors) cannot be reached inside Phase 1 either.
  • Suggested resolution: Decide how Phase 1 is defined. Preferred: Phase 1 runs from FID (Month 12) to first-block energization (Months 42-48), with Months 12-36 as the construction-start window. Success is then tested at the Phase 2 FID (about Months 54-60), after 12 months of operating data. Make permit-dependent works conditional on the permit decision and ANSSI review. Remove 'energized' from the Months 12-36 pitch bullet.

2. EUR 750M hard cap vs split-campus default and tranche calendar (🔴 High) — needs a project decision

  • Executive summary (Timeline and Budget); canonical phase0_budget_cap and phase0_tranche_caps: Phase 0 is a "EUR 750M hard cap (no overspend)" in four tranches of 150/250/200/150, with tranche 2 covering Months 3-6.
  • Review 1 (#1); premortem FM1 and FM4; self-audit #13 and #18; Review 4 (#2): Review 1 treats the split pivot (EUR 250M-500M) plus design rework (EUR 100M-250M) as a Phase 0 cap problem. Premortem FM4 says split-from-start adds EUR 100M-250M and breaches the cap. Self-audit #13 calls EUR 250M-500M 'Phase 0 sunk cost'. Review 4 releases tranche 2 'after the Month 4 topology lock'.
  • Why it conflicts: The calendar default to split at Month 4 is the likely outcome, yet it needs Phase 0 money above a cap called hard, and no source is named. The EUR 250M-500M premium is Phase 1 capex (5-10% of EUR 5B), not a Phase 0 cost. Tranche 2 starts at Month 3, before the topology decision. Tranche 3 spans Months 7-9 and cannot sit in escrow until the Month 9 gates have been decided.
  • Suggested resolution: Keep the EUR 250M-500M premium in Phase 1 capex and remove it from Phase 0 cap discussions. For split-from-start Phase 0 work (up to EUR 250M over the cap, canonical) the committee must decide the funding source: a lender and co-investor approved cap increase, scope cuts within EUR 750M, or doing per-node validation after the gate. Split tranche 2 into a Month 3-4 part and a part released after the topology decision.

3. Meaning of the ~1 GW grid kill test vs the 500 MW gate and the shortfall response (🔴 High) — needs a project decision

  • Executive summary (Focus, Purpose); premortem FM2; canonical grid_kill_test and rte_phase1_gate: "RTE grid hosting capacity above ~1 GW is the primary kill test"; gate (1) is only 500 MW within 36 months. FM2 stop rule: cancel Phase 1 only if RTE gives under 500 MW at all nodes and there is no path to ~1 GW cumulative by Month 12.
  • Review 5 (#1); executive summary (Feedback 3); premortem FM2: Review 5 triggers a 250 MW downsize if the interim RTE estimate is below 750 MW per topology. Executive summary feedback says grid below 500 MW means a 250 MW downsize. FM2 says under 500 MW at the lead node means a 250 MW re-baseline or a split.
  • Why it conflicts: A project can pass the Month 12 gate with 500-999 MW and still meet the user's failure definition (no hosting above ~1 GW). The executive summary never says what 'kill' ends: the 9 GW ambition, the single square or Phase 1. A Month 6 letter for 500 MW cannot answer a >1 GW question. A 750 MW trigger appears nowhere else, and the same shortfall is met with downsize, split, re-baseline or cancel depending on the document.
  • Suggested resolution: Separate the two tests. (1) Phase 1 gate: written letter for at least 500 MW at the lead node (Month 6), firm offer targeted at Month 12. (2) 9 GW ambition test: documented path to more than ~1 GW cumulative in any topology; failure ends the Phase 2+ ambition (single node or cancel), not necessarily Phase 1. Drop the 750 MW trigger or label it a proposed early-warning level. State one consequence table.

4. What 'Phase 1' is under a split campus (MW unit) (🟡 Medium) — needs a project decision

  • Project plan (Goal Statement); canonical topology_decision_rule and phase1_base_case: Goal: "deliver a 500 MW Phase 1 base case at Cambrai/E-Valley"; canonical nodes: Cambrai 500 MW, Dunkirk 250 MW, Valenciennes 250 MW.
  • Pitch (Land Fragmentation); premortem FM2; executive summary (Key Deliverables): Split campus is the default at Month 4 ("2-3 nodes of 250-500 MW", "at least 80% per node"); FM2 tripwire: "RTE indicates < 500 MW at any candidate node". Executive summary: "500 MW at Cambrai or split-campus topology".
  • Why it conflicts: The documents do not say whether a split Phase 1 is 500 MW in total (for example 250+250), Cambrai 500 MW plus other nodes, or Cambrai only. The 30% tenant gate, the EUR 3B debt gate, the RTE letter, the EUR 250M-500M premium and the EUR 10B ceiling each depend on that answer. A 250 MW node cannot satisfy a 500 MW per-node RTE tripwire.
  • Suggested resolution: Decide whether Phase 1 is a fixed 500 MW total (split across nodes) or one 500 MW node (Cambrai) with other nodes as Phase 2 candidates. Then restate each gate (RTE letter per node or total, 30% denominator, debt, premium) on that basis.

5. Land gate: parcel basis and acquisition premium (🟡 Medium) — needs a project decision

  • Project plan (Measurable); canonical land_option_gate and ecology_and_farmland; premortem FM4: Gate: "at least 70% of the chosen topology's target parcel" optioned at no more than 15% above benchmark (first check Month 3, confirmed Month 4). Phase 1 node is about 900 ha; land for the full square is EUR 0.24B-0.40B for 16,100 ha.
  • Review 14 (#3): Farmland relocation priced "at 1.5-2.0x benchmark value (EUR 15,000-25,000/ha for ~900 ha per 500 MW node = EUR 13.5M-45M per node)".
  • Why it conflicts: A 1.5-2.0x price fails the 15% non-coercive option gate, so it cannot be a budgeted Phase 1 cost under the same plan. The arithmetic mixes 1.0x (EUR 13.5M) and 2.0x (EUR 45M). It is also unclear whether the 70% test applies to the full 161 km² square or the roughly 900 ha Phase 1 node, which are very different tasks to complete by Month 3-4.
  • Suggested resolution: Define 'target parcel' (Phase 1 node plus option on expansion reserve, versus the full square) in the topology rule. Cost land at no more than 1.15x benchmark (EUR 15.5M-25.9M per 900 ha node, recomputed). Treat 1.5-2.0x as the gate-failure scenario that triggers the split.

6. Phase 1 cost stack composition, totals and headroom (🟡 Medium)

  • Canonical fallbacks_vs_budget_and_dates and phase1_ceiling_headroom_500mw: Stack of EUR 1.55B-4.2B covers grid, split premium, carrying, remediation and fiber/subsea. Ecology, security, community and firm connection sit outside it (EUR 0.5B-1.15B), giving EUR 7.05B-10.35B in total.
  • Review 1 (#3), Review 3 (#3), Review 11 (#3), Review 12 (#3); pitch (Stacked Contingent Add-Ons): Reviews 1, 11 and 12 put ecology, security and community inside the stack. The pitch lists 'Ecological remediation and expansion EUR 200M-500M' inside the stack and ecology again outside it. The pitch line items sum to about EUR 1.35B-3.4B (recomputed), not EUR 1.55B-4.2B. Review 3 states 'likely EUR 6.5B-7.5B for 500 MW'.
  • Why it conflicts: The same lines are counted inside and outside the stack, so totals and headroom cannot be reproduced. The EUR 6.5B-7.5B estimate is not supported by EUR 6.55B-9.2B or EUR 7.05B-10.35B.
  • Suggested resolution: Publish a single line-item table using the canonical split: stack lines (grid, split premium, carrying, remediation, fiber/subsea) summing to EUR 1.55B-4.2B, and outside-stack lines (ecology, security, community, firm connection). Remove the EUR 6.5B-7.5B claim. Keep the ceiling at EUR 10B and the maximum breach at EUR 0.35B.

7. USD hardware inside the ceiling: what the EUR 2.7B-3.5B represents (🟡 Medium)

  • Review 11 (#2); Review 8 (#2): "If hardware is included in the EUR 10B ceiling and funded by the campus company ... about EUR 2.7B-3.5B remains for infrastructure". Review 8: hardware inclusion "leaving about EUR 2.7B-3.5B for infrastructure at the 500 MW base".
  • Canonical phase1_budget_range, usd_hardware_scope_open_decision, phase1_ceiling_headroom_500mw: Infrastructure base for 500 MW is EUR 5.0B. Hardware is EUR 1.5B-2.3B. 10 - 5.0 - (1.5 to 2.3) = EUR 3.5B-2.7B, which is headroom above the base, not an infrastructure budget.
  • Why it conflicts: EUR 2.7B-3.5B is the headroom left if hardware sits inside the ceiling. Calling it the infrastructure budget implies the EUR 5B base is cut roughly in half, and the forced 'scope reduction' follows from that misreading. The open decision (is hardware inside the EUR 5B-10B) stays open.
  • Suggested resolution: Reword: if hardware is inside the EUR 10B ceiling, headroom above the EUR 5.0B base falls from EUR 5.0B to EUR 2.7B-3.5B (before the stack), so the stack of up to EUR 4.2B can breach the ceiling. If outside, headroom is unchanged. Keep the inclusion question as a Month 1 committee decision.

8. Foreign co-investor equity cannot be bound at FID vs equity-binding gate (🟡 Medium) — needs a project decision

  • Pitch (Ethical Considerations - National Security): "foreign co-investor equity cannot be bound at FID before that clearance"; no binding foreign commitment beyond Phase 0 without a favorable informal ANSSI opinion and Month 12 written confirmation.
  • Executive summary (Purpose, Key Deliverables); canonical debt_financing_gate; review plan (Review 7): Month 12 gate requires equity sources bound for Phase 1 (EUR 2B+ equity commitments); the investor profile is a consortium with sovereign-adjacent co-investors.
  • Why it conflicts: If sovereign-adjacent or other foreign capital supplies a material share of the EUR 2.0B equity, the equity-binding gate cannot be met at Month 12, because formal clearance comes at about Months 25-31. The documents do not say how much equity is foreign or who covers a gap.
  • Suggested resolution: State the foreign share of the EUR 2.0B equity and decide who backstops it: EU-domiciled non-controlling co-investors or sponsor equity (premortem FM6 option), or a conditional commitment that the gate accepts. Otherwise treat the Month 12 equity gate as conditional on clearance.

9. Energy shock sensitivities, pass-through framing and trigger levels (🟡 Medium)

  • Review 6 (KPI 2); executive summary (Feedback 5); canonical energy_volume_and_price: Energy (EUR 60/MWh) is "passed through to tenants", yet a +EUR 30/MWh move 'adds about EUR 112M annual opex' and takes DSCR to 0.96x.
  • Premortem; self-audit; Reviews 1, 4, 5, 6: Early-warning triggers differ for the same event: above EUR 70/MWh (premortem A2, FM3, Review 6), above EUR 75/MWh (self-audit #15, #20), EUR 80/MWh lease-revision level (Reviews 4 and 5), with a +/-EUR 5 collar (Review 6). Review 1 describes +EUR 30 as '50-70 to 100'.
  • Why it conflicts: With pass-through the shock is a tenant-affordability and demand risk, not an NOI loss. The 0.96x DSCR applies only without pass-through (canonical). Three thresholds for one trigger confuse escalation. EUR 112M corresponds to +EUR 30 (for example 70 to 100); 50 to 100 is +EUR 50 (about EUR 186M, recomputed).
  • Suggested resolution: Use one trigger (keep EUR 70/MWh as the proposed escalation level, since the premortem gates use it) and one lease-revision level. State that the DSCR 0.96x result is the no-pass-through stress, and that under pass-through the effect is tenant demand and lease discount. Correct the '50-70 to 100' wording.

10. Energization and Phase 1 start dates cited in the reviews (🟡 Medium)

  • Review 6 (KPI 3); Review 16 (#1); Review 14 (#2): "If only 250 MW is signed by Month 36 energization"; "go live by Month 36 energization"; Phase 1 ramp tests framed from "Month 24 Phase 1 start".
  • Canonical phase_schedule_and_capacity and permitting_and_schedule_realism; executive summary: Phase 1 starts at Month 12; first-block energization is Months 42-48 (downside 48-60).
  • Why it conflicts: The same milestone carries Month 36 in the reviews and Months 42-48 elsewhere, and Phase 1 start is given as Month 12 and Month 24.
  • Suggested resolution: Replace with Months 42-48 energization and Month 12 Phase 1 start; set the dashboard go-live and the ramp test dates to match.

11. DREAL screening opinion: Month 6 vs Month 9 (⚪ Low)

  • Executive summary (Timeline and Budget): "RTE letter, water opinion, ANSSI preliminary and DREAL screening by Month 6".
  • Project plan (Permits, Compliance Actions); pitch; canonical ecology_and_farmland: DREAL screening opinion by Month 9; permit file submitted Months 8-9. The executive summary's own Month 6 action list omits DREAL.
  • Why it conflicts: The same milestone has two dates, and a Month 6 screening would come before the permit-file submission.
  • Suggested resolution: Keep Month 9 (canonical) and delete DREAL from the executive summary's Month 6 list.

12. EDF 'binding contract' timing and the claimed EDF/tenant deadlock (⚪ Low)

  • Review 4 (#3): "EDF's binding contract (target Month 9 or later)".
  • Canonical power_procurement_edf; executive summary; Reviews 5, 6 and 13: EDF non-binding LOI by Month 6, term sheet by Month 9, binding contract not before FID; indicative price range requested by Month 4.
  • Why it conflicts: A binding contract at Month 9 contradicts the plan. The 'both gates depend on each other' deadlock in Reviews 8 and 13 also overlooks that the Month 4 indicative price and Month 6 LOI come before tenant term sheets at Month 9.
  • Suggested resolution: Keep 'LOI Month 6, term sheet Month 9, binding at or after FID'. Describe the deadlock risk as only the case where the Month 4 and Month 6 EDF items slip.

Summary

Most canonical numbers (budget caps, tranches, DSCR, financing, gate thresholds) are used consistently, and many earlier conflicts have been fixed. Substantive problems remain in how Phase 1 is defined against energization, permitting and ANSSI clearance. The documents also do not say who funds a split-from-start overrun above the EUR 750M cap, what the ~1 GW kill test ends, or what a split-campus Phase 1 comprises in MW. The rest is repairable: cost-stack composition, hardware headroom wording, energy triggers, stray Month 36 energization dates and a DREAL date.

How the canonical facts were reconciled

Arithmetic was recomputed for every product, annuity and percentage; most chains held (EUR 299M debt service, 1.34x and 1.15x DSCR, 3.72 TWh, EUR 750M tranche sum, 1.55B/4.2B add-on stack). Errors corrected: land intensity was 17.9 ha/MW and is 1.8 ha/MW (0.0179 km²/MW), the RTE-based energization (36 months after a Month 1–3 = 2026-11-17 to 2027-01-17 request) is Months 37–39 (2029-11-17 to 2030-01-17) not 39–42, the permit decision range is Months 26–39 (2028-12-17 to 2030-01-17), the ANSSI 12–18 months run from the Month 13 (2027-11-17) review start, and the Phase 2 increment covers 2–2.5 GW. Sequencing and consistency conflicts were fixed or flagged: the Month 4 (2027-02-17) topology decision cannot require an RTE ≥1 GW letter due at Month 6 (2027-04-17) (split campus is the default), the 12-year debt-tenor floor gives DSCR 1.15x against the 1.30x covenant, the 15% land-premium gate conflicts with the 1.5–2× compensation prices, the 1.30 design-day PUE trigger sits below the expected 1.35–1.5 hot-weather PUE, and the Phase 2 gate is relabelled as a proposed threshold. A new fact, phase1_ceiling_headroom_500mw, closes the gap on free headroom under the EUR 10B ceiling: the remediation reserve is counted once, and cost lines outside the stack could breach the ceiling by up to EUR 0.35B.

Initial Prompt

Plan:
Assume today's date, Saturday 17 October 2026, is Month 0. Assume the provisional sponsor is a private hyperscale data-center developer backed by an infrastructure-fund consortium with sovereign-adjacent co-investment discussions, and that Phase 0 spend carries high exploratory risk appetite but no committed capital until the Phase 0 gate. The 12.7 km × 12.7 km square is a notional planning envelope to be stress-tested, not a fixed requirement: evaluate the single square skeptically, then compare it honestly against a split-campus model, and recommend whichever is feasible. Create a rigorous, skeptical, red-team plan for an intentionally extreme hyperscale AI data center campus in Hauts-de-France, France, focused on the industrial AI belt around Cambrai / E-Valley, Valenciennes / Denain / Escaudain, Dunkirk, Saint-Omer, and nearby industrial or brownfield land. The project has a fixed notional footprint of 12.7 km × 12.7 km — approximately 161 km² / 40,000 acres — and a full-buildout power target of 9 GW over 10–15+ years. Budget in EUR throughout for capital, land, labor, grid, power, permitting, taxes, financing, and public-benefit commitments: assume Phase 0 feasibility and site control of about €250M–€750M, Phase 1 of about €5B–€10B for 500 MW–1 GW, about €25B–€45B to expand to 3 GW, and about €100B–€140B+ for the full 9 GW buildout; treat these figures as estimates to validate and challenge rather than facts, and track USD exposure separately for GPUs/TPUs, networking hardware, selected software, and international vendor contracts, with FX hedging assumptions wherever USD-denominated hardware procurement materially affects the budget. Include cost drivers such as grid upgrades, substations, nuclear-backed power contracts, cooling systems, fiber, land acquisition, brownfield remediation, environmental mitigation, security, financing costs, French labor, permitting, public benefit commitments, and community compensation.

The core feasibility question must drive everything: can Hauts-de-France realistically host a 9 GW, 161 km² AI/hyperscale compute campus without overwhelming the grid, land market, water systems, permitting process, local communities, and environmental constraints? Do not assume the answer is yes, and never invent binding commitments from RTE, EDF, DGSI, ANSSI, tenants, municipalities, or prefectural authorities; treat all external approvals, grid commitments, security clearances, tenant contracts, and public-sector commitments as uncertain until the plan defines a realistic process to obtain them, and mark any milestone depending on an external authority as "uncontrolled" unless it is backed by a contract, permit, formal decision, or signed term sheet. Select Hauts-de-France as the only location because of its strong industrial redevelopment and reindustrialization narrative, existing logistics, port, rail, steel, refinery, military, and brownfield land contexts, Cambrai / E-Valley as a large redevelopment zone, Dunkirk as a heavy-industry and port-logistics hub, a better cooling climate than southern France, low latency to Paris, London, Brussels, Amsterdam, Frankfurt, and northern Europe, geopolitically safer positioning than Russia-adjacent regions, and a stronger public narrative than a pure greenfield rural megaproject.

The campus serves high-density GPU/TPU clusters for AI training, fine-tuning, batch inference, sovereign AI, and selected enterprise inference, with a PUE target of 1.15–1.25, direct-to-chip liquid cooling by default plus an optional 50–100 MW immersion cooling pilot, and zero- or ultra-low-water cooling preferred, treating freshwater or evaporative cooling as high risk. Use low-to-mid-rise data halls, typically 14–20 m tall with a maximum of 25–30 m, individual halls of 20,000–100,000 m² with some above 150,000 m², and 50–100+ major buildings at full buildout, and explain why taller buildings are usually less suitable for AI-scale data centers. Do not assume most of the 161 km² should be buildings: build a land-use model covering data halls, substations, BESS, backup generation, roads and logistics, fiber corridors, stormwater, biodiversity buffers, heat-reuse infrastructure, security setbacks, expansion reserve, community buffers, agricultural or ecological continuation zones, and brownfield remediation zones. Power strategy uses the French low-carbon grid, nuclear-backed contracts, EDF/RTE coordination, PPAs, BESS, grid flexibility, and limited backup generation. Connectivity needs diverse fiber to Paris, London, Brussels, Amsterdam, Frankfurt, Marseille, and subsea/transatlantic routes. Security covers national-security review, hardened perimeter, cyber/OT separation, anti-drone systems, supply-chain security, and resilience against sabotage or grid/fiber disruption.

The plan must analyze whether 161 km² can even be assembled, whether the single square footprint is realistic, whether a split-campus model across nearby industrial zones is superior, grid and transmission feasibility, power procurement and price risk, cooling and water risk, heat-reuse opportunity, fiber latency and route diversity, brownfield remediation risk, agricultural displacement, permitting and national-security review, local political support, public opposition risk, tenant demand, financing credibility, and scalability from 1 GW to 3 GW to 9 GW.

Then produce a complete plan with an executive summary, selected site rationale, land-use model, single-site vs split-campus analysis, phased roadmap, budget model, power model, cooling model, connectivity strategy, permitting path, stakeholder map, environmental and water strategy, community and social-license strategy, security strategy, tenant strategy, workforce strategy, public benefit strategy, risk register, decision gates, kill criteria, open questions, and a first 180-day action plan. Structure the phased roadmap as follows. Phase 0, Years 0–1: feasibility, site control, land assembly, grid hosting capacity, EDF/RTE engagement, cooling and water feasibility, environmental baseline, community risk, fiber feasibility, anchor-tenant validation, financing pre-commitments, permitting path, national-security review, and a no-build alternative; the decision gate is to proceed only if Phase 1 power, land, water, permits, tenants, financing, fiber, and social license are credible. Phase 1, Years 1–3: build 500 MW–1 GW with 8–20 data halls, a dedicated substation, BESS and backup, a liquid-cooling loop, diverse fiber, a hardened perimeter, first tenants, a public benefit agreement, a local workforce program, and environmental monitoring; the decision gate is to expand only if power reliability, PUE, water, security, and community targets are met and creditworthy anchor tenants have signed take-or-pay or equivalent capacity commitments for at least 30–50% of the next expansion tranche — no credible anchor tenants means no FID for the next phase. Phase 2, Years 3–7: scale to 1–3 GW with more halls, additional substations, transmission upgrades, heat-reuse pilots, expanded fiber, a supplier ecosystem, and public-benefit payments. Phase 3, Years 7–11: scale to 3–6 GW with sovereign AI zones, high-security compute partitions, standardized liquid cooling, resilience testing, and lifecycle replacement planning. Phase 4, Years 11–15+: reach 9 GW only if demand, grid capacity, financing, environmental permits, and social license remain strong. Define success explicitly as completing Phase 0 and Phase 1 within budget with credible tenants and a Phase 2 FID supported by signed anchor-tenant commitments, and define failure explicitly as failure to secure grid hosting capacity above ~1 GW, inability to assemble an adequate parcel, absence of creditworthy anchor tenants, sustained community or political opposition, financing that cannot be structured, or environmental constraints (water, grid, ecology) that cannot be mitigated.

The output must stay skeptical rather than promotional: identify explicitly what would make the project infeasible and what must be proven before serious capital is committed, and treat downsizing, splitting the campus, delaying expansion, or cancelling the project entirely as legitimate recommendations if feasibility fails.
